--[p361]-- 10.5.4 Examples of emission spectra and comparison with experiment

In this respect we must quote the pioneering work by $\mathrm { C e r j a n } ^ { 7 7 }$ on solid Sn targets irradiated by 1064-nm 7.5-ns pulses.

===== [p74-75] EUV Source Requirements for EUV Lithography > 2.4 Cost of Ownership (8块) =====
--[p75]-- For LPP systems parts of the drive laser must be exchanged on a regular basis, and within the discharge volume, the target delivery systems and collection optics must be considered as replaceable parts as well.
Looking at today’s status of development, it is not possible to give an accurate estimate of what the CoO of the first tools will be. Large error bars will be there, and even some of the future spare parts are still in the definition phase right now.
--[p75]-- Real values, which include detailed analyses of the system, should be used for this calculation. The throughput has a major influence on the CoO of the complete system; let us take it fixed at, say, 100 wafers/h and calculate an example CoO of the source as a function of initial source cost and source consumables cost. An example similar to that in Ref. 12 is considered, and the following values on a yearly basis are used in the calculation:
--[p75]-- It is clear that the main driver of the CoO is the purchasing price of the source itself. At the same time one should not disregard the price of consumables in the evaluations.
The target consumables–spare-part cost should be optimized to a value where present photolithography tools are operational in the field.
--[p75]-- • $\delta 5 0 0 / \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ has been assumed for the cost of the clean-room floor.
• The number of hours per year equals $2 4 \times 3 6 5 \times 6 5 \%$ utilization = 5700 h.
• The fraction 1/5 represents 5-year depreciation; 1/10, 10% interest; and 1/25, a 4% service cost.
• Footprint + service area: $2 0 \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$
• Throughput: 100 wafers/h.
Figure 2.7 presents the results of these analyses.
--[p74]-- 2.4 Cost of Ownership
The purchase of photolithography equipment is a complex decision. Many aspects need to be weighed against one another in order to justify the preference for a specific supplier. In view of the ever-increasing purchasing cost per unit, this evaluation needs to be performed very accurately. One important parameter is the cost of ownership (CoO) of the exposure tool, to which the operating cost of the source is a considerable contributor.
--[p75]-- A simplified model (2.4) similar to Ref. 12 can be used for the CoO of the source. It is apparent that the total CoO will depend on such quantities as the power of the source, optical system throughput, and resist sensitivity, and on the throughput as well. But once a certain throughput for certain system parameters is evaluated, the formula for the CoO per wafer level exposure can be written as
$$
--[p75]-- \begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { { C o O = \frac { \ s i z e \cdot ( p r i c e \ p e r m ^ { 2 } ) } { t h r o u g h p u t \cdot ( h o u r s / y e a r ) } + \frac { \ s i n i t i a l \ c o s t } { t h r o u g h p u t \cdot ( h o u r s / y e a r ) } \cdot \left( \frac { 1 } { 5 } + \frac { 1 } { 1 0 } + \frac { 1 } { 2 5 } \right) } } } \\ { \mathrm { { + \frac { \ c o n s u m a b l e s } { t h r o u g h p u t \cdot ( h o u r s / y e a r ) } \cdot } } } \end{array}
$$
--[p74]-- The cost of source operation involves many aspects. Roughly they can be split into operating costs, consumables, and clean-room area costs.
Examples of operating costs are those of wall-plug power, fuel material such as Xe or Sn, various gases, and cooling water. Consumables are parts that need to be exchanged due to operational wear or as part of preventive maintenance. Examples for DPP systems are the electrode set, collection optics, and parts of the mitigation system.

===== [p263-265] Z∗ Code for DPP and LPP Source Modeling > 8.2.2 EUV emission and radiation transport (14块) =====
--[p265]-- It is related to the radius r and angle φ of the direction of this projection by $x = \sqrt { r _ { \mathrm { o u t } } ^ { 2 } - r ^ { 2 } \sin ^ { 2 } \varphi + r }$ cos ϕ, where $r _ { \mathrm { o u t } }$ is some external radius, and where the boundary conditions on radiation may be described as stating that only outgoing radiation exists at $r = r _ { \mathrm { o u t } }$ , i.e., $I _ { \omega } | _ { r = r _ { \mathrm { o u t } } } = 0$ at $\pi / 2 < \Phi < 3 \pi / 2$ The coordinate z of a trajectory is defined by the formula $z = z _ { \mathrm { o u t } } + x$ cot θ, where ${ \it Z } _ { \mathrm { o u t } }$ is the coordinate of the intersection of the trajectory and the surface $r = r _ { \mathrm { o u t } }$ The Eq.
--[p265]-- As a rule the characteristic size of the DPP or LPP plasma of interest is much smaller than the distance traversed by the radiation during the evolution time, and a quasi-stationary approximation may be applied, i.e., the time derivative in Eq. (8.5) may be neglected. Between the spectral radiation flux density and the energy density, an important correlation follows from Eq. (8.5), viz., in the quasi-stationary case,
$$
--[p263]-- Also, at such high temperatures the radiation field is formed in a plasma-dynamic process, affecting the microstates of the plasma ions and the radiative properties of the plasma. Likewise the microstates of the ions determine the emissivity and spectral absorption coefficients of the plasma. Reabsorption in the spectral lines can change the ionization stage and internal energy of the plasma at the same electron temperature, for these are strongly coupled to the electrons via level kinetics.
--[p265]-- I _ { \omega } ( r , z , \varphi , \theta ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { \tau } \frac { j _ { \omega } } { \kappa _ { \omega } } e ^ { \tau ^ { \prime } - \tau } d \tau ,\tag{8.7}
$$
--[p263]-- The ionization kinetics and radiation transport therefore require a self-consistent description.
The radiation transfer equation for spectral intensity $I _ { \omega }$ with photon energy h¯ ω, without free-electron scattering processes, has the form
$$

===== [p408-409] Dense Plasma Focus Source > 12.1 Introduction (8块) =====
--[p408]-- 12.1 Introduction
--[p409]-- Apart from the main application of large-scale DPF devices for fusion research (typically operated with single pulses), low-energy instruments (with less than ∼1-kJ stored energy) with submicrosecond pulse duration and sometimes higher repetition frequencies have also been investigated as radiation sources by several groups.<sup>12–16</sup> Our choice of the DPF configuration was born out of related work on coaxial plasma guns and plasma thrusters for space applications.<sup>17–20</sup> At Cymer Inc., we have adopted the DPF source technology because small-scale configurations can be constructed with very low discharge-circuit inductance and only moderate electrical power consumption while showing at the same time excellent prospects for reliable multikilohertz operation and high EUV gene
--[p408]-- With the emergence of EUVL as the chosen technology for next-generation lithography (NGL) systems, significant effort has been spent in developing light sources consistent with the challenging requirements of the scanner manufacturers<sup>1</sup> as well as meeting the aggressive demands of the end users for high-volume manufacturing (HVM).<sup>2</sup> A light source with extremely high power and brightness is required for integration into a scanner tool based on reflective optics with multilayer (ML) coatings, since it needs to be designed for highest throughput at a wavelength of 13.5 nm. Over the past six years at Cymer Inc., we have pursued the research and development of DPPs to meet the demands for commercial HVM tools.
--[p409]-- ration efficiency.
--[p409]-- Strong magnetic forces created by the high discharge current then lead to a pinch event after plasma compression, with a hot dense microplasma zone developing on the axis near the end of the inner electrode. This highly ionized plasma is confined for a short time and emits intense EUV and soft x-ray radiation.
--[p409]-- and discuss the various areas of investigation we have concentrated on during our efforts to optimize the performance of the light source. The main focus is on the characterization of the various EUV output parameters for different operating conditions. We also discuss thermal management, modeling efforts, debris mitigation, light collection, scalability, and risk areas.
--[p408]-- A dense plasma focus (DPF) configuration was chosen because it provides an open geometry with large possible collection angle and can be operated over a wide parameter range. The main thrust of our research and development is devoted to achieving the challenging industry demands on light-source performance, requiring extremely high output power (>100 W), cleanliness, and component lifetime.
In this chapter we review the DPF development efforts at Cymer Inc.
--[p409]-- More extensive and detailed discussions of some particular aspects of the DPF source are described in our previous annual progress reports on source development.<sup>3–9</sup>
The plasma-focus scheme was developed independently several decades ago by Mather<sup>10</sup> and by Filippov et al.<sup>11</sup> In a typical Mather-type DPF configuration, an annular sliding plasma discharge is first produced between coaxial electrodes in a so-called rundown phase.

===== [p214-214] Radiative Collapse in Z Pinches > 6.4 Neck Instabilities in Pinch Plasmas: Radiative Collapse (3块) =====
--[p214]-- 6.4 Neck Instabilities in Pinch Plasmas: Radiative Collapse
In the preceding sections we have discussed different ways for the formation of the plasma column in axially symmetrical discharges (ASDs). The characteristics of the prephase (e.g., the duration, resistance, and inductance of the plasma) may essentially depend on the geometry of the electrodes, the methods of supplying of the working material into the interelectrode gap, and the engineering characteristics of the discharge circuit.
--[p214]-- We are going to show below that for plasmas of heavy ions (e.g., Xe, Sn) all types of ASD under discussion with a total stored electrical energy in the range 2–20 J emit EUV during the RC phase. For plasmas of light elements (e.g., Li), EUV radiation (such as the Ly-α line of H-like $\operatorname { L i } ^ { 2 + } )$ could be radiated in the plasma-column necking mode as well, while that process is no longer a radiative collapse.
--[p214]-- Nevertheless, after a plasma column has been formed on the discharge axis, further plasma development has many common features in almost all types of axially symmetric discharges. First of all, the plasma columns are unstable, and often neck instabilities are the first to develop. For plasmas containing strongly radiating heavy atoms the necks may develop in the regime of strong radiative losses mainly due to line radiation.<sup>14</sup> This regime is known as radiative collapse (RC).

===== [p415-416] Dense Plasma Focus Source > 12.8 EUV Spectra (6块) =====
--[p415]-- 12.8 EUV Spectra
Spectral analysis of the emitted EUV radiation is important for the determination of the partitioning of inband and out-of-band emission, for estimation of the mean electron temperature, and for characterization of the spectral output stability at different DPF operating conditions. Measurements of the EUV emission spectra from the DPF were carried out for a variety of source elements and with special emphasis for the case of xenon.
--[p415]-- Later on, we employed a transmission-grating arrangement with a CCD camera that allowed recording of single-pulse xenon spectra at lower resolution.<sup>7,8</sup> The DPF spectrum for tin near 13.5 nm was also measured with this detection scheme.<sup>9</sup> A high-resolution spectrum of xenon is displayed in Fig. 12.7 together with a typ ical theoretical reflectance curve for a Mo/Si MLM.
--[p416]-- Generally, larger changes were observed for the short-wavelength regions of the spectra, corresponding to emission from more highly ionized xenon in the hottest zone of the plasma. The main features of the xenon spectra can be analyzed by a comparison of our results with similar data for a capillary discharge obtained by Klosner and Silfvast.<sup>28</sup>
--[p416]-- It was found that the emission of xenon depends strongly on the operating conditions, as previously seen in the xenon spectrum of a preionized Z pinch by McGoech.<sup>27</sup> The spectral distribution changes when the deposited energy, the discharge current, the gas mixture, or the gas pressure is changed.
--[p415]-- In our early work we discussed the lithium spectra<sup>3</sup> and the spectra of xenon and various other source gases<sup>5</sup> using step-bystep recording with a grazing-incidence spectrometer at a resolution of 0.02 nm.
--[p416]-- Spectra at increasing input energies showed an increase of the emission of more highly ionized xenon, indicating a higher average electron temperature.<sup>5,21</sup> On the other hand, for fixed DPF operating conditions subsequent single-pulse spectra exhibited only small intensity fluctuations that may be attributed to differences of the final compression and heating of the pinch plasma from one pulse to the next.

===== [p184-185] Atomic Physics of Highly Charged Ions and the Case for Sn as a Source Material > 5.1 Introduction and Background (10块) =====
--[p185]-- Shevelko et al.<sup>6</sup> subsequently undertook an extensive study of the spectra of a large number of elements from LPPs with a KrF excimer laser focused to a power density of $1 0 ^ { 1 2 } \mathrm { W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ onto planar targets, including tin, and found that the maximum intensity was in fact obtained for Ge and Re targets under these conditions.
--[p185]-- However, the duty cycles of all of these sources are ultimately limited by heat dissipation. All of the CEs reported to date for these devices are close to 0.5%. The optimum in-band efficiency obtainable from LPPs appears to be of the order of 1%; therefore, xenon is not the optimum choice if 3% conversion is required.
--[p185]-- To surmount this problem, liquid jet targets were developed so that plasma formation could take place far away from the nozzle, and CEs of the order of 0.75% have been reported with this setup.<sup>13</sup> In addition, a wide variety of pulsed discharge sources using xenon or xenon-helium mixtures are being actively investigated by a variety of companies and laboratories.
--[p185]-- There is a line group in the spectrum of xenon that has been shown by a number of researchers to arise from $\mathrm { 4 d ^ { 8 } - 4 d ^ { 7 } 5 p }$ transitions in Xe XI.<sup>7,8</sup> These lines have recently been measured to an accuracy of 0.01 nm by Churilov et al.,<sup>9</sup> who have identified all of the lines in this range by comparison with atomic structure calculations using the suite of codes developed by Cowan.<sup>10</sup> The population of this ion stage needs to be optimized to attain maximum intensity. Note that, depending on the type of source and hence ion density, optimization is not always necessarily the same as maximizing a given ion population because of opacity effects.
--[p184]-- 5.1 Introduction and Background
Projection lithography schemes based on 13.5-nm multilayer mirrors (MLMs) have been under intense scrutiny since the mid-1990s.<sup>1</sup> Stearns and coworkers<sup>2</sup> first demonstrated a reflectivity of 61% at this wavelength using Mo/Si multilayer optics, a figure that has been improved in the intervening period to a present value close to 72%.
--[p184]-- Ceglio and Hawryluk<sup>3</sup> proposed that a suitable scheme would require a 1% conversion efficiency (CE) of incident laser pulse energy to soft x rays in a 0.3-nm band centered at this peak. Kauffman et al.<sup>4</sup> attained this figure using 7.5-ns, 300-mJ frequency-doubled Nd:YAG pulses focused to a power density of $2 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 1 } ~ \mathrm { W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ onto a tin target.
--[p185]-- For example, Cymer has developed a dense plasma focus (DPF) device that can give a CE of 0.42% at 12.4 J of input energy at repetition rates of a few hundred hertz.<sup>14</sup> JMAR, Philips, and AIXUV have all built compact pinch discharge sources, again with CEs of the same order, and a capillary discharge source has been developed at Sandia National Laboratory capable of operation at repetition rates up to 1.7 kHz.<sup>15</sup>
--[p185]-- However, all of their work was with solid targets that produced significant debris in the form of both ions and particulates of various sizes. The need to reduce particulate emission led to the choice of xenon, which as an inert gas should provide a debris-free source.
--[p185]-- Considerable work has been expended on exploring the feasibility of using LPPs of xenon clusters, produced by supersonic jets or gas puffs from nozzles,<sup>11</sup> or from solid xenon targets. The highest CE (1.2% into 2% bandwidth) has been achieved using solid xenon,<sup>12</sup> because plasma formation causes damage to nozzles, which in turn produces more debris.
--[p184]-- This figure has now been revised upwards because of the increased costs of producing a suitable exposure tool, to better than
3% CE into 2% bandwidth, because this is necessary for the successful commercialization of such a source.
Because of the debris problems associated with the use of tin, other target materials were sought with strong emission in the 13–14-nm region. Jin and Richardson<sup>5</sup> used mass-limited water ice targets that emitted O VI lines near 13 nm to limit the debris.

===== [p317-320] HEIGHTS-EUV Package for DPP Source Modeling > 9.4 Detailed Radiation Transport (22块) =====
--[p317]-- In such a condition the radiation transfer is carried out by those photons, the frequency of which corresponds to the wings of the emitting lines and results in the absorption in colder areas of those photons emitted from the hotter plasma parts.
In studying the transfer of the radiant energy, one needs to distinguish two aspects of the modeling of a DPP device.
--[p318]-- In numerical simulation of the radiation transport processes, the radiant energy flux is calculated by integrating the radiation transport equation (RTE),<sup>10,11</sup> which represents the conservation of emitted and absorbed energy along the direction of the transfer.
--[p319]-- The energy and the trajectory of photon movement are determined by the Monte Carlo technique. It is supposed that each portion is a monochromatic set of photons. The total energy of a portion is a sum of the energies of the component photons, and the portion is called a macrophoton or photon bundle. The number of test photon bundles is determined by the hydrodynamic parameters of a cell and analyzed by the MCRT method.
--[p319]-- Integrals over solid angles are approximated by numerical quadrature, the choice of which defines the directions of the DRT. The solution is carried out simultaneously with the energy-balance solution to provide the distribution of the local energy source, temperature, and density profiles. The method is timeconsuming and resource-intensive. This makes it difficult to conduct a parametric study of a DPP device in practice.
--[p319]-- N = V \int _ { E _ { \mathrm { m i n } } } ^ { E _ { \mathrm { m a x } } } \frac { \kappa _ { \mathrm { e m i } } ( T , \boldsymbol { \rho } , \varepsilon ) \varepsilon ^ { 2 } } { \hbar ^ { 3 } \pi ^ { 2 } c ^ { 2 } } \bigg ( e ^ { \varepsilon / T } - 1 \bigg ) ^ { - 1 } d \varepsilon .\tag{9.11}
$$
--[p318]-- First, solving the hydrodynamic part of the problem requires correction (redistribution) of the plasma internal energy and, accordingly, correction of the evolution of the whole pinch dynamics. The key is the accurate and detailed calculation of the radiant energy redistribution in the whole plasma domain over the very broad spectral range of participating photons.
--[p318]-- The second aspect is the detailed calculation of the effective radiation of the EUV source within the operating energy range of 13.5 nm $\pm 2 \%$ . In this case, the calculation of the radiation transport must be restricted to take account of only those photons whose energies are in the mentioned range.
--[p318]-- \mathbf { S } _ { \mathrm { r a d } } = \int \Bigg [ \int _ { 0 } ^ { 2 \pi } \delta \varphi \int _ { 0 } ^ { \pi } I _ { \mathrm { E } } ( \theta , \varphi ) \cos { \theta } \sin { \theta } \delta \theta \Bigg ] d E .\tag{9.10}
$$
Finally, the radiation energy loss in each cell is found from $Q _ { \mathrm { { r a d } } } = \nabla \cdot S _ { \mathrm { { r a d } } }$ . Essentially, this method is the result of finite-differencing of the directional dependence of the RTE.
--[p318]-- Deterministic transport methods divide the computational domain in space, energy, and angles.<sup>12</sup> The radiation intensity along each direction is determined by integrating the RTE, and the directions are given by the angles of the chosen numerical quadrature.
--[p319]-- (9.3) due to radiation transport is found, knowing the number and the energy of emitted and absorbed photons in each cell of the hydrodynamic domain:
$$
Q _ { \mathrm { r a d } } = \sum _ { i } ^ { N _ { \mathrm { a b s } } } \varepsilon _ { i } - \sum _ { j } ^ { N _ { \mathrm { e m i } } } \varepsilon _ { j } .\tag{9.12}
$$
To improve the efficiency of the method, we utilize weight factors of the statistically collected events.
--[p318]-- In contrast to the direct resolution of the integrodifferential RTE, where one calculates a continuous function of the radiation intensity, the probabilistic model of the energy redistribution operates in discrete ranges of the radiative energies.<sup>11</sup> Given the importance of the correctness and the accuracy of the radiation transport, we are using both methods to ensure and benchmark the validity of our simulation.

===== [p312-313] HEIGHTS-EUV Package for DPP Source Modeling > 9.1 Introduction (9块) =====
--[p312]-- Because of its influence on the whole dynamics of the discharge, radiation transport for both continuum and lines with detailed spectral profiles is modeled by various discrete-ordinate and Monte Carlo methods. The developed models have been integrated into the HEIGHTS-EUV computer simulation package.
--[p312]-- The features of the package allow one to study the hydrodynamics and radiation of two-gas mixtures in dense plasma focus (DPF) devices in the presence of impurities and erosion products that can affect radiation output.
The goal of this chapter is to provide an overview of methods and techniques we use to simulate MHD and optical processes that occur in DPP devices of various electrode constructions.
--[p312]-- Regions with differing propagation speeds of perturbation require accurate numerical solutions of the MHD equations. The total variation diminishing (TVD) scheme in the Lax-Friedrich formulation for the description of magnetic compression and diffusion in a cylindrical multidimensional geometry is the most suitable and is used in our model.
--[p312]-- 9.1 Introduction
This chapter presents an integrated model that is being developed to describe the hydrodynamic and optical processes that occur in DPP devices for EUVL applications. The developed model will eventually address the following subjects: plasma evolution and magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) processes, atomic data and plasma properties, detailed photon radiation transport, and interaction between plasma/radiation and material.
--[p313]-- The general types of DPP devices that can be simulated within the HEIGHTS-EUV package are schematically shown in Fig. 9.1: (a) the DPF device, (b) the Z-pinch device, and (c) the hollow-cathode triggered pinch plasma source.<sup>1–3</sup> The electrodes are drawn solid and shown in gray.
--[p313]-- The plasma is an element of the electric circuit, which gets its discharge current from the feeding capacitor $C _ { 0 }$ . The simulation of the discharge by using the external (experimentally recorded) current may lead to the violation of the selfconsistency principle, because the energy balance is not conserved and the plasma dynamics can be distorted. The physical processes that take place in these DPP devices are identical and can be described within the same mathematical model.
--[p313]-- The device is filled with xenon gas under an initial pressure in the range of several tens of millitorr at room temperature, corresponding to an initial density of the gas in the range of $1 0 ^ { 1 4 } – 1 0 ^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ . It is also assumed that a preionization step heats the gas to a temperature of near 1 eV and initiates the discharge.
Typical representatives of the DPP devices are the conduction-type devices.
--[p312]-- Depending on the complexity of the problem and the availability of computer time, a combination of various atomic and plasma models is being developed for populations of atomic levels, ion concentrations, plasma properties, and opacities. These include a collisional radiation equilibrium plasma model, a Hartree-Fock (HF) self-consistent-field atomic model, and a Hartree-Fock-Slater (HFS) method with splitting of atomic levels.
--[p313]-- The distinguishing features of each particular design can also be affected by the initial and boundary conditions, such as the design and geometry of solid walls, the initial plasma parameters, the parameters of the electric circuit, and the methods of turning the device on and off. The MHD processes, radiation transport, and thermal conduction are implemented as a part of the HEIGHTS-EUV package, while design-specific features are implemented as additional blocks.

===== [p489-491] High-Power GDPP Z-Pinch EUV Source Technology > 15.1.2 First wall (19块) =====
--[p489]-- As an example relevant to the Star Pinch with xenon operated at 10-J input, 2 J of radiation in the 10–15-nm band is incident in a 50-ns pulse on the nearest surface at 9 mm from the plasma. This surface, which is that of the central insulator, has temperature jumps of $4 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in pBN and $3 0 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in SiC.
--[p490]-- Scaling from Table 15.1, the temperature jump is estimated to be only $2 2 ^ { \circ } \mathbf { C }$ . In the equatorial direction, magnetic insulation reduces the intensity of the plasma impact by several times (evidenced by a reduced erosion rate, discussed below), so the equatorial insulator, at 9 mm, is estimated to respond to the 8-J plasma with a temperature jump of less than $1 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$
When a pulse of energetic exhaust ions strikes the first wall, there is heating, but also sputter erosion.
--[p489]-- We consider several wall materials interacting with either the xenon 10– $1 5 \mathrm { - n m } \ \mathrm { b a n d } ^ { 2 }$ or the tin 12–16-nm band.<sup>3</sup> Typical metal wall materials are copper and tungsten, and insulators are pyrolytic boron nitride and silicon carbide (the latter is partially conductive).
--[p490]-- Although application of the same scaling to the Star Pinch is still speculative, we will make the approximation that the number of ions is proportional to the pulse energy.
--[p491]-- The erosion rate in this direction is about 5 times less than we would expect for isotropic expansion, because there is effective magnetic insulation by the pinch magnetic field, which persists at a relatively high level during the initial plasma expansion. The ion stream is directed by the magnetic and electric fields toward the cathode end of the pinch in a beam of solid angle less than 1 sr.

--[p490]-- There are many deleterious effects of sputter erosion: (1) changing the shape of the wall (in extreme cases breaking through to cooling channels); (2) evaporating (sputtering) wall material that can leave the source and reduce the reflectivity of the collection optics; (3) introducing new radiating species into the plasma that dissipate energy but may not contribute at 13.5 nm; (4) in the case of multilayer collector mirrors, eroding layers and reducing reflectivity; and (5) in the case of grazing-incidence collector optics, degrading the smoothness of the surface, reducing reflectivity. Sputter erosion is of equal concern in LPP and DPP sources, in each case being the main limiter of source life.

--[p489]-- 15.1.2 First wall
The temperature jump due to the combined effect of prompt radiation and plasma impact must not melt the first wall; otherwise small droplets of wall material can be ejected. The prompt radiation temperature jump is determined by distance from the hot plasma, the absorption depth in the wall, and the thermal constants of the wall material.
--[p490]-- Drawing on experience from DPP sources, sputter erosion can be incorporated into a simple model for source life. Erosion is proportional to the number of ions in the plasma times the number of pulses, N. We estimate the number of ions in the expanding plasma based on the known initial gas density (considering xenon for now) and the estimated volume swept into the pinch.

===== [p64-66] EUV Source Requirements for EUV Lithography > 2.2.1 Choice of wavelength (7块) =====
--[p66]-- Thus, depending on the type of light source, it is possible to achieve only a 5%– 10% increase in the optical throughput of a system by accurate spectral matching for emitters other than Li. The same shift for a Li-based source would make its use in EUVL impossible. That is not desirable at this early stage of development of EUVL. Currently, therefore, 13.5 nm is the wavelength of choice for EUVL.
--[p65]-- A more quantitative choice relates to the final adjustment of the system wavelength within a given spectral window of the Mo/Si mirror. The source emission characteristics play a major role in that choice.
A number of sources have potential for EUVL.<sup>2–7</sup> Due to their emission characteristics, the working materials that are used in those sources are usually Xe, Sn, and Li.
--[p64]-- Strong emission in the 11-nm region has been demonstrated for LPP Xe sources; see Fig. 2.2. Nevertheless, because the spectral width of the ML mirror in the shorter wavelength region is narrower than in the longer wavelength region, the total power at the wafer for Mo/Be mirrors does not exceed that of Mo/Si mirrors. Coupled with the manufacturing and safety problems of Mo/Be mirrors, that has led to a choice of wavelength in favor of Mo/Si mirrors.
--[p64]-- 2.2.1 Choice of wavelength
The optics used in the EUVL tools is based on multilayer mirrors (MLMs). Different combinations of multilayer pairs are possible. The most common for the EUV region are Mo/Si and Mo/Be pairs. The Mo/Be mirrors’ spectral range is larger than that of the Mo/Si mirrors. The cutoff wavelength for Mo/Si mirrors is about 12.5 nm in the shortwave region. No source, though, has been found so far that can make effective use of this fact.
--[p65]-- The amount of energy lost due to nonoptimal spectral alignment can be evaluated. This type of analysis has been done for a white-light source with a wavelength-independent spectrum.<sup>9</sup> In this case, the integrated reflectivity of the system, with 10 mirrors, is only 5% lower for 13.5 nm than for 14.4 nm, as mentioned by Stuik et al. in Ref. 9. However, the final analysis has been done with a combination of the optical throughput and the light-source spectrum in Ref. 10.
--[p65]-- Figure 2.2 presents a calculated near-normal-incidence reflectivity, based on the model of Ref. 11, for an 11-mirror reflective system. In contrast with a white spectrum, real Xe-, Sn-, and Li-based sources<sup>8</sup> have a maximum near 13.5 nm. Alteration of the peak wavelength by 0.5 nm might cause light losses of 60%– 100%. The light loss induced by placing the tool wavelength at 13.5 nm for Xe and Sn emitters does not exceed 5%–10%.
--[p65]-- Li, being a line emitter,<sup>7,8</sup> is the most sensitive to the choice of operating wavelength of the lithographic tool. Li radiates at 13.50 nm with a linewidth of 0.03 nm. The choice of a central wavelength differing from 13.50 nm by even a small amount can eliminate the possibility of using Li as a working material in the source for EUVL. On the other hand, a nonoptimal choice of the wavelength of the sources with other radiators means loss of power as well.

For a Doppler-broadened line with the center wavelength $\lambda _ { 0 }$ , the optical depth for the homogeneous plasma is given $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { b y } } ^ { 2 2 }$

It is evident that at low temperatures this line radiance is a very strong function of the temperature. Above about 60 eV it increases approximately as $( k T ) ^ { 2 }$ till it reaches the Rayleigh–Jeans regime and scales with $( \romannumeral 1 ) ^ { 3 / 2 }$ above 300 eV.

This implies cooling times in the nanosecond range for LPPs and in the hundred-nanosecond range for pinch plasmas with densities of $1 0 ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$

--[p245]-- At very high optical depths τ (optically thick plasma), the spectral radiance of the emission approaches the source function $S _ { \lambda }$ , which corresponds to the Planck function of a blackbody of the same temperature if the level distribution is thermal: it thus reaches maximum brilliance for the given temperature.
--[p245]-- The broadening of the optically thick line depends only weakly on the optical depth $\tau _ { 0 }$ at the line center, so that $\Delta \lambda \sim 2 \Delta \lambda _ { \mathrm { D o p p l e r } }$ is a good approximation for a single, initially Doppler-broadened line, and τ is in the range from 5 to 50.<sup>22,23</sup> Hence, the Planck radiance of a single line at 13.5 nm (92 eV) is
$$

where 1 $\mathrm { R y } = 1 3 . 6 ~ \mathrm { e V }$ is the Rydberg.
--[p248]-- Based on these arguments, the radiator CE can be estimated as the inband energy emitted per steradian divided by the input energy. The input energy is the energy invested to generate the plasma, i.e., to heat the substance to the emitting ground state (amounting to $\mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { i o n } }$ per ion) and, during its existence, to cover the radiative (and other) losses.
--[p249]-- Because the system is extremely complicated and many basic material data are not available, such models can only be useful in close collaboration with experiments. Some rather important properties of a pinch discharge, however, can be simulated with astonishingly good accuracy by rather simple models, which give useful hints to optimize the source efficiency.
--[p248]-- For example, there will always be electrode losses, losses via heat conduction to the walls, and losses due to ohmic heating of the device. Also, parasitic currents, which bypass the pinch plasma and dissipate energy elsewhere, cannot be avoided in a practical source.<sup>39</sup> Spectral efficiencies have been determined experimentally for the EUV range only.

===== [p349-349] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.5.1.3 Configuration interaction (3块) =====
--[p349]-- For instance, in the $\mathbf { M o } ^ { 1 5 + }$ spectrum, the configuration $3 \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 } 3 \mathrm { p } ^ { 6 } 3 \mathrm { d } ^ { 8 } 4 \mathrm { s }$ could not deexcite toward $3 \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 } 3 \mathrm { p } ^ { 5 } 3 \mathrm { d } ^ { 1 0 }$ via a single-electron dipolar electric transition; but a mixing through CI of the former configuration with other configurations such as $3 \mathrm { s } 3 \mathrm { p } ^ { 6 } 3 \mathrm { \bar { d } } ^ { \mathrm { \bar { 1 } 0 } }$ or $\bar { 3 \mathrm { s } } ^ { 2 } 3 \mathrm { p } ^ { 6 } 3 \mathrm { d } ^ { 9 }$ makes the transition possible. Formalisms such as the UTA method or the supraconfiguration approximation cannot include such effects, but detailed methods are usually able to take them into account.
--[p349]-- 10.5.1.3 Configuration interaction
In some cases the optical transitions in dense plasmas cannot be described by a transition array associated with a one-electron transition between well-defined initial and final configurations. In the atomic physics theory this means that in the diagonalization procedure the multielectron levels must be expanded in a basis belonging to two or more configurations.
--[p349]-- Although in such a situation the terminology based on a one-electron basis cannot be rigorously applied, we will keep using it to refer to the dominating configuration in the multiconfiguration expansion.<sup>63</sup> This CI may result in a strong redistribution of the transition probability between the various configurations. A striking illustration of this fact will be given below (Sec. 10.5.3).
Another possible effect is the presence in the spectrum of apparently forbidden electronic transitions due to mixing.

===== [p68-69] EUV Source Requirements for EUV Lithography > 2.2.3 Repetition frequency (3块) =====
--[p69]-- To deliver more than those numbers of pulses in 7.8 ms, repetition frequencies more than 14.4, 9.2, and 6.4 kHz are needed, respectively. It is stated in the joint requirements that the repetition frequency must be higher than 7–10 kHz, depending on the design of the exposure tool.
The width of the slit is limited because the number of mirrors in the projection optics is limited. The width is assumed to be 2 mm in the typical wafer throughput model.
If the width changes, the requirement of the integrated energy stability or the repetition frequency may change.
--[p68]-- Therefore, the average EUV power in the slit is $6 4 2 \mathrm { m W } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ . The exposure time is 7.8 ms at a point on a wafer if the resist sensitivity is $5 \mathrm { m J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$
In a case where the energy stability budget of the EUV source for dose control is 0.2% (3σ), 0.25% (3σ), or 0.3% (3σ), EUV light must expose the point with 112.5, 72, or 50 pulses, respectively, if the integrated energy stability over 50 pulses is 0.3% (3σ).
--[p68]-- 2.2.3 Repetition frequency
The repetition frequency is determined from a specification of dose uniformity. The dose uniformity depends not only on the integrated energy stability of the EUV source, but also on the control and measurement accuracy of the dose in the exposure tool.
The power at the wafer is 0.321 W in the typical wafer throughput model. The slit exposure area on the wafer is assumed to be $\bar { 2 } \times 2 5 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ .

===== [p191-191] Atomic Physics of Highly Charged Ions and the Case for Sn as a Source Material > 5.3 Alternatives to Xenon; the Case for Tin (1块) =====
--[p191]-- 5.3 Alternatives to Xenon; the Case for Tin

===== [p213-214] Radiative Collapse in Z Pinches > 6.3 Discharge Source for EUVL: High-Power, High-CE Alternative Concept Source (14块) =====
--[p214]-- 6.2, where a laser beam was focused on the edge of the cathode disk.<sup>12(b)</sup> A discharge took place between the focus of the laser and the corresponding sector of the anode. Radiation was collected in the radial direction, where less debris is expected to be produced by the discharge. The main experiments presented below were performed using this concept prototype installation PROTO I, working at repetition rates up to 1000 Hz.
--[p213]-- It was demonstrated that the CE could be 3–4 times higher than in the case of Xe; in our experiments the CE exceeded 2%.<sup>12</sup> Nevertheless the expected average heat load was still too high—50 kW for a small discharge geometry. Successful results of using tin as a working material in EUVL sources are reported as well in Chapters 16 and 18 of this volume.
The second direction of pursuit—source multiplication—did not result in successful solutions for gas systems.
--[p213]-- (The physical reasons for the benefits of using Sn are given, e.g., in Chapters 4 and 8 of this book.) Experiments with LPP types of EUV sources have proven the possibility of increasing the CE by using Sn plasmas rather than Xe (see Chapter 24 and references there). Nevertheless, tin was not considered for a rather long time as a possible working material for discharges. The reason was the difficulty of creating tin vapors with sufficient density and axial symmetry.
--[p214]-- That assumes that every elementary discharge source must have full axial symmetry and its diameter must be at least a few millimeters, or even a few centimeters, depending on the type of the discharge and the stored electrical energy.
--[p214]-- It is well known that ablation by a laser pulse or by an electron beam results in reasonably good axial symmetry of vapors relative to the normal to the target surface. It was found experimentally that with the proper initial material (vapor) configuration the vacuum discharge conserves the internal axial symmetry even at significant deviation of the electrode system from such symmetry.
--[p213]-- In 2002 we reported successful use of laser ablation of a tin cathode for the initiation of a vacuum spark.<sup>12(a)</sup> The first experiments were carried out using a standard vacuum spark geometry. The cathode was a hollow metal cylinder filled with tin. The anode was placed at a changeable distance of 3 to 5 mm from the cathode. Low inductance (≈ 10 nH) allowed delivery of currents up to 30 kA at a stored energy of 5 J.
--[p213]-- 6.3 Discharge Source for EUVL: High-Power, High-CE Alternative Concept Source
A number of EUV discharge source configurations—such as Z pinch, plasma focus, and capillary discharge—have been or are under investigation as possible solutions for industrial applications in EUVL. The history of these efforts and the results achieved are well presented in this book.
In the beginning Xe was explored mostly as the working material.
--[p213]-- The initial discharge symmetry and reproducible gas distribution needed for successful development of the discharge column was easily provided by the axial symmetry of the electrodes. With the initial conditions and a distance between electrodes not exceeding a few millimeters, the size of the EUV-radiating source was below $5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 2 }$ cm, which was in good agreement with the technical specifications of an EUVL apparatus.
--[p213]-- Strong concern, though, existed in regard to the power scalability of the EUV source based on Xe. Commercial lithography apparatus, in order to become commercially viable, must employ EUV sources, which, depending on the collector configuration, produce about 0.5–1 kW of EUV radiation in a 2% spectral band in $2 \pi$ solid angle. Experiments have shown that it is hardly possible to expect a conversion efficiency (CE) for Xe higher than 0.5%–1%.
--[p214]-- One might envision that the easiest solution would be a rotating configuration, where a new elementary discharge source replaces the previous one at the focus of the optical imaging system.<sup>11,12(b),13</sup>. As we pointed out earlier, the axial symmetry necessary in the gas discharges was provided by the axial symmetry of the electrode system.
--[p213]-- That would result in the necessity to dissipate about 100–200 kW of electrical power in a rather small volume, less than $1 ~ \mathrm { { c m } } ^ { 3 }$ . Such high power would unavoidably destroy the electrodes. Definitive characterizations of the difficulties one meets in using a Xebased discharge as an industrial EUV source are given in other chapters of this book.
There are two directions in which the solution for this problem might be sought.
--[p213]-- The first one is the use of a material (element) that is expected to have stronger radiation near 13.5 nm than Xe. The second is the so-called multiplication ofsources, an approach where the heat load is supposed to be distributed between a number of elementary discharge sources.<sup>11</sup>
For the first approach the candidate was evident: Sn, an element with atomic number 50.
--[p214]-- To build a discharge system consisting of tens or hundreds of elementary discharge sources would first of all be excessively expensive; secondly, at an expected repetition rate of the source of the order of 10 kHz these elementary discharge sources must move with a very high velocity, approaching 100 m/s. Both conditions made this approach rather unrealistic.
A simple solution for the source multiplication approach is found as soon as we turn to ablated tin vapor.
--[p214]-- Finally, we found that normal Z-pinch-like discharge development is maintained even for a flat configuration of both electrodes. Application of flat electrodes did not significantly change the dynamics of pinching. The CE was conserved also on the same level, approximately 2%. This result immediately made the whole concept of source multiplication fully feasible. The first rotating system was accomplished in a form of two rotating disks (cathode disk and anode disk) as shown in Fig.

--[p422]-- 12.13 Lifetime Limitations and Power Scaling
The lifetimes of the inner electrode and the collector mirrors are the limiting parameters during use at high duty cycles. Fast exchange of the inner electrode and (less frequent) exchange of the collector assembly can be arranged. Erosion data derived from weighing of inner electrodes after exposure to millions of pulses at continuous operation at ≈50 Hz were consistent with the thermal results.
--[p422 [表]]-- In order to reach EUV power levels above 100 W at the IF, even under favorable conditions, a thermal extraction power of 100 kW or more will be required in the case of a Xe-based DPF source. However, as shown in the last column of Table 12.1, due to its higher CE number, tin as source element will meet these requirements for HVM already at 35-kW extraction power.
Table 12.1 Output power scaling for the DPF source operated with Xe or Sn.
Today | Future | Required | Required
--[p422]-- The weight loss per pulse was measured for several different electrode materials, including various forms and alloys with tungsten. Tungsten has favorable impulsivity characteristics.<sup>7</sup> The electrode lifetime decreases with increasing repetition rate. Operation with negative polarity at the inner electrode resulted in a 2 times reduction of the erosion rates of the electrode material of choice. Test runs indicate that the electrode life is extendable to beyond 100 million pulses.
--[p422]-- At present, the projected collector optics lifetime is above 300 million pulses. It is ultimately connected with the efficiency and acceptable reduction in EUV transmission of the debris shield. The economical use of an assembly of replicated collector shells can be envisioned.
The power scaling of the DPF source can be estimated based on the present results. Table 12.1 shows the various factors that govern the inband EUV power obtainable at the IF.
--[p422]-- With the present state of the DPF technology, using xenon as the source element, at 3.1-kW thermal extraction power and 140-W generated inband EUV power, about 14 W of EUV power will be obtained at the IF. The collection efficiency and the transmission factors are listed in Table 12.1. Future developments should enable the generation of 300-W EUV power (for Xe, at higher CE and thermal power extraction; see Table 12.1).

===== [p44-44] EUV Source Technology: Challenges and Status > 1.3.1 Measurements (5块) =====
--[p44]-- For FC, an accuracy of better than 3% is estimated for absolute EUV power measurements on a beamline.<sup>38</sup> These absolute accuracies are good for the Xe-based system only. For Sn-based EUV sources, because of varying spectral correction factors, an FC-type device with special 2%-BW mirrors has been used.
--[p44]-- Metrology for measurements at IF is still being developed.<sup>33–35</sup> Since measurements at IF are more cumbersome and IF metrology equipment is more expensive, power measurements are likely to continue to be taken directly at source.
Absolute EUV power is measured using one or more multilayer mirrors and EUV diodes, although absolutely calibrated charge-coupled devices (CCDs) combined with spectrometers can also perform these measurements.
--[p44]-- 1.3.1 Measurements
The EUV source requirements are specified at the intermediate focus (IF) in the 2% BW around 13.5 nm. However, most measurements are now performed by directly observing the EUV source. Consequently, the power estimated at the IF requires the estimation of losses between the source and IF.
--[p44]-- Both mirror and diodes are calibrated at beamline. SEMATECH has sponsored the Flying Circus (FC) project to independently assess source performance,<sup>4</sup> cross-calibrate the suppliers’ EUV sensors, and cross-calibrate other commercial EUV energy sensors.<sup>4,36,37</sup> Such measurement campaigns have resulted in confidence in the source power measurements and source performance data.
--[p44]-- The special multilayer mirrors, designed to simulate the performance of the 11-mirror system, allow one to esti mate the EUV radiation in the 2% BW around 13.5 nm, without spectral feature information for the Sn source in a wide-spectral-range calibration. 39

===== [p343-345] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.4.2 Simple spherical target (9块) =====
--[p344]-- The atomic physics data required for this code were acquired from the Opacity Project database.<sup>27</sup> The Opacity Project was implemented to calculate and compile the atomic data necessary for estimates of stellar envelope opacities. The database consists of atomic data for the astrophysically abundant elements, $Z = 1 { - } 2 6$ . Coupled with these data, the Spectra code produces synthetic spectra from 1 to 1000 nm.
--[p344]-- As is shown in the companion chapter by Richardson et al. (Chapter 26), this model reproduces quite well the pseudospherical expansion of the plasma from the spherical target, even with one-directional laser irradiation. An example of this is shown in Fig. 10.5.
Modeling the line emission from water droplets (oxygen) was accomplished with the Spectra code.<sup>26</sup> This code assumes LTE and calculates the ionization distribution, excited-state populations, and allowed transitions.
--[p345]-- The average is over the electron velocity v.

and widths of the individual line emission in the 10–18-nm range. The agreement between the code predictions and the measured data is remarkably close.

===== [p202-202] Atomic Physics of Highly Charged Ions and the Case for Sn as a Source Material > 5.3.5 Debris (4块) =====
--[p202]-- Using 500 mJ of 1.064-µm radiation delivered in a 18-ns pulse, it was found that most debris is emitted 2–3 µs after the pulse and that 98% of the particulates travel slower than $6 4 0 ~ \mathrm { m } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 } .
--[p202]-- \dot { 5 } 3$ The mass deposition rate at 5 cm from the target was 1 $\mu \mathrm { g } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ per shot.<sup>54</sup> Subsequently, the mass-limited cryogenic target was proposed, and the feasibility of using ice droplets demonstrated.<sup>5</sup> More recently this target has been modified to include a small percentage of tin.<sup>55</sup> Other proposals have been to illuminate a thin film of tin, which evaporates upon irradiation by a laser pulse; to view the EUV emission from behind, i.e., in a direction opposite to the plasma expansion;<sup>56</sup> or to confine the tin plasma in a channel and again view the emission in a direction away from the expanding plume.<sup>57,58</sup> For slab targets, the debris is minimized if tin-doped glasses or ceramics are used.
--[p202]-- The use of repeller fields has also been suggested,<sup>54</sup> and if all the debris were ionized, by using mass-limited, cavity-confined or prepulse-pulse-generated plasmas from slab targets, then fields could be quite efficient in deflecting the debris away from the multilayer optics.
--[p202]-- 5.3.5 Debris
Debris generation from solid targets produced by laser blowoff has been the subject of much investigation, for deposition on nearby condenser optics poses a major constraint on any commercial exploitation of LPP soft-x-ray sources. The use of a low-pressure (0.2-torr) He background gas has been successful in reducing the emission of small particles (<0.3 µm) but has had minimal effect on larger particulates.

===== [p39-41] EUV Source Technology: Challenges and Status > 1.2.1 DPP versus LPP (8块) =====
--[p39]-- 1.2.1 DPP versus LPP
The conversion efficiency (CE) is the ratio of energy radiated by the EUV source in a 2% bandwidth (BW) around 13.5 nm to the input energy to the EUV source. The CE is used to estimate the utility requirements, choose the fuel, and understand the limits of power scaling. The fundamental CE for a fuel represents the upper limit of CE for that particular fuel.
--[p41]-- 3 | Resist resolution sensitivity and line edge roughness (LER)
Unranked issues
Reticle protection during storage handling and use Source power
Projection and illuminator optics quality and lifetime
--[p39]-- For DPP, the input energy is the electrical energy consumed by the entire system (energy dissipated in the plasma plus energy lost in the electrical system). However, sometimes the CE values presented in the literature take into account only the energy deposited in the plasma. In DPP, some of the energy is lost in the electrical components; therefore, the reported CE will depend on system-specific details.
--[p39]-- Without those details, it is difficult to separate the CE from the fundamental CE limits for a given fuel. Reference 4 gives an example of the CE for the entire system as well as the fundamental CE. For a given fuel, it is possible to optimize the system operation to maximize its $\mathrm { C E . } ^ { 5 }$ One may note that many times the highest CE reported for a fuel and source design combination does not correspond to optimal operating conditions.
--[p39 [表]]-- In this situation, it is best to use the CE for optimal operating conditions to get a realistic utility consumption estimate and understand the limits of power scaling. For the LPP system, the laser power and EUV output in the 2% BW around 13.5 nm is used to estimate the CE. However, for LPP systems, the overall conversion for the entire system is much less than for DPP because of the low wall-plug-to-laser-light CE of a laser system, which is typically less than 10%.

--[p150]-- 4.3 Results of the Calculations

--[p150]-- Only the transitions with A values higher than $A _ { \mathrm { m a x } } / 1 0$ are given for the complex configurations, because the full tables take too much space in these cases. The transitions in the tables are sorted according to the energy of the upper level in each ion. Figure 4.1 shows these data in convenient visual form.
--[p150]-- Tables with the results of the calculations are presented in the appendix. --[p150]-- Calculations of the odd-level systems were made in a configuration-interaction approach in which several highly excited configurations responsible for large correlation effects were added: $4 \mathrm { p } ^ { 6 } 4 \check { \mathrm { d } } ^ { M - 1 } n \mathrm { f } ( n = 5 , 6 ) , 4 \mathrm { p } ^ { 3 } 4 \mathrm { d } ^ { M + 3 } , 4 \mathrm { p } ^ { 5 } 4 \mathrm { d } ^ { M - 1 } 5 \mathrm { \check { p } } ^ { 2 }$ , and $\mathrm { 4 p ^ { 5 } 4 d } ^ { M - 1 } \mathrm { 5 f } ^ { 2 }$

--[p150]-- It should be noted that each ion starting from Sn VII has a clearly seen array of intense lines, whose maximum shifts to shorter wavelengths with increasing ionization stage.

===== [p415-415] Dense Plasma Focus Source > 12.7 EUV Source Size and Spatial and Angular Distribution (7块) =====
--[p415]-- 12.7 EUV Source Size and Spatial and Angular Distribution
The EUV source size must be small in order to achieve a very high brightness. Moreover, the etendue has a direct influence on the attainable collection efficiency.<sup>1,26</sup> Therefore, we have measured the source size by means of EUV imaging techniques.
--[p415]-- Depending on the operating conditions, the averaged DPF source volume has an elongated shape with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) in the range of 0.3–0.4 mm and 2.5–4.5 mm perpendicular and parallel to the axis, respectively. Studies of the source size were carried out using a back-illuminated CCD camera and a thin metal foil for spectral filtering.
--[p415]-- At first, measurements were performed both on axis and off axis, using a pinhole-imaging technique, for both single-pulse and pulse-averaged spatial images.<sup>5,6</sup> However, such data contain also some contributions from more energetic out-of-band radiation and typically lead to an underestimation of the true source size.
--[p415]-- In order to obtain more accurate inband data, we have therefore employed a pinhole-free at-wavelength imaging technique using spherical $\mathbf { M L M s } ^ { 7 , 8 }$ and have also included in the pinhole arrangement a reflection from a MLM at 45-deg incidence in front of the CCD camera.<sup>9</sup> The latter arrangement is show in Fig. 12.6.
--[p415]-- High angular emission correlation was also observed for other detector combinations. These results indicate that for individual pulses the pinch dynamics leads to similar emission characteristics irrespective of the different angular directions. Pulse averaging improves this correlation even further.
--[p415]-- A comparison of inband measurements using the EUV monitor and the integrated CCD signal on a pulse-to-pulse basis has yielded almost perfect agreement, with a correlation coefficient > 0.97. The corresponding source position stability was also determined from the fluctuations of the centroid in measurements of the source size and was found to be typically less than 0.05 mm rms.
--[p415]-- The dose stability and the uniformity of the filling of the entrance pupil of the illumination optics are directly connected with the angular stability of the source. Therefore, the emission from the source was examined by correlation measurements at different angles, using pairs of our calibrated EUV monitors. High correlation (>0.95) of the inband EUV emission was detected for DPF operation at both low and high (2 kHz) repetition rates.

===== [p445-445] Hollow-Cathode-Triggered Plasma Pinch Discharge > 13.4 Summary and Outlook (4块) =====
--[p445]-- It is important to stress that progress is needed in all parameters, since one parameter can hardly compensate shortage in another one. A CE of 0.5% for Xe with an acceptable short pinch length below 3 mm for xenon discharges is achieved, but it is not expected to increase the xenon efficiency much above 1%. In particular, it means that xenon is not an option for HVM sources because of its intrinsic low CE due to the spectral distribution of the EUV light.
--[p445]-- 13.4 Summary and Outlook
The HCT concept has proven successful in a number of relevant parameters. Frequency scaling up to 8 kHz was demonstrated. Thermal and cooling properties were successfully demonstrated to power levels in excess of 15-kW input power. Further, an electrode lifetime of 200 million shots and a collector lifetime of at least 500 million shots were demonstrated. All of this makes the concept well suited to meet HVM specifications.
--[p445]-- Progress, however, is needed in all relevant parameters. The following combination is targeted as the final specification:
Input power: 30 kW
CE: >2%
Collection efficiency: >25% of 2π sr, meaning a collector with 3 sr
opening and an average reflectivity of 60%
Debris mitigation: Light transmission of 80%
Together, these parameters will lead to >120 W of usable light at the IF.
--[p445]-- In Sn pinch plasmas, a CE higher than 2% and also a higher collection efficiency than with current xenon pinches have been successfully demonstrated.
The authors believe that the employed source concept is well suited to meet the targeted specifications. As this will be necessarily based on a Sn discharge, the main challenge will be handling of metal vapor and corresponding protection of the collector.
Since every concept will have to use metal vapors, a generic solution to serve all sources might soon become an option.

===== [p251-253] Fundamentals and Limits of Plasma-based EUV Sources > 7.7 Atomic Physics, Radiation, and Ionization Modeling (15块) =====
--[p252]-- The method of escape factors,<sup>43</sup> however, can be applied to estimate which part of the spectrum will be affected by opacity and to predict trends.<sup>39</sup>
Up to now we have discussed only the radiation properties of various ions in the EUV spectral range. The computation of the abundances of the various ion stages in the transient plasma requires ionization and recombination rate coefficients.
--[p252]-- This or similar methods have been applied by various authors to compute (optically thin) spectra of interesting xenon and tin ions.<sup>36–39</sup> Actually such spectral calculations<sup>40</sup> led the community to move from xenon to tin as radiator: whereas only one xenon ion, $\mathrm { X e ^ { 1 0 + } }$ , radiates near 13.5 nm, several tin ions, viz., $\mathrm { S n ^ { 8 + } - }$ $\mathrm { S n } ^ { \dot { 1 } \dot { 2 } + }$ , have strong transitions in this spectral range.
--[p251]-- 7.7 Atomic Physics, Radiation, and Ionization Modeling
Since only the EUV radiation in a narrow inband wavelength region of 13.5 nm $\pm 1 \%$ can be used in the reflecting optics of the illuminator, it is of essential importance to generate a spectrum that is strongly peaked in this region. On the other hand, the OOB radiation in other wavelength regions, which would lead only to unwanted energy losses and heating of the electrode system, must be minimized.
--[p251]-- Besides energy levels, transition probabilities (Einstein A coefficients) and electron impact excitation rates are also calculated. These data allow in the next step the evaluation of excited-state populations of each ion by balancing its electron impact excitation and de-excitation and photonic transitions as a function of the surrounding plasma’s parameters.
Assuming a Maxwellian electron energy distribution, the plasma is described by its electron density and temperature.
--[p252]-- For ions with many inner-shell electrons in high-density plasmas this is a very complicated matter, for dielectronic processes and intermediate metastable states become very important. The calculation of effective rates considering these processes is a subject of current research; see for example Ref. 35. The situation becomes even more complicated if one takes into account that photoabsorption affects the population of excited states.
--[p251]-- In the highly transient pinch discharges described here, the plasma conditions change rapidly during the compression. All three situations are such that a complete CR description is required to compute the total radiation and the spectra of individual ions as functions of electron temperature and density.
--[p252]-- A thorough simulation of these effects requires the solution of the radiation transport equations (RTEs) at each time step of the transient plasma simulation.<sup>41,42</sup> Besides the immense computational effort, this also requires data about shapes and broadening mechanisms for thousands of spectral lines. Moreover, radiation absorption contributes considerably to the power balance and must therefore be coupled to the MHD model to compute temperature and density profiles.
--[p251]-- The intermediate situation is called collisional radiative (CR) equilibrium.<sup>34</sup> These regimes appear in Fig. 7.9, showing the populations of three excited $\mathrm { X e ^ { 1 0 + } }$ states of the configuration $4 \mathrm { d } ^ { 7 } 5 \mathrm { p }$ near 13.5 eV as a function of electron density for an electron temperature of 51 eV, which was found to be a typical value for optimized emission at our device.
--[p251]-- In the low-electron-density limit where electron impact deexcitation is negligible compared to photonic decays, this leads to a corona equilibrium. In this case the excited-state populations—and hence the radiated power per ion—are proportional to the electron density. In the other limit of a very dense plasma, the photonic decays are much slower than collisional processes, and the excited-state populations—and consequently the emitted radiation—are independent of the electron density.
--[p251]-- These requirements led to the choice of 13.5 nm: the resonant first Lyman line, 2p-1s, of hydrogenlike $\operatorname { L i } ^ { 2 + }$ is exactly at this wavelength. In the following we will show, however, that besides the technological problems, also the spectral properties of lithium are not optimal.
The evaluation of the spectral emissivity is based on the atomic structure— energy levels, oscillator strengths, and electron impact excitation rates—of the ions of interest.
Compared to neutral atoms, the Coulomb interaction with the nucleus has a larger effect on the energy levels.
--[p252]-- And even $\mathrm { X e ^ { 1 0 + } }$ has a large fraction of useless OOB radiation near 11 nm. Therefore, one expects and observes up to 5 times higher spectral efficiency [(inband radiation)/(OOB radiation)] with tin plasmas than with xenon plasmas. Consequently the heat load associated with a given inband radiation can be reduced by a factor of up to 5, for generating the same amount of inband radiation.
--[p252]-- A more exact prediction of the inband efficiency of EUV sources is rather complicated; especially during the high-density phase of the transient discharge, when most of the EUV radiation is generated, photoabsorption strongly affects the emission. For example, the radiation of $\mathrm { X e ^ { 1 0 \bar { + } } }$ near 11 nm is considerably reduced, but also other lines from various xenon or tin ions are absorbed.
--[p251]-- Fortunately this allows for rather accurate calculations of the atomic structure in the Hartree-Fock approximation with relativistic extensions, as for example with the widely applied Cowan code.<sup>33</sup> For ions with open d shells, the high angular momentum of the outer electrons and configuration mixing cause a splitting into thousands of energy levels and consequently almost continuous, grasslike spectra.
--[p252]-- Consequently also the effective ionization and recombination rates will depend on the radiation fields.
Knowing these effective rates, it is in principle possible to compute the equilibrium ionization, i.e., the abundances of the various ions, as a function of electron temperature and density.
--[p253]-- The plasma parameters in the highly transient discharges, however, change so fast that ionization equilibrium will not be achieved; a proper simulation should therefore include the full transient ionization dynamics.

===== [p220-221] Radiative Collapse in Z Pinches > 6.7 Experimental Observation of Neck Instabilities; Plasma Outflow (8块) =====
--[p221]-- It often happens that during further development (compression) the neck is split into two or more subnecks (frame 7), keeping the aspect ratio of the sausage $( \gamma = \mathrm { { l e n g t h / r a d i u s } } )$ approximately constant $( \gamma \approx 2 – 5 )$ .
--[p220]-- On the other hand, it is a well-known fact that even in gas-filled Z pinches the EUVradiating plasma has a smaller axial dimension than the cathode-anode gap. This observation would be difficult to understand without the assumption that a hightemperature zone is created inside the main discharge column. Time-integrated pinhole images show that the radial size of the EUV source is also smaller than the initial discharge radius.
--[p220]-- Simultaneous registration of time-gated and space-resolved spectra show that radiation around 13.5 nm is mostly responsible for the formation of the bottom images. Horizontal lines indicate the positions of cathode and anode, with a distance of 3.5 mm between them.
EUV radiation from the pinch starts only when the plasma column locally (at a distance of approximately half a millimeter from the cathode) shrinks to a diameter $\approx 0 . 3 – 0 . 4$ mm (frame 4).
--[p220]-- The images have been recorded with the help of a time-gated open-microchannel plate camera sensitive to radiation below 150 nm (www.schulz-si.com). No filters are used for the upper images. They are formed, therefore, by integrated radiation between 1 and 150 nm. The bottom images are filtered by a Zr/Si filter and are thus formed by EUV radiation between 8 and 16 nm.
--[p220]-- 6.7 Experimental Observation of Neck Instabilities; Plasma Outflow
Neck instabilities are known to be a common feature of almost all axial discharges. They have been observed in discharges over a wide current range—on vacuum sparks and Z pinches with currents between 50 and 200 kA, and in Z pinches and plasma foci with currents of a few megamperes.<sup>2,8</sup> The presence of necks in lowcurrent (10–30 kA) discharges was also expected but is not yet demonstrated.
--[p220]-- Nevertheless, direct observations of discharge-column necking are of interest and are shown in Fig. 6.5.
Figure 6.5 presents a series of pinhole images of a vacuum spark discharge recorded on the concept tool PROTO I with a current of about 20 kA in tin vapors. Time frames were of about 20-ns duration. The time shift between the frames (numbered) is 10 ns. Thus exposure times of different frames are partly overlapped.
--[p221]-- The observed duration of EUV radiation corresponds well with an estimate of the sausage lifetime due to plasma outflow: $\tau \approx \gamma r / V _ { \mathrm { S } }$ where $V _ { \mathrm { { S } } }$ is the ionic sound velocity in the plasma. At a velocity of $1 0 ^ { 6 }$ cm/s and a radius of 0.01–0.015 cm, expected lifetimes are 20–50 ns, which corresponds fairly well to the experimental observation.
--[p221]-- At maximum radiation the plasma has a diameter of about 0.2 mm and a length in the axial direction close to 1 mm. More than one neck may appear, and the position of maximum narrowing of the plasma column—the neck—gradually moves from the cathode to the anode.

--[p378]-- 11.3 Power Balance Model
We analytically estimate a scaling law for the CE of the laser intensity from a power balance consideration.<sup>21</sup> We consider a target of which the initial density is higher than the laser critical density, where the electron plasma frequency equals the incident laser frequency. Since laser light propagates up to the critical density in plasma, laser absorption occurs only near the surface of the target, and hot plasma spurts out.

--[p284]-- A set of simulations was performed for fast capillary discharges in a geometry close to that of the experimental MPP discharge device established at EPPRA. The MPP radiation source is unique among the DPP sources in operating at a stored electrical energy ${ \ll } 1 ~ \mathrm { J }$ . It relies on a very low inductance discharge geometry to allow current of several kiloamperes to be delivered to a preionized discharge channel in several nanoseconds, despite the small energy used.
--[p286]-- Since the plasma temperature does not reach the optimal value under the discharge conditions simulated, the percentage of EUV radiation may be increased if the current is increased. Such an optimization simulation was performed at a higher charging voltage of 20 kV, with other parameters in closely similar conditions. The inband EUV emission was found to increase by 4 times instead of the increase of less than 3 times predicted by simple $I ^ { 2 }$ scaling.
--[p283]-- 8.4.1.1 3D plasma compression
In most EUV capillary radiation sources so far developed,<sup>33–36</sup> the operating gas is fed from one electrode and exhausted through the opposite electrode. The exhaust electrode connects the discharge system to the vacuum pumping system. Due to the almost Knudsen flow in the pressure regime of the operating discharge, a pressure gradient is established within the capillary between the two electrodes.
--[p283]-- This solution shows that the plasma flows along the Z axis from the lower-density region to the higher-density region and thus the plasma is compressed three-dimensionally, unlike the 2D compression in the homogeneous cylindrical case. The formula (8.21) allows the density distribution $\rho _ { 0 } ( z )$ and capillary profile $R _ { 0 } ( z )$ to be optimized for more efficient radiation production.
--[p284]-- Many of these simulation results have been reported in various EUVL meetings.<sup>35–38</sup>
In the following, we present details of some results on simulations obtained by $Z ^ { * }$ using the geometry presented in Fig. 8.7(b). An alumina capillary with internal diameter 1.6 mm and length 12 mm is placed between the electrodes.
--[p284]-- The structure is shown schematically in Fig. 8.7(a). Various capillary diameters, from 0.8 to 3.2 mm, and lengths $l = 6 { - } 1 2$ mm, with various gas compositions—including pure Ar, Kr, and Xe or their admixtures with He—at a range of pressures from 1 mTorr to 1 Torr, were examined.
These simulations were carried out with different driving parameters, including cell capacities and cell voltages, and different types of generator circuits.
--[p283]-- The compression time of the discharge plasma decreases as the linear mass decreases $( t _ { \mathrm { c } } \propto \stackrel { - } { m } ^ { 1 / 2 } c R _ { 0 } / I )$ , and the plasma near the anode therefore compresses faster than that near the cathode. Such a difference in the compression dynamics effectively causes faster increase of the magnetic field pressure near the anode and produces an axial compression wave along the capillary axis from the anode to the cathode.

===== [p279-279] Z∗ Code for DPP and LPP Source Modeling > 8.3.3 Multigroup radiation transport model (10块) =====
--[p279]-- To examine radiation within the EUV spectral band of interest, special radiation groups are prepared for the range near 13.5 nm and the adjacent bands. The calculated EUV spectrum and details of the part of the spectrum within the band 13– 14 nm are presented in Fig. 8.6. By summing over a given bandwidth it is possible to generate a time profile of the emission power and to find a conversion efficiency (CE) for the plasma EUV source, particularly for comparison with experimental measurements.
--[p279]-- In the multigroup approach, the full spectral range is divided into M spectral bands $( 0 \to \omega _ { 1 } , \dots , \omega _ { m - 1 } \to \omega _ { m } , \dots , \omega _ { M - 1 } \to \infty )$ , including the most important intervals for the energy balance. To find the radiation energy, the quasistationary transport Eq. (8.7) must be integrated along trajectories under cylindrical symmetry conditions.
--[p279]-- To continue the classical solution, the multigroup approach is extended to the angular coordinate, i.e., the volume is also divided into groups $0 $ $\varphi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \varphi _ { k - 1 } \to \varphi _ { k } , \ldots , \varphi _ { K - 1 } \to 2 \pi$ for the azimuthal angle $\Phi ;$ , and $0 $ $\theta _ { 1 } , \dots , \theta _ { l - 1 } \to \theta _ { l } , \dots , \theta _ { L - 1 } \to \pi$ for the angle $\theta .$ .
--[p279]-- Then, to find the spectral radiation energy $U _ { \omega }$ in a cylindrical geometry, the integral over the volume of the cell and over the angular group is evaluated analytically; after that it is used in the energy balance Eq. (8.18).
This approach is much more complicated than the diffusion or quasi-diffusion model widely used to model the radiation transport.
--[p279]-- In the method used in $Z ^ { * }$ , the self-consistency of the nonlinear radiation transport and the non-LTE dependence of the plasma state on radiation energy are taken into account by means of an approximation of the radiative coefficients,<sup>13,20</sup> as described earlier in Sec. 8.3.1. The result is realized through internal iterations, which are stable.
--[p279]-- In $Z ^ { * }$ a semianalytical approximation is used to obtain an expression for the intensity. The emission and absorption coefficients $j _ { \omega } , \kappa _ { \omega }$ in Eq. (8.7) depend on the coordinates r and $z .$ In the approximation, the integral in Eq.
--[p279]-- However, diffusion methods cannot be applied for semitransparent or transparent plasmas, for there is no physical basis for such applications. In a plasma where only strong lines may be reabsorbed, the main part of the photons have mean free paths comparable to or even larger than the plasma size. The radiation in the plasma is necessarily anisotropic and must be subjected to the transport Eq. (8.1).
--[p279]-- By choosing specially oriented angle groups, the radiation flux to any diagnostic EUV detector may be also simulated.
--[p279]-- (8.7) is integrated analytically inside each cell, where the coefficients $j _ { \omega } , \kappa _ { \omega }$ do not depend on the coordinates, since numerical integration in the case of high reabsorption $( \Delta \tau \sim \kappa _ { \omega } \Delta x / \sin \theta \gg 1 )$ can lead to large error.
--[p279]-- 8.3.3 Multigroup radiation transport model
Specific attention in $Z ^ { * }$ is paid to radiation-transport simulation. The classical solution developed to tackle radiation transport in dense plasmas involves a multigroup approach to limit the radiation energy band. An averaged absorption and emission coefficient for the radiation is derived for each group, and a table containing detailed properties in connection with the equation of state is used.
