--[p241]-- The basic investment is always what is needed to heat the plasma to a temperature (thermal energy in electrons and ions) sufficiently high to yield a high abundance of ground-state ions of interest (potential energy), and then to excite the ions to the upper level for photon emission. With a probability depending on the branching ratio of the involved radiative transitions, one gains a usable photon.

===== [p202-202] Atomic Physics of Highly Charged Ions and the Case for Sn as a Source Material > 5.4 Conclusions (2块) =====
--[p202]-- Preliminary measurements indicate that CEs of 3% should be readily attainable if opacity effects are minimized (by controlling the concentration of tin in the target and the target geometry) and if the laser pulse shape and power density are carefully matched to the target conditions. Moreover, the use of dilute targets reduces the amount of out-of-band EUV emission, which is another problem that must be addressed.<sup>55</sup>
--[p202]-- 5.4 Conclusions
We have shown that from both atomic-structure and plasma considerations the brightness attainable from a plasma containing a small percentage of tin is considerably greater than from xenon-based sources.

===== [p458-462] High-Power GDPP Z-Pinch EUV Source Technology > 14.4 Discharge Electrode System, Source Collector, and Electrode Lifetime (23块) =====
--[p460]-- 14.7 the temperature at the surface of the electrode has been calculated for an example of discharge geometry after switching on the Z-pinch EUV source at a repetition rate of 1000 Hz. At each excitation pulse with approximately 5-J energy input into the plasma, the temperature at the electrode surfaces rises very fast by about 2500 K.
--[p459]-- Pre-ionization (i.e., uniform seeding of the plasma discharge volume with electrons prior to the initiation of the main discharge) is necessary in order to form a uniform glow discharge, so as to avoid arcing and to allow a homogeneous pinching effect.
--[p461]-- Experimentally achieved discharge-unit lifetimes for XTREME technologies’ GDPP Z-pinch sources are discussed below.
Unfortunately, without additional means of plasma confinement, these discharge configurations produce larger plasma volumes and therefore have lower CEs. Additional means to confine the plasma are necessary.
--[p461]-- The locally confined target-material evaporation supports small plasma volumes, which are to a certain extent independent of the electrode size.
The laser-assisted GDPP EUV source principle of Ref. 34 can be applied not only with stationary but also with moving electrodes, because the laser beam fixes the location of the tin vapor in this configuration.
--[p458]-- Today, available Wolter-type grazing-incidence collectors have a maximum opening angle of 1.8 sr, i.e., ±45 deg. Wolter telescopes with π-sr opening angle as EUV source collectors are in principle producible.
Usually the diameter for GDPP sources in general and for Z-pinch sources specifically stays well below 1 mm. With both tin and xenon GDPP Z-pinch sources, we have achieved plasma diameters for full width at $1 / e ^ { 2 }$ between 0.6 and 0.9 mm.
--[p460]-- Because of the finite heat transfer time, the background temperature of the electrode surface increases before the next excitation pulse is delivered to the discharge. The background temperature level saturates because the energy delivered into the surface volume of the discharge electrode by a single excitation pulse decreases relative to the total amount of energy originating from all previous excitation pulses.
--[p459]-- The parameters that affect the pre-ionization, such as threshold value, seed electron density, and uniformity, are heavily dependent on the design of the discharge electrode system, such as the type of electrode and profile, gas pressure of the target material, duration of pre-ionization, electron loss processes, time delay between pre-ionization and main discharge, and rise time of the discharge voltage, as well as on the overall discharge-system geometry.
--[p458]-- Therefore, the numerical aperture (NA) and etendue allow geometrically the transmission of the entire EUV energy of the diameter. Because of the cylindrical symmetry of all GDPP sources, the shape of the EUV-emitting volume can be approximated as an ellipsoid with the main axis typically longer than the diameter. With Z-pinch sources using both xenon and tin, XTREME technologies Z-pinch sources have generated lengths between 1.0- and 8.0-mm full width at $1 / \bar { e } ^ { 2 }$
In Fig.
--[p459]-- XTREME technologies Z-pinch sources use a sliding surface-discharge pre-ionization, which improves the energy stability over the non-pre-ionized operation of the Z pinch by a factor of 4. For experimental data on energy stability, see below.
With this type of pre-ionized Z-pinch discharge unit the EUV-emitting plasma ellipsoid size of <0.6-mm diameter and 1.0-mm length (FWHM) is sustainable, which corresponds to approximately 80% etendue acceptance for a π-sr collector at $3 .
--[p459]-- According to the discussions above, the development of highly efficient GDPP EUV sources has the goal to keep the plasma size, for efficiency reasons, below the etendue limits of the EUV scanner. For reasons of higher stability and better uniformity of the illumination in the EUV scanner, however, the plasma size should be somewhat larger than the etendue limit (so-called overfilling of the illumination system).
--[p460]-- 3 \mathrm { - m m } ^ { 2 }$ · sr etendue. Maximum etendue acceptance factors of above 95% have been realized.
The most critical issue in GDPP EUV source technology is the lifetime of the electrode discharge system. In the following we discuss simulations that show that the distances between plasma and walls should be maximized to increase the lifetime of the discharge electrode system and also to improve the heat management of the discharge unit. In Fig.
--[p461]-- The electrode lifetime is defined as the number of EUV pulses generated in the system until the mass loss of the electrodes has led to a significant change of the electrode shape. Because of the linear increase of average excitation power with increasing repetition rate, the electrode lifetime decreases accordingly. The three configurations differ in geometry by the size of the discharge system.
--[p460]-- The limit on the total average excitation power (product of excitation pulse energy and repetition frequency) that can be delivered into the discharge unit is that the maximum surface temperature of the electrodes should be lower than the melting temperature of the electrode material. Otherwise, at higher temperatures the mass loss is increased significantly by the emission of droplets from the electrodes.

--[p461]-- At the normalized distance d the electrode lifetime stays well above $\bar { 1 } 0 ^ { 9 }$ pulses up to 4-kHz repetition frequency. For a plasma-wall distance of $d / 3$ the lifetime decreases by more than two orders of magnitude. If a configuration with 3 times larger plasma-wall distance is possible, the lifetime of the electrodes increases to above $\mathrm { \bar { 1 0 } ^ { 1 0 } }$ pulses.
--[p459]-- An etendue transmission factor of 80–90% seems to be a reasonable goal as a practical compromise according to our calculations. For a π-sr collection angle this requires a plasma length of 1 mm or less.
In order to maximize the usable power at the IF, appropriate electrode discharge systems for Z-pinch EUV sources have been developed at XTREME technologies as depicted in Fig. 14.6. The anode of the Z-pinch discharge allows an obscuration-free emission solid angle of 2.0 sr.

--[p461]-- A very promising approach is the combination of localized laser evaporation and excitation of the target with subsequent GDPP EUV power generation.<sup>34</sup> In this approach the target can be injected separately from the electrodes in several ways (for example, as droplets, as discussed in Chapter 19 in this volume), or the electrode itself can be used as the target supply.

While for the 1.8-sr collector the geometrical transmission for the 1.6-mm-long plasma is above 95%, for the π-sr collector it is decreased to 65%. Because of the constancy of the etendue [see Eq. (14.1)], the increase in the collection angle <sub>collector</sub> is compensated by the decrease of the collectible plasma length l<sub>collectable</sub>.
--[p462]-- Moving the electrodes extends the static increase of the discharge electrode dimension to a serial dimension because different electrode locations are used in a temporally multiplexed way as described by Borisov et al.,<sup>35,36</sup> Banine,<sup>41</sup> Koshelev et al.,<sup>46</sup> and Pankert.<sup>42</sup> The rotating electrodes in laser-assisted GDPP sources give the potential of increasing electrode lifetimes by orders of magnitude to the required HVM lifetime specifications.
--[p458]-- 14.4 Discharge Electrode System, Source Collector, and Electrode Lifetime
As explained in Sec. 14.1.2, the limited etendue of the optical system of the EUV scanner and the numerical-aperture specification at the IF limit the usable size and volume of the EUV-emitting plasma. The smaller the plasma size, the larger is the allowed opening angle of the source collector optics (see Sec. 14.1.2).
--[p458]-- Therefore, the geometrically transmitted power into the IF with right etendue increases only weakly with increasing collector angle as soon as the plasma length reaches $l _ { \mathrm { c o l l e c t a b l e } }$ . The use of collectors with larger opening angle requires the generation of a sufficiently short plasma. For the current development status a collector opening angle of approximately 2 sr seems to be the most efficient and practical solution.

===== [p420-420] Dense Plasma Focus Source > 12.11 Debris Mitigation and Contamination Studies (5块) =====
--[p420]-- Our previously reported results with multichannel arrays simulating debris shields<sup>6,7</sup> showed that EUV-catalyzed carbon deposition significantly exceeded the rate of all other sources of debris generation. The analysis of subsequent experiments under improved vacuum conditions with 3 million pulses showed that the coating of witness samples generated by debris contained carbon, oxygen, aluminum, and xenon.
--[p420]-- Therefore, a significant portion of our EUV development program is addressing debris mitigation and environmental control in order to maintain a clean collector optic.
--[p420]-- We have previously demonstrated that debris from the inner electrode can be efficiently suppressed by a debris shield with long channels, exhibiting typical reduction factors of ${ \sim } 1 0 0 / \mathrm { c m } .$ .<sup>6</sup> In order to verify the stopping power of channels with different diameters and to better understand the debris-suppression scaling, we have also used a multichannel test fixture consisting of an array of channels with different lengths and orientation angles relative to the pinch axis;<sup>7</sup> see Fig. 12.11. Furthermore, we have continued to eliminate potential sources of hydrocarbon outgassing and improved our vacuum system by utilizing magnetically levitated turbomolecular pumps.
--[p420]-- No evidence of electrode material was seen, and the observed rate of carbon buildup<sup>9</sup> was 100 times lower than in the previous experiments. Although we have made a considerable improvement in the system cleanliness, we have not yet identified all of the source terms for carbon in our system. Future experiments will require additional measures of cleanliness handling, using ultraclean electropolished vacuum vessels.
--[p420]-- 12.11 Debris Mitigation and Contamination Studies
The lifetime of the first collection mirror is of major concern for all EUV light sources. The generated debris contains fast ions and neutrals. Even if the debris is effectively shielded, the optics lifetime can still be limited by degradation due to contamination leading to oxidation or EUV-catalyzed carbon growth on the mirror surface.

===== [p352-353] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.5.1.7 Collisional-radiative codes (11块) =====
--[p352]-- In the HULLAC code<sup>69</sup> or other DTA codes,<sup>65–67</sup> ionic states are described at the fine-structure level, including the configuration interactions. This is clearly the pertinent approach to model emission structures that are known to be sensitive to the CI effects. However, this method can require a very large number of levels in order to obtain a correct calculation of population kinetics and of the emission features in the spectrum.
--[p353]-- But the ab initio formulation of the transition rates and the approximations used to calculate them are not always unique. Empirical formulas, fitted to experimental data, may exist also. In the third non-LTE kinetics workshop,<sup>81</sup> held in 2003 at Gaithersburg, a significant dispersion between results of non-LTE codes a priori similar has been observed in several cases. Actually, realistic non-LTE calculation is still an open problem.
--[p353]-- 10.5.1.1, a single fictitious electron configuration populated with a noninteger number of electrons is used to represent the average excited species of the plasma. The description of the electron structure with this single-configuration approximation is too coarse to produce a representative emission spectrum of the plasma, but it can be used to initialize a (noninteracting) detailed-configuration accounting approach (see Sec.
--[p353]-- Though these codes cannot allow for the configuration interactions, they can easily take into account all relevant ions and their configurations. They can be useful for estimating the non-LTE ionic distribution, and for providing information on the relative strength of different bound-bound transitions, as well as the bound-free spectrum.<sup>30</sup>
In the SCAALP code<sup>78</sup> and the similar non-LTE AA model<sup>79,80</sup> introduced in Sec.
--[p352]-- This is particularly true for the laser-produced xenon or tin plasma sources of interest, in which ions may have one or several open shells. In practice, for these applications, only a limited number of parent configurations (which are split into detailed multielectron levels by the code) can be taken into account.
--[p352]-- 10.5.1.7 Collisional-radiative codes
In the situations where the plasma is not in LTE (see Sec. 10.3.3), the densities of the various ionic states cannot be found from the general principles of statistical physics. In the general case, the population kinetics of each excited species is given by a rate equation that represents the population balance due to the microscopic processes in the plasma. The principal radiative and collisional processes involved in the plasma are described in Sec.
--[p352]-- 10.3.3. The rate equation for the ionic states i reads
$$
{ \frac { d N _ { i } } { d t } } = - N _ { i } \sum _ { j \neq i } R _ { i  j } + \sum _ { j \neq i } N _ { j } R _ { j  i } ,\tag{10.15}
$$
where $N _ { i }$ is the population density $( \mathrm { i n } \mathrm { m } ^ { - 3 } )$ of species i, and $R _ { j  i }$ and $R _ { i \to j }$ (in $\mathbf { s } ^ { - 1 } )$ are the rates of population and depopulation of species i due to the various processes in the plasma.
--[p353]-- In order to limit the number of ionic states while keeping a realistic description of the plasma, it is possible to use collisional-radiative codes based on the superconfiguration approach,<sup>70,72</sup> described in Sec. 10.5.1.5. In the SCROLL code,<sup>73</sup> an iterative process is used to define the supershells, starting from a single supershell gathering all orbitals, and refining the supershells till the spectrum converges.
--[p353]-- The AVERROES<sup>74</sup> code defines the supershells as Layzer complexes, i.e., by grouping orbitals of the same principal quantum number n. In practice, this allows one to reduce the number of relevant superconfigurations to a few hundred. The populations of the superconfigurations obey a set of rate equations similar to Eq. (10.6), except that the global transition rates are computed as average values of the configurationconfiguration rates belonging to the superconfigurations.
--[p353]-- 10.5.1.2) resulting in a more detailed spectrum.<sup>52</sup> A similar approach has been proposed in Ref. 80, in which the AA wave functions are used in order to construct detailed configurations and calculate their optical and collisional transition rates. To ensure the convergence of the code to the LTE limit, detailed balance is applied between the collisional rates and their inverse processes.
--[p352]-- The set of coupled rate equations, one for each ionic state, must be solved simultaneously in order to obtain the population kinetics. Therefore, an essential characteristic of a collisional-radiative code is the representation of the ionic states of the plasma, which will determine the size of the rate equations to be solved, and thus the numerical cost of the method.

===== [p462-466] High-Power GDPP Z-Pinch EUV Source Technology > 14.5 Pulsed Power Excitation of Z Pinches (19块) =====
--[p462]-- The contribution to the 13.5-nm emission from xenon comes from the 10+ ionization state (Xe <sub>XI</sub>). For efficient EUV emission an ion density of $( 3 { - } 6 ) \times 1 0 ^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ is necessary. Such concentrations can only be obtained by very high pump energy densities, on the order of $1 { - } 3 \ \mathrm { J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ , supplied in a short time interval of about $\mathrm { i } 0 ^ { - 7 }$ s, usually by a high-power discharge pulse.
--[p464]-- The lifetime of thyratrons in high-power operation, however, is rather limited. Therefore, high-voltage semiconductor switching devices such as thyristors or integrated gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs) are used in high-power Z-pinch sources. This all-solid-state switching technology constitutes a major advance toward highly reliable industrial systems, since semiconductor solid-state switches have practically unlimited lifetime.
--[p464]-- Because of the longer current rise times of semiconductor switches, subsequent pulse compression is needed. To compress the switching pulse from the semiconductor switch, magnetic pulse compression is used for high-power Z-pinch EUV sources. A corresponding circuit layout for C-C transfer with magnetic pulse compression is depicted in Fig. 14.10.
--[p463]-- The discharge circuit used for the excitation of GDPP Z-pinch sources is either the capacitor transfer (C-C transfer) circuit or the inductor-capacitor inversion (L-C inversion) circuit. While a C-C transfer circuit is the simplest design for low-repetition-rate $Z$ pinches, efficient Z-pinch excitation circuits use one or more magnetic pulse compression stages to shorten the driving pulse of the plasma.
The conventional C-C transfer circuit (see Fig.
--[p462]-- Besides the charging section, the power supplies of GDPP EUV sources usually consist of a network of inductors and capacitors (discharge circuit), which is designed to closely match the dynamic behavior of the gas discharge, where the ohmic resistance is rapidly changing with time due to the plasma pinching and heating.
--[p466]-- With the above parameters, electrical pulsed-power-circuit losses (which are easily managed thermally) amount to less than 30%. EUV emission efficiencies of 1% to 2% from power deposited into the Z-pinch plasma to 13.5-nm EUV output have been realized, depending on the emitting fuel (see below).
--[p463]-- 14.9) employs simple matched energy transfer from a storage capacitor $C _ { 1 }$ , which is initially charged to the required high voltage, to the discharge peaking capacitor $C _ { 2 }$ . Once the voltage on $C _ { 2 }$ and with it the pinch electrode voltage has risen to the level necessary for discharge initiation, the energy is switched into the discharge.
--[p462]-- 14.5 Pulsed Power Excitation of Z Pinches
As discussed in Sec. 14.2, the GDPP EUV sources require pulsed electrical excitation of the discharge because of the EUV plasma physics. To realize the pinch effect in a low-pressure gas discharge and to allow efficient emission at the 13.5- nm EUV wavelength, the target atoms such as xenon or tin must be highly ionized. For tin the ionization state of ions contributing to the 13.5-nm band is between 8+ and 13+.
--[p465]-- where $t _ { 1 }$ and $t _ { 2 }$ are the transfer times of loops 1 and 2, respectively, and $L _ { \mathrm { M S } } ^ { \mathrm { s a t } }$ is the saturated inductance of $L _ { \mathrm { M S } }$ .
--[p465]-- The associated disadvantage of increased switching currents at the lower voltage is compensated by the addition of one or more pulse compression stages.
Practical values used in XTREME technologies’ Z-pinch sources are 2–20 J of electrical energy per pulse, stored in the first capacitors switched by high-voltage, high-current switches such as thyristors or IGBTs, with fast current rise of up to 100 kA/s. Discharge breakthrough voltages range from 2 to 10 kV, depending on the storage capacity.
--[p464]-- The magnetic switch is realized by a saturable inductor employing ferrite or amorphous metal as core material. The nonsaturated, high inductance of the inductor does not permit significant current flow and therefore constitutes the open position of the switch. Switch closure is effected by driving the inductor into saturation, which reduces the inductance to close to the equivalent air-core value.
--[p465]-- Typically achieved compression ratios for a single stage range from 2 to $5 ,$ , and several stages can be cascaded to achieve overall pulse compression ratios of several orders of magnitude.<sup>25</sup> Since saturable inductors are passive switching elements, they can be designed for very high peak currents and holdoff voltages and have a virtually unlimited lifetime.
--[p464]-- Total energy transfer between successive loops is achieved if the energy transfer time from $C _ { 1 }$ to $C _ { 2 }$ is matched to the time required for the inductor $L _ { \mathrm { M S } }$ to be driven into saturation (holdoff time). The pulse compression ratio $\delta$ between the loops is
defined as
$$
\delta = \frac { t _ { 2 } } { t _ { 1 } } = \sqrt { \frac { L _ { 1 } } { L _ { \mathrm { M S } } ^ { \mathrm { s a t } } } } ,\tag{14.6}
$$
--[p462]-- GDPP sources are therefore invariably pumped by a power supply that delivers the stored electrical energy directly into the gaseous target material. The pumping schemes are well developed, for similar schemes have been applied over more than 20 years to excimer laser pumping. They involve efficient switching of the stored electrical energy into the discharge system in a very short time and with a well-defined spatial and temporal profile (for an overview see Refs. 23 and 24).
--[p465]-- An excitation circuit for Z-pinch GDPP sources that can use lower input voltages at the semiconductor switch is the $L { - } C$ inversion circuit. Figure 14.11 shows the circuit diagram of an $L { - } C$ inversion circuit with single-stage pulse compression. The $L { - } C$ inversion circuit has the advantage of voltage doubling and therefore halves the operating voltage for the switch.
--[p464]-- In magnetic pulse compression circuits the electrical energy is not delivered to the Z pinch in a single step (as, e.g., in the case of the simple C-C transfer circuit), but is initially transferred on a slow time scale by the semiconductor switch from the primary energy storage capacitor $C _ { 1 }$ to an intermediate energy storage capacitor $C _ { 2 }$ , from where it is transferred rapidly to $C _ { 3 }$ and the discharge electrode system by the magnetic switch $( L _ { \mathrm { M S } } )$ . Because of the low initial transfer rate, peak currents carried by the semiconductor switch can be reduced, allowing it to operate well below its rise-time and peak-current limits and therefore not being lifetimelimiting.
--[p463]-- The loop inductance $L _ { 2 }$ consists of the stray inductance of the pinch electrode system and can be kept at a few tens of nanohenrys, resulting in a fast current pulse and extreme power deposition levels.
The simplest high-voltage switch for use in combination with the circuit in Fig. 14.9 would be a thyratron, i.e., a low-pressure hydrogen- or deuterium-filled electron tube with cathode, anode, and control grid.
--[p462]-- This determines the discharge uniformity and—in turn—influences the spatial and temporal stability of the extracted EUV light. The excitation conditions needed impose severe requirements on the pumping scheme of GDPP sources in terms of peak currents and voltage rise times.
--[p465]-- Impedance matching is the design goal to achieve low losses in the pulsed power circuit. Typical values for the impedance are 20–30 m. Typical voltage, current, and EUV output waveforms are shown in Fig. 14.12. The EUV pulse is emitted after the voltage at capacitor $C _ { 3 }$ has reached the negative maximum. The EUV signal shown in Fig. 14.12 is the response of the photodiode. The duration of the EUV pulse is approximately 100 ns.

===== [p189-190] Atomic Physics of Highly Charged Ions and the Case for Sn as a Source Material > 5.2.2 Plasma considerations (10块) =====
--[p189]-- Unfortunately, in xenon the neutral absorption is well known to be dominated by a 4d → εf shape resonance in the photoionization continuum,<sup>26</sup> which peaks near 15 nm but still has a cross section of 20 Mb at 13.5 nm.<sup>27</sup> In gas-jet plasmas evidence for neutral absorption is also evident.<sup>28</sup> In the first two ionization stages this feature persists, yielding cross sections of 25 and 22 Mb, respectively.
--[p189]-- 5.2.2 Plasma considerations
Typical Q-switched lasers used for EUVL generation emit pulses with energies in the range from 200 mJ to 1 J on time scales from hundreds of picoseconds to tens of nanoseconds. The Nd:YAG lasers used in our work emit 1.1 J and 500 mJ of $1 . 0 6 4 \ – \mu \mathrm { m }$ radiation in 15 ns and 170 ps, respectively.
--[p189]-- When these lasers were focused onto a solid target to a focal spot size of diameter 40 µm, the maximum average power densities attained were $\phantom { - } 1 . 4 6 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 2 }$ and $5 . 8 5 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , though they were typically used at ${ \sim } 1 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 1 }$ and ${ \sim } 1 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 2 } \ \mathrm { W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ .
--[p189]-- Recently a calculation of the emission from xenon, with allowance made for opacity effects, was performed using the HULLAC code.<sup>32</sup> This calculation showed a reduction at 13.5 nm and also an even more spectacular effect on the 11-nm band, whose intensity was reduced so that it almost matched that at 13.5 nm.
In addition, from the results of a calculation for the variation of ion population with electron temperature (Fig.
5.4) it is evident that the maximum concentration of $\mathrm { X e ^ { 1 0 + } }$ attainable is only of the order of 40%.
--[p189]-- In our case, the dominant ion stages are anticipated to be 15 and 20 times ionized. Theoretically, the maximum electron density depends on the cutoff density, which scales as $\lambda ^ { - \bar { 2 } }$ and for Nd:YAG radiation has a value of approximately $1 0 ^ { 2 1 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ and decreases rapidly away from the interaction region, which is approximately 100 µm in extent.
--[p189]-- According to the collisional radiative (CR) equilibrium model,<sup>24</sup> the corresponding electron temperatures $T _ { e }$ , which depend on laser flux density according to $T _ { e } \propto \Phi ^ { 3 / 5 }$ , are 49 and 194 eV. Calculations based on the CR model give
$$
\frac { N _ { z + 1 } } { N _ { z } } = \frac { S ( z , T _ { e } ) } { \alpha _ { r } ( z + 1 , T _ { e } ) + n _ { e } \alpha _ { 3 b } ( z + 1 , T _ { e } ) }\tag{5.4}
$$
--[p189]-- for the ratio of the population of ions of charge $z + 1$ to that of charge $z ,$ where $S ( z , T _ { e } )$ is the total collisional ionization rate coefficient, $\alpha _ { r } ( z + 1 , T _ { e } )$ is the total radiative recombination rate coefficient, and $n _ { e } \alpha _ { 3 b } ( z + 1 , T _ { e } )$ is the total threebody recombination rate coefficient. Note that dielectronic recombination is not explicitly included in this model.
--[p189]-- $^ { 2 9 , 3 0 ^ { - } } \mathrm { B y \ X e ^ { 4 + } }$ this feature has been replaced by discrete 4d → 4f transitions, which yield a strong autoionizing line again near 13.5 nm,<sup>31</sup> so absorption by neutrals and low ionization stages, if present on the periphery of the source, will greatly reduce the available intensity.
--[p189]-- The ion expansion velocity is of the order of $1 0 ^ { 6 } { - } \dot { 1 } \dot { 0 } ^ { 7 } \mathrm { c m } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ . As the plasma expands, it cools, so absorption at the cooler margins is possible. Moreover, Filevich et al.<sup>25</sup> have recently shown that the EUV emission itself causes a cooler plasma to be generated in a region surrounding the expanding plasma plume, so radiation tangential to the surface can be absorbed in a cold plasma layer.
--[p190]-- Therefore, any advantages of using xenon based on its gaseous nature and inherent cleanliness must be weighed against the disadvantages of the low density of emitting ions, the fact that the transition involved is at least a factor of 10 weaker than those occurring in the 11-nm band, and the fact that the wavelength of choice almost coincides with that of maximum absorption in the neutral and low ion stages.

===== [p296-296] Z∗ Code for DPP and LPP Source Modeling > 8.4.3 LPP emission efficiency (2块) =====
--[p296]-- All these factors may be considered in their complexity through modeling.
To simulate the LPP EUV sources with the code Z<sup>∗</sup>, the laser energy transfer process is implemented in a special version with zero electromagnetic field. Details of the model adopted for the laser interaction with materials are presented in Appendix C.
--[p296]-- 8.4.3 LPP emission efficiency
Optimization of the LPP EUV source is a complex problem, despite the absence of the considerable influence of the electromagnetic fields found in the DPP. Achieving EUV emission efficiency from the LPP depends on several requirements: efficiency of laser energy absorption by the plasma, attainment of the optimum plasma temperature and density for efficient inband radiation, and minimization of radiation reabsorption by the expanding plasma.

--[p433]-- Furthermore, the models known in the literature make use of a hybrid description of a two-fluid model in combination with a Monte Carlo ansatz for ionizing processes and the evolution of beams.
We have chosen a model that fully describes the ignition in a Monte Carlo model, since the fluid description is not valid for proper description of the ignition phase. The electrons have large mean free paths and thus high average energies, which are not consistent with a fluid description.

===== [p431-432] Hollow-Cathode-Triggered Plasma Pinch Discharge > 13.2.1 General remarks (8块) =====
--[p431]-- 13.2.1 General remarks
The principle of the present concept for generating pinch plasmas, which are emitters of thermal radiation in the EUV, is the pseudospark discharge. Since its discovery in 1978,<sup>7</sup> this kind of low-pressure gas discharge has been extensively investigated both theoretically and experimentally.
--[p432]-- A hollow-cathode plasma builds up, which shifts the anode potential close to the cathode walls as shown in Fig. 13.1. The electrical field increases to values sufficient for the ignition of cathode spots and evaporation of material. With the ignition of the cathode spots, the storage capacity can be discharged, leading to peak currents of typically 10 kA. Current attachment at the cathode is preferred to attachment in the gap and at the borehole wall.
--[p432]-- Electrons are extracted by the anode, which leads to a positive cloud of remaining slow ions. This cloud extends into the hollow cathode, forming a virtual anode. This process is illustrated in Fig. 13.1, following the simulation in Ref. 9. This virtual anode leads to the pendulum effect for electrons in the hollow cathode. The effective path for such electrons increases, which leads to very effective ionization.
--[p431]-- This concept is called the HCT pinch plasma discharge. There are numerous publications dealing with problems, especially for pseudospark switches, with regard to ignition, electrode lifetime, electrode erosion, and means of triggering the discharge, which are also of interest for the HCT concept. However, especially for the ignition and the high-current phase, there remains a variety of open questions.
--[p431]-- These have led to investigations of high-power light-source development, which are described in detail in the subsequent sections.
The design of the HCT lamp in its basic form is very simple: Two parallel plates with opposing central boreholes are connected to a capacitor bank. The connection must have a very low inductance to allow for fast current buildup during the pinch phase. On the anode side, the electrode system is open for outcoupling of the light.
--[p431]-- The main focus has been on its use as a high-current switch for pulsed-power applications and as a source of highly brilliant electron and ion beams.<sup>8</sup> The main difference for its use as an EUV source is that a high, pulsed current for compression and heating of the working gas is used, which is usually a high-Z element. A general description of the pseudospark discharge is found, e.g., in Ref. 8. The basic concept for use as an EUV emitter is presented in Refs. 2 and 3.
--[p432]-- The pulsed current leads to a compression and heating of the plasma channel across the gap, leading to a pinch plasma several hundred microns in diameter and of length from 1 mm to several millimeters, depending on the particular geometry of the boreholes.
--[p432]-- On the cathode side, a hollow recess is connected to the borehole to form the hollow cathode. The electrode system is in a low-pressure environment of usually 10–100 Pa of a heavy gas, leading to operation on the left branch of the Paschen curve. On applying a voltage, typically in the range of several kilovolts, to the electrode system, ionization processes take place along the long electrical field lines in the vicinity of the boreholes.

===== [p335-335] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.1 Introduction (9块) =====
--[p335]-- Not only does it require a thorough understanding of the plasma state, but more important, and much more difficult to model, is the understanding of the detailed radiation transfer from all these transitions. To our knowledge this has not yet been accomplished completely. Thus, this chapter is a report on progress toward this end. First we summarize those basic processes in laser plasmas that are relevant to the plasma regime involved in EUV sources.
--[p335]-- They pose new challenges in the understanding, characterization, and design of laser plasmas.
This chapter addresses one of these challenges. The EUV roadmap requires a bright source in a narrow spectral band in the vicinity of a 13-nm wavelength. This wavelength and the width of the spectral band (≈0.26 nm) are set by the characteristics of the collection and imaging optics employed.
--[p335]-- We focus on the theory of laser-light interaction, plasma expansion, and radiant emission, seeking plasmas that are most likely to meet these needs. Thus we consider here spherical, 1D models of laser plasmas dominated by inverse bremsstrahlung absorption (IBA), thermal excitation, and classical energy transport. We focus on plasmas formed from ions that have strong emission lines in the 13-nm region. There are several candidates, including Li, O, Xe, Sn, and others.
--[p335]-- Then we describe the application of conventional plasma fluid models to the laser light’s interaction with the plasma and its subsequent expansion. Finally, we go on to describe in some detail the various aspects of modeling the radiation from high-Z plasmas, particularly the emission spectra as derived from detailed atomic physics codes.
--[p335]-- It must be a high-repetition-rate source to satisfy dose stability. Moreover, strong consideration must be given to constraining the particulate and ion emission from the source: protecting the EUV illumination optics from degradation or erosion for long exposure times is one of the principal challenges. This combination of requirements forces consideration of features of laser plasmas outside the focus of most studies.
--[p335]-- In satisfying the needs for a source, our challenge from a theoretical viewpoint is to understand and model this emission, at least under conditions that are likely to satisfy the intense brightness requirement in a practical system.
It is for these reasons that in this chapter we concentrate on laser plasmas that have characteristics conducive to the creation of high-brightness, high-repetitionrate point EUV sources.
--[p335]-- 10.1 Introduction
Although plasmas produced by lasers have been the subject of intense study over the past 40 years, those that are being considered as sources for EUVL offer new challenges in both design and understanding. The requirements of these sources are unique relative to other interests and applications of laser plasmas. EUVL demands a source that emits strong radiation only in one radiation band. The plasma must be small and be stable in position and light emission.
--[p335]-- Low-Z materials such as Li and O have been examined in previous studies, and are now thought to be incapable of providing sufficient emission, or to be too impractical as a source. Here we examine mostly emission from so-called unresolved transition arrays (UTAs), tightly packed emission lines from multitudes of excited-state transitions in multiple ions in materials such as Xe and Sn. Theoretically this is a very challenging problem.
--[p335]-- The brightness required, which can be expressed in several ways [115 W of inband radiation at ≈13.5 nm, 2% bandwidth, at the intermediate focus (IF), or perhaps, more fundamentally, ≈400 W of inband radiation within 2π sr at the source], challenges the limits of laser and laser-plasma technology. Laser plasmas emit radiation that is both characteristic of the plasma conditions and characteristic of the excited ion states created in the plasma.

===== [p468-470] High-Power GDPP Z-Pinch EUV Source Technology > 14.7 Debris Mitigation and Collector-Optics Protection (12块) =====
--[p469]-- To increase the optics lifetime of the source collector to these values, several design criteria have to be implemented in the collector.
First, one may increase the distance between plasma and collector to the highest technically possible values. The flux of fast particles decreases quadratically with increasing distance from the plasma, for geometric reasons. The larger space between plasma and collector can be used to efficiently mitigate debris.
--[p470]-- This is already one-tenth of the HVM optics lifetime requirements.
Once sputtering is reduced to the required level, contamination of the optics by electrode material and, in the case of tin, also by the target material itself may play the most important role (see below and Refs. 37, 38). These effects must be studied in further detail to achieve the required collector lifetime.
--[p469]-- Second, research into sputter-resistant materials for collector coatings must be intensified. Third, the use of additional means for ionization of fast particles in combination with debris filtering by electric and/or magnetic fields may be necessary to reduce the sputtering effects further.
Using projected debris-filter collector optics design configurations suited for β tools, an optics lifetime of 5–10 billion pulses can be extrapolated from experiments with the microbalance device.
--[p468]-- While xenon at room temperature is in the gaseous state, tin is in the solid state, and tin tends therefore to condense on the optical surface. In addition, because of erosion of the discharge electrode system, material from the electrodes may reach the collectoroptics surface and, depending on the energies, either erode the collector surface or also condense there. All these interactions lead to a limited lifetime of the collector optics.
--[p468]-- 14.7 Debris Mitigation and Collector-Optics Protection
The EUV-emitting plasma is a source of high- and low-energy particles such as ions, atoms, and electrons with a wide range of energies from a few electron volts up to several times 10 keV. The interaction of these particles with the collectoroptics surface depends on the emitting material, i.e., xenon or tin.
--[p469]-- For a debris filter device as shown in Fig. 14.15 the sputter rate has been measured and compared with the sputter rate without a filter. The comparison is given in Fig. 14.16. With the debris filter in place the sputter rate at the optics is reduced by a factor of approximately 5000.
--[p468]-- To achieve sufficient lifetime of the source collector optics, collector protection and debris mitigation is one of the crucial tasks in EUV source development.
To measure debris-related effects that limit the lifetime of the source collector optics, two types of measurements are routinely carried out. One is the quartzcrystal microbalance technique, which is a well-developed and mature diagnostic metrology method.
--[p468]-- It allows one to measure the change of mass, either loss or deposition, of detectors coated with relevant grazing-incidence collector coating materials. The quartz crystal oscillator vibrates at a certain frequency in the megahertz range. The change of the frequency caused by sputtering (mass loss) or contamination (deposition of material) is measured. As mass is deposited on the surface of the oscillator, the frequency of the oscillator decreases.
--[p468]-- This is true both for xenon and for tin fuel in the source. For collector-optics samples placed at a distance of 11 cm from the pinch plasma the reflectivity decreases by 5% on exposure to 50,000 pulses of the xenon target source. The EUV inband energy per pulse amounts 35 mJ, so that the total EUV dose accumulated during 50,000 pulses is 1.75 kJ.
Debris filters have been developed at XTREME technologies that allow significant reduction of the sputter rate at the optics surface.
--[p468]-- While optics sample irradiation experiments are time-consuming (irradiation of samples may take weeks) the microbalance method gives results after short measurement times (a few tens of minutes).
With the above diagnostic techniques we came to the following conclusion: The dominant effect that limits the lifetime of the source collector without any means for debris reduction between EUV-emitting plasma and collector is sputtering of the optics surface by high-energy ions and atoms.
--[p469]-- Currently collector-optics lifetimes from several hundred million pulses up to 1 billion pulses have been achieved with a collector distance of 11 cm for an EUV source with 35-W power at 1000-Hz repetition frequency (see below). For HVM, a 3000-h collector lifetime should be the target specification. At 10 kHz this corresponds to $1 . 1 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 1 }$ pulses.
--[p468]-- Sputtering of the oscillator coating material results in increasing oscillation frequency. The second kind of measurements uses small optics witness samples made with the manufacturing technology of grazing-incidence source collector optics. The relative or absolute reflectivity and its change are measured with 13.5-nm EUV detectors.

===== [p200-201] Atomic Physics of Highly Charged Ions and the Case for Sn as a Source Material > 5.3.4 Effect of prepulses (7块) =====
--[p201]-- This can be understood as follows: The prepulse generates a small compact plasma that only expands to a few tens of microns before the prepulse ends, and the emitting volume is very small. The plasma expands outward from the target, and the main pulse interacts with this larger plasma volume. After 5 ns, the plasma volume and density are optimum to ensure good coupling with the laser pulse. At longer delays the density drops below that needed for optimum heating and the EUV output decreases.
--[p200]-- 5.3.4 Effect of prepulses
It is known that the use of a prepulse can greatly increase the EUV emission from a LPP. For example, a tenfold increase was recently observed for laser-irradiated ice droplets.<sup>52</sup> In that experiment laser pulse durations ranging from 200 fs to 120 ps for pulse energies ranging from 20 to 100 mJ were employed.
--[p200]-- In our case, in a series of experiments, the emission from a plasma produced on a tin oxide in a glass target at a tin concentration of ∼1% as a function of prepulse-pulse time delay was studied by synchronizing outputs from the 1.1-J, 15-ns Nd:YAG with that from the 500-mJ, 170-ps system. When the latter illuminated the plasma formed by the nanosecond system, an intensity enhancement of 75% was attained after a delay of 9 ns.
--[p201]-- The main pulse was then passed around an optical delay line and the output intensity at 13.5 nm monitored as a function of interpulse delay and prepulse-pulse ratio. The results are presented in Fig. 5.14, from which it is evident that the optimum conversion is attained with a time delay of 5 ns and a prepulse-pulse ratio of 1:9.
--[p200]-- If one assumes this enhancement is attained at all target compositions, then for the 2% tin in glass the efficiency using this arrangement could be increased to 2%–3% into 2π sr. With more careful illumination control and optimum target compositions, the figure 3% should be attainable.
Using the 170-ps system by itself, the beam was divided by inserting a 99% mirror at 45 deg and intercepting a controllable fraction. In this way any fraction desired could be removed to serve as a prepulse.
--[p201]-- A prepulse used in this way only produces a small amount of material, which is then further ionized by the main pulse. Experimentally, the debris quantity is proportional to the energy directly incident on the target. Thus, the volume of debris produced is greatly reduced in comparison with that from a single pulse of the same total energy.
--[p200]-- The best CE without a prepulse was found for the longest pulses, with a CE of 0.2% in 2.5% bandwidth into 4π sr at 13.0 nm on the 2p-4d lines of Li-like O VI. Addition of a prepulse increased the CE, and a maximum of 2% into 2.5% bandwidth was attained for 2-ps pulses at a 3-ns delay.

===== [p221-221] Radiative Collapse in Z Pinches > 6.8 Dissipation of Electrical Energy in the Discharge (4块) =====
--[p221]-- The ablating laser pulse must be optimized to mitigate unnecessary energy loss. The EUV signal and a strong dissipation of electrical energy start after approximately 50 ns and correlate with the appearance of neck in the plasma column. Evidently that dissipated energy is spent on plasma heating, ionization, and emission of radiation. The EUV signal for these specific discharge conditions consists of two unresolved peaks.
--[p221]-- 6.8 Dissipation of Electrical Energy in the Discharge
The pinch dynamics shown in the previous figure correlate well with electrical and EUV signals recorded by an oscilloscope. An example is shown in Fig. 6.6. The discharge current starts to deviate from the ideal $L C$ contour current immediately after breakdown. The initial energy dissipation is most probably connected with low conductivity of the rear plasma near the anode.
--[p221]-- Such an EUV signal structure is usually associated with the occurrence of two or more subsequent micropinches—a so-called zippering effect (see below). The duration of every subpeak is about 30–40 ns. Expansion of the necks causes a slight increase of the current. Nevertheless, at this moment most of the stored electrical energy is dissipated in the discharge. Less than 15% of the initial electrical energy is still present in the capacitor bank and in the circuit inductance.
--[p221]-- Thus more than 70% of the stored energy was dissipated during the useful phase of the pinch.

===== [p489-489] High-Power GDPP Z-Pinch EUV Source Technology > 15.1.1 Pulsed plasma conditions (5块) =====
--[p489]-- 7 \mathrm { - m m } ^ { 3 }$ volume, reaching an estimated electron density of $4 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 9 } \ \mathrm { e c m } ^ { - 3 }$ and a temperature greater than 30 eV. At its hottest, the plasma radiates broadband EUV power at the rate of 20 MW, so it cannot be sustained continuously. In the case of xenon plasma discharges, approximately 20% of the dissipated energy is released promptly in a 50-ns burst of radiation, most of it in the 10–15-nm band.
--[p489]-- The remaining energy is carried by the expanding plasma toward the facing walls, where ion sputtering is the main erosion mechanism.
The typical plasma particle energy impacting the wall is roughly between 300 eV and 1 keV. We reach this number by considering the case of a plasma comprising $\mathrm { X e ^ { 1 0 + } }$ ions (the ionization state that contributes most strongly to 13.5-nm radiation) that expands adiabatically from an initial temperature of 30 eV without recombination.
--[p489]-- At asymptotic distances the electron kinetic energy is low and Xe ions carry the energy formerly stored by the electrons, totaling 300 eV. In practice, di-electronic recombination occurs very rapidly through many of the xenon ionization stages before the plasma has even doubled in diameter. As that occurs, the electron density is reduced, but the electron temperature tends to be raised.
--[p489]-- Highly excited ions produced in recombination further heat electrons via superelastic collisions, but most of this electron energy is then imparted to the ions as electron pressure drives the expansion. The net effect is for much of the xenon ionization energy (totaling $8 0 7 ~ \mathrm { e V } ) ^ { 1 }$ to be added into the radial kinetic energy and for the expected asymptotic ion energy range to lie roughly between 300 eV and 1 keV.
--[p489]-- 15.1.1 Pulsed plasma conditions
In EUV sources of the plasma type, either LPP or DPP, the challenge is to achieve rather hot and dense plasma conditions repetitively for at least $1 0 ^ { \overline { { 1 0 } } }$ pulses without damaging the illumination or collector optics, chamber walls, and (in the DPP case) electrodes. --[p41]-- 1.2.2 Xe, Sn, and Li conversion efficiency

===== [p283-283] Z∗ Code for DPP and LPP Source Modeling > 8.4.1 Capillary-discharge EUV source (3块) =====
--[p283]-- 8.4.1 Capillary-discharge EUV source
Fast capillary discharges are simple and efficient means of producing high-energydensity radiation systems. In such a system, a high current is made to pass rapidly through a small-diameter insulating tube of millimeter dimension scale. The operation of a gas-filled capillary discharge with small dimension requires the proper preparation of the initial current conduction path in order to avoid a wall-initiated sliding spark discharge.
--[p283]-- This preionization condition can be produced in a number of ways, including the injection of a tight e-beam to create an ionization channel. By mating a suitable hollow-cathode structure to a capillary discharge, a selfgenerated on-axis electron beam is produced as a result of the transient hollowcathode effect<sup>16</sup> and leads to the formation of a preionized conducting channel on axis, where the main current begins to develop.
--[p283]-- This highly effective preion ization process is inherent in the operation of the HCT Z pinch pioneered by Philips Extreme<sup>45</sup> and the micropulsed plasma (MPP) radiation source developed at EPPRA.<sup>36</sup>

===== [p90-91] Chapter 3 Atomic Xenon Data > 3.6 Benchmarking Output Data (9块) =====
--[p90]-- The measured spectrum from the well-characterized plasma can then be compared with the calculated spectrum, with no (or relatively few) adjustable parameters. To my knowledge, no type A benchmark comparisons have been completed by the EUVL community.
At the request of Intel, my group at NIST has been producing type A benchmark data using the EBIT.
--[p91]-- Type B benchmarks are important because they take place in plasmas that correspond more closely to those that will be used in real EUVL light sources. An example of such a type B benchmark has been published by researchers at $\mathrm { C y m e r .
--[p90]-- 3.6 Benchmarking Output Data
These benchmarks fall into two classes. In what I call type B benchmarks, spectra from a plasma of unknown electron energy distribution are compared with model calculations. Either the model parameters or the experimental parameters are adjusted to optimize the agreement. In contrast, for what I call type A benchmarks the plasma electron energy distribution is well known and can be used as fixed input to the plasma model.
--[p90]-- Type A benchmarking is highly desirable given that the main goals of EUVL modeling are extrapolative: (1) determining the ultimate efficiency limits of EUVL light sources, and (2) assisting in the discovery of new source designs that will change the plasma output sufficiently to meet the design specifications of the semiconductor industry. Both of these goals involve extrapolation to regimes that are considerably beyond those achieved to date.
--[p90]-- A variety of NIST EBIT type A benchmark data are presently available for double-blind comparisons. An example of an EBIT EUV spectrum for Xe is shown in Fig. 3.5. More samples of EBIT data that can be used for benchmarking xenon models were published recently in a special cluster of articles on EUV light sources for semiconductor manufacturing.<sup>21</sup> Additional data can be generated to suit the specific needs of particular modeling groups.
--[p90]-- The cancellation of errors in type B benchmarks can frequently be adjusted to give good agreement with observations, but it will hold up less frequently when extrapolated to new plasma conditions outside those in the fit.
--[p90]-- The NIST EBIT is described in detail elsewhere.<sup>18–20</sup> By comparing plasma models (suitably modified to take into account the proper energy distribution and observation angle), one can avoid the key weakness of type B benchmarks, namely that various inaccuracies in the model are compensating for each other and producing a reasonably good fit to the observed spectra, albeit for the wrong reasons.
--[p90]-- The EBIT has the particular advantage of not only having a very well-defined electron energy distribution, but also a very sharply peaked (nearly delta-function) and oriented (unidirectional) distribution. This makes it possible to very selectively test various collision processes that contribute to the overall light output of the plasma, and to allow for the possibility of testing polarization effects.
--[p91]-- } ^ { 2 2 }$ Although these calculations give good agreement with the experiments, they predict that even more light output could be achieved at somewhat longer wavelengths (just under 15 nm) and lower plasma temperatures (around 25 eV); this prediction is not in agreement with the model calculations of the Argonne group.<sup>16</sup>
Other type B benchmark tests have been completed by the Saclay $\mathrm { g r o u p } ^ { 2 3 }$ and by Sasaki and collaborators.<sup>24</sup>

===== [p235-235] Fundamentals and Limits of Plasma-based EUV Sources > • Radiator efficiency (η<sub>rad</sub>) (2块) =====
--[p235]-- • Radiator efficiency (η<sub>rad</sub>)
After the driver energy is deposited into the radiating matter, there is an intrinsic efficiency for the radiation in the desired spectral band of use. Radiator efficiency is usually given in the same units as the total efficiency, with respect to 1 sr or 2π sr. The radiator efficiency is governed by two main factors:
1.
--[p235]-- Plasma efficiency $\left( \boldsymbol \eta _ { \mathrm { p l a s m a } } \right)$ , which is the fraction of the power deposited in the plasma that is radiated per steradian by the plasma in a specified direction.
2. Spectral efficiency $( \eta _ { \mathrm { s p e c t r a l } } )$ , which is the fraction of the totally emitted radiation (into the defined solid angle) that can be used within the 2% bandwidth around the central wavelength.

===== [p287-288] Z∗ Code for DPP and LPP Source Modeling > 8.4.1.2 Influence of preionization (7块) =====
--[p287]-- The plasma is assumed to be motionless. The geometry of the MPP capillary shown in Fig. 8.7(b) was simulated. The ionization dynamics obtained is shown in Fig. 8.11.
During almost 2 ns an electron beam of several keV energy, initiated near the cathode, passes mainly along the axis of the capillary.
--[p287]-- Near the cathode, the electrons have lower energy and ionize more effectively. Near the anode, where all electrons come together, the ionization also rises more quickly. Due to the increased plasma conductivity, the electric field becomes localized between these clouds of plasma, and two ionization waves are observed to move respectively from the anode and from the cathode toward the middle, and meet each other after 3 ns.
--[p287]-- At 4 ns the conductive channel occupies half the diameter of the capillary, but the high-density region is localized on axis. This preionized channel is similar to the initial condition chosen for simulation of the main discharge development.
To study the influence of the preionized channel size on the EUV emission yield from the MPP discharge, simulations with different preionization conditions were carried out for a Kr:He gas mixture with $Z ^ { * }$ . The results are shown in Fig.
--[p288]-- The measurements were made in discharges with a fixed He pressure of 20 mTorr, measured at the anode side, but with different percentages of Kr admixture. Experimentally, it has been shown that a high percentage of Kr will lead to a large preionization channel. Qualitative agreement with the simulation results can be seen in the emission.
--[p287]-- 8.4.1.2 Influence of preionization
In simulations of the MPP capillary discharge at EPPRA, the best fit to experiment is obtained if the initial preionization is localized in a tight channel of 100-µm diameter along the capillary axis. To understand the preionization dynamics and the hollow-cathode effect, a special version of the code $Z ^ { * }$ was developed, where MHD was replaced by electron hydrodynamics as described in Sec. 8.2.4 and ionization kinetics was implemented.
--[p288]-- 8.12(a), which shows the radiation pulse behind a Zr filter as calculated in two cases: tight on-axis preionization and broad volume preionization. A large first radiation peak is observed for the tight preionization case. In Fig. 8.12(b), a series of experimental measurements taken with a fast diode behind Zr filter is shown, primarily looking at the radiation in the 8–16-nm band.
--[p287]-- The beam is tight, about 70 µm in diameter, due to a combination of electric field refracted onto the axis, as a result of the high dielectric constant of the capillary material (about 8.5 at such frequencies), and the self magnetic field. The beam and (mainly secondary) electrons produce ionization in time. At the same time electrons are exposed to the electrostatic turbulence, and the dynamics is rather complicated.

===== [p193-197] Atomic Physics of Highly Charged Ions and the Case for Sn as a Source Material > 5.3.2 Origin of UTA intensity (17块) =====
--[p197]-- As a result, tin is not the brightest potential EUV source and has a relatively large bandwidth, though it is less sensitive to opacity effects, since the overlap of discrete $\Delta n = 0$ transitions in the UTA in adjacent ion stages is less complete, especially in stages below $\mathrm { S n ^ { 9 + } }$ .
--[p197]-- Thus, the emission band is brightest and narrowest in the lanthanides. Under our experimental conditions it is in fact optimum in cerium, where a CE of $( 4 . 2 \pm$
1.5)% at 8.8 nm using cerium-doped glass targets has been measured.<sup>51</sup> However, at present no suitable MLMs have been developed for use at these wavelengths.
--[p194]-- As a result, the different $4  { \mathrm { d } } ^ { n } \to 4  { \mathrm { d } } ^ { n - 1 }  { n }  { \mathrm { f } }$ transitions have appreciable oscillator strength and are generally stronger than the 4d → np lines. With increasing ionization, the inner potential well becomes deeper and narrower, and the 4f wave function gradually contracts into the core region and has a large spatial overlap with the 4d wave function.
--[p193]-- The first minimum, with its center near $a _ { 0 }$ (the Bohr radius), is close to the 4d wave function peak but lacks sufficient depth to support a bound level, and, as in xenon, the 4d → f channel is dominated by a 4d → εf shape resonance that forms when the outgoing f electron has sufficient energy to overcome the centrifugal barrier. The outer shallow well, centered near 16a<sub>0</sub>, is essentially hydrogenic in character and contains the 4f level.
--[p196]-- As already pointed out, the UTA emission is not due to 4d-4f transitions alone, but arises from $4 { \mathrm { p } } ^ { 6 } 4 { \mathrm { d } } ^ { n } - 4 { \mathrm { p } } ^ { 5 } 4 { \mathrm { d } } ^ { n + 1 } + 4 { \mathrm { d } } ^ { n - 1 } 4 { \mathrm { f } }$ transitions, which merge to form a UTA consisting of tens of thousands of lines.
--[p196]-- However, inclusion of CI effects effectively removes the dependence on 4d occupation and causes the oscillator-strength envelope of the transition array to narrow and overlap at the same energy position in successive ion stages. The strength of this interaction again depends on the magnitude of 4d | 4f.
Thus, to optimize the brightness of an array, three criteria must be satisfied:
• The ion stages produced should contain an open 4d subshell.
--[p193]-- Because there is essentially no overlap with the 4d wave function in this region, transitions of the type 4d → nf are absent, and the discrete spectrum will be dominated by $4 \mathrm { d } \to n \mathrm { p }$ lines.
--[p194]-- With increasing ionization the centrifugal barrier disappears and 4f wave function contraction into the inner well region results in a transfer of oscillator strength from the continuum to the discrete spectrum.<sup>37–41</sup> The labeling of the discrete states is very sensitive to the choice of basis used in any calculations, since the lowest $4 \mathrm { d } ^ { n } n \mathrm { f }$ states are strongly LS-coupled and their wave functions are highly term-dependent.<sup>42,43</sup> In fact, if the average energy of configuration $( E _ { \mathrm { a v } } )$ is used as the basis, then there is considerable hybridization amongst the different nf functions, and transitions to these states have appreciable oscillator strength by virtue of their sizable $4 \mathrm { f _ { a v } }$ component.
--[p196]-- • The 4f radial wave function should be completely localized in the ionic core in each ion stage. Consequently both $| \langle 4 \mathrm { d } | \mathrm { r } | 4 \mathrm { f } \rangle |$ and CI effects, which cause overlapping and narrowing of the UTA, are maximized.
• The plasma should be optically thin to these UTA.
For tin, the 4d | 4f overlap increases with increasing ionization and only stabilizes past $\mathrm { S n ^ { 9 + } }$ (see Fig. 5.8).
--[p194]-- As the inner well deepens, the nf level separation increases, the 4f and $4 \mathrm { f _ { a v } }$ functions become essentially the same and the oscillator strength becomes concentrated in the $4 \mathrm { d } ^ { n }  4 \mathrm { d } ^ { n - 1 } 4 \mathrm { f }$ transitions. This behavior has been studied for a number of isonuclear sequences. In Fig.
--[p196]-- Single-configuration calculations show that for $4 \mathrm { d } ^ { n } - 4 \mathrm { d } ^ { n - 1 }$ 4f transitions the strongest lines are displaced to the highenergy side of the interval between the centers of gravity of both configurations and that this displacement is essentially determined by the magnitude of the 4d | 4f radial overlap integral and the number of electrons in the 4d subshell.
--[p195]-- The EUV spectra of Sn through $\mathrm { S n ^ { 4 + } }$ should be dominated by a 4d → εf continuum resonance. Since such phenomena are essentially many-body in nature, the appropriate theoretical description should reflect this.
--[p193]-- 5.3.2 Origin of UTA intensity
In neutral tin the radial potential experienced by an l = 3 electron contains both an attractive Coulomb term defined by its interaction with the nucleus and a repulsive centrifugal term, which effectively excludes the nf wave functions (top of Fig. 5.8) from the core region and resulting in a bimodal potential with two pronounced minima (bottom of Fig. 5.8).
--[p195]-- Two such theoretical prescriptions are many-body perturbation theory<sup>44</sup> and the random-phase approximation with exchange.<sup>45</sup> Another theoretical approach is the time-dependent local density approximation (TDLDA).<sup>46</sup> This approach has been shown to be very useful for studying changes in the 4d cross section with increasing ionization in iodine and cesium.<sup>47,48</sup> In this work the relativistic TDLDA code DAVID<sup>49,50</sup> was used to calculate the continuum cross section of each species above the 4d threshold. In all of these species it predicts a peak cross section of 24 Mb near 17 nm (73 eV). The calculated cross sections are included for comparison in Fig. 5.10.
--[p197]-- Our calculations have also shown that production of more highly ionized ions with $4 \mathsf { p } ^ { n }$ ground configurations is, in general, undesirable, since 4p-4d transitions move to longer wavelengths with increasing n and therefore would, if present, broaden the UTA.
For the rare-earth elements the 4f orbital is localized in the core region, and consequently the rate of change of  4d | 4f with increasing ionization is very small.
--[p194]-- 5.9 the transfer of oscillator strength from a broad continuum resonance to discrete 4d → 4f lines along the cesium isonuclear sequence is shown. Since these resonances, which evolve into $\Delta n = 0$ transitions, are the strongest features observed in neutral photoabsorption spectra, the corresponding arrays in the spectra of highly ionized atoms must correspond to the strongest emission features attainable.
--[p195]-- It should be noted that the absorption cross section of these ions at 13.5 nm is close to 15 Mb, so that their presence in any source will lead to significant radiation transport problems.

--[p273]-- Non-LTE plasma characteristics, viz., the average ion charge $\bar { Z } ( T _ { \mathrm { e } } , \rho , U )$ , spectral opacity $\kappa _ { \omega } ( T _ { \mathrm { e } } , \rho , U )$ and emissivity $j _ { \omega } ( T _ { \mathrm { e } } , \rho , U )$ , are then obtained by means of interpolation of the respective values for a transparent plasma defined at $U = 0$ calculated in CRE and for a plasma in LTE defined for Planckian radiation $U = U _ { \mathrm { p } }$ using a nonequilibrium parameter $\xi = U / U _ { \mathrm { p } } . { } ^ { 1 3 , 2 0 }$ The parameter ξ is calculated by solving the self-consistent nonlinear radiation transfer equation together with the plasma dynamics.
--[p272]-- 8.3.1 Databases of radiation and ionization plasma properties
Most experimental plasmas under conditions of interest in practical applications exist in the non-LTE regime. The plasma properties are functions of the temperature, the mass density, and the local spectral radiation energy density and time.
--[p272]-- The Gaussian widths are given by Doppler broadening, taking into account an additional width calculated in the intermediate coupling scheme.<sup>32</sup> Photoionization processes are considered in the average-atom approximation with corrections for configurations. Inverse bremsstrahlung is computed using the self-consistent potential and taking into account degeneracy effects. The equation of state is derived from the grand thermodynamic potential.
--[p273]-- To take into account the dependence of the plasma properties in non-LTE conditions on the local spectral radiation energy density $\mathbf { U } _ { \omega }$ and to avoid online calculations of complicated level kinetics, an analytical interpolation non-LTE model was developed,<sup>13</sup> using, as a main parameter, the ratio of the absorbed local radiation intensity to its equilibrium value.
--[p273]-- 8.1) and the corresponding steady-state value $f _ { \mathrm { e q } }$ are recalculated and interpolated by means of a corresponding interpolating function $\Phi ( f )$ [normalized to unity by the maximum value $\Phi _ { \operatorname* { m a x } } ( f ) = 1 ]$ from tables prepared in preprocessing.
--[p275]-- The influence of the magnetic field on multicharged-ion plasma kinetic coefficients is taken into account in the general case by conversion of field coefficients using Braginskii’s formulas, or using formulas taken directly from Ref. 14 for the case of an ideal plasma.
--[p272]-- The Hartree-Fock-Slater quantum-statistical model of a self-consistent field for the matter is used in the code with the Dirac equation for atomic shells. For opacity calculations the ion state probabilities are obtained from a renormalized Gibbstype distribution. The line shapes are Voigts with Lorenz widths given by electron pressure broadening, natural broadening, and the Stark effect.
--[p273]-- Xenon emission has a maximum at $Z _ { 0 } = 1 0$ too. Under the same ionization degree $Z _ { 0 } = 1 0$ , the share of EUV emission from xenon is 6 times less than that from a tin plasma.
The behavior of the emission for the discharge depends on both radiation transport and plasma dynamics. The detailed tables obtained are used for calculations of the nonstationary ionization process together with radiation transport, through an interpolation procedure.
--[p275]-- For a solid, volumetric compression coefficients are introduced from published tables. The phase transition from solid to gas (plasma) is represented by the corresponding sublimation temperature and sublimation enthalpy. The liquid phase is ignored, but the transition energies are taken into account.
--[p273]-- The tables of plasma parameters are calculated beforehand by the code THERMOS over a wide range of temperature $T _ { \mathrm { e } }$ and mass density ρ in the transparent CRE and LTE limits.
--[p273]-- Other values from the tables for the EOS and the plasma kinetic coefficients, prepared by THERMOS over a wide range, are interpolated as functions of the temperature, density, and mean charge using this parameter ξ. Using this formalism, it is possible to approximate non-LTE values and to reduce considerably the computing time of radiation transfer calculations in the RMHD computations.
Beyond the calculated region of the tables, extrapolations by Saha or Thomas– Fermi models are applied.
--[p272]-- The detailed atomic structure and databases of spectral lines and ionization edges for Xe and Sn plasmas including I–XX ions are calculated by the code TERM.<sup>43</sup> By using this database the calculation of spectral opacities and emissivities is made with the code THERMOS. The nonlinear steady-state Eqs. (8.4) for level occupancies are solved by iteration cycles.
--[p272]-- Thermodynamic functions of electrons and nuclei are taken as the additive ones.
The databases are calculated in steady-state approximations, and to be able to take into account nonstationary effects on the plasma state, the rates of atomic processes are also calculated. For comparison, the calculated ionization degree of a tin plasma at the two limits of LTE and CRE, as functions of temperature and mass density, are represented in Fig. 8.3.
--[p272]-- Values of energies and oscillator strengths are found by solving the system of Hartree-Fock-Slater equations with obtained occupation numbers $N _ { v }$ . At a given temperature and density, the level of excitations depends on the radiation intensity and is calculated using interpolation between the two considered limits. The results for the calculated spectral emissivity of a tin plasma at the two limits of LTE and CRE are represented in Fig. 8.4.
--[p272]-- For comparison of the EUV emission from Sn and Xe plasmas, relative emissivity properties are presented in Fig. 8.5 as the ratio of the emissivity within a
2% band around 13.5 nm to the spectrum-integrated total emissivity. This relative value is important for definition of the necessary plasma parameters to optimize an EUV source. The emission of the tin plasma has a first maximum at $Z _ { 0 } = 1 0$ and increases again until $Z _ { 0 } = 1 5$ .
--[p272]-- The databases on the EOSs for any materials and mixtures and on the spectral and plasma transport coefficients are calculated in $Z ^ { * }$ in preprocessing by the code THERMOS<sup>5,23</sup> in both the optically thick LTE and the transparent non-LTE limit. The actual non-LTE condition is modeled by analytical interpolation, described in the following, between those two limits.

===== [p492-492] High-Power GDPP Z-Pinch EUV Source Technology > 15.1.3 Magnetic insulation (5块) =====
--[p492]-- Magnetic insulation is not ideal in this case, but the erosion data show substantial anisotropy (further details discussed below). The initial axial expansion that occurs during the magnetic field pulse has the effect of lowering the plasma temperature, so that once radial expansion is free to occur, the resulting terminal radial ion velocity is less than the axial ion velocity, leading to a lower sputter coefficient on equatorially located surfaces.
--[p492]-- In addition, a very useful degree of radial confinement is available for several hundred nanoseconds after the peak-current moment (when 13.5-nm emission occurs), with the result that the early plasma expansion is directed more toward the poles than toward the equator. The effectiveness of this magnetic insulation is greatest when the duration of the current pulse, $\tau _ { \mathrm { I } } ,$ , exceeds the characteristic time $\tau _ { \mathrm { X } }$ for axial plasma expansion.
--[p492]-- 15.1.3 Magnetic insulation
By definition, the magnetic field around the pinched plasma is sufficient to radially confine it at the relevant density and temperature for 13.5-nm emission. In fact, the peak azimuthal magnetic field is approximately 15 T in the Star Pinch.
--[p492]-- Without either magnetic insulation or another form of plasma barrier, the life limit imposed by sputter erosion of first-wall components is very severe for both LPP and DPP sources. A magnetic field barrier of 0.6 T has been shown to be partially effective at slowing down the energetic ions from a laser-produced tin plasma.<sup>6</sup>
--[p492]-- For a plasma of charge state Z, ion mass $m _ { \mathrm { i } }$ , temperature $T .$ , and axial dimension $h ,$ the expansion time is $\tau _ { \mathrm { x } } = h ( m _ { \mathrm { i } } / Z T ) ^ { 1 / 2 }$ , which is of the order of 400 ns for typical Star Pinch conditions. The full duration of the current pulse is 600 ns, with 13.5-nm emission occurring halfway through, thereby providing 300 ns of insulation as the current and magnetic field decay.

===== [p250-250] Fundamentals and Limits of Plasma-based EUV Sources > 7.6 Plasma Simulation: Tool for Source Optimization (7块) =====
--[p250]-- Prerequisites are that all relevant processes be taken into account and that both input and output allow direct coupling to real experiments, which means that the whole experimental chain from the properties of the generator up to the electrode geometries must be modeled and that the output must be compiled for direct comparison with experimental source diagnostics. In the following sections, we describe—as an example—the modeling of a DPP.
--[p250]-- Typical discharge parameters are peak currents around 10–20 kA and durations ranging from 100 to 500 ns. Stored electrical energies are in the range of few joules to a few tens of joules.
The most promising emitters currently discussed are xenon and tin, as intense broadband emitters, and lithium, with its freestanding Lyman-α line at 13.5 nm.
--[p250]-- Because the system is extremely complicated and many basic material data are not available, such models can be useful only in close association with experiments.
--[p250]-- The intention is to develop a feeling for possible optimization potentials based on modeling of the EUV emission of a pinch plasma in a real system and to compare this with the current status of development.
In general, in a discharge plasma a gas is heated and compressed by a pulsed current to temperatures in the range of several tens of electron volts, which leads to thermal emission due to transitions in the EUV. The pulsed current is produced by fast discharge of a storage capacitor.
--[p250]-- As discussed already, the method to generate the plasma, the efficiency of coupling power from the generator into the plasma, plasma dynamics, and radiative transport may be significant in maximizing the single-pulse efficiency. This all must be accomplished under additional boundary conditions in that electrode cooling, gas flow, and material aspects play significant roles when developing an effective EUV source.
Plasma modeling and simulation can support and accelerate cutting-edge experimental and engineering development of sources for EUVL in many aspects.
--[p250]-- The following section will describe the theoretical models required for simulating the EUV emission pinch plasmas: Atomic physics and radiation models are needed to compute the important spectral intensities. Furthermore, they supply material data such as radiative power losses and ionization and recombination rates for MHD models to calculate the highly transient plasma properties, for example, of a pinch discharge.
--[p250]-- 7.6 Plasma Simulation: Tool for Source Optimization
Simple stationary estimations are not sufficient to optimize all aspects of practical plasma-based sources. This is of special importance for discharge-based systems, because they usually have more relevant processes involved and more complex geometries than LPPs.

===== [p232-233] Fundamentals and Limits of Plasma-based EUV Sources > 7.1 Introduction (12块) =====
--[p232]-- Several types of LPPs and DPPs are under investigation by several groups as EUV sources for the first EUV exposure tools.<sup>3–18</sup> Within the last three years such sources have demonstrated improvements of several orders of magnitude with respect to relevant parameters such as power and component lifetime.
--[p232]-- 7.1 Introduction
EUVL exposure tools for more than 100-wafer/h throughput require highly efficient sources of EUV radiation.
--[p233]-- In this chapter we discuss efficiencies of pulsed plasma systems, starting from basic principles, in order to define combinations of suitable plasma parameters for the generation of the EUV-generating plasma sources.
