Usually the radiator efficiency is given for a specified solid angle, i.e., 1 sr or 2π sr. The collector efficiency is governed by the solid angle  of the collector and the relative amount of flux that is usable with the etendue of the projection optics.
--[p233]-- The input power to the EUV sources directly influences the cost of ownership (CoO) of the source with respect to both investment costs and operational costs. In addition, because the lifetime of source components degrades with increasing power input, a source with the highest CE and hence the lowest driving power has the best chances for technical realization and for achieving lowest CoO.
--[p232]-- It is commonly accepted that the development of suitable EUV sources is one main risk factor in bringing this promising technology to a cost-effective implementation in high-volume semiconductor manufacturing fabs.<sup>1,2</sup> While investing enormous efforts in developing such sources, it has become obvious that the requirement can be met only if these sources operate close to the physical limits and the limits of thermal engineering.
--[p233]-- Common to all approaches and all concepts is that an optimized conversion efficiency (CE), η, is of major importance because this minimizes the driving power, $P _ { \mathrm { i n } }$ , for a demanded EUV power, P<sub>EUV</sub>:

--[p233]-- This is of special importance for discharge sources, where the ultimate limiting factor is expected to be the cooling of the electrodes and their lifetime. With LPPs, the CoO is expected to be determined mainly by the high-power laser, which will be in the 5- to 30-kW class.
For LPPs, the efficiency is maximized by finding an optimized set of parameters for the laser driver matched to the target of choice.
--[p233]-- For the two basic concepts of DPP and LPP, the definition of CE is slightly different: While for DPPs we calculate efficiencies with respect to the electrical input power $P _ { \mathrm { e l e c t r } }$ , LPP conversion is stated in relation to the average laser power $P _ { \mathrm { l a s e r } } .$ , not taking into account the conversion from electrical energy into laser energy.
--[p232]-- On looking at the present performance of EUV sources with up to 2% radiator efficiency into 2π sr, repetition rates of up to 10 kHz, input powers beyond 20 kW, and component lifetimes on the order of more than $1 0 ^ { 1 0 ^ { \circ } }$ pulses, the development of EUV sources that can meet the performance specifications seems feasible, if only this pace of progress can be sustained.
In principle, there are many different concepts to generate LPPs and DPPs.
--[p233]-- Suppliers have plans for up to π-sr collectors for DPP and up to 5-sr collectors for LPP. Often the collector efficiency is given as a percentage of the collectable solid angle or as a percentage of 2π sr.
--[p233]-- For DPPs, the efficiency depends critically on the concept to generate a suitable plasma and on the parameters to operate such a device, which govern how much power can be effectively coupled to the radiating plasma. The chances of succeeding in developing a viable source rise with decreasing demands on the electrical power to be handled in the discharge volume.

--[p443]-- Such a system is not easy to build, nor is a concept available yet that satisfies the lifetime requirements of the industry. The subject will remain a research topic for quite some time.

--[p443]-- The shells are coated with metal layers of (e.g.) Au, Pt, Pd, Ru, or Mo and have a reflectivity that is strongly dependent on the reflection angle. In practice, angles above 20 deg will not have acceptable reflectivity. The reflectivity is dependent on surface roughness and contamination. The pinch plasma creates, in addition to EUV photons, high-energy ions and neutrals of the radiating species (Xe, Sn). The energy of the particles can be as high as several keV.
--[p443]-- Furthermore, metal vapor or clusters will leave the pinch in all directions. The metal vapor originates either from the electrodes or, in the case of a Sn discharge, from the radiating species itself. High-energy particles will quickly sputter the collector surface. Metal vapor eventually deposits on the surface and reduces the reflectivity. All of this damage must be prevented by an effective debris mitigation system.
--[p444]-- Details on the diagnostics for the grazing-incidence reflectivity will be published elsewhere.
--[p442]-- 13.3.4 Electrode lifetime, debris, and collector lifetime
The lifetime of the lamps is largely determined by the lifetime of two critical components: electrodes and collector.
The electrodes are subject to excessive heat load, sputter load, and current load. It is important to note that sputter and current load also occur when the lamp is operated at relatively low average power.
--[p442]-- Because of the very short exposure time, the surface can reach a very high temperature during the pulse. This temperature rise can amount to as much as 2000 K above the steady-state temperature. The physical process is determined by the heat capacity and density of the material and the thermal conductivity. During the 100 ns, the heat is mostly stored in a very thin surface layer and conducted away on a much longer time scale. In Fig.
--[p442]-- In practice however, the material choice is limited because of the required high melting temperatures. Refractory materials like W and Mo are good compromises.
As a result of electrode damage, the lamp will change its performance over time. As a general rule, we have observed that the overall generation of EUV with good CE is tolerant of even severe changes in electrode shape. On the other hand, the size and position of the pinch are highly sensitive to the detailed electrode shape.
--[p442]-- It is important to note that improved cooling technology can only reduce the average background temperature, not the pulsed surface heating. The only way to cope with this phenomenon is to reduce the surface heat load (e.g., by lowering the pulse energy, extending the pinch duration, or increasing the plasma-to-wall distance) or to increase the thermal conductivity and heat capacity of the material.
--[p442]-- Sputter load occurs on all surfaces exposed to the plasma, and is proportional to the number of plasma pinch events generated over time. Current load depends on the accumulated amount of charge transported through the system, again strictly proportional to the number of pinch events accumulated over time.
Thermal load, by contrast, is a property of average and peak load. Heatis dissipated during a time interval of 100 ns, i.e., with a duty cycle of 1:1000 in the case of 10-kHz operation.
--[p442]-- 13.8 a typical model calculation for W electrodes, 3 J pulse energy, and an electrode-to-pinch distance of 5 mm is shown. The background temperature is assumed to be $1 4 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ It can be seen that the surface temperature can rise up to the melting temperature of ${ \textrm { W } } ( \approx 3 4 0 0 { \textrm { K } } )$ while the temperature rise of the material as little as 10 µm below the surface is only 100 K.
--[p443]-- In practice, this means that collection efficiency is the more critical parameter to watch than CE. The biggest progress achieved so far has been the distribution of the current over a large surface by introducing the multiple-borehole concept. In Fig. 13.9, the results are presented for a life test of 200 million shots.
Another severe lifetime problem is damage to the collector. For the collector design we are using grazing-incidence nested collector shells.

===== [p46-46] EUV Source Technology: Challenges and Status > 1.3.2.3 Gas transmission (2块) =====
--[p46]-- 1.3.2.3 Gas transmission
Absorption of EUV light by a background gas such as Xe is expected in DPP and LPP systems. Although absorption-versus-pressure data are readily available,<sup>43</sup> suppliers do not provide pressure data because of pressure gradients and the proprietary nature of such data. From the FC2 experiment,<sup>36</sup> for 2.1 mTorr of Xe, a loss of 15% for a 900-mm distance in an EUV source can be expected.
--[p46]-- Suppliers usually expect a 15% loss, or 85% transmission, for Xe, which indicates the path length and gas pressure of EUV radiation to the IF.
For Sn-based DPP systems, the choice of carrier gas is not publicly known. Experiments with various Sn halides have shown that absorption by carrier gases can be a problem.<sup>44</sup> An 85% value is used in Table 1.3, but measurements need to be performed to assess the practical transmission for Sn-based DPP EUV sources.

--[p439]-- 13.3.3 Collection efficiency
Next to CE, collection efficiency is the most important parameter in characterizing lamp properties. The overall collection efficiency is defined as the fraction of inband photons that can be processed by the scanner. The reference point is the intermediate focus. Determining factors are the etendue match between the source and the scanner, and the geometrical and material properties of the collector.
--[p441]-- The CCD image is taken at a fixed angle; the line scan is a direct scan of the CCD signal, so the length scale is divided by the sine of the observation angle to obtain the true length of the pinch. In all cases, the pinch is not well represented by a simple Gaussian intensity distribution. Just looking at FWHM values may hence be misleading.
--[p441]-- This volume must be stable in space and, for thermal and sputter reasons, stay as far as possible away from any walls and other parts of the system.

--[p374]-- 11.1 Introduction
Some EUV light sources have been promoted that use LPPs, and some that use DPPs (see, for example, Ref. 1). Although each proposed source has significant advantages, the LPP offers an especially attractive prospective application range due to advances in laser technology and tunability of the source emission by targetmaterial selection.

===== [p338-339] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.3.1 Laser coupling and interaction processes (13块) =====
--[p338]-- This process of plasma heating by laser radiation is known as IBA. Although elastic and inelastic collisions generally take place at the same time, the cascade ionization is especially important in the starting phase of the plasma.
IBA plays a central role in heating the plasma. The electrons, while oscillating under the action of the laser electric field, collide with the ions, giving rise to transfer of EM energy to the plasma. The absorption coefficient for IBA can be written as<sup>15</sup>
--[p338]-- 10.3.1 Laser coupling and interaction processes
As laser light propagates in the plasma, several mechanisms can account for the transfer of energy from the laser electromagnetic (EM) wave to the plasma, according to the interaction regime. Initial ionization of laser-plasma target material takes place by photoionization processes.

The absorption coefficient for IBA is then proportional to the electron density squared (neglecting the $n _ { \mathrm { e } }$ dependence of the Coulomb logarithm).

===== [p210-211] Radiative Collapse in Z Pinches > 6.1 Introduction (6块) =====
--[p210]-- 6.1 Introduction
Emission of radiation at short wavelengths demands hot plasmas, which are readily produced by the pinch effect. This term describes the self-constriction accompanied by heating of discharges by the magnetic field B of the current I in a discharge plasma. Pinching starts when the magnetic field pressure $B ^ { 2 } / 2 \mu _ { 0 }$ exceeds the plasma particle pressure p, and it stops when the two are equal; this condition describes a magnetically confined plasma column.
--[p211]-- A cylindrical shock wave running ahead of the piston is characteristic of fast discharges. Several calculations are presented in this book; see, for example, Chapter 11. In this chapter we focus on the development of a magnetically confined plasma cylinder consisting of strongly radiating ions after it has been formed on the axis. In this state, energy is transferred to the plasma mainly by Joule heating.
--[p211]-- However, the transformation of electrical energy into plasma is rather inefficient in -pinch devices of short length; thus nearly all discharge-based EUV sources employ the linear geometry. A typical Z-pinch discharge proceeds as follows: high voltage is applied to the electrodes of the discharge tube, and after breakdown the current starts to flow in a thin cylindrical low-temperature plasma shell adjacent to the insulating wall.
--[p211]-- This current produces a corresponding magnetic field outside the shell, which accelerates the plasma like a piston or a slug toward the axis till it stagnates on the axis. For rough estimates, modeling of the compression employing a simple “snowplow” model suffices, although a detailed description of the plasma state requires solving MHD equations combined with kinetic codes for ionization and population of the atomic species, taking into account also radiative transport.
--[p211]-- Both discharges are operated in a pulsed mode, since the high currents required can conveniently be supplied only by discharging properly designed capacitor banks. Operation in pulsed mode is useful also for other reasons: the lifetime of hot plasma columns is limited by plasma losses at the ends of the column on the one hand, and on the other hand these plasmas are prone to hydromagnetic instabilities, which are extremely serious in the case of the Z pinch.<sup>1</sup>
--[p210]-- There are two complementary geometries: the linear, or $Z$ , pinch and the  pinch (Fig. 6.1).
Both are axially symmetric. In the Z pinch the current flows along the axis (Z direction) and the plasma is confined by the azimuthal magnetic field of the current. In the second arrangement an azimuthal current (in the  direction) is induced in the plasma column by a rapidly varying current in a single-turn coil around the discharge vessel, and the confining magnetic field is parallel to the axis.

===== [p357-358] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.5.3.1 Atomic-physics properties of the 4d-nf and 4d-np transitions (7块) =====
--[p358]-- The same observation has been made for similarly charged Xe ions at the tokamak of Fontenay-aux-Roses,<sup>40</sup> and confirmed by synchrotronradiation photoionization experiments by Bizau et al.<sup>84</sup>
As pointed out in a previous publication,<sup>30</sup> this effect strongly narrows the 100– 110-Å emission band from the xenon plasmas typical for the XUV lithography experiments, while it hardly affects the 135-Å lines in the $\mathrm { X e ^ { 1 0 + } }$ ion.
--[p357]-- 10.5.3.1 Atomic-physics properties of the 4d-nf and 4d-np transitions
A first significant feature concerns the evolution of the repartition of the 4d-εf oscillator strength as a function of the f electron energy ε. It is known that the effective potential acting on the f electrons has a double well resulting from a competition between the electrostatic potential and the centrifugal barrier.
--[p358]-- This is due to the fact that the 100–110-Å band comes from 4-4 transitions, while the 135-Å structure is mainly associated with the 4d-5p lines, weakly perturbed by CI effects.
--[p358]-- For two decades, in particular owing to the work by Mandelbaum et al.<sup>85</sup> on highly charged lanthanide ions, it has been well known that CI is present in the excited states belonging to $4 \mathrm { p } ^ { 6 } 4 \mathrm { d } ^ { N - 1 } 4 \mathrm { f }$ and $\mathrm { 4 p ^ { 5 } } 4 \mathrm { d } ^ { N + 1 }$ configurations.
--[p358]-- A similar effect in the case of Cs has been described by Cummings and O’Sullivan.<sup>86</sup> Moreover, in praseodymium $( Z = 5 9 )$ it was demonstrated that the position of the resulting structure depends weakly on $Z ^ { * }$ (i.e., on the net ion charge), and therefore the corresponding arrays for the various ions coalesce in a strong structure.
--[p357]-- For neutral xenon and its low-charge ions (charge ≤ 4), the 4d-εf oscillator strength belongs mostly to the bound-free spectrum, resulting in a giant resonance in the continuum.<sup>30,84</sup> For large ion charge states, the 4f wave function collapses in the inner well and the main oscillator strengths shift to the 4d-4f transition, since the 4d and 4f wave functions significantly overlap.
The second effect present in Xe and Sn ions is the CI.
--[p358]-- This CI may result in the quenching of many lines, and it may strongly shift and narrow transition arrays associated with the lines between the $\mathsf { 4 p } ^ { 6 } 4 \mathsf { \bar { d } } ^ { N }$ ground state and the above-mentioned excited states.

===== [p348-348] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.5.1.2 Detailed configuration accounting method (7块) =====
--[p348]-- 10.5.1.2 Detailed configuration accounting method
In principle the formulas describing the interaction of multielectron LTE plasma ions with photons require the calculation of all excited eigenstates of ions of different charges. Even for low-Z elements the number of such eigenstates may be very large. For this reason, at the early stage of the development of the plasma photoabsorption codes, the usual procedure was to avoid the diagonalization of the atomic Hamiltonian.
--[p348]-- These transitions form UTAs that can be represented by Gaussian functions of the photon frequency. The three moments characterizing such a UTA can be calculated exactly from closed formulas that can be found in the mentioned literature.<sup>59–62</sup> The one-electron states of each configuration are usually obtained in a common self-consistent potential calculated for that specific configuration.
--[p348]-- An important advance that gave the DCA approach a firm theoretical basis is associated with the rigorous statistical methods proposed by Bauche, Bauche-Arnoult, and Klapisch.<sup>59–62</sup> These methods are based on the notion of the UTA and its relativistic version, the spin-orbit split array (SOSA). The statistical methods proposed in Refs. 59–62 deal with optical transitions between all states belonging to two different configurations.
--[p348]-- However, some early opacity codes were based on ad hoc approximate formulas using the averaged configuration energies. The use of such early direct configuration accounting (DCA) approaches has been criticized in the literature as leading to errors in the bound-bound absorption and emission structures, especially in the case of the $\Delta n = 0$ transitions;<sup>56,57</sup> a discussion of this issue can be found in Ref. 58.
--[p348]-- All levels were supposed to have a degenerate energy that could be found without diagonalization.<sup>55</sup> A configuration can be constructed starting from one-electron subshells (defined by the n, l or n, l, j quantum numbers found in the AA approximation) and choosing integer occupation numbers of these subshells that do not exceed the subshell degeneracies. This set of quantum numbers, together with their integer occupation numbers, defines a detailed configuration.
--[p348]-- The corresponding self-consistent potential can be calculated for each configuration. One may do that using the density-functional approach or using the restricted HF approximation, which takes the exchange into account explicitly.<sup>56</sup> Again, as in the case of the AA, the one-electron states obtained from the configuration selfconsistent potential cannot be directly used in the formula for the photoabsorption cross sections.
--[p348]-- In the original literature the absorption or emission structures obtained from these moments are usually referred to as UTAs only in the nonrelativistic approach.<sup>59,60</sup> If the one-electron states are calculated in the relativistic formalism (full Hartree-Fock-Dirac approach or approach based on the Pauli correction<sup>55</sup>), they are referred to in this literature as SOSA absorption or emission structures.<sup>61</sup> The SOSA and UTA approaches have been widely used to interpret opacity measurements in various laboratory plasmas.

===== [p466-467] High-Power GDPP Z-Pinch EUV Source Technology > 14.6 Discharge-Electrode Thermal Management Technology (7块) =====
--[p466]-- Direct liquid cooling offers the potential for high heat flux.
The electrodes are designed with flow channels. Water or oil is injected into and removed from the system via these channels. With optimized liquid-cooled Z-pinch discharge designs a heat removal of up to 12 kW has been achieved.
A further significant improvement of the cooling efficiency is achieved by employing a cooling technology called porous-metal cooling.
--[p467]-- With the current technical realization, heat removal of up to 20 kW has been obtained from the discharge electrode assembly of XTREME technologies’ GDPP Z-pinch sources.
--[p467]-- Key components include an inner copper shell, an outer copper shell, a divider ring, and the porous metal layer. The water coolant flows into the annular porous layer from the top. As it flows through the layer, it absorbs heat conducted from the tip through the inner wall. As it reaches the bottom of the assembly, the coolant is redirected around the divider ring, and then passes upward and out of the assembly.
--[p466]-- The development of efficient cooling systems for Z-pinch sources is therefore targeting a heat removal of up to 50 kW at heat fluxes of up to 5 to 10 $\mathrm { k W } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ . Because the discharge electrodes are connected to high voltage, the cooling system must be electrically isolated. Thermal cycling of the discharge electrode system from room temperature to above $1 0 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ will occur.
--[p466]-- Several cooling arrangements for the discharge electrode system have been developed and tested with XTREME technologies’ Z-pinch EUV sources.
In the simplest arrangement the electrodes are in good thermal contact with a liquid- (water- or oil-) cooled heat sink. With such arrangements up to 5 kW of heat could be removed from the discharge region.
In a more complex arrangement the electrodes have been designed to be directly liquid-cooled.
--[p466]-- 14.6 Discharge-Electrode Thermal Management Technology
From the power requirements for GDPP EUV sources for high-volume chip manufacturing derived in Sec. 14.1.2, one can estimate the cooling requirements for the discharge electrode system. Under the assumption of 3% CE (estimate for tinfueled Z-pinch sources) from electrical power to EUV inband radiation, between 23 and 46 kW of electrical power must be removed from the discharge system.
--[p467]-- In this technology, highly efficient heat removal is obtained through use of a porous medium with microchannels for extended surface heat transfer (see Fig. 14.13). Parts of the electrodes are manufactured of porous metal with a very large surface, similar to a sponge. Water is forced by high pressure through the porous metal, and high heat exchange from the surface to the water is obtained. The porous-metal heat-sink version of an electrode assembly is shown in cross section in Fig. 14.14.

===== [p304-306] Z∗ Code for DPP and LPP Source Modeling > Appendix B: Estimations for the Motion Dynamics of a Sheath in the Ionized Gas via the Snowplow Model (11块) =====
--[p305]-- To estimate the influence of sheath stretching, let us suppose, contrary to the snowplow model, that the density of the ambient plasma does not attach to the sheath, but instantly flows down along the sheath, because a sheath in a radiating plasma has a finite thickness. In this case the upper limit for the sheath velocity is the magnetic sound speed in the plasma.
--[p305]-- Another picture takes place if the gas density in front of the sheath is high enough and preionized. The magnetic field diffusion equation written for the azimuthal component $B$ is
$$

===== [p411-411] Dense Plasma Focus Source > 12.5 Operation at High Repetition Rates (3块) =====
--[p411]-- On excluding the initial transient in the burst, pulse energy stability variations were typically ≈7%–8% rms at high repetition rates.
The EUV output energy was also measured for continuous operation at a repetition rate of 2 kHz at negative polarity using second-generation direct water-cooled electrodes. Employing an EUV monitor with debris suppression tube, inband output energies of 38 mJ/pulse (into 2π sr, 2% bandwidth) were observed, corresponding to 76 W of continuous average output power.
Furthermore, additional test runs with continuous operation at 50% duty cycle and 5-kHz repetition rate were carried out.
--[p411]-- The shape of the characteristic transient at the beginning of the pulse burst is highly dependent on operating conditions such as electrode geometry, gas recipe, and preionization system. The EUV output energy is strongly correlated with the degree of coupling of the stored pulse energy to the discharge. This indicates that the energy stability is strongly affected by details of the discharge formation process and energy coupling mechanisms.
--[p411]-- 12.5 Operation at High Repetition Rates
Stable performance of the source at high repetition rates is important for high exposure dose and accurate dose control. Burst-mode operation at increasingly higher repetition rates has been demonstrated on several of our DPF systems. Figure 12.4 shows the variation of the time-integrated inband output energy during a burst of more than 300 pulses for a positive-polarity DPF with uncooled electrodes at 5 kHz.

===== [p436-438] Hollow-Cathode-Triggered Plasma Pinch Discharge > 13.3.1 Design of the HCT lamp (10块) =====
--[p438]-- If these holes are far apart, the pinch can be far away from any wall. In our experiments, we have realized wall distances as large as 15 mm. In Fig. 13.4, EUV pictures of an eight-hole cathode are shown on a linear scale and on a logarithmic scale to amplify the radiation from single holes. It appears that the radiation intensity at noncentral positions is only a minute fraction of the intensity at the central position.
--[p437]-- Moreover, the timing of the pulses is now entirely determined by the timing of a low-power trigger pulse. A recent study of the effect of a blocking electrode on a xenon-operated discharge is found in Ref. 17.
The development of a multiborehole cathode has remedied the heavy thermal and sputter load on the electrodes and, as already mentioned, suppressed the deformation of the cathode geometry by distributing the attaching current over a larger surface.
--[p438]-- Here, the holes are connected to one single hollow cathode and provide each hole a fraction of the total current. The single hollow cathode controls the breakdown process and leads to simultaneous discharge in all channels. Upon choosing the right discharge conditions, it is possible to have currents in single holes sufficiently small not to form an individual pinch while the joint current of all holes is sufficiently large to form a pinch in the middle of the array of holes.
--[p438]-- The heat-load problem is addressed in more detail in Sec. 13.3.4. Generally, the most effective means of reducing the heat load is to increase the distance of the hot pinch plasma from the electrode surface.
A typical plasma-wall distance for a single-hole electrode system is 5 mm. An extension of the pseudospark concept—again known from switches—is a device with more than one borehole connecting the hollow cathode with the gap (Fig. 13.4).
--[p437]-- This electrode is connected via a low-power switch to the cathode and is at a positive potential relative to the cathode during the charging cycle of the capacitors. Its basic function is to remove the initial electrons in the hollow cathode prior to breakdown, hence impeding the breakdown itself. This comes down to shifting the Paschen curve to an effective Paschen curve that is higher in breakdown voltage (Fig. 13.3).
--[p436]-- There is no single optimum parameter set; the lamp can be operated in a broad range of parameters, which allows optimization for other parameters such as the lifetime of the electrodes and the pinch size.
Compared to competing concepts such as the Z pinch or plasma focus, the key advantages of the HCT concept are the absence of insulating materials near the pinch region, and self-breakdown.
--[p437]-- The first property allows far more effective cooling and protection against sputter damage; the second property allows for simple design of the electrical circuitry in that no high-current switches are necessary.
In a further development stage, the simple HCT concept has been supplemented by a trigger electrode that is inserted into the hollow cathode (Fig. 13.3).
--[p436]-- Upon increasing the voltage, the breakdown occurs spontaneously at a certain voltage. If the parameters of the electrical circuitry are chosen appropriately, current buildup leads to pinch formation and EUV radiation. Typical circuit parameters are an inductance below 10 nH, capacitance between 50 nF and $2 \mu \mathrm { F } ,$ and voltage between 2 and 20 kV.
--[p436]-- 13.3.1 Design of the HCT lamp
Typical geometrical dimensions are 5–10-mm plate distance and borehole diameter. The hollow cathode itself may have a diameter between 10 and 50 mm. The lamp head, including the electrode system and the storage capacitors, needs to be connected to a power supply and put in a vacuum system where a controlled gas pressure can be imposed. The pressure, voltage, and geometrical dimensions of the device determine the breakdown conditions.
--[p437]-- When the capacitor is charged to a voltage below the effective Paschen curve, but above the corresponding curve without a trigger voltage, switching the trigger off will immediately move the system into breakdown. It is important to note that the trigger circuit does not carry a high current. The effect of the trigger is a widening of the operation margins. In particular, it allows operation over a wide pressure range.

===== [p353-355] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.5.2.1 Elementary radiative transfer and Kirchhoff’s law (17块) =====
--[p355]-- A simple way to estimate the emission spectra is to assume that the plasma is nearly homogeneous and can be characterized by a single electron temperature and ion density. This allows one to simplify the expression of the self-emission and get
$$
I _ { \ v } ( \tau _ { v } ) = S _ { \ v } ( 1 - e ^ { - \tau _ { v } } ) .\tag{10.21}
$$
For example, let us consider a plane target irradiated with a laser pulse at normal incidence.
--[p355]-- However, even in the latter case, fitting the emission spectrum with Eq. (10.21) allows one to estimate roughly the mean properties of the plasma (average temperature and density, optical depth). The ef fect of reabsorption on the emission spectrum of a laser-produced xenon source was qualitatively studied in Ref. 30 using Eq. (10.21) under the assumption of LTE, i.e., for
$$
S _ { v } = B _ { v } ( T ) .\tag{10.22}
$$
A similar approach was used in Ref.
75 to model DPPs, with the source function evaluated in coronal equilibrium.
--[p354]-- This point is particularly important for the interpretation of spectra from a nonuniform plasma, as the observed intensity at different frequencies reflects conditions at different depths into the plasma.
For a system in thermal equilibrium, emission and absorption must balance, resulting in Kirchhoff’s law:
$$
\begin{array} { r } { \eta _ { \nu } = B _ { \nu } \alpha _ { \nu } , } \end{array}\tag{10.19}
$$
where $B _ { \mathbb { V } } ( T )$ is the Planck function:
$$
--[p354]-- I _ { \mathrm { v } } ( \tau _ { v } ) = I _ { \mathrm { v } } ( 0 ) e ^ { - \tau _ { v } } + \int _ { 0 } ^ { \tau _ { v } } S _ { \mathrm { v } } ( \tau _ { v } ^ { \prime } ) e ^ { - ( \tau _ { v } - \tau _ { v } ^ { \prime } ) } d \tau _ { v } ^ { \prime } ,\tag{10.17}
$$
where $S _ { v } = \eta _ { v } / \alpha _ { v }$ is called the source function, and $\tau _ { \nu }$ (dimensionless) is the optical depth of the plasma, defined by the formula
$$
--[p354]-- \tau _ { \mathbb { v } } ( s ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { s } \alpha _ { \mathbb { v } } ( s ^ { \prime } ) d s ^ { \prime } .\tag{10.18}
$$
The first term on the right-hand side of Eq. (10.17) represents the attenuation along the ray of the external radiative field of intensity $I _ { \ v } ( 0 )$ , whereas the second term is the self-emission of the plasma in that direction. This expression illustrates several important points. For optically thick material $( \mathrm { i } . \mathrm { e } .
--[p355]-- In the previously cited thesis,<sup>31</sup> it is shown that reabsorption can substantially modify the ratio between the main emission band at 10 nm, due to the 4d-4f and 4p-4d transition arrays mixed by configuration interaction and originating from $\dot { \mathrm { X e } } ^ { 1 0 + } ~ \mathrm { t o } ~ \mathrm { X e } ^ { 1 3 + }$ , and the emission structures at 13.5 nm, due to 4d-5p transitions of $\mathrm { X e ^ { 1 0 + } }$
The radiative transfer equation written in the form Eq.
--[p353]-- 10.5.2.1 Elementary radiative transfer and Kirchhoff’s law
Studies of radiation transfer are very important in LPPs. Radiation is a critical energy transport (and loss) mechanism and is also a key part of the ionizationrecombination balance. Much of the early work on radiation transfer was done in the context of astrophysics, and there is an extensive astrophysical literature on the subject (see, for instance, Ref. 82).
--[p355]-- 10.4.3, treat these problems in a consistent manner, using greatly simplifying approximations (screened-hydrogenic AA model for atomic physics, multigroup diffusion approach to radiation transfer, etc.) in order to keep computation times reasonable. Codes such as CRETIN<sup>83</sup> attempt to self-consistently combine more detailed atomic-physics treatments with general radiative-transfer algorithms, particularly for situations where important lines are optically thick.
--[p355]-- It also introduces a nonlocal coupling through photon transport, which can extend well beyond the simple estimate of one optical depth. Specialized computational techniques are used to self-consistently solve for the radiation field along with the material properties. Codes such as CHIVAS,<sup>32</sup> mentioned in Sec.
--[p354]-- The most common macroscopic description of the interaction of matter with radiation uses the equation of radiative transfer, which describes the balance between emission, absorption, and transport of photons:
$$
\frac { d I _ { v } } { d s } = \left( \frac { 1 } { c } \frac { \partial } { \partial t } + \pmb { \Omega } \cdot \nabla \right) I _ { v } ( s ) = \eta _ { \mathsf { v } } ( s ) - \alpha _ { v } ( s ) I _ { v } ( s ) ,\tag{10.16}
$$
--[p354]-- , \tau _ { v } \gg 1 )$ , the intensity approaches the source function: $I _ { \ v } \to S _ { \ v }$ . For optically thin material, $I _ { \nu }$ need not have any relationship to the local value of $S _ { \ v }$ , but is directly determined by values of $S _ { \ v }$ within about one optical depth. Finally, the emission spectrum measured along a line of sight corresponds to photons that escape the plasma within about one optical depth of the surface.
--[p355]-- Equation (10.21) represents a reasonable approach to model the emission spectrum measured in the transverse direction, because the lateral expansion of the plasma is almost self-similar with limited gradients of temperature and density. On the other hand, Eq. (10.21) is not well suited to simulate the emission intensity of the plasma measured longitudinally along the beam axis, since in that direction larger gradients can be expected.
--[p354]-- The specific intensity $I _ { \nu }$ is proportional to the photon distribution function, and Eq. (10.7) can be recognized as a Boltzmann equation with the absorption and emission terms arising from collisions between photons and matter.
The formal solution of Eq. (10.16) (i.e., for specified emission and absorption) can be written analytically as
$$
--[p354]-- B _ { \ v } ( T ) = { \frac { 2 \pi h v ^ { 3 } } { c ^ { 2 } } } { \frac { 1 } { e ^ { h v / k T } - 1 } } .\tag{10.20}
$$
This property is a consequence of the principle of detailed balance in a system with a Maxwellian electron distribution. Although this relationship does not hold in general, it often provides a handy benchmark for quick estimates.
--[p354]-- The quantities $\alpha _ { \mathrm { v } }$ and $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { \Delta } } \boldsymbol { \mathrm { \eta } } _ { \boldsymbol { \mathrm { \Delta \xi } } }$ are the macroscopic absorption (in $\mathbf { m } ^ { - 1 } )$ and emission (in $\mathrm { ~ \dot { ~ } W } \mathrm { m } ^ { - 3 } \mathrm { H z } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { s r } ^ { - 1 } )$ coefficients, respectively, which ultimately derive from the microscopic processes.
--[p354]-- where s is measured along the beam in the propagation direction, and $I _ { \nu }$ is the specific intensity (in $\mathrm { { W m } } ^ { - 2 } \mathrm { { H z } } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { { s r } } ^ { - 1 } )$ .
--[p355]-- (10.17) is deceptively simple in that it hides the fact that the absorption and emission coefficients depend on the local properties of the material (temperature, density, population distributions), which themselves depend on the radiation field. The radiation introduces a nonlinear coupling between different physical processes (e.g., in hydrodynamic and cross-section calculations) by altering the energy balance, ionization balance, and excited-state distributions.

===== [p483-483] High-Power GDPP Z-Pinch EUV Source Technology > 14.11 Summary and Conclusion (5块) =====
--[p483]-- The progress has resulted in a continuous EUV power of 200 W into 2π sr at 4.5-kHz repetition rate. The usable IF power for these sources is in the range between 12 and 26 W, depending on the collector optics design, on the transmission of the optical path to the IF, and on the etendue specification. The plasma shape of xenon sources, however, will likely prevent transmission through the source collector with sufficient efficiency to support HVM.
--[p483]-- Because of their favorable plasma shape and spectral emission characteristics, Z-pinch sources with tin fuel have been developed. These sources have demonstrated 400-W EUV output power into 2π sr at 4.5 kHz in continuous operation. The IF power for existing collector designs is calculated to range between 36 and 50 W inband EUV power, depending on etendue specifications. The power requirements for HVM EUVL will be met without additional inventions.
--[p483]-- Significant progress has also been made in the lifetime of the discharge electrodes and the source-collector optics. Current development projects lead to the projection that the lifetimes required for HVM use of GDPP sources will also be reached. The research programs at XTREME technologies are focused on demonstrating required HVM lifetimes in 2006.
--[p483]-- 14.11 Summary and Conclusion
Z-pinch EUV sources at XTREME technologies are currently the most powerful GDPP sources in the world. Prototypes of commercial machines with xenon as emitter and an EUV power of 35 W into 2π-sr solid angle have been developed and are integrated in EUV microsteppers. These EUV microsteppers are used as pathfinders for EUVL in the semiconductor industry.
--[p483]-- The microstepper EUV source XTS 13-35 is equipped with a debris filter to protect the grazing-incidence collector optics. An optics lifetime exceeding 100 million pulses at 1-kHz repetition frequency is achieved. The same lifetime is obtained for the components of the discharge system itself.
On a laboratory scale, xenon-fueled GDPP sources have been developed with an available EUV inband power increased by more than 2 orders of magnitude over the status 3 years ago.

===== [p149-149] Chapter 3 Atomic Xenon Data > 4.2 Theoretical Approach (7块) =====
--[p149]-- The difference of the two average energies is then applied as a correction to the states within that configuration after the Hamiltonian is diagonalized.
The radiative transition rates are calculated in the single-multipole approximation. This means that the interference between different multipoles is not taken into account, although rates corresponding to arbitrary multipoles can be calculated.
--[p149]-- To reduce the error of level energies due to the use of this less than optimized potential, a special correction procedure is applied. Before the potential for the mean configuration is calculated, an optimized potential for each configuration is obtained, and the average energy of the configuration using this potential is calculated. The average energy of each configuration is then recalculated using the potential optimized for the mean configuration.
--[p149]-- The bound states of the atomic system are calculated in the configuration-mixing approximation with convenient specification of mixing schemes; the radial orbitals for the construction of the basis states are derived from a modified self-consistent Dirac-Fock-Slater iteration on a fictitious mean configuration with fractional occupation numbers, representing the average electron cloud of the configurations included in the calculation.
--[p149]-- • A fully relativistic approach based on the Dirac equation is used throughout the entire package, which allows its application to ions with large nuclear charge.
--[p149]-- The mean configuration in the construction of the potential is used in order to take into account the screening of more than one configuration involved in the physical processes to be calculated. This mean configuration is usually obtained by distributing the active electrons in the initial and final states. Therefore, the potential obtained is not optimized to a single configuration; rather, it is a compromise to accommodate different configurations.
--[p149]-- • It combines the strengths of existing atomic codes [CIV3, SUPERSTRUC-TURE, multiconfiguration Hartree-Fock (MCHF) and multiconfiguration Dirac-Fock (MCDF) codes, and the HULLAC package] with modifications to numerical procedures made to extend the capability and improve the efficiency and robustness.
• It has a uniform, flexible, and easy-to-use user interface for accessing all computational tasks and performing bulk-scale calculations.
--[p149]-- 4.2 Theoretical Approach
The FAC authored by Ming Feng Gu has been chosen for the calculations of energy levels and transition probabilities of Sn ions. The FAC is a publicly available<sup>1</sup> complete software package for the computation of various atomic data. The choice was caused by the following advantages of the FAC:

===== [p191-193] Atomic Physics of Highly Charged Ions and the Case for Sn as a Source Material > 5.3.1 Atomic structure considerations and UTA (11块) =====
--[p191]-- It was further shown that if the tin concentration was reduced to approximately 10%, the peak brightness actually increased.<sup>16</sup> Furthermore, if the remaining 90% of the constituents were low-Z materials, the radiation emitted was concentrated in a band 1–2 nm wide centered near 13.4 nm and the ordinary recombination continuum from the plasma was suppressed in comparison with that from a pure tin target.
--[p191]-- From work ongoing at University College Dublin (UCD) since the late 1970s, tin was identified as potentially the strongest emitter at 13.5 nm, since the UTA is centered near that wavelength.
--[p191]-- 5.3.1 Atomic structure considerations and UTA
The same UTA as that in xenon at 11 nm is also observed in adjacent elements.<sup>33</sup> Since in every case it arises from $4 \mathrm { p } ^ { 6 } 4 \mathrm { d } ^ { n } - 4 \mathrm { p } ^ { 5 } 4 \mathrm { d } ^ { n + 1 } + 4 \mathrm { d } ^ { n - 1 }$ 4f transitions, the peak position is sensitive to atomic number and moves to shorter wavelengths as Z increases (Fig. 5.5).
--[p191]-- In this figure the in-band intensity was determined using a calibrated CCD detector housed in a 0.25-m flat-field grazingincidence vacuum spectrometer supplied by Jenoptik Microtechnik.
--[p193]-- Theoretically, the profile width is determined to a large extent by final-state $4 \mathrm { p } ^ { 5 } 4 \mathrm { d } ^ { n + 1 } + 4 \mathrm { d } ^ { n - 1 } 4 \mathrm { f }$ configuration interaction, which also causes the features to overlap in successive ion stages. The result of Hartree-Fock calculations with the Cowan code are presented in Fig. 5.7.
As in xenon, in performing these calculations, scaling factors for the Slater-Condon factors were chosen to best fit the observed UTA.
--[p193]-- The energy overlap in successive stages, like the intensity, is strongly related to the localization of the 4f radial wave function and its overlap with the 4d wave function.
--[p193]-- With decreasing concentration the populations essentially decrease uniformly, so that the emission at the wings decays more rapidly than from the center, because the plasma never becomes optically thin at the peak wavelength.
--[p191]-- In fact, if pure targets are used, the recombination continuum contains most of the emitted radiation. It extends throughout the EUV, and if absorbed by the multilayer optics, could cause heating, distortion, and loss of focus. These results have been verified in a controlled study with tin-doped glass targets and are summarized in Fig. 5.6.
--[p193]-- In pure targets the UTA essentially appears as a modulation of the recombination continuum and there is considerable self-absorption, while from targets containing only a few percent of the element of interest the plasma becomes optically thin.<sup>34</sup> The observed increase in the intensity of the UTA with the decrease in the concentration agrees with the data of Choi et al.,<sup>35</sup> who, in a space-resolved study of emission from tin metal and tin oxide targets, found that the emission from a $\mathrm { S n O } _ { 2 }$ film target was every where greater than that from a tin slab target.
--[p191]-- It is evident that the brightness attainable with slab targets at 2% concentration is some 45% greater than with a pure tin target, but the optimum concentration needs to be clarified and will be sensitive to the laser pulse profile and focusing conditions, as these determine the ion-stage distribution that controls both emission and absorption. For 2% concentration the efficiency is estimated to be approximately 1.7%, based on the detector calibration and source geometry.
Both intensity and profile are very sensitive to concentration.
--[p193]-- For mass-limited targets, the peak intensity is essentially unaltered, but the profile width decreases as the tin concentration is reduced.<sup>36</sup> Presumably this reflects the fact that the emission at the UTA center is from the dominant ions for which the plasma is optically thick, while that from the wings emanates from both higher (shorter wavelength) and lower (longer wavelength) ion stages for which the plasma is closer to being optically thin.

===== [p494-494] High-Power GDPP Z-Pinch EUV Source Technology > 15.2 Directed Discharges (4块) =====
--[p494]-- 15.2 Directed Discharges
A new approach to pinch discharges, the Star Pinch,<sup>14</sup> was introduced in order to develop very high power DPP 13.5-nm sources with life exceeding $1 0 ^ { 1 0 }$ pulses at 5-J dissipated energy. The two main problems that had to be overcome were first-wall temperature rise and first-wall sputter erosion, both of which mandated an increased distance between the plasma and the first wall.
--[p494]-- The state of the surface began to have a significant influence on the discharge azimuthal uniformity, and also on the 13.5-nm stability. Experiments then began with a type of discharge previously studied for possible use in high-current closing switches<sup>15</sup> that had shown volumetric ignition at lower pressures than possible with the Z-pinch geometry.
--[p494]-- This was more related to spatial (azimuthal) inhomogeneity of the high-current plasma than to any nonuniformity of preionization. It was exacerbated by the need to evolve to lower-pulse-energy and higher-repetition-rate operation, when lower gas density became essential, and ignition began to be dominated by discharges feeding on the release of surface material rather than using gas available volumetrically.
--[p494]-- A third problem, that of cathode life, was solved in the process of solving the first two. A fourth problem, the need for volumetric ignition, was the key to taking the next step: toward directed discharges. Early in PLEX’s development cycle on Z pinches it had been found that even with a symmetrically preionized cylindrical plasma<sup>2</sup> the distance of the first wall could not be increased much beyond 12 mm before the positional stability of the emitting plasma began to degrade.

Calculation of the emission spectra from the small-size plasma of high-current pulsed systems and LPPs requires the consideration of reabsorption of the radiation by the plasma in the presence of high-intensity nonequilibrium radiation.

When gas-dynamic processes proceed much more slowly than collisional and radiative ones, the quasi-stationary approximation can be applied. This type of quasi-stationarity is defined by rate processes, for example, as in the coronal equilibrium model<sup>11</sup> and the collisional-radiative equilibrium (CRE) model,<sup>4,12,13</sup> which are widely used.
--[p260]-- In a sufficiently simple case the problem may be considered by using the Biberman– Holstein approximation, which is valid when spectral lines do not overlap. This is not applicable, however, for a multicharged-ion plasma, where there are a lot of overlapping spectral lines. On the other hand, the full system of the levelpopulation kinetic equations, including the processes induced by the nonequilibrium radiation field, is complicated for direct calculations.
--[p260]-- In addition, in a detailed approach, it is difficult to describe correctly all important states and transitions with all necessary processes in multicharged plasmas such as plasmas of xenon or tin in the tenth degree of ionization. However, these factors alone do not limit the wide application of the full level kinetics.
For practical applications, the numerical procedure should be simple enough and its cost, in terms of computation time, must be low enough to be used in 2D RMHD simulations.
One suitable solution is to use an average-atom model<sup>4</sup> where all possible states and transitions are taken into account.

===== [p296-298] Z∗ Code for DPP and LPP Source Modeling > 8.4.3.1 Xe and Sn slab targets and Xe gas puff (8块) =====
--[p297]-- Lower plasma density means exponentially lower EUV reabsorption in that direction. This is particularly important in the case of Xe, where the absorption coefficient at the inband wavelength is large.
The maximum in EUV emission is reached at 5.7 ns in both cases. At the brightest region in EUV emission, the electron temperature is $T _ { \mathrm { e } } \approx 5 0 – 6 0 \ \mathrm { e V } ,$ and the mass density is $\rho \approx 0 . 1 \mathrm { - } 0 .
--[p298]-- 2 \ \mathrm { g } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ , which is lower than the critical density for 248-nm wavelength. The inband (13–14 nm) radiation efficiency was presented in Ref. 38. The result has been recalculated for a 2% bandwidth, and Fig. 8.20 shows the EUV radiation efficiency for the Xe and Sn slab targets as a function of laser energy input.
In this calculation, reabsorption of EUV by the expanding plasma was taken into account in the multigroup radiation transport.
--[p296]-- The dynamics of the plasma evolution for the Xe and Sn targets are presented in Fig. $8 . 1 9 ^ { 3 8 }$ for a laser energy of 0.12 J, corresponding to an intensity of 2.3 TW/cm<sup>2</sup>.
In general, the plasma dynamics is similar in the two targets.
--[p296]-- 8.4.3.1 Xe and Sn slab targets and Xe gas puff
Calculations were done with a simple slab solid-target geometry, and simulations were performed for short-wavelength 248-nm KrF laser light, since xenon has a high absorption (more than tin) in this case. The laser-beam profile was set at 10-ns FWHM with a focal spot of 25-µm diameter. The laser energy was varied between 0.01 and 1 J. A solid xenon target under cryogenic initial temperature and a metallic tin target were modeled.
--[p298]-- The average attenuation in the hot plasma is about 0.5 at the moment of maximum emission. As we can see, the EUV efficiency for the Sn target has a maximum $\mathrm { C E } \approx 2 . 6 \%$ around a laser energy of 0.1 J for 248-nm laser wavelength. The optimum condition for the Xe target is at a higher laser energy, ≈0.6 J, with a CE ≈1.5%. From Fig. 8.19 we can see also that at the end of the laser pulse, craters of about 80 µm in diameter appear in the targets.
--[p297]-- Due to the different EOS, a higher density is created behind the shock wave in tin. The tin plasma splashes, with the formation of a cumulative dense jet on the axis (this jet sometimes produces intense short emission spikes). Approximately half of the absorbed laser energy is reemitted.
In neither case does the plasma expand isotropically. It is more rarified along the laser beam axis due to plasma heating in this region through bound-bound laser-light absorption.
--[p298]-- The material from them contributes to debris.
In the same Fig. 8.20, the efficiency of a xenon gas-puff target is presented. It is significantly lower due to lower laser absorption by the relatively low-density plasma. The gas-puff plasma modeling was performed for the experiment at FOM.<sup>41</sup> It is illustrated in Fig. 8.21, showing the shock-wave excitation by a double laser pulse to increase the plasma density.
--[p296]-- The laser light is absorbed at first in regions with high enough density; a plasma is created and expands; the laser light penetrates deeper into regions with density 0.1–0.2 g/cm<sup>3</sup> and heats up the plasma volume, creating an intense shock wave, which propagates into the solid material.
In detail, some differences in the dynamics can be seen. Tin absorbs a little less laser energy (0.05 J) than xenon (0.07 J), but due to its lower atomic weight expands faster.

===== [p298-299] Z∗ Code for DPP and LPP Source Modeling > 8.4.3.2 Spherical Xe and Sn targets (5块) =====
--[p298]-- 8.4.3.2 Spherical Xe and Sn targets
Some of the experiments on LPP EUV sources were performed with IR glass lasers at 1064-nm wavelength using spherical droplet targets. $Z ^ { * }$ was used to model such
LPP sources. A flat laser pulse of 15-ns duration and 30–300-mJ energy, focused to a 40-µm-diameter spot, was considered in the simulations. The target was either a solid tin or a cryogenic xenon droplet, with a 30-µm diameter.
--[p299]-- Laser absorption and EUV emission are localized mainly at the critical density. The interaction of the laser light with plasma at critical density is unstable, and the emitting shell consists of hot spots. The brightest points in EUV have a high temperature of 67 eV and a mass density of 0.018 g/cm<sup>3</sup>.
--[p299]-- The inband EUV yield recalculated to a 2% bandwidth from the Sn target reaches 2.46 mJ, or 1.48 mJ in 2π sr, recalculated to a solid angle around the laser beam. The CE is about 3%. This is higher than that obtained for the xenon droplet, at 0.32 mJ in 2π sr and CE ≈0.65%.
It should be noted that the effective total emission solid angle is less than 4π, as there is a shadow behind the dense plasma due to the target. The emitting plasma has the shape of a conical shell.
--[p299]-- The source position of the EUV-emitting region moves in time, moving more than 5 µm up due to plasma expansion in the first half of the pulse, and then 25 µm down due to target ablation and acceleration of the remaining dense part under the ablation pressure (rocket motion).
--[p299]-- We shall compare Xe and Sn target emission efficiencies in the EUV band at an incident laser energy of 50 mJ. The dynamics of Xe and Sn LPPs are represented in Fig. 8.22. In Fig. 8.23, graphs of the laser-power absorption by Xe and Sn targets are presented together with the EUV emission pulses.
The xenon target has absorbed 34 mJ, and the Sn target absorbed 48 mJ, due to a higher bound-bound absorption.

• The spectral efficiency is rather low. Although for a given temperature this source emits the highest flux, 98.5% of the emission is OOB. The consequence is obvious: an effective emitter must be tuned to higher spectral efficiency by reducing the OOB emission while keeping the inband emission as close as possible to the Planckian limit.
For a short-pulsed transient emitter, overheating may be an effective strategy if the excess energy is gained in the cooling phase.
--[p237]-- This optimized Planckian radiator would emit about $1 0 ^ { 7 } \ \mathrm { W / m m ^ { 2 } s r }$ of EUV inband radiation (dotted line in Fig. 7.2; the broken line gives the total radiance). In order to keep it emitting, at least the total power emitted must be replenished, which corresponds to driving powers of at least $1 0 ^ { 9 } \mathrm { W } .$ . It is thus obvious that highly efficient EUV sources must be operated in the pulsed mode.
--[p236]-- For a blackbody radiator to be most efficient for a selected spectral band, the emission of use must be tuned to be as large as possible compared to the rest of the emission, which is usually referred to as out-of-band (OOB) emission. The Stefan-Boltzmann law gives the emission integrated over the full spectral range. By definition, the radiator efficiency equals the radiator efficiency for an ideal Planck radiator.

===== [p281-282] Z∗ Code for DPP and LPP Source Modeling > 8.4 EUV Radiation Source Simulations (13块) =====
--[p281]-- DPP EUV radiation sources belong to a class of discharge plasmas where a driving current flows along a mainly axial direction—the Z pinch. In the Z pinch, a high-density plasma (HDP) is created by the driving current through electromagnetic forces, and heated to a high temperature by the same current. Properly designed, such a high-energy-density, tight plasma structure can transform electrical energy efficiently into radiation.
--[p281]-- In a fast Z pinch, the influence of MHD instability is less significant and the pinch is controlled, but the compression may not be very high, due to shock formation and preheating of plasma ahead of the compression. To obtain a high enough temperature in a fast Z pinch, it is necessary to have a high rate of current rise $( > \mathrm { { i 0 } ^ { 1 2 } \ A / s ) ^ { 1 5 } }$ and high current density $( > 1 0 ^ { \dot { 5 } } \mathrm { ~ A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } )$ .
--[p281]-- At the same time, it is known from the experience of Z-pinch plasma study that such a plasma is unstable to $m = 0$ MHD neck instability and $m = 1$ 3D kink-mode instabilities.
From instability considerations, Z pinches may be classified as follows: fast Z pinches with current pulse time shorter than the inertial time $t _ { \mathrm { c } }$ of Z-pinch compression,<sup>30</sup> and slow ones with pulse time much greater than the MHD time.
--[p282]-- This gas can trigger an additional current path, or current leakage, when the local voltage increases as a result of inductive and resistive effects during plasma pinching.
In a small-volume discharge, as is typical in a capillary discharge, another situation takes place. Due to the physical size of the capillary, the plasma dimension is less than the skin depth. There is no current sheath in this case, and the discharge plasma is compressed volumetrically by the magnetic field.<sup>21</sup>
--[p282]-- To find optimal parameters for the emission under complicated conditions within different plasma devices, detailed numerical simulations were carried out. The plasma characteristics and radiation performance of these devices in the EUV spectral band are presented.
--[p282]-- In cylindrical systems, it compresses down onto the axis, i.e., the column of plasma pinches down. Because the compression rate is higher than the local sound speed, a shock wave is produced ahead of the compressing sheath structure. It ionizes and collects the gas during its motion, but some part of the gas is not captured into the motion and rests behind the sheath.
--[p282]-- This point of extremely high energy density can be achieved when the radiation rate is higher than the heating rate in a plasma column undergoing compression by its own magnetic pressure, a phenomenon sometimes referred to as “radiative collapse” or, more appropriately, radiation-assisted magnetic compression.
--[p282]-- In the simulations represented below we shall consider the influences of some of these described effects on the radiation emission. A series of simulations using $Z ^ { * }$ on plasma configurations such as the capillary discharge, dense plasma focus, and LPP has been performed, with a view to evaluating the functionality and suitability of such plasma systems for the purpose of plasma EUV radiation sources.
--[p282]-- The density and temperature are limited by plasma outflow and consequent destruction of the MHD Z-pinch structure.<sup>31</sup> On the other hand, in a high-Z plasma, such as that encountered in the DPP EUV sources, the radiation rate is high and it is possible to utilize this neck structure to create an intense radiation point.
--[p282]-- Yet another classification can be considered from the point of view of the current-sheath formation. The plasma conductivity limits a rising current to flow within a certain thickness on the surface of the plasma, defined by the skin depth. In a large-volume discharge the current flows initially in a layer much thinner than the chamber size and forms a current sheath. The sheath is accelerated by the magnetic field pressure and compresses the plasma ahead of it.
--[p281]-- In slow $Z$ pinches, plasma compression is ahead of current rise and the motion is oscillatory, i.e., compression is followed by expansion and the cycle repeats. After a few oscillations the Z pinch is destroyed by MHD instability.
The neck or sausage instability creates a localized region of high density and high temperature.
--[p281]-- 8.4 EUV Radiation Source Simulations
DPP and LPP radiation sources have demonstrated promising features to satisfy the conditions necessary for a source in EUVL. The exact plasma characteristics most suitable for optimum EUV radiation are not clear and have not been reported in any detail. This hampers the scaling of each of the different types of discharges for EUV to higher radiation yield and has made objective comparison of DPP and LPP difficult.
--[p282]-- The key issue for EUV source application is whether this phenomenon can be controlled and whether the electrical energy in the system can be transferred to this pointlike structure, in time and in space, and can be efficiently converted to EUV radiation.<sup>44</sup> The neck formation may be induced by means of, for example, the initial density distribution, or by a special electrode form, or by organization of the special dynamics of the current sheath.

This set of equations is significantly smaller and simpler than Eq. The implicit nonlinear dependence between the radiation and the material properties remains the same.
--[p357]-- Here, the radiation field is discretized in frequency, and the absorption and emission coefficients are averaged over a single frequency interval:
$$

$$
--[p357]-- The main complication arises from the fact that photons can be emitted and reabsorbed many times in optically thick spectral regions before being emitted, and escaping, in an optically thin spectral region. This behavior is reflected in slow convergence rates for the numerical solution unless special techniques are used. Developing general techniques that can be used with the variety of atomic models mentioned above remains an area of active research.

$$

$$
This is most appropriate in the optically thin limit, i.e., when $\tau _ { \ v } \ll 1$ .
--[p357]-- This equation is used heavily for radiation-hydrodynamics calculations and does quite well in many applications, due to the use of the two absorption coefficients with their different properties. However, the restriction to (near) LTE situations remains.
For conditions far from LTE, it is usually the case that some significant portion of the spectrum is optically thin and the full radiative-transfer equation must be solved.
--[p356]-- In plasmas that are optically very thick, the radiation at large optical depths will be nearly isotropic. In this case, the radiative-transfer equation can be well approximated by a diffusion equation:
$$
\frac { 1 } { c } \frac { \partial J _ { v } } { \partial t } - \nabla \frac { 1 } { 3 \alpha _ { v } } \nabla J _ { v } = \boldsymbol { \eta _ { v } } - \alpha _ { v } \boldsymbol { J _ { v } } ,\tag{10.23}
$$
where
$$

===== [p259-259] Z∗ Code for DPP and LPP Source Modeling > 8.1 Introduction (11块) =====
--[p259]-- 8.1 Introduction
An EUV source is a critical component for the industrial extension of EUVL to feature sizes of 45 nm and beyond. In the ITRS road map,<sup>1</sup> the current specification requires an EUV source capable of producing inband radiation at 13.5 nm in excess of 115 W collectable over a 2% bandwidth at the intermediate focus (IF). This calls for extreme plasma parameters of unprecedented radiation efficiency.
--[p259]-- DPPs, such as the hollow-cathode-triggered (HCT) Z-pinch, capillary discharge, and dense plasma focus (DPF), and also LPPs, are considered as possible candidates for the creation of a compact EUV radiation source. In plasma discharges, low-Z materials such as Li $( Z = 3 )$ or various high-Z materials such as Sn $( Z = 5 0 )$ , In $( Z = 4 9 )$ , or the gases Kr $( Z = 3 6 )$ and Xe $( Z = 5 4 )$ , for instance, are considered for the generation of EUV radiation.
--[p259]-- 8.4, a number of case studies utilizing $Z ^ { * }$ for both DPP and LPP will then be presented, allowing us to highlight some of the unique features of both $Z ^ { * }$ and the specific plasma configurations of interests. The strengths and weaknesses of $Z ^ { * }$ in its current implementation can be seen for these examples.
--[p259]-- In such sources the complicated atomic and plasma physics, the nonstationary, nonequilibrium ionization process, and the radiation transport and plasma dynamics with self-consistent electromagnetic field (for discharge plasmas) interact strongly with each other. In a DPP plasma, heating is effected through several physical mechanisms: Joule dissipation; viscous kinetic energy dissipation, driven by the magnetic j × B force, in compression waves; and P dV work of the preheated plasma.
