In Sec. 8.3, we will describe the numerics developed in $Z ^ { * }$ to allow treatment of this physics in real-world plasmas with realistic boundary conditions. In Sec.
--[p259]-- In this chapter, we will briefly describe the physical fundamentals of a strongly radiating, high-energy-density plasma, before expanding on the numerical methods adopted in $Z ^ { * }$ to accurately and effectively simulate such a plasma. We will cover in Sec.
--[p259]-- The 5p-4f transitions in xenon ions Xe XI and 4d-4f resonances of a set of tin ions Xe V–XIV emit intensely in the 13.5-nm 2%-bandwidth spectral band.<sup>2</sup> Knowledge of the behavior of discharge plasmas with low- and high-Z elements is critical for the study of DPP or LPP and is of vital importance in the design of EUV sources.
A suitable source of radiation in the case of a high-Z radiator is the radiating multicharged ion plasma heated up to tens of electron volts.
--[p259]-- The energy deposition in the discharge often exceeds 10 keV per ion to create the highly charged ion plasma. The ionization degree may reach 10 or higher. A significant part of the deposited energy is radiated. Radiation may be partially trapped, especially in the most intense lines. Optical properties and the plasma equation of state (EOS) are, as a rule, in conditions far from local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE), i.e., in a non-LTE state.
--[p259]-- $Z ^ { * }$ is a computational code,<sup>3</sup> designed at EPPRA in collaboration with the RRC Kurchatov Institute, the Troitsk Institute of Innovation and Fusion Research (TRINITI), and the Keldysh Institute of Applied Mathematics, Moscow, Russia, to focus specifically on the modeling of a multicharged ion plasma in experimental and industrial facilities, using a radiative magnetohydrodynamics (RMHD) approach.
--[p259]-- Modeling of complete plasma dynamics together with ionization phenomena and radiation transfer demands a rigorous approach such as that developed in high-energy-density physics (HEDP).
--[p259]-- To find optimal conditions for the emission under complicated plasma behavior with an extensive set of parameters, it is important to use computer simulations. In view of requirements for size and stability, the emitting plasma source should be close to spherical or cylindrical symmetry. A complete plasma simulation tool with at least 2D effects should be used to model the transient plasma and to evaluate the radiation production.

===== [p271-271] Z∗ Code for DPP and LPP Source Modeling > 8.3 Computational RMHD Code $Z ^ { * }$ (5块) =====
--[p271]-- Plasma radiation properties, ionization, and the EOS, as well as excitation and ionization rates and plasma kinetic coefficients, are calculated by means of interpolations from a set of tables prepared in preprocessing. Another set of tables prepared by the preprocessor is used for the postprocessing treatment of data obtained by the RMHD processor, to calculate detailed spectra of the plasma emission with high resolution in specific spectral bands—EUV or other regions as desired.
--[p271]-- It has been developed to perform calculations in complex geometries of electrodes and insulators with improved cold-start ionization processes and radiation transfer in nonequilibrium regimes, and to provide a high robustness at the same time.
The code $Z ^ { * }$ is designed on the basis of the MHD equations of multicharged ion plasma in a 2D axially symmetric geometry with full radiation transport.
--[p271]-- Interpolations of preliminary prepared databases allow the code to avoid online calculations of a variety of processes such as plasma dynamics, atomic physics, and ion kinetics. As a result, the robustness of the code and accuracy of calculations of the main processes can be considerably increased.
The code $Z ^ { * }$ also includes an interactive interface for graphical adaptive computation-grid construction.
For exploration of calculated data and presentation of results, a standard graphical package is applied.
--[p271]-- 8.3 Computational RMHD Code $Z ^ { * }$
The code $Z ^ { * }$ is a numerical modeling tool developed for complete simulations of the behavior of a multicharged ion plasma in experimental and industrial facilities, using an RMHD formalism. It is derived from the well-proven code ZETA,<sup>18</sup> developed for the purposes of plasma modeling in HEDP by the same team that put together $Z ^ { * }$ .
--[p271]-- Using ZETA, various plasma systems on different large pulsedpower generators such as ANGARA-5 in TRINITI (Russia),<sup>19</sup> the ${ \cal Z }$ accelerator at SNL (USA),<sup>20</sup> and others have been simulated. ZETA was also successfully applied to simulate EUV radiation sources on the basis of capillary discharges on nanosecond<sup>21</sup> and microsecond<sup>22</sup> time scales.
$Z ^ { * }$ is a special development designed specifically for complete simulations of industrial plasmas.

===== [p386-387] Conversion Efficiency of LPP Sources > 11.4.2 Detailed atomic model with use of HULLAC code (8块) =====
--[p386]-- It is shown by O’Sullivan that the configuration interaction (CI) changes the EUV spectrum of Xe and Sn significantly.<sup>41,42</sup> We investigate the effect of CI by comparing the calculations including different sets of configurations using $\mathrm { \dot { H } U L L A \dot { C } ^ { 4 3 } }$ and GRASP.<sup>44</sup> It is shown that the binding energy of the ground configuration $( 4 \mathsf { d } ^ { n } )$ is shifted by amounts up to 10 eV by the CI effect with twoelectron excited states such as $\dot { 4 } \mathrm { d } ^ { n - 2 } 4 \mathrm { f } ^ { 2 }$ . However, the wavelengths of 4d-4f and 4d-5p transitions are found to be rather sensitive to the CI between upper states, because in the presence of orbital collapse these configurations have similar excitation energies.
--[p387]-- The calculated wavelengths of the resonance lines of Xe and Sn ions are summarized in Fig. 11.5. Here the HULLAC code was used in the calculation of the energy-level structure. In the case of Sn, the effect of the CI brings the wavelength of both 4p-4d and 4d-4f transitions of $\mathrm { S n } ^ { 8 + - 1 2 + }$ near 13 nm. In the case of Xe, it is shown that 4d-5p transitions of 10+ ions make the main contribution to the EUV emission in the 13.5-nm band.
--[p386]-- 11.4.2 Detailed atomic model with use of HULLAC code
A detailed atomic model is required for predicting the spectral profile of the transition array, which depends on atomic number, ion charge, and plasma conditions, and estimating the fraction of emission power in the desired bandwidth. The plasma temperature for the lithographic EUV source is between 20 and 50 eV, where the ion charge is around 10. The near-10+-ionized Xe and Sn have a ground configuration of $4 \mathrm { d } ^ { i }$ .
--[p386]-- These N-shell ions exhibit strong emission through 4d-4f resonance lines at the EUV wavelength.<sup>40</sup> Because of the half-filled N-shell configuration, the emission line consists of a large number of fine-structure transitions. Furthermore, the emission lines from several different charge states overlap each other, and the observed spectrum of 4d-4f transitions usually appears as a broad transition array with $\Delta \lambda / \lambda \approx 0 . 1$ .
In the case of Xe and Sn, the 4d-5p transition array also appears in the same wavelength region.
--[p387]-- Since the inclusion of a large number of multiply excited and inner-shell-excited configurations is necessary in order to calculate the spectrum, we apply a mixed model approach, in which the detailed term accounting (DTA) model is used for the resonance lines, whereas finestructure transitions are averaged to form unresolved transition arrays<sup>46</sup> (UTAs) for satellite lines.
--[p387]-- The present model allows us to practically reproduce the experimental spectrum, which originates from overlapping millions of fine-structure transitions. Furthermore, for the accurate estimation of the CE of the EUV source, we calculate the wavelengths and the spectral distribution of the resonance lines using HULLAC, including the effect of the CI.
--[p387]-- On the other hand, the wavelengths and widths of satellite lines are obtained from calculations without the CI, because the CI is less critical for the wavelength of individual lines.
With the present atomic model, we calculate the emissivity and opacity of Xe and Sn plasmas in CRE. Furthermore, we calculate the EUV spectrum to study the experimental spectral structure, as will be discussed in Sec. 11.5.3.
--[p387]-- We calculate the ion abundance and level population of Xe and Sn ions using the collisional radiative model<sup>45</sup> (CRM), taking into account the energy-level structure, which is similar to those shown in Fig. 11.6.

===== [p54-54] EUV Source Technology: Challenges and Status > 1.3.4.4 Li LPP (3块) =====
--[p54]-- Remaining challenges for Li LPP technology are the laser power and additional system issues that may surface as the source performance data becomes available for Li LPP-based EUV sources.
--[p54]-- 1.3.4.4 Li LPP
Li LPP was recently chosen by a supplier as the technology for achieving highpower EUV sources.<sup>9,16,71</sup> The supplier has demonstrated a 2.5% CE using a 351- nm excimer laser. The initial spectra have shown smaller OOB radiation than for Sn LPP. Due to their smaller atomic weight, Li ions cause less erosion of the collector mirrors, and the deposited Li metal can be removed by heating the mirrors to $4 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ .
--[p54]-- The same supplier has also demonstrated a coating for collector mirrors that may be able to control the diffusion of Li into the mirrors. In addition, a Li droplet delivery system with droplets of 50-µm diameter and operation frequency of 48 kHz has been demonstrated. No EUV source power results have been yet reported.
Similarly to Sn LPP, 149 W of power can be estimated for a 15-kW power input. However, if SPFs are not necessary for Li LPP, higher EUV source power may be achieved.

===== [p240-241] Fundamentals and Limits of Plasma-based EUV Sources > 7.4 Fundamental Processes (6块) =====
--[p240]-- 7.4 Fundamental Processes
In order to generate a small volume of plasma as an effective pulsed emitter of EUV radiation, matter must be heated and ionized to the ground state of an ion that has radiative transitions of suitable wavelengths, and finally these transitions must be excited by electrons of sufficient energy and density.
In a first approximation the ionization potentials of ions of interest all are about $4 / 3$ of the energy of the photons to be generated.
--[p241]-- Typical rate coefficients S for ionization are in the range of $1 0 ^ { - 7 } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } / \mathrm { s }$ for neutral atoms (i.e., removing the first electron), and in the range of some $1 0 ^ { - 8 } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } / \mathrm { s }$ for all the other outer-shell electrons. For low-Z elements two to five stages of ionization must be undergone, and for high-Z elements 10 or even more stages.
--[p241]-- As the time constant of ionization is the rate coefficient times the electron density, single ionization in 10 ns requires a minimum electron density of at least $1 0 ^ { 1 \dot { 6 } } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - \overline { { 3 } } }$ . The ionization is governed by the confinement parameter $\Phi = t _ { \mathrm { p l a s m a } } n _ { \mathrm { e } } S$ for the corresponding ionization stage. If $\Phi < 1$ , then ionization does not occur effectively.
--[p241]-- If $\Phi > 1$ , then ionization can be completed. A good tuning of the EUV plasma is to generate electron densities such that $\Phi \approx 1$ for the radiating ion of interest. Then ionization into the ground state is achieved, while over-ionization is avoided. Hence, $1 0 ^ { 1 6 } – 1 0 ^ { 1 8 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ can be seen as the minimum and in some respects the optimum electron density for effective EUV emitters.
--[p240]-- For EUV around 13.5 nm this leads to ionization potentials of 120–130 eV. This estimation is based on the knowledge that the first resonance lines (as, e.g., the Lyman-α lines in hydrogenlike ions) are of highest intensity. In plasmas, as a rule of thumb, a given ion is best emitting, i.e., is of high abundance, if the electron temperature is in the range of $1 / 5$ $1 / 4$ of the ionization potential.
--[p240]-- This gives the range of desirable electron temperatures as $1 / 4$ to $1 / 3$ of the desired photon energy, which results in an estimate of 23 to 31 eV; this is nearly the same value as the blackbody approach demands.
Ionization and excitation must be accomplished within the lifetime of the plasma.

===== [p357-357] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.5.3 Influence of atomic physics on models (1块) =====
--[p357]-- 10.5.3 Influence of atomic physics on models
The atomic physics of multiply charged ions relevant for nanolithography, either xenon or tin, is mainly related to the 4d-4f and 4d-5p transition arrays’ properties. They will be discussed first; then we will focus on their consequences for the tin emission spectrum as calculated by the HULLAC code, and finally we will examine to what extent the SCO code may describe the plasma emission.

===== [p409-410] Dense Plasma Focus Source > 12.2 Overview of the Source (7块) =====
--[p409]-- 12.2 Overview of the Source
The main features of our present-generation DPF machines have been described in detail previously.<sup>6–9</sup> Using a reliable, all-solid-state pulsed-power system that is scalable to high repetition rates (6–10 kHz), fast 4.2-kV pulses are delivered to the coaxial electrode set of the discharge with low inductance via a magnetic pulsecompression scheme.
--[p410]-- In order to address several development areas in parallel, in our investigations seven DPF machines were assembled. They served to focus on different issues such as plasma optimization, thermal engineering, power scaling, metrology, and debris mitigation. In most of our past work we used the “conventional” DPF configuration with a positively biased central electrode (anode) and grounded outer electrode (cathode).
--[p410]-- Higher efficiencies may be attained by optimization of the plasma conditions and also by using better-matched source elements and collector designs with high acceptance angle and coatings for high reflectivity. As described below, significant improvements were obtained in most of these areas.
--[p410]-- However, strong EUV generation with similar conversion efficiencies (CEs) was also observed when a negative voltage was applied to the inner electrode. In this case the DPF can also be operated without preionization in a self-breakdown mode. In agreement with other DPF discharges,<sup>22</sup> the optimum pressure is found to be lower for the negative-polarity DPF, leading to a reduction of absorption by xenon gas.
--[p409]-- The electron temperature, the ion distribution, and therefore also the spectral distribution of the EUV output are dependent on the energy input as well as the gas flow, the pressure, and the pumping speed.<sup>21</sup> Although the majority of our development studies were carried out with xenon gas, we have also operated our sources with good success using metal fuels such as lithium<sup>3,4</sup> and tin.<sup>9</sup>
--[p410]-- Very recently, we described the effects of the electrode polarity on the source performance in a detailed study.<sup>23</sup>
The source output can be scaled by increasing repetition rate, CE, and collection efficiency. This requires improvements and optimization in various areas: the pulsed-power system, thermal extraction, gas dynamics, and electrode materials, as well as geometry and preionization.
--[p409]-- After preionization from separately energized electrodes, an annular moving current sheet is formed between anode and cathode in the discharge gas. The J × B forces then accelerate and compress the plasma to a small dense region on the axis. The pinch event occurs in time near the current maximum (about 40 kA) at a location in front of the electrodes. The highly ionized excited species formed by collisions in the pinch region give rise to intense emission of EUV radiation near 13.5 nm.
For a Xe light source, the DPF operation at a given pressure can be optimized by injecting helium gas in addition to xenon.

===== [p346-347] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.4.3 Xe and Sn emissions (12块) =====

In order to understand in detail the interaction between the laser and the Xe droplet spray, Auguste from CEA-Saclay has developed<sup>38</sup> a code in which this interaction is modeled in a real 3D geometry. In this model one takes into account individual droplets in the spherical approximation, as in the method used previously by Garloff et al.<sup>39</sup> to calculate the interaction of a water droplet with laser light.
--[p347]-- Moreover, in Auguste’s model each realistic configuration of many droplets in the interaction zone is taken into account by 3D laser ray tracing, including calculated absorption and reflection. At the end the results are averaged over all possible droplet configurations. In the paper by Garloff et al.,<sup>38</sup> the plasma density in the droplet is taken for simplicity as being homogeneous inside the sphere.
--[p346]-- The calculation with the CHIVAS code leads to expansion velocities varying between $8 \times 1 0 ^ { 6 }$ cm/s in the coronal regime to $2 \times 1 0 ^ { 6 }$ cm/s for the denser region of the expanding target. Such expansion leads to a macroplasma within a time equal to a fraction of the laser pulse duration. Let us note that these values obtained for the droplet expansion velocity are not far from the sound velocity of an LTE Xe plasma at 30 eV, which is roughly $1 .
--[p346]-- Introducing the experimental conditions into the code, the electron temperature $T _ { \mathrm { e } }$ in the droplet is found to be of the order of 30–35 eV at the laser intensity peak, and the electron density $n _ { \mathrm { e } }$ is found to be slightly lower than $3 . 7 \times 1 0 ^ { 2 0 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ .
--[p346]-- For instance, one may ask whether during the laser action the droplets have enough time to expand and form a macroplasma interacting with the laser in a rather complicated manner. The expansion velocity obtained from the modeling of single droplet with the CHIVAS code performed by the EXULITE group<sup>37</sup> indicates that the formation of such a macroplasma could be possible. Taking into account the specific gravity of liquid xenon as $3 .
--[p346]-- These results, obtained by considering the droplets in the slab approximation, have been checked against possible 2D effects by Auguste,<sup>35</sup> who used the Castor code.<sup>36</sup> The results stemming from the 2D calculations are not different from the results in the slab approximation assumed in the CHIVAS modeling.
An interesting question that relates to this droplet target is whether the lasertarget interaction can be modeled in the approximation of a single droplet.
--[p347]-- In Auguste’s code the assumed fixed form of each droplet density is a Gaussian function.<sup>39</sup> The results obtained from this modeling indicates that important droplet expansion occurs at the beginning of the laser pulse, which results in a rather inefficient overall coupling between the laser and the spray.
--[p346]-- Using a simple collisional-radiative model based on the original work by Colombant and Tonon,<sup>34</sup> one gets that the dominant ion stage is $\mathrm { X e ^ { \overline { { 1 0 + } } } }$ The plasma electron density obtained in this way is quite close to the value established as a necessary (but not sufficient) condition for the LTE regime.

===== [p336-337] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.2 EUVL Source Requirements (9块) =====
--[p336]-- 10.2 EUVL Source Requirements
There is considerable hope for laser plasmas being able to meet the requirements for an EUVL source. This stems from several features. The plasma and the source that is energizing it are separate. The plasma source can be located in free space, far from any secondary sources of debris. With most target designs this allows large angular access to the source, in principle larger than 2π sr.
--[p336]-- Laser plasmas of Xe have been investigated with various target formats. Initially, Xe gas sprays were used.<sup>5</sup> Then, in efforts to increase the fractional emission within the 13.5-nm (2% bandwidth) band, clusters,<sup>6</sup> microscopic jets,<sup>7</sup> and high-speed droplet streams<sup>8</sup> were used.
--[p336]-- The fraction of out-of-band radiation (the radiation that is not reflected by the XUV optics and is therefore largely absorbed by the first collector mirror) must be below its thermal loading limits. Moreover, the particulate and ion emission from the source, usually transmitted by line of sight, must be very strongly inhibited from impinging on the first mirror, in order to preserve its life over many months of operation.
--[p336]-- The separation of laser and EUV source allows for high repetition rates without fear of thermal loading. Nonetheless, the current EUV source requirements are very severe, and significant progress needs to be made to achieve the required performance within acceptable cost scenarios.
The principal performance requirements of an EUVL laser-plasma source are well known and have been summarized in Chapter 2.
--[p336]-- At source brightness levels of ≈400 W in 2π sr and 2% spectral bandwidth at 13.5 nm, the pulse-to-pulse stability must be ${ \sim } 1 \%$ , assuming source repetition rates >10 kHz. The source must be small (<1 mm in size), be stable in position, and be capable of continuous operation for ${ > } 1 0 ^ { 1 1 }$ shots, with ${ < } 3 \%$ downtime for scheduled maintenance. Two other challenging requirements must also be met.
--[p337]-- More recently a new format for delivering microscopic droplet targets of Sn has been devised.<sup>9</sup> As a target material, Sn’s advantage is that the main UTA transitions from many Sn ions $\mathrm { ( S n ^ { + 7 } { - } S n ^ { + 1 2 } ) }$ can contribute to the EUV emission (as with Xe, at a certain plasma temperature—for Sn, $T _ { \mathrm { e } } \approx 2 8$ eV—primarily three ionization states are created). Thus, many more emission lines can contribute to the emission (Fig. 10.3).
--[p336]-- This led very quickly to the selection of Xe, and to a lesser extent ${ \bf O } _ { 2 }$ , as the source materials of preference.<sup>3,4</sup> Both are gaseous, and therefore less threatening with respect to debris. Li-like oxygen emits a strong narrow line from the 4d-3p transition at 13.1 nm. A Xe plasma at a temperature of ≈30 eV will consist predominantly of $\mathrm { X e ^ { + 1 0 } }$ (Fig. 10.1), which has a band of emission in the region of 13.5 nm (Fig. 10.2).
--[p336]-- These considerations have led to several laser-plasma source scenarios with different source media. Early studies<sup>1,2</sup> showed that several source materials can produce emission at the required wavelength (such as Li, ${ \bf O } _ { 2 }$ , Xe, and Sn), but that experiments with massive solid planar targets produced copious levels of particulate debris.
--[p337]-- In principle, tin-doped droplet laser plasma targets should be more efficient in generating 13-nm emission than Xe. Some evidence for this is already available.<sup>10</sup> However, the challenge to make this source sufficiently clean of particulate matter is certainly more difficult.
This chapter focuses mainly on the modeling of Xe and Sn laser plasma sources, since these are the most likely candidates. From a modeling standpoint they are also the most challenging.

===== [p470-473] High-Power GDPP Z-Pinch EUV Source Technology > 14.8 First Commercial Sources for Exposure Tools—EUV Source XTS 13-35 (10块) =====
--[p471]-- Theoretically the combination of the source with a collector optics module with 10% total efficiency would lead to 3.5-W EUV inband power at the IF.
A typical emission spectrum of the xenon-fueled source is shown in Fig. 14.19. The emission spectrum of the radiation is routinely measured with a reflectiongrating spectrograph, which consists of a flat-field grating and a CCD detector.
The spectrum of the Z-pinch source shows a distinct peak around 13.5 nm.
--[p473]-- To estimate the expected collector optics lifetime, samples of grazing-incidence collector optics were placed at 110-mm distance to the plasma. The reflected radiation at grazing incidence was monitored using an EUV inband energy monitor<sup>29</sup> equipped with two multilayer mirrors, a freestanding filter, and a photodiode. A reference signal was monitored simultaneously with an identical detector, which faced the plasma directly.
--[p470]-- 14.8 First Commercial Sources for Exposure Tools—EUV Source XTS 13-35
The development program for Z-pinch EUV sources at XTREME technologies has led to the completion of the first commercial GDPP EUV source prototypes of the type XTS 13-35 (see Fig. 14.17). The sources operate with xenon as fuel. They have been integrated into the EUV microstepper MS 13 developed by EXITECH, Oxford, UK.<sup>26,27</sup> The source design is modular.
--[p470]-- Intel has announced the installation of the EUV microstepper and recently presented first promising imaging results.<sup>28,39</sup> A second EUV microstepper is installed at the International SEMATECH ISMT-North facility in Albany, USA.
The main performance parameter of the source is the output power of 35 W of EUV inband radiation (2% bandwidth) into a solid angle of 2π sr. The nominal repetition rate is 1000 Hz, and the pulse-to-pulse stability is 3σ < 20% (see Fig. 14.18).
--[p473]-- The ratio of the two signals corresponds to the normalized reflectivity of the optics sample. Running the source at the nominal output power of 35 W, the sample reflectivity was kept constant for more than 170 million pulses (see Fig. 14.21).
The noise of the measurement data is related to the online measurement with the two EUV inband energy monitors directed through the debris filter. One of the monitors is behind the optics sample; the other directly measures the inband energy of the source.
--[p473]-- The normalized reflectivity curve in Fig. 14.21 was calculated by dividing the signals of the two detectors.
Further progress in debris mitigation at XTREME technologies has led to optics lifetimes derived from quartz-crystal microbalance devices in the above collector configuration of between 500 million and 1 billion pulses for advanced XTS-type sources with xenon fuel. The achieved lifetime is mainly determined by erosion of the optics surface as discussed in Sec. 14.7.
--[p472]-- The CE into the 13.5-nm band of 2% bandwidth and 2π-sr solid angle is 0.7%.
Extensive lifetime testing of components and optics has been performed with the XTS 13-35 to evaluate the performance and the reliability of the system. Power stabilization, which keeps the output power constant, was simulated by controlling the high voltage of the discharge manually.
--[p470]-- The source is equipped with a debris mitigation system, which was developed at XTREME technologies and extends the optics lifetime (until the reflectivity drops below 90% of the initial value) to more than 100 million pulses. The collector optics used with the source was designed and manufactured by Carl Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany. The EUV microstepper with the XTS 13-35 EUV source will be used for process development in the semiconductor industry.
--[p470]-- The plasma generator (discharge head) must be connected to the vacuum beamline of the EUV exposure tool. A first part of the pulsed-power excitation circuit is directly integrated into the EUV discharge head. A first supply module contains fast high-voltage electronics of the pulsed-power circuit, which must be installed adjacent to the EUV source head. A second supply module, which contains power supplies and computer control, can be installed at a larger distance from the source head.
--[p472]-- Running the source at its nominal output power of 35 W into 2π sr, a discharge lifetime in excess of 100 million pulses was achieved (see Fig. 14.20). With recent improved configurations with larger electrode dimensions the lifetime of the electrode system could be improved to 80 h at 1-kHz repetition frequency, which is equivalent to 300 million pulses.

===== [p260-260] Z∗ Code for DPP and LPP Source Modeling > 8.2 Fundamentals of the Physics of EUV-Emitting Plasmas (2块) =====
--[p260]-- Such self-consistent modeling of plasma dynamics together with plasma radiation is considered in the RMHD approach. In the following, we will discuss the elements that must be considered in such a modeling approach.
--[p260]-- 8.2 Fundamentals of the Physics of EUV-Emitting Plasmas
One of the main characteristics of a plasma emitting intensely in a narrow EUV band is the presence of high-intensity nonequilibrium radiation in a wide spectral range. The plasma cannot be in LTE, for EUV emission occupies only a small part of the blackbody spectrum. The plasma dynamics must therefore be considered self-consistently with a nonequilibrium radiation field.

===== [p288-288] Z∗ Code for DPP and LPP Source Modeling > 8.4.2 Dense-plasma-focus dynamics (4块) =====
--[p288]-- 8.4.2 Dense-plasma-focus dynamics
The DPF configuration attracts attention because the radiation source is outside the interelectrode space and allows radiation to be collected from a large solid angle, almost 2π sr. In addition, in a DPF it is possible to realize nearly all the mechanisms of plasma heating in the discharge through kinetic energy, Joule heating, and P dV work on the plasma, while in other pinch configurations the input of kinetic energy into plasma heating is comparably small.
--[p288]-- The electric power is supplied to the DPF by means of an LC circuit, with the capacitor $( C = 1 . 3 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { F } )$ charged initially up to $U _ { 0 } = 6 . 7$ kV. The switching is performed by an inductive switch LS, changing in inductance from $L _ { 1 } = 7 5$ nH to $L _ { 2 } = 1 . 8$ nH in 50 ns. Together with the impedance of the DPF, the circuit provides a peak current of 70–80 kA, about 140–150 ns from the start of the discharge.
--[p288]-- The vessel is filled by a gas mixture of 10% Xe and 90% He, with total pressure in the range 0.1–2 Torr, the initial gas distribution being homogeneous, with a density $\rho = \mathrm { ( 0 . 1 - 2 . 0 ) } \times 1 0 ^ { - 6 } \ \mathrm { g / c m } ^ { 3 }$ . An initial temperature of 1 eV is imposed in the plasma along the insulator, bridging the electrodes, to simulate preionization of the gas. The ambient gas is at room temperature.
--[p288]-- In Ref. 39, it was reported that in the 13.5-nm EUV spectrum (2% bandwidth), ≈55 mJ per pulse in 2π sr was obtained from a DPF, with an EUV efficiency of 0.45%.
The parameters of the DPF published in Ref. 39 were used as the basis for $Z ^ { * }$ modeling. Simulations were performed in the geometry as presented in Fig. 8.13. Steel is used as the material for the anode and cathode. Alumina is used as the material for the insulator between them.

Solid objects such as electrodes, insulators, and rigid walls are treated with the same set of equations except the equation of motion (they are either motionless or moving with given speed), but with different conductive, nonconductive, radiative, and heat-capacity properties, until they are heated up to sublimation temperature and evaporated.

--[p276]-- The Euler-Lagrange variables<sup>24</sup> retain the advantages of the Lagrange and the Euler variables but reduce their disadvantages. Specifically, the Lagrange variables have no numerical diffusion and allow more precise solution of the MHD equations using implicit schemes, but there are problems of grid crossing that are computationally expensive to solve.
--[p276]-- While the Euler variables have no problem associated with grid crossing, they do have large numerical diffusion due to plasma convection, and thus demand very detailed grids.

--[p276]-- 8.3.2 Effective conservative schemes for plasma RMHD modeling
The physical model established in $Z ^ { * }$ includes the quasi-neutral plasma RMHD equations with self-consistent electromagnetic fields [Eq. (8.8)] and the radiation transport Eqs. (8.5) described above in Secs. 8.2.2 and 8.2.3. The mathematical model is based on a completely conservative, implicit difference scheme in Euler-Lagrange variables.
--[p278]-- To summarize this subsection, the detailed, fully conservative approach described here in the numerical modeling of a plasma RMHD and the bounding surfaces allows $Z ^ { * }$ to carry out robust and reliable simulation of complicated objects, such as multicharged ion plasmas with realistic boundary conditions.
--[p277]-- To realize the completely conservative scheme from the equations of balance, we define values of the density, specific energy, temperature, and pressure in each cell, and of velocity, electric field, and thermal and radiation flux at each node. The corresponding control volumes V are grid cell volumes (for mass and energy equations), or volumes constructed around each node (for the momentum equation), which together form the consistent system.
--[p278]-- This approach allows the code to simulate sophisticated experimental geometries without change of algorithm, and also the introduction of additional boundary conditions. Interaction of the plasma with the external power supply is realized through boundary conditions on the electric $( { \bf E } | _ { \Gamma } )$ and magnetic $( { \bf B } | _ { \Gamma } )$ fields, self-consistent with the electric circuit equations. --[p280]-- In the postprocessor the distributions of plasma parameters such as the density, temperatures, ionization stage, radiation field, and velocities obtained during the RMHD simulation are used as instant background data for recalculation of necessary functions, together with some additional physical processes.
--[p280]-- (8.5) is solved self-consistently along the observation path, both in continuum and in spectral lines, with simulation of the Doppler effect in a moving plasma. The equations of population kinetics are solved in steady-state approximation or chosen to fit the ionization stages calculated during the RMHD simulation by means of the simplified nonstationary ionization model (8.15).
--[p280]-- Ionization and excitation rates, distributions of energy levels, oscillator strengths and widths of spectral lines, and detailed (up to 5000 points) spectral absorption and emission coefficients are calculated by using the code THERMOS, with corrections from known experimental data. Such details are necessary to provide simulation output for benchmarking with experimental observations and to allow the modeling tool to be used for plasma optimization and diagnostic purposes.

--[p280]-- 8.3.4 Spectral ray-tracing postprocessing
The number of radiation spectral energy intervals and angular sectors in a multigroup RMHD simulation cannot be high enough to obtain detailed radiation spectra from a high-Z plasma. The integral approach characteristic of the multigroup method also does not permit the monitoring of particular points in the plasma for diagnostics.

===== [p46-47] EUV Source Technology: Challenges and Status > 1.3.2.4 Spectral purity filter transmission (11块) =====
--[p47]-- Remember that these specifications for OOB are at the IF, and not all of the OOB emitted at the source will be collected there, due to etendue limits and the finite reflectivity of optical elements between the source and IF.
Until recently, the potential need for a spectral purity filter (SPF) has not been widely acknowledged, causing the neglect of precise measurement of OOB radiation and development of SPF technology.
--[p47]-- Today, complete source spectral purity requirements for OOB radiation are not agreed on among major scanner manufacturers. For 130–400 nm, spectral purity requirements are <3–7% (compare the power in this region with the power in the 2% BW around 13.5 nm), and spectral purity for the region >400 nm is not specified. The spectral requirements outside the 2% BW in 18–130 nm have not been addressed by scanner manufacturers, because the multilayer reflectivity in that range is very small.
--[p47]-- The source operation parameters (temperature and density) will affect the OOB radiation; hence systematic measurements of OOB radiation are needed as a function of those parameters.
In today’s EUVL microsteppers, a thin film is used as the SPF, which also doubles as a debris filter and vacuum barrier. Although such filters work well at lower EUV powers, they will not be able to tolerate the thermal load at high EUV power.
--[p47]-- Note that LBNL’s SPFs are based on multilayer mirrors and the efficiency numbers refer to the percentage reflectivity of a multilayer, which is estimated to have an upper limit of absolute reflectivity of 70% at 13.5 nm. It is assumed that a multilayer SPF will replace one of the mirrors in the EUVL scanner, and its insertion will cause an additional loss factor of 30%.
--[p47]-- The experimental data available for Xe DPP<sup>4,50</sup> show that OOB radiation at the source is more than allowed by specifications at IF. It has been shown that in the 5–18-nm region 46%, and in the 18–80 nm region, 9.8% of the total radiation is expected,<sup>49</sup> which may not meet the OOB requirements for an EUV source. Measurements<sup>4</sup> have shown that in the 130–400-nm region, the OOB radiation is 14%.
--[p47]-- Any SPF designed for high-power manufacturing will need to address the thermal load. Recent work has shown the experimental SPF efficiency based on the diffraction rating to be 55%, and the theoretical efficiency to be 60%.<sup>50</sup> Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) has measured the efficiency of its multilayer SPFs to be $4 0 \% ^ { 5 1 }$ but predicts that an SPF efficiency >70% is well within reach (see Refs. 50 and 51 and the references cited in the latter).
--[p46]-- The main radiation bands of concern are 130–400 nm and >400 nm. In the 130–400-nm band, multilayers have significant reflectivity, transmitted radiation will cause flare at the wafer, and the longer-wavelength radiation will heat the optics, reticle, and wafers, causing overlay problems<sup>45</sup> and the need to cool the optics. In addition, there is some concern about the ionization of environmental contamination by vacuum ultraviolet (VUV) light.<sup>46</sup>
--[p47]-- For Sn LPP, data are available for a mass-limited droplet-based LPP system. OOB radiation in the 130–325-nm region was found to be negligible. However, in the 325–850-nm region it is 13%, compared to 9% measured for Xe DPP<sup>4</sup> in the same region. Absolute spectral measurements of OOB radiation for various fuels are needed.
--[p46]-- 1.3.2.4 Spectral purity filter transmission
EUV sources radiate over a range from the EUV to the infrared (IR). The multilayer optics in the EUVL scanner (Fig. 2.6) and grazing-angle collector also reflect in most wavelength regions. This combination of source emission and optics reflectivity will result in a wide spectrum of radiation being transmitted through the system and reaching the wafer. Radiation out of a 2% BW around 13.5 nm is called out-of-band (OOB) radiation.
--[p47]-- One of the scanner manufacturers has made public its estimate for the entire OOB requirements.<sup>45</sup> By assuming that a total OOB radiation at the wafer will need to be <10%, together with OOB radiation of <1% in the <400- nm region and total OOB radiation absorption by a single mirror of <10%, it is estimated that a specification of <3% OOB radiation will be needed in the region of 130–400 nm, 10% in 400–800 nm, and 0.2% in >800 nm to address flare and thermal issues.
--[p47]-- In a recent industry panel discussion, all major scanner manufacturers publicly acknowledged the need for SPFs and agreed that even if they are not included in the final design, it is too risky to assume that SPFs will not be needed.<sup>47</sup> In a recent industry forum,<sup>48</sup> the majority of stakeholders (scanner manufacturers and source suppliers) agreed that SPFs will be needed.

===== [p51-52] EUV Source Technology: Challenges and Status > 1.3.4.1 Laser power (12块) =====
--[p52]-- The laser power density of $1 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 1 } \mathrm { W / c m } ^ { 2 }$ is now believed to be the optimum for generating Sn LPP plasmas with Nd:YAG lasers.
--[p52]-- It expects to increase the laser power per module to 1200 W. In addition, this supplier has demonstrated multiplexing of three lasers to realize 3 kW of laser power and believes that higher power can be achieved by multiplexing.
Reliable $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ lasers with continuous output of 10–20 kW are commercially available. However, they need to be switched to produce the desired pulse shapes. A 30–40% switching efficiency is expected for these lasers.
--[p52]-- The supplier was then able to combine up to three such chains and deliver 4.5 kW of power. No single laser module is expected to meet these laser power requirements. Laser modules will need to be multiplexed to deliver such power.
--[p52]-- Operation has been demonstrated at 4 kHz with a 100-mJ pulse energy per power amplifier, which provides output power of 800 W using a single laser frame with two excimer power amplifiers. With input power of 50 kW, it has a 1.6% wall-plug light efficiency. The supplier roadmap shows an increase to two laser frames and increased operation frequency to 8 kHz per amplifier or 32 kHz overall, with a pulse energy of 220 mJ to deliver 7 kW of power.
--[p52]-- Initial experiments have shown CEs of $0 . 6 \% ^ { 1 2 }$ and $0 . 7 \% ^ { 1 \bar { 5 } }$ with targets for $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ laser pulses.
In addition, excimer lasers have been proposed as the driver for LPP sources for an HVM environment.<sup>16,32</sup> The excimer drive laser in such a source uses a tripleharmonic Nd:YLF seed laser that has been frequency-shifted to match the XeF emission at 351 nm.
--[p52]-- Nd:YAG lasers, $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ lasers, and excimer lasers are being considered for LPPbased EUV sources for HVM. Since a weak dependence of CE on laser wavelength has been shown,<sup>16</sup> the ultimate choice will most probably be decided by the cost of ownership (CoO) of lasers.
A supplier developed a 1.5-kW Nd:YAG laser module using master oscillator– power amplifier (MOPA) architecture<sup>62</sup> and demonstrated reliable operation of 1.5-kW lasers.
--[p52]-- However, because further increases in Nd:YAG laser power are not deemed feasible and cost-effective,<sup>12</sup> this supplier plans to use pulsed $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ lasers as drivers for high-power sources. A third supplier has demonstrated a 1.2-kW, 16.6-ns Nd:YAG pulse laser,<sup>11</sup> which gives a 1% CE and produces 12 W of power at IF. A fourth $\mathrm { s u p p l i e r } ^ { 1 3 }$ has demonstrated operation of a 1-kW Nd:YAG laser module.
--[p52]-- Based on an output of 3.5 kW per frame with 150-kW input power, the supplier expects to achieve 2% wall-plug CE for its XeF excimer drive lasers. This supplier has also demonstrated the feasibility of a sub-100-µm Sn droplet delivery system operating at 36 kHz that can use its high-frequency laser system. There is, however, disagreement on the wall-plug efficiency for excimer lasers; estimates as low as 0.5% have been proposed as realistic.<sup>31</sup>
--[p52]-- This was recently demonstrated in experiments<sup>66</sup> by scanning the Sn targets through the minimal focus of a laser beam (with a maximum intensity of $1 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 2 } \mathrm { W } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } )$ and seeing double peaks corresponding to CE maxima.<sup>66</sup> Experimental and modeling efforts are underway to understand these power density limits in order to develop ways to achieve the maximum CE for Sn LPP.<sup>66</sup> Experimental and modeling results<sup>16</sup> indicate that the required optimum laser power density increases with decreasing laser wavelength.
--[p51]-- Multiplexing high-power lasers has been demonstrated, in which three 1-kW lasers were spatially and temporally multiplexed.<sup>13,24</sup> Although there is no hard technical basis for predicting how many chains can be used for multiplexing, it is a good estimate that up to 15 kW of laser power can be achieved. In principle, higher laser power can be achieved by further multiplexing, thus giving this technology the scalability to enable higher EUV power than current specifications.
--[p51]-- 1.3.4.1 Laser power
High-power lasers are the key enablers of LPP EUV source technology. Consequently, their limitations must be fully understood to understand the limitations of LPP EUV sources. A high average power (15-kW range) and high peak power (hundreds-of-millijoules to 1-J pulses with a width of ${ \approx } 1 0 ~ \mathrm { n s } ) ^ { 6 2 - 6 4 }$ are needed.

--[p315]-- When a neutral atom appears in the hot area, it is ionized, losing energy equal to the ionization energy. At still higher ionization states, the electronic thermal conduction is a main contributor, which is given by the classic Spitzer formula with the correction for nonideality of the plasma. Similarly, we can also calculate the ionic thermal conduction, but it is substantially weaker than the electronic conduction.
--[p316]-- • Thermal conduction conditions are set at the boundaries of the domain and include the given temperature of the wall, the condition of the insulating wall, and the conditions of incoming and outgoing heat flux.
--[p316]-- • Magnetic conditions are set on the magnetic field and include the condition of the driven current in the electric circuit in the area of the feeding voltage, the condition at the conductive walls, and the condition at the axis of symmetry to provide the cylindrical symmetry of the magnetic field.
--[p315]-- The process of energy transfer by the photons emitted from the hotter areas and absorbed by the colder ones is included directly in the form of radiation transport, as described below.
In view of the cylindrical symmetry of a DPP device, we wrote the general set of MHD Eqs. (9.1)–(9.4) in cylindrical coordinates $( r , \varphi , z )$ ; we neglected the plasma motion in the ϕ direction and assumed that the magnetic field had only one component $B _ { \varphi }$ .
--[p315]-- At such different temperatures, several mechanisms can contribute to the thermal conductivity. At low temperatures with low charge state, the classical elastic scattering by neutral atoms gives the main contribution to the total thermal conductivity. Correction is needed to allow for the dependence of the atom diameter on the energy of impact. At higher ionization states, an ambipolar diffusion—the diffusion of the neutral atoms in the plasma—contributes to the total value.
--[p315]-- • Hydrodynamic conditions are set on the boundaries of the hydrodynamic domain and include the condition of free pass, the conditions on the inflow and outflow, and the condition of the symmetry of the device.
--[p315]-- These simplifications allowed us to reformulate the problem in coordinate form, which provided efficient numerical implementation and various easily implemented enhancements.

===== [p448-449] High-Power GDPP Z-Pinch EUV Source Technology > 14.1 Introduction (5块) =====
--[p449]-- This chapter gives an overview of GDPP Z-pinch source basics and an update of the development status of these EUV light sources at XTREME technologies GmbH, operating in Jena and Göttingen, Germany, including some recent achievements (early 2005). Opportunities, challenges, and risks in developing Z-pinch GDPP sources to HVM lithography specifications are discussed as well.
--[p449]-- Thus Z-pinch sources are currently the most powerful EUV sources for lithography development. Their EUV output power is likely scalable to high-volume manufacturing (HVM) requirements. Moreover, with appropriate electrode design, the lifetime requirements of source components also seem to be reachable.
--[p448]-- 14.1 Introduction
The timely availability of EUV light sources, measurement tools, and integrated test systems is of major importance during the development phase of EUVL for use in high-volume chip manufacturing, which is expected to start in 2009. The cost estimates of an EUV exposure tool in combination with sophisticated throughput models lead to a throughput requirement of 80–120 wafers (300-mm diameter) per hour for economic use of EUVL.
--[p448]-- The projection for the necessary EUV output power from the light source is 115 W at a 13.5-nm wavelength at the entrance of the illuminator system for an estimated resist dose of 5 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup>. The EUV power requirement, in combination with the necessary lifetimes of source components and collector optics, has made source technology one of the most critical issues in developing EUVL.
--[p449]-- Gas-discharge-produced plasma (GDPP) EUV sources that are based on socalled Z-pinch arrangements are a promising technological approach to critical technical issues in EUV sources. GDPP Z-pinch sources have been proven to possess a high intrinsic efficiency and very good stability as well as low complexity. Since 2001 the EUV output power of Z-pinch sources at XTREME technologies GmbH has been increased by two orders of magnitude to 400 W in 2π sr in continuous operation (see Fig. 14.1).

===== [p413-414] Dense Plasma Focus Source > 12.6 Thermal Management (6块) =====
--[p413]-- Surface temperature distributions in the range of 650 to $2 0 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for different DPF configurations were examined by means of thermographic imaging. We found that in comparison with negative-polarity operation, a larger energy fraction is deposited at the inner electrode in the case of positive polarity.
--[p414]-- Figure 12.5 shows an example of calorimetric data, at different repetition rates, for the total extracted power as obtained from thermocouple sensors at different positions at the inner and outer electrodes and the chamber. Our results indicate that DPF operation at negative polarity leads to a smaller relative heat dissipation fraction at the inner electrode than does positive polarity.
--[p413]-- 12.6 Thermal Management
Several factors contribute to the heating of the source during operation: Energy is transferred by radiation from the plasma to the electrodes, the chamber, and the debris-shield–collector assembly. Heating by conduction from the plasma and ohmic heating of the electrodes also leads to sizable amounts of transferred energy.
--[p414]-- Computer simulations have been updated using empirical data to more accurately model the detailed thermal loading on the inner electrode. The resulting temperature distribution calculated for the electrode shows good correlation between areas of high temperature in the model and those of highest erosion observed in experiments. Thermal modeling predicts manageable inner-electrode temperatures for up to 3-kHz operation with our second-generation cooling design.
--[p414]-- Thermal test runs at steady-state repetition rates of up to 2300 Hz have been carried out with a total energy of >28 kW removed from the electrodes and the vessel, including the coolant pumping power. Lifetimes of up to 35 million pulses have been demonstrated, the end of life being characterized by noncatastrophic coolant leakage.
--[p414]-- Thermal engineering of the discharge region of our DPF light source has included the testing of different water-cooled designs for the inner electrode using open annular channels, porous-metal channels, and microchannels. Water cooling was also applied to the outer electrode and the vacuum vessel. In addition, manufacturing techniques to produce electrodes using refractory metals such as tungsten and molybdenum and discharge insulator development have progressed significantly.

Data from surrounding charge states are needed because the charge state of the emitter evolves from ionization from below $( q < 1 0 )$ and recombination from above $( q > 1 0 )$ .

Because of the huge volume of type I data needed, it helps to have some sort of scheme to organize it, think about it, and discuss it. This section presents one such scheme.

--[p84]-- The consensus of the FDWG is that $q = 1$ to $q = 1 8$ is needed in order to accurately model EUVL light sources, and that the range $q = 7$ to $q = 1 8$ is particularly crucial. The latter range is thus the focus of this chapter.
The third axis of the energy array gives the energy level within the ion that is specified by the first two axes.
--[p84]-- To uniquely specify the energy level from a fundamental point of view, one needs a complete set of quantum numbers corresponding to the eigenvalues of the exact Hamiltonian. Unfortunately, the latter is not available in practice. Typically, the quantum numbers are specified assuming LS coupling, and then the wave functions are “corrected” by mixing in small components of nearby $L S$ eigenstates. For example,
$$
\Psi = 0 . 9 8 \Psi _ { 1 } + 0 . 0 2 \Psi _ { 2 } .\tag{3.1}
$$
--[p85]-- Industry plasma modelers have already considered thousands of levels in their calculations, and are concerned that this may not be enough. In addition to the levels that directly lead to transitions in the desired wavelength band, other levels can be important because of their indirect influence on the desired radiation (radiative cascade from recombination into higher-lying levels, for example).
--[p85]-- (3.2) is dominant, differences between calculations may result in uncertainties in the coefficients sufficient to make the level identification ambiguous. The need for good ties to clean experiments, therefore, is even greater than usual.
An alternative, operational approach is to delineate the energy levels by the values of their energies. One might hope to compare one calculation with another by comparing line lists.

For each of the many levels in the energy array, there are a large number of associated fundamental data points associated with the variety of dynamical processes that can occur in the plasma (ultimately shifting the electronic occupation of this level). --[p86]-- In some cases, so-called “forbidden” transitions can be stronger than “allowed” ones.
Furthermore, which energy levels are negligible can depend on the details of the plasma processes. For example, dielectronic recombination can indirectly alter the light emitted at 13.5 nm by changing the amount of $q = 1 0$ charge state and/or by leading to excited states that then cascade down to the ground state through multiple steps.
--[p86]-- Which of these transition energies is important is determined not only by their correspondence with the desired wavelength of the emitted light (13.5 nm), but also by the selection rules that allow or forbid transitions between them.
In the case of highly charged ions, where many of the usual selection rules appear to be violated due to strong configuration interaction (level mixing), the question of which transition energies are significant is complex.

===== [p417-417] Dense Plasma Focus Source > 12.9 Spectral and Plasma Modeling (6块) =====
--[p417]-- A more extensive discussion of the Xe spectra, the line group assignments, and the model calculations for different electron temperatures with inclusion of opacity effects is given elsewhere.<sup>21</sup>
For inclusion of a time-dependent fluid description of the plasma, we used the magnetohydroradiative-dynamic research (MHRDR) code described in Refs. 29 and 30. It includes thermal conduction, radiation, ionization, and material properties in an equation-of-state formulation.
--[p417]-- 12.9 Spectral and Plasma Modeling
Modeling of radiative interactions and of the plasma magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) leads to a better understanding of the critical parameters influencing energy coupling and plasma emission. More detailed analysis of the xenon spectra was obtained from a comparison with Hartree-Fock (HF) model calculations.<sup>21</sup> They were carried out in order to obtain information on the various spectral contributions for different pinch conditions.
--[p417]-- A comparison of single-pulse spectra measured with the transmission grating at the same total gas pressure but for different Xe flow rates is shown in Fig. 12.8.<sup>8</sup> An analysis of the relative intensity changes of the Xe IX to Xe XII line groups indicates that the average plasma temperature increases with decreasing xenon flow rate.
--[p417]-- The timing of the pinch is optimized to the discharge circuit with the time constant fixed externally. The circuit and gross electrode geometry can thus be optimized for best plasma performance.
--[p417]-- The calculations reproduce the main features of the experimental spectrum, in particular for the wavelength region at around 13.5 nm that is assigned to many overlapping 4d-5p transitions of $\mathrm { \bar { X e } ^ { 1 0 + } }$ ions. The model calculations also revealed that the influence of the optical thickness on the spectral emission intensities is significant and larger for the 4d-4f transitions than for 4d-5p, due to their higher oscillator strengths.
--[p417]-- Figure 12.9 shows the calculated radial kinetic energy and discharge current as a function of time during the discharge for different lengths of the inner electrode. The magnitude of the radial kinetic energy peak at the instant of the plasma pinch is a measure of the coupling efficiency. The length for which the kinetic energy is maximized corresponds to the best transfer of magnetic energy to internal plasma energy.

===== [p42-43] EUV Source Technology: Challenges and Status > 1.2.3 Utility requirements (9块) =====
--[p43]-- For an Nd:YAG laser, the wall-plug-to-laser-light CE (wall-plug efficiency) is estimated to be 10%, which means 120 kW of power will be needed to generate 12 kW of laser light, which is the amount necessary to produce the required 115 W of power—hence increasing the power requirement for EUV sources by 70 kW over that of a light source for a 193-nm scanner. For 10 scanners this will mean an additional 700 kW of power, which, although a substantial increase, may be acceptable.
--[p42]-- Based on current data, the utility requirements in 300-mm fabs have been estimated.<sup>29,30</sup> In a
HVM 300-mm fab (defined as 30,000–40,000 wafer starts per month), the average power requirement for the entire fab is 50 MW. For a typical fab, 40% of the energy consumed is used by tools. In today’s fabs, 193-nm scanners are the leading-edge-technology scanners. On average in an HVM fab, 10 scanners of leading-edge technology are needed for patterning critical layers.
--[p43]-- The utilities for a 193-nm scanner are rated for 75 kW, which makes consumption by 10 scanners 750 kW, or 4% of the total tool power consumption. For this discussion, the power rating for equipment has been used for the actual power consumption by the tool. In reality, the actual power consumption is less; however, data on it are not readily available.
--[p43]-- However, high-power Nd:YAG lasers do not seem to be technically feasible or cost-effective.<sup>12</sup> Suppliers are looking at a pulsed $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ laser, which is expected to demonstrate ≈8% wall-plug efficiency. The main concern for utility requirements, however, comes with excimer lasers. Present wall-plug efficiency estimates range from $0 . 5 \% ^ { 3 1 }$ to 2%,<sup>32</sup> or a power input from 600 kW to 2.4 MW to generate 12 kW of laser power.
--[p42]-- 1.2.3 Utility requirements
Utility requirements for EUV sources and for a wafer manufacturing fab in general should be considered, since these requirements allow an understanding of why some potential EUV source technologies may not be cost-effective. Although firm numbers are not available for laser utility requirements and full-scale scanners, utility consumption estimates can still point out potential issues.
EUVL is expected to be implemented in a 300-mm HVM fab.
--[p43]-- For an alpha-level EUVL scanner with 25 W of a Sn DPP source, utilities are rated for 150 kW. A good estimate assumes that for a production-level EUVL scanner, ≈ 150 kW of energy will be required, meaning only a modest increase in power consumption is expected in the HVM environment for one EUVL scanner, and ≈750 kW for 10 EUV scanners.
The utility estimate for EUVL scanners will be different if LPP-based EUV sources are used.
--[p43]-- This would mean additional power requirements of 550 kW to 2.35 MW per EUV source, or 5.5 to 23.5 MW for 10 such EUV sources, as compared to 193-nm light sources. Such estimates of additional utility requirements could render excimer-laser-driven LPP EUV sources not cost-effective.
--[p43]-- A 40-W, 193-nm laser used in a 193-nm scanner has utilities rated for 50 kW.<sup>32</sup> An HVM Sn DPP EUV source is expected to consume 30 kW of power; therefore, for DPP EUV sources, no increase in utilities (power consumption or cooling requirements) is expected. Today’s EUVL microsteppers are rated for 100 kW of power usage. Their Xe DPP EUV sources generate 1 W of power using ≈2 kW of power input (based on a 0.5% CE for Xe), or 2% of the energy.
--[p43]-- The power scaling for DPP sources is limited due to thermal management limits on electrode cooling. If future applications of EUVL demand higher power, LPP can provide the needed power scaling. However, the utility requirements for LPP raise concern, depending on the type of laser employed by the EUV source.

===== [p476-478] High-Power GDPP Z-Pinch EUV Source Technology > 14.9.2 Scaling of performance to HVM requirements (13块) =====
--[p476]-- However, because of the size of the EUV-emitting plasma and the observed EUV spatial background of xenon-fueled sources under real conditions with debris mitigation schemes, it is unlikely that etendue acceptance factors above 80% can be achieved without additional means of plasma confinement. The maximum IF power achievable from xenon sources we estimate at 40–80 W. On the way to HVM sources, more efficient emitters will likely have to be used.
As discussed in Sec.
--[p476]-- 14.3, because its emission spectrum is well matched to the reflectivity of the 13.5-nm optics, tin is the most promising candidate for a GDPP source fuel.<sup>18,30,38,39</sup> Tin-vapor-based GDPP EUV sources have been built at XTREME technologies. At the same electrical input energy, the CE for tin was measured to be higher than for xenon by at least a factor of 2. Emission spectra from tin and xenon under the same excitation conditions are shown in Fig. 14.24.
--[p476]-- The intensity of the 13.5-nm emission peak for tin is 2 times higher than that for xenon. Absolute CEs into the 13.5-nm band vary from 1.7% to 2.9%, depending on the method of tin vapor generation: by gaseous supply or by electron-beam or laser-beam evaporation.
In Fig. 14.25 the output power of the tin-fueled source is given in comparison with the xenon-fueled source under identical excitation conditions. The tin-based
--[p478]-- With further development of existing contamination protection schemes, lifetimes in excess of 100 million pulses are expected for mid-2005. This lifetime is about 2 orders of magnitude below the optics lifetime in xenon sources and 3 orders of magnitude below HVM requirements. We discuss this gap further below.
--[p478]-- EUV source can be operated at the same maximum repetition frequency as the xenon source. This repetition frequency is given by the maximum heat removal capability of the porous-metal-cooled electrode discharge unit, which is 20 kW. The maximum power from the tin source amounts to 400 W into 2π sr for 20 kW of power dissipated in the plasma at 2% CE. With existing and manufacturable source collector mirror designs, the power into 2π sr corresponds to 50 W of available power at the IF plane.
--[p476]-- Under these provisions we estimate a maximum EUV power achievable with xenon Z-pinch sources of 600–1000 W emitted in a solid angle of 2π sr. This is the order of magnitude that was estimated to be needed for HVM sources in Sec. 14.1.2.
--[p476]-- 14.9.2 Scaling of performance to HVM requirements
In order to estimate the potential and limits of xenon-fueled sources with respect to HVM requirements, we predict the following possible improvements in development:
1. Improvement of the cooling technology and enlargement of the dimensions of the discharge electrode system will allow heat removal of 30–50 kW from the discharge region.
2. A CE of 2% from electrical power deposited into the plasma to EUV inband radiation can be reached.
--[p478]-- In comparing the tin-fueled with the xenon-fueled sources, it is important to emphasize that the spatial emission from the tin source is more concentrated. In Fig. 14.26 the EUV-inband-emitting plasma shapes are depicted for the xenon source (a) and the tin source (b) under identical excitation conditions. The scale of both inband images of the pinches is the same.
--[p478]-- As for xenon, optics lifetimes of 350–700 h, i.e., 5–10 billion pulses, are projected for β-tool sources today. The application of the developed protection schemes leads to similar results for optics lifetimes in tin sources with respect to sputtering. Because of the well-developed protection against sputtering, the lifetime of optics in tin sources is limited only by contamination today.
--[p478]-- It can be seen that the xenon plasma is more smeared while the emission of the tin plasma has sharp edges and a rather homogeneous intensity distribution. The spatial background emission in the xenon source contains significant energy. The tin plasma shows no visible background radiation. This means that the etendue acceptance factor for the tin source is larger than that of comparable xenon sources. For HVM sources it is also expected to reach values of around 0.9.
--[p478]-- Figure 14.27 shows the normalized reflectivity measured online during irradiation of grazing-incidence collector-optics samples versus the number of pulses while applying both contamination protection and sputtering protection. The reflectivity stays nearly at the same level for about 20 million pulses. The fluctuations in the signal are related to the reference measurement of the pulse energy behind the debris filters. The lifetime is limited by contamination of the optics by tin compounds.
--[p478]-- Despite the high usable IF power of tin GDPP sources, contamination of optics by tin fuel is a new challenge that comes in addition to requirements for optics protection against fast particles, which is also needed for xenon sources. Because the mass and ion energies of tin are comparable to those of xenon with respect to sputtering, similar protection schemes are necessary (see above).
--[p478]-- Therefore, overall collection efficiencies from plasma to IF well in excess of 10% are expected for HVM tin sources.
From currently achieved data, 45 W of the available EUV power could be used in the EUV scanner, provided the collector can withstand the high input power load.

===== [p341-341] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.3.3 Local thermodynamic equilibrium and non-LTE plasmas (6块) =====
--[p341]-- Plasmas produced by nanosecond lasers pulses from high-Z materials cannot generally be considered to be in LTE. Considerable energy is converted into radiation—both line radiation and blackbody Planckian emission—and this radiation plays an important part in determining the population of the available energy states. This is the so-called non-LTE (NLTE) regime. A much more complicated energy transfer situation exists, with the opportunity for many more physical processes to occur.
--[p341]-- However, many laser plasmas can be described as being in local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE), where the populations of available energy levels is determined by electron-ion collisions, and it is assumed that the effects of radiation processes on these populations are negligible.
--[p341]-- 10.3.3 Local thermodynamic equilibrium and non-LTE plasmas
Laboratory plasmas do not satisfy the conditions for thermal equilibrium (TE), i.e., that all electrons, ions, and radiation are strongly coupled and share the same temperature.
--[p341]-- LTE conditions are more likely to be satisfied in laser plasmas of low-Z materials, where collisional processes are dominant over radiative processes, and in plasmas that are optically thin, so that radiation can escape from the plasma. For a Maxwellian electron distribution, the plasma will be optically thin if the electron density $n _ { \mathrm { e } }$ fulfills
$$
n _ { \mathrm { e } } ~ ( \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 } ) \geq 1 .
--[p341]-- 7 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 4 } T _ { \mathrm { e } } ^ { 1 / 2 } \Delta E _ { \mathrm { u } , 1 } ^ { 3 } ,\tag{10.6}
$$
where $T _ { \mathrm { e } }$ is the electron temperature and $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { u , 1 } }$ is the transition energy, both expressed in electron volts. If the plasma is optically thick, that is, radiation generated within the plasma is coupled to the ions and electrons, then lower values of $n _ { \mathrm { e } }$ can be used.
--[p341]-- In addition to electron collisions, radiative deexcitation and photoelectric and recombination processes will come into play. Modeling these processes in an exact way is more challenging.

===== [p430-431] Hollow-Cathode-Triggered Plasma Pinch Discharge > 13.1 Introduction (6块) =====
--[p431]-- Philips Extreme UV, as a joint venture of Philips and Fraunhofer ILT, is running an extensive program to realize high-power sources well suited for production. The source concept is the hollow-cathode-triggered (HCT) gas discharge.
--[p431]-- Many aspects of it have been published in a series of preceding papers.<sup>2–6</sup> The program includes fundamental research on ignition and pinch formation, but mainly focuses on the many engineering problems, such as power scaling, electrode lifetime, collector protection, and closed-loop dose control. So far, Xe has been used as a radiator, which, however, is considered as having insufficient conversion efficiency (CE) to meet the long-term power requirements.
--[p430]-- 13.1 Introduction
The light source has been identified as being the most critical single component on the way to realizing EUVL. The requirements on the source are derived from a throughput model for the processing of up to 120 wafers per hour in a commercial EUV scanner. In the current status of design of the scanner, this means a requirement of 115-W collected inband EUV.<sup>1</sup> The 115 W refers to the power emitted in a 2% band around the center wavelength of 13.5 nm.
--[p431]-- To address this issue, a research program using Sn as a radiator has been started. Sn is well known for its favorable spectral distribution; however, it has the disadvantage of being more difficult to handle. Handling problems occur both in its delivery to and in its removal from the system. Nevertheless, it seems to be the only possibility for ever achieving the required high power levels.
The chapter addresses some of the problems associated with both Xe and Sn sources. In Sec.
--[p430]-- For etendue limits imposed by the optical system, the radiation must be emitted out of a small volume of a few cubic millimeters in order to be collectable by the optical system. Typical collector openings are limited to a geometrical opening of 2–3 sr; collector efficiencies are on the order of 50%–80%. The source power is defined to include all of these above effects.
--[p431]-- 13.2, the physics of ignition and pinching of an HCT source will be described. Section 13.3 summarizes the results achieved so far in developing commercial EUV sources. Emphasis is put on the physical principles rather than the engineering aspects.

===== [p434-436] Hollow-Cathode-Triggered Plasma Pinch Discharge > 13.2.3 High-current phase and basic lifetime considerations (9块) =====
--[p434]-- 13.2.3 High-current phase and basic lifetime considerations
The generation and modeling of EUV radiation by the emission of highly charged ions in the pinch phase is extensively discussed in another chapter of this book.<sup>12</sup> This subsection will focus on the state of the art for the transition from the glow phase of the pseudospark discharge to the arc phase and give some general discussion of electrode erosion.
--[p436]-- Relevant rates and time scales shift drastically when operating with xenon.
The cathode surfaces of HCT electrodes have been investigated by means of electron microscopy. Traces of type 1 and type 2 (following the nomenclature of Anders and $\operatorname { A n d e r s } ^ { 1 5 }$ ) are found on the polished metal surfaces, as in other highcurrent applications of the pseudospark discharge.
--[p436]-- Although the glow-to-arc transition is understood qualitatively in the pseudospark discharge, there is still work to be done for further understanding of the spatial current distribution over the electrode surface for the EUV light source, so as, for example, to minimize electrode erosion by operating in a mode of lowest erosion rate. Most of the existing work refers to hydrogen or helium, which are preferred in switches.
--[p434]-- Generally, in any kind of low-pressure pinch plasma discharge the current density is of the order of $1 0 \mathrm { k A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { \hat { 2 } }$ . The occurrence of cathode spots and thus the evaporation of electrode material, which are delivering the required current from the electrode surface, is unavoidable. The special feature of the pseudospark discharge is the possibility of a relatively homogeneous and simultaneous ignition of cathode spots over a large area.
--[p434]-- The transition from the glow plasma in the hollowcathode phase to the high-current arc phase has been discussed qualitatively in several contributions.<sup>13,14</sup> The hollow-cathode plasma leads to a sheath thickness of typically several tens of microns and a voltage drop on the 100-V scale. This leads to electrical fields in the range of $1 0 ^ { 7 } { - } 1 0 ^ { 8 } \ \mathrm { V / m }$ , which is sufficient for the ignition of cathode spots.
--[p436]-- For low-pressure gas discharges the type 1 spots have the lowest erosion rate: 1–10 $\mu \mathrm { g } / \mathrm { C }$ in a single spot. The net erosion is usually one order of magnitude lower, since most of the evaporated electrode material is redeposited onto the electrode surface after the discharge. Typical erosion rates are on the order of a few micrograms per coulomb, or a few times $1 0 ^ { - 4 } \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 } / \mathrm { C }$ , for metal cathodes.
--[p436]-- Thus strategies must be applied in order to reduce the influence of the electrode geometry in general on the pinch plasma properties and keep the deformation as small as possible. One means is the use of multiborehole arrangements, which is described below. This strategy is also used in other concepts.<sup>16</sup>
--[p436]-- For an HCT EUV source, such an erosion rate would lead to a removal of around 1 $\mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ , or 10 g, after $1 0 ^ { 9 }$ shots. The electrode geometry, however, determines the pinch geometry and also the CE. An erosion of 1 $\mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ would be unacceptably high for a system with a single cathode borehole.
--[p434]-- Typical current densities in the transition phase are in the range of $1 0 { - } 1 0 0 \ \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ . The transition to high-current transport is on the 10- ns scale, which is typically one order of magnitude smaller than the pinch-current duration.

===== [p224-224] Radiative Collapse in Z Pinches > 6.10 Equilibrium Radius versus Linear Density Trajectory (4块) =====
--[p224]-- We emphasize that sliding along the $r ( N )$ path is due to plasma outflow from the neck and this outflow determines the time characteristics of the process. During the evolution the plasma in the neck passes through the temperature interval corresponding to the appearance of ions radiating in the EUV—indicated as $\Delta T _ { \mathrm { E U V } }$ . The range in radial size of the EUV-radiating source is shown as $\Delta R _ { \mathrm { E U V } }$
--[p224]-- 6.10 Equilibrium Radius versus Linear Density Trajectory
Some important features of the neck development can be illustrated using a trajectory on a plane whose coordinates are the compression radius r and the total number of charged particles in the neck cross section, $N = n _ { \mathrm { i } } ( 1 + Z ) \times \pi r ^ { 2 } \approx n _ { \mathrm { e } } \times \pi r ^ { 2 }$ (Fig. 6.7).
--[p224]-- In a simplified approximation the total number of charged particles, N, is straightforwardly connected to the plasma temperature through the Bennett relation $\hat { ( T \propto I ^ { 2 } / N ) }$ . We assume also a constant current in the pinch. The starting point of the trajectory (A) indicates that the initial plasma column was created with a radius $r _ { A }$ , the total number of particles was $N _ { A }$ , and the corresponding initial plasma temperature was $T _ { A }$ .
--[p224]-- The neck development can be seen as the result of plasma outflow from the neck with a subsequent increase of the plasma temperature and plasma compression. Rather soon the plasma reaches the equilibrium radius (dashed curve), and further neck development follows the path $r = R _ { \mathrm { E Q } } [ T ( N ) ]$ (solid line), which may slightly deviate from the equilibrium radius trajectory.

===== [p76-76] EUV Source Requirements for EUV Lithography > 2.5 Conclusions (2块) =====
--[p76]-- 2.5 Conclusions
The joint requirements for EUV sources have been specified by exposure-tool manufacturers, and their bases have been explained above. They will be helpful for source developers and source suppliers. More detailed requirements or specifications for EUV sources are needed for exposure-tool manufacturers; many of them depend on both exposure-tool design and source design. Information exchange between exposure-tool manufacturers and source suppliers will be needed individually.
--[p76]-- However, source development is still the most critical issue for EUVL. The illuminator transmission and the sensitivity of the photoresist, which determine the required source power, need to be improved to relax the requirement for source power.

--[p377]-- Here $g _ { \mathfrak { n } }$ is the statistical weight of the nth level, and $f _ { \mathrm { n ^ { \prime } n } }$ is the oscillator strength. The EUV radiation at 13.5 nm with 2% bandwidth is mostly due to the 4f-4d, 4p-4d, and 5p-4d transitions for tin and xenon.
--[p377]-- If we assume that $l _ { \mathrm { O D = 1 } } = 1 0 – 1 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ , the oscillator strength is $( g _ { \mathrm { n ^ { \prime } } } / g _ { \mathrm { n } } ) f _ { \mathrm { n ^ { \prime } n } } = 1$ , and the abundance of the ions emitting the EUV radiation is 0.1, then the ion density required can be in the range of $1 { \stackrel { \smile } { 0 } } ^ { 1 8 } - 1 0 ^ { 2 0 } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ .
--[p377]-- The required plasma density can be estimated as follows: we consider a planar plasma in which the number density of ions emitting the EUV radiation at 13.5 nm with 2% bandwidth is given by $n ^ { * }$ and of which the length is of the order of $l _ { \mathrm { O D = 1 } }$ defined as the distance corresponding to optical depth 1 for 13.5-nm photons.
