--[p376]-- It should be noted that the etendue of an LPP is mainly determined by the plasma diameter, since the plasma thickness is smaller than the diameter, as will be discussed below.
Since the plasma expansion speed is determined by the ion sound speed $c _ { \mathrm { { s } } } .$ , the diameter of the source plasma can be larger than the plasma expansion distance, if $\Phi > c _ { \mathrm { s } } \tau _ { \mathrm { L } }$ , where $\tau _ { \mathrm { L } }$ is the laser pulse duration.

===== [p423-424] Dense Plasma Focus Source > 12.14 Summary and Conclusion (10块) =====
--[p423]-- Using the burst mode, we have operated at up to 5 kHz with approximately 200 W of inband power. Charging the DPF with negative polarity allows operation in either a selfbreakdown mode or a preionized mode, with slightly different source parameters. The thermal load distribution is more favorable in this case. The trend in CE seems to indicate a saturation at 0.5% with xenon for both positive and negative polarity.

Comparison of our xenon spectra with HF model calculations yielded good agreement and gave valuable information on the transitions contributing to the EUV emission.

--[p424]-- A nestedshell collector arrangement working at grazing incidence angles is suited best for the discharge source. Data collected so far show promise that a rugged, low-cost method is available with a clear path towards higher collection efficiencies. The electrode wear is considerable, and inner-electrode exchange is required after extended operation at high repetition rates.
The power levels required for HVM can be achieved in a DPF source with tin as the source element at thermal extraction powers on the order of 35 kW.
--[p423]-- 12.14 Summary and Conclusion
Significant progress has been made in all aspects of DPF source development over the past years. We have demonstrated continuous improvements of inband EUV output power, CE, and other source parameters. A summary of the source parameters achieved by the end of the year 2003 is given in Table 12.2 for both Xe and Sn. The highest inband output power obtained with xenon in continuous operation mode at 2-kHz repetition rate was 76 W (emitted into 2π sr).
--[p424]-- The use of MHD plasma modeling codes such as MHRDR has allowed us to explore design regions that are not easily accessible experimentally. Reasonably good qualitative agreement has been observed between the variation of modeled and experimentally measured source parameters as a function of electrode length and gas pressure.
Measurements of debris reduction with single- and multiple-channel shields showed reduction factors of 100 per centimeter of channel length.
--[p423]-- Likewise, high degrees of correlation were obtained for EUV emission into different angles from measurements of the angular distribution stability. Imaging arrangements for source size measurements were refined in several steps and yield now consistent and reliable data on the size of the emitting hot plasma zone.
We are continuing to make progress in the thermal engineering of the pulsedpower system and discharge electrodes.
--[p423]-- With the changes outlined in this chapter we expect to be able to operate the pulsed-power system in a continuous mode at >5-kHz repetition rate. The high degree of coupling of stored energy to the discharge (>90%) enables us to operate with a lower total stored energy in the pulsedpower system. The tested electrode cooling designs have demonstrated the capability to extract >21 kW of total discharge power from the electrode with >11 kW from the smaller inner electrode.
--[p423]-- We have successfully demonstrated tin and lithium as more efficient metal target elements. For tin, at equivalent operating conditions, approximately a fourfold increase in EUV output energy and CE was observed over operation with xenon gas. We have implemented several advanced source metrology systems employing EUV photodiodes for output power measurements, and CCD cameras for source size measurements. Both detection schemes show excellent correlation on a pulseto-pulse basis.
--[p424]-- Extrapolation of these results suggests that channel lengths of 4 cm are required. Results of debris mitigation and potential optics contamination studies indicate that low levels of hydrocarbon contamination in the vacuum system continue to be a problem. Significant improvements in the control of the vacuum environment will be required to eliminate EUV- and DUV-catalyzed carbon growth on mirror surfaces.

===== [p395-398] Conversion Efficiency of LPP Sources > 11.5.3 Xenon: effects of satellite lines and opacity (18块) =====
--[p397]-- We here compare analytical spectra with the emission from liquid Xe jet $\mathrm { t a r g e t s } ^ { 4 }$ to clarify these effects, which are shown in Fig. 11.14. In Fig. 11.14(a), the experimental spectrum exhibits a dominant peak near 11 nm accompanied by weaker peaks at longer wavelengths.
--[p396]-- In particular, with the electron density of the emitting region above $1 0 ^ { 2 0 } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ , we find that the population in the plasma approaches LTE, leading to an optical depth of the typical LPP greater than one; thus the opacity effect should be taken into account.<sup>50</sup> As shown in the previous analysis of the spectrum of the 3d-4f transition array from LPP,<sup>51</sup> the satellite lines form a tail structure, called the red wing, on the longer-wavelength side of the resonance lines. As the optical depth of the resonance lines increases, the intensity of the resonance lines saturates due to self-absorption. Consequently, the relative intensity of the satellite lines will increase, resulting in broad spectral width of the transition array.
--[p398]-- Figure 11.15 shows the spectral emissivity of Xe plasma at the ion density $4 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 9 } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ and electron temperature 30 eV. The comparison of the emissivities with and without the effects of CI and satellite lines shows that the broad structure originates mainly from the satellite lines. Furthermore, we have estimated the spectral efficiency, which is defined as the ratio of the inband to the total EUV emission intensity.
--[p398]-- 11.14(c), the emission spectrum calculated including the effect of satellite lines and opacity reproduces the experiment fairly well. Thus, in order to perform a radiation hydrodynamics simulation to predict the CE, we calculated and tabulated the emissivity and opacity of Xe and Sn plasmas as functions of the electron temperature $T _ { \mathrm { e } }$ and the ion density $n _ { \mathrm { i } }$ , using the present atomic model, in which CRE and an optically thin plasma are assumed.
--[p395]-- 11.5.3 Xenon: effects of satellite lines and opacity
We apply the power balance model for a xenon target. Figure 11.13 shows the laser-intensity dependence of the electron temperature and the various loss fluxes. The dependences are almost the same as those with tin, shown in Fig. 11.3.
--[p398]-- We found that since the main part of the emission appears in the 11-nm band in Xe, the spectral efficiency is approximately 1/6 of that of Sn. We also found that the high efficiency is obtained within a limited temperature range, where the $\mathrm { X e ^ { 1 0 + } }$ ion has a significant abundance. It is interesting that the optically thick calculation, shown in Fig. 11.14, yields similar spectral efficiency.
--[p395]-- The power balance model gives a CE of approximately 2% at about $1 0 ^ { 1 1 } \ \mathrm { \bar { W } } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ with 1.2-ns pulse duration, with the use of atomic data obtained from the average-ion model. However, atomic data obtained from the detailed atomic model introduced in Sec. 11.4.2 show that the inband emission is about 1.5% of total emission at an electron temperature of 25 eV, and it decreases with increasing electron temperature, as will be discussed below.
--[p398]-- Absorption between 11 and 12 nm is mainly due to 4d-4f satellites, such as $4 \mathrm { d } ^ { i - 2 } 4 \mathrm { f } n \hat { l } \to 4 \mathrm { d } ^ { i - 1 } n l$ transitions, where nl indicates the orbit of the spectator electron. It is also shown that 4d-5p resonance lines from each charge state have satellites lines, $4 \mathrm { d } ^ { i - 2 } 5 \mathrm { p } n l  4 \mathrm { d } ^ { i - \bar { 1 } } n l$ transitions, on their longer-wavelength side.
--[p396]-- We find from our collisional radiative model calculation that the multiply excited and inner-shell-excited configurations are significantly populated in high-density plasmas, resulting in considerable emission and absorption through 4d-4f and 4d-5p satellite lines.
--[p395]-- Therefore, the CE of 2% could be an overestimate.
The theoretical value of the optimum laser intensity does not agree with experiments. Most of the experiments shown in Fig. 11.1 show that the maximum CE appears at higher intensity, around $1 0 ^ { 1 2 } \mathrm { W / c m } ^ { 2 }$ or more. However, none of the experiments with xenon were carried out with a laser spot size (and target size) greater than 500 µm, as may be required for the validity of the 1D expansion assumed here.
--[p397]-- It is found from our collisional radiative model that for the electron densities $> 1 0 ^ { 2 0 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ and a temperature of 25 eV, all atomic states can be assumed to be in LTE, where the ionization balance and level populations can be determined from the Saha-Boltzman relation. For a spherical plasma in LTE, the radiation intensity $I _ { \nu }$ from its surface is also simply calculated using an analytical formula $\mathrm { a s } ^ { 5 5 }$
$$
--[p398]-- It is found that the emission on the longer-wavelength side of the 4d-4f transition array (11.5– 13 nm) and the background level of the $4 \mathrm { d } \mathfrak { - } 5 \mathrm { p }$ transition arrays (12–16 nm) can be explained only by considering the satellite lines, as shown in Fig. 11.14(c).
Figure 11.14(d) shows the contribution of each satellite channel to the absorption coefficient of the plasma.
--[p396]-- A small target size causes large kinetic loss and thus requires higher laser intensity. We have recently found that experiments with larger target size show that the optimum laser intensity appears around $1 0 ^ { 1 1 } \ \mathrm { W / c m ^ { 2 } }$ , which agrees with the power balance model.
We now discuss the effect of detailed atomic processes on the CE of the Xe plasma in terms of satellite line emission and the opacity of the emission lines.

===== [p350-351] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.5.1.5 Superconfiguration approximation (9块) =====
--[p350]-- The method treats one-electron transitions between all states belonging to two different superconfigurations, starting from the assumption that these transitions can be represented by a Gaussian function of frequency.
--[p351]-- The superconfiguration approximation does not require any a priori knowledge of the relevant ions and transitions involved. For instance, in the case of the SCO code<sup>72</sup> based on that approach, one has just to define a series of supershells that regroup ordinary nl or nlj orbitals.
--[p351]-- It consistently includes the thermodynamics (under the LTE hypothesis; but there exist superconfiguration codes SCROLL<sup>73</sup> and AVERROES<sup>74</sup> that take account of the collisional radiative rate equations).
--[p350]-- 10.5.1.5 Superconfiguration approximation
The UTA and SOSA formalisms are also used as an essential part of the superconfiguration approximation.<sup>70</sup> This approximation is especially useful in mediumand high-Z-element plasmas in conditions in which the number of configurations can be too large for the DCA approach.
--[p351]-- For a given temperature and density, the SCO code then computes a series of relevant superconfigurations, which are defined by a set of integer population numbers for each supershell, such as $[ ( 1 { \mathrm { s } } 2 { \mathrm { s } } 2 { \mathrm { p } } ) ^ { 1 0 } ( 3 { \mathrm { s } } ) ^ { 2 } ( 3 { \mathrm { p } } 3 { \mathrm { d } } ) ^ { 6 } ( 4 { \mathrm { s } } 4 { \mathrm { p } } 4 { \mathrm { d } } ) ^ { 1 } ]$ .
--[p351]-- It is important to stress that both the UTA and the SOSA approach in the DCA as well as the STA-type methods are based on the assumption that the CI can be neglected. This approximation is usually justified in hot dense plasmas.
As will be seen later, detailed atomic codes such as MCHF and MCDF, and parametric potential codes such as the HULLAC code, bear the common drawback that they require some prior knowledge of the relevant atomic parameters for the emission process.
--[p350]-- The three moments characterizing a STA can be calculated via rapid and efficient recurrent formulas<sup>70,72</sup> at the price of the following approximation: the energy of the configuration C that is used in the Boltzmann probability factor $P _ { C } = A \exp ( - E _ { C } / T )$ (A is the normalization factor) has been expressed as
$$
E _ { C } \approx \sum _ { i } q _ { i } ^ { ( C ) } \varepsilon _ { i } + \Big \langle E _ { 1 } ^ { ( C ) } \Big \rangle _ { S } .
$$
--[p351]-- This approximation means that only the term linear in the subshell populations $q _ { i } ^ { ( C ) }$ (i runs over all subshells) is taken into account explicitly, while the term quadratic in the population numbers is averaged over the superconfiguration. In practice the assumption seems to be justified when the energy differences between configurations belonging to the same superconfiguration are of the order of the temperature.
--[p350]-- In the superconfiguration approximation, first proposed in the supertransition array (STA) code,<sup>70,71</sup> the configurations are grouped into superconfigurations that are close in energy. The self-consistent potential (used to obtain the one-electron basis) is now calculated for each superconfiguration, which means that it is averaged over all configurations belonging to that superconfiguration.

===== [p456-457] High-Power GDPP Z-Pinch EUV Source Technology > 14.3 Emitter Materials for 13.5-nm Z-Pinch Sources (12块) =====
--[p457]-- An interesting approach to tin supply is the laser-assisted GDPP EUV source principle as described in Ref. 34, where a laser evaporates tin from electrodes or a separate target and an electrically excited gas discharge uses this tin as target gas.
--[p456]-- The maximum efficiency at Z = 50 can be explained by a manifold of strong 4d-4f transitions that fall into the 13.5-nm band for a range of ionization stages between 8+ and 13+. This emission feature is called an unresolved transition array (UTA), since several thousand transitions occur in a narrow band of roughly
0.5-nm width.<sup>15</sup> The emission characteristic of high-Z elements is a spectral quasicontinuum with lower spectral brightness.
--[p457]-- After substantial progress with xenon GDPP sources, more recently tin sources have been investigated in more detail to explore the limits of the EUV power that can be generated in GDPP sources and to study the debris contamination with tin. Tin has been supplied to the discharge region also in gaseous form after evaporation from solid tin or tin compounds. XTREME technologies’ Z-pinch GDPP sources have achieved CEs of 1.0% with xenon and 2.0–3.0% with tin. For details see Secs. 14.8–14.10.
--[p456]-- A systematic experimental survey of medium- and high-Z elements was performed in the mid-1990s to evaluate the efficiency of EUV plasma emission at 13.5 nm.<sup>14</sup> In order to allow easy experimental access, selected elements with atomic numbers Z ranging from 13 to 82 were excited by a Nd:YAG laser with a pulse width between 7.5 and 30 ns. The EUV efficiency was recorded in a narrow channel around 13 nm.
--[p457]-- The theoretical efficiency of xenon is lower than that of tin because the strong 4d-4f UTA peaks at about 11 nm, while the 13.5-nm radiation originates from a weaker 4d-5p UTA.<sup>17</sup> Because of its condensation-free operation, xenon has been used widely in the development of GDPP EUV sources.<sup>5,6,18–22,40</sup> Xenon is simply supplied in its gaseous state to the pinch region at pressures of approximately 1 Pa.
--[p457]-- Detailed configurations, which use in the simplest case rotating electrodes, are described for a rotating-disk-electrode GDPP source by Borisov et al.,<sup>35,36</sup> and for a laser-triggered multiplexed source by Banine,<sup>41</sup> Koshelev et al.,<sup>46</sup> and Pankert.<sup>42</sup>
In view of the high CE of lithium under laser excitation reported in Ref. 33, lithium may be reconsidered as a fuel for GDPP sources also.
The required density may not be achieved with pure GDPP arrangements. Therefore, laser evaporation is a likely approach for the target supply.
--[p457]-- Kubiak et al.<sup>16</sup> suggested, as a compromise between efficiency and condensation properties, using xenon as target material in order to eliminate condensation of target material on the collector optics.
--[p456]-- Several groups have investigated the efficiency of EUV generation from low-Z elements, such as Li, O, and F, which emit only a few separated lines in a narrow band at 13.5, 13, and 12.8 nm, respectively,<sup>7–10</sup> mostly with laser excitation. With increasing efforts in the development of GDPP sources, investigations of emitters in such sources have also been performed on a larger scale.<sup>11–13</sup>
--[p456]-- 14.3 Emitter Materials for 13.5-nm Z-Pinch Sources
The emitter wavelength is determined by the Mo/Si multilayer-coated mirrors in the illumination and imaging beam path of the EUV scanner and by convention of the community to be 13.5 nm. The convention also reflects the fact that certain emitter materials are available with strong emission transitions at this wavelength.
--[p457]-- However, the choice of the emitter material for EUV sources is not governed by the requirement of high efficiency alone, but also driven by stringent requirements on source cleanliness. Because the first source-collector optics is only 10–20 cm away from the plasma (see above), one of the inherent requirements of lithography sources is that no condensation of the target material on the optical surfaces is allowed.
--[p456]-- For LPPs a conversion efficiency (CE) into 2π sr of close to 0.5% was achieved with a fluorine-rich target excited with the second harmonic of a Nd:YAG laser.<sup>8</sup> Recently Hanson et al. reported a CE of 2.7% obtained with lithium targets under laser excitation.<sup>33</sup>
--[p456]-- Figure 14.4 gives a graphic summary of the measured efficiency as a function of the atomic number.
As a general trend it was observed that the efficiency increased with increasing atomic number. Pronounced maxima appear around atomic numbers of 26 (Fe) and 50 (Sn), respectively. The highest efficiency was achieved with tin and antimony, while high-Z elements such as gold were slightly less efficient.

===== [p48-49] EUV Source Technology: Challenges and Status > 1.3.2.6 Other factors affecting source power requirements (7块) =====
--[p48]-- Because the resist sensitivity depends on how many times a resist molecule causes a reaction, more reaction means increased sensitivity but also higher LER. Today it appears that the alpha specification for resist sensitivity $( 5 \mathrm { m J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } )$ for a given resolution cannot be met without sacrificing LER (see Table 1.4). Data 1 is for one type of resist; data 2 and 3 are for another type.
--[p48 [表]]-- Resist performance needs to improve; otherwise, higher source power may be necessary to achieve the required throughput.

--[p49]-- More source power can be demanded to compensate for loss of reflectivity in the mirrors and collector optics in an EUVL scanner.
1.3.2.6.3 Other factors. Other factors that can potentially affect power requirements are overhead time and number of mirrors. According to the EUVL scanner throughput model, out of a total of 36 s spent per wafer in the EUV scanner, 27 s is devoted to overhead time, and only 9 s is spent on exposing the photoresist on the wafer.
--[p49]-- It has been shown that a higher reflectivity of 70% is possible,<sup>56</sup> and a reflectivity >67% that can be obtained and sustained can reduce power requirements. At the same time, the reflectivity of collectors and mirrors decreases as they erode. Currently, a 10% reflectivity loss is accepted as the end of lifetime for optics; present lifetime estimates for mirrors are 1000 h.<sup>57</sup> Therefore, this factor can also weigh against the source power requirements.
--[p48]-- 1.3.2.6 Other factors affecting source power requirements
Because the requirement for 115 W of power arises from a throughput model (see Table 2.3), the EUV source power requirements can increase, depending on how some of the requirements change. It is important to consider some of the major factors that may increase or decrease source power requirements.
1.3.2.6.1 Resist sensitivity.
--[p48]-- The EUVL scanner throughput model assumes an EUV resist sensitivity of $5 ~ \mathrm { m J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ . Although this is the only characteristic mentioned in the throughput model, an EUV resist must meet many additional specifications [e.g., line edge roughness (LER) and resolution]. There is a trade-off between sensitivity, LER, and resolution.<sup>55</sup> For example, increasing absorption will improve the resist sensitivity but will worsen the profile and resolution.
--[p49]-- Ota et al.<sup>2</sup> discuss the basis of the overhead time chosen in the throughput model. A small decrease in overhead time can mean a decrease in the required source power. Also, if the number of mirrors for certain scanner designs increases as EUVL is implemented at smaller nodes, more power will be needed.

--[p21]-- It also organizes numerous technical workshops and symposia involving technologists and decision-makers from around the world to foster global, pre-competitive cooperation and to drive consensus solutions for future semiconductor manufacturing technology. Continued progress in the development of EUVL is a prime example of SEMATECH’s efforts in this regard, and this book is a direct result of such collaboration.
Kevin Kemp

SEMATECH
--[p21]-- Among the technical challenges facing the semiconductor industry, lithography presents some of the most formidable problems, particularly the search for a nextgeneration lithography solution that can provide for high-volume manufacturing of computer chips at the 32 nm node and beyond. Extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUVL) is the leading candidate to succeed optical lithography at the currently used wavelength of 193 nm.
--[p21]-- The amount of available source power translates directly to the wafer throughput that can be achieved by an EUV exposure tool. Source component lifetime affects the cost of maintaining the tool, including the amount of time that a tool must be taken out of productive service for maintenance. Both these factors in turn drive the per-wafer processing cost for the technology.
--[p21]-- Introduction
In semiconductor manufacturing, progress is measured in terms of the industry’s continued ability to adhere to Moore’s Law, which states that the number of transistors on a chip doubles about every two years. The International Technology Roadmapfor Semiconductors (ITRS) dictates expected performance specifications for chip manufacturing technology to ensure continued adherence to this law.
--[p21]-- However, the technical challenges of source power, source component and optics lifetime, resist performance, and mask defectivity still must be addressed to ensure the cost-effective and timely implementation of EUVL. Furthermore, the industry infrastructure in these key areas needs to be developed rapidly to support planned manufacturing at the 32 nm generation.
Source power and associated source component lifetime are among the most critical of all the EUVL challenges.
--[p21]-- SEMATECH is a consortium of the world’s leading semiconductor manufacturers, and is a powerful catalyst for accelerating the commercialization of technology innovations into manufacturing solutions for the semiconductor industry. Its lithography division conducts targeted research projects to accelerate technology and infrastructure development to meet the lithography requirements of the ITRS.
--[p21]-- The past four to six years have seen a concerted effort on the part of suppliers and researchers to achieve the power levels and component lifetimes required to produce commercial EUV sources for lithographic applications. This volume celebrates the successes along this path and provides a reference for practitioners in the field and other interested readers.
--[p21]-- Accomplishing these specifications in turn requires the development and perfection of new technologies at a pace that is unmatched by any other industry. No single company can hope to do this alone: The increasing complexity of the technical challenges and the rising cost of development call for an unprecedented level of resource and risk sharing among semiconductor manufacturers, tool and materials suppliers, and research institutions and consortia.

===== [p474-476] High-Power GDPP Z-Pinch EUV Source Technology > 14.9.1 β-tool source requirements and performance for xenon fuel (7块) =====
--[p476]-- Taking into account all these parameters, xenon-fueled Z-pinch sources will enable the timely adoption of EUV β tools in semiconductor fabs to prepare for manufacturing integrated circuits with EUVL.
--[p474]-- With 20-kW electrical power deposited in the plasma (limited by the cooling capabilities; see Sec. 14.6), the repetition rate of the discharge source can be increased to 4500 Hz in continuous operation. The electrical input energy per pulse is kept constant by adaptation of the pulsed power supply circuits. Also the CE was preserved at the same value as at low repetition rates.
--[p474]-- The output power curve for the sources operated with xenon fuel shows a linear dependence on the repetition rate, and 200-W output power into 2π sr is achieved (see Fig. 14.22). This is currently the highest power obtained in continuous operation over several hours from a xenon-fueled GDPP EUV source.
Figure 14.23 shows the output power and high voltage at the discharge electrode system. The adjustment of the high voltage allows one to stabilize the output power at 200 W.
--[p474]-- 14.9.1 β-tool source requirements and performance for xenon fuel
EUV-source power and lifetime scaling, including collector power handling and collector lifetime scaling, is the major critical issue in the development of EUV technology. Because of the contamination-free operation available with xenon, the development efforts in the past have been directed to a large extent to xenon-based EUV sources to explore the limits of the technology.
--[p474]-- The development of source collector mirrors for β-tool use is focused on implementing efficient cooling technology at the collector mirror to enable the handling of the thermal load introduced by the high input power from the source.
With designs of larger electrode discharge systems, electrode lifetimes of several billion pulses are also projected for xenon-fueled β-tool sources.
--[p474]-- They have the significant advantage of having no problem of optics contamination by the inert xenon. Debris filters to suppress fast-particle sputtering of the collector mirror have been tested at XTREME technologies for β-tool sourcecollector designs. These tests indicated collector lifetimes achievable by suppression of sputtering amounting to 5–10 billion pulses, i.e., 350–700 h at 4 kHz.
--[p474]-- The inband EUV power of 200 W into 2π-sr solid angle corresponds to an available IF power of 25 W for the existing 1.8-sr source collector design, taking into account the losses due to the debris filters, shadowing by mechanical parts in the beam path, and residual-gas absorption in the source collector module. In the etendue of β-tool optical systems, 10–20 W of the available IF power can be used. Xenon-fueled Z-pinch sources are therefore well suited for β- tool use.

===== [p71-72] EUV Source Requirements for EUV Lithography > 2.2.6 Etendue of source output and positioning stability (9块) =====
--[p72]-- On the other hand, the etendue, $E _ { \mathrm { I } }$ , of the light that impinges on the reticle is obtained by
$$
E _ { \mathrm { I } } = \pi { \left( A m ^ { 2 } \right) } \left( \sigma \cdot { \frac { \mathrm { N A } } { m } } \right) ^ { 2 } = \pi \sigma ^ { 2 } A \cdot \mathrm { N A } ^ { 2 } ,

where $\sigma$ is the coherence factor and m is the magnification.
--[p72]-- The zeroth-order diffraction light from the reticle is reflected at the same angle as incident light. However, the first-order diffraction light is reflected at a different angle from that of the zeroth order. Therefore, the etendue becomes bigger after the reticle.
Whether an integrator is necessary or unnecessary in an EUV illuminator depends on the characteristics of the EUV source (e.g., the spatial uniformity and angular uniformity) and their temporal stability.
--[p71]-- 2.2.6 Etendue of source output and positioning stability
Etendue is an optical invariant and is called by many different names.<sup>14</sup> One of the names is “light-gathering power.” As implied by this terminology, when light enters an optical system with smaller etendue from another optical system with larger etendue, the former optical system fails to transmit some part of the light. Thus, an illuminator cannot transmit all light from an IF with larger etendue than that of the illuminator.
--[p72]-- It is shown in the joint requirements that the etendue must be smaller than $1 { - } 3 . 3 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ sr.
If the center of gravity of EUV light at the IF moves, the movement results in both etendue enlargement and deterioration of illumination uniformity. If the range of the movement is less than 10% of the beam size, it seems to cause few problems. However, the required positioning stability has not yet been agreed on in the joint requirements.
--[p72]-- When there is an integrator in the illuminator, $E _ { \mathrm { I } }$ is the etendue of the light that is outgoing from the integrator and transmitted through a downstream part of the illuminator after the integrator. It is found that $E _ { \mathrm { P } }$ is different from $E _ { \mathrm { I } }$ unless $\sigma$ is 1. This means that etendue is not necessarily conserved before and after the reticle.
--[p71]-- Therefore, a given EUV power with a larger etendue than that of the requirement is substantially equivalent to a smaller EUV power with the etendue of the requirement. The light that cannot be transmitted through the illuminator becomes thermal energy, and extra cooling is needed. The etendue at the IF must be smaller than that of the requirement.
--[p72]-- The required characteristics of the integrator also depend on the characteristics of the EUV source. When an integrator is used in the illuminator, the integrator enlarges the etendue.
If the area A is $5 0 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ , NA is 0.25, and σ is 0.6, then $E _ { \mathrm { P } }$ is $9 . 8 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ sr and $E _ { \mathrm { I } }$ is $3 . 5 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ sr. The coherence factor is changed for various device patterns and may become smaller.
In such a case, $E _ { \mathrm { I } }$ becomes smaller than $3 .
--[p72]-- When area A on a wafer is exposed with uniform intensity and uniform numerical aperture, NA, the etendue, $E _ { \mathrm { P } }$ , of the projection optics is obtained by
$$
E _ { \mathrm { P } } = A 2 \pi { \left( 1 - \sqrt { 1 - \mathrm { N A } ^ { 2 } } \right) } \approx \pi A \cdot \mathrm { N A } ^ { 2 } .
$$
This is the etendue of the light exposed on the wafer and is also the etendue of the light that is outgoing from the reticle and is transmitted through the projection optics.
--[p72]-- 5 \ \mathrm { \bar { m m } } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { s r }$ If an integrator is used, the etendue of the light that falls on the integrator (i.e., the etendue of the light that is outgoing from the IF and is transmitted through an upstream part of the illuminator before the integrator) may be much smaller than $E _ { \mathrm { { I } } } ;$ it is $1 \mathrm { \overline { { ~ m m } } } ^ { 2 }$ sr in one optical design of the illuminator.

===== [p453-456] High-Power GDPP Z-Pinch EUV Source Technology > 14.2.1 Physical principle (14块) =====
--[p453]-- 14.2.1 Physical principle
A well-known and the most efficient method of plasma generation is an electrical gas discharge—for example, a spark or flash. Unfortunately, to generate EUV radiation the densities and temperatures of conventional gas discharges such as those used in discharge lamps or excimer lasers are not sufficient. However, a cold lowdensity plasma can be compressed by magnetic fields to a hot, high-density plasma with maximum intensity at an emission wavelength of 13.5 nm.
--[p454]-- From this plasma, charged particles as well as ultraviolet radiation are propagating into the main discharge region of the Z-pinch assembly (step 1). A short time after the pre-ionization, a pulsed high-current discharge is ignited close to the insulator walls (step 2) and immediately compressed to a hot high-density plasma column (step 3). After the current pulse, the plasma pressure becomes higher than the magnetic pressure due to the decreasing magnetic field.
--[p453]-- P _ { \mathrm { m a g } } = P _ { \mathrm { p l a s m a } } \Rightarrow \frac { B ^ { 2 } } { 2 \mu _ { 0 } } = \big ( \langle Z \rangle + 1 \big ) n _ { \mathrm { i } } \cdot k T \Rightarrow k T = \frac { \mu _ { 0 } I ^ { 2 } } { 8 \pi ( \langle Z \rangle + 1 ) N _ { \mathrm { i } } } ,\tag{14.5}
$$
--[p453]-- The plasma temperature can be estimated from the balance between the pressure of the magnetic field $( P _ { \mathrm { m a g } } )$ and the thermal pressure of the plasma $( P _ { \mathrm { p l a s m a } } ) ^ { 3 }$
$$
--[p454]-- Recent experiments to generate 13.5-nm radiation with GDDP sources have been made with xenon gas as the emitter.<sup>4</sup> From the above relation and the requirements for EUV sources for lithography (plasma diameter about 1 mm, almost spherical) the current I necessary to generate a plasma temperature k T of 20 eV can be estimated at about 20 kA for gases such as xenon. The magnetic field is about 20 T and compresses the plasma cylinder to about 2000-bar pressure.
--[p454]-- The design of the Z-pinch source supports an accessible emission solid angle for collection of more than π sr, i.e., ±60 deg. Gas or vapor is used as the target material, which is typically continuously flowing through the discharge region. When the gas is converted to the plasma state and heated, EUV light is emitted. Key for the high emission stability of the Z-pinch source is a highly efficient surface-discharge pre-ionization device included in the source.
--[p453]-- where B is the magnetic field of the discharge current $I , \mu _ { 0 }$ is the magnetic field constant, $n _ { \mathrm { i } }$ is the ion density, $\langle Z \rangle$ is the average degree of ionization, $k T$ is the plasma temperature, and $N _ { \mathrm { i } }$ is the line density. Here, $N _ { \mathrm { i } } = n _ { \mathrm { i } } \pi r ^ { 2 }$ and $B = \mu _ { 0 } I / ( 2 \pi r )$
--[p454]-- The operation of the device can be separated into four steps. The pre-ionization of the working gas is spatially separated from the main discharge region. A high-voltage pulse is applied to an electrode system, which is isolated by a ceramic insulator. By collisions of free surface electrons with bound electrons on this surface, a cloud of electrons is generated. This electron gas ionizes the ambient gas phase and forms a cold plasma with low density.
--[p456]-- • the discharge-electrode thermal management technology,
• the control of electrode and wall erosion,
• the debris mitigation and collector-optics protection system,
• the collector and source-collector contamination cleaning system.
In the following sections the above-listed technologies and components are discussed in more detail.
--[p454]-- Then the plasma starts expanding into the vacuum phase in both radial and axial directions (step 4).
In the Z-pinch design the length and diameter of the EUV-emitting volume can be varied by changing the separation between anode and cathode, as well as their shapes, and the gas dynamics. This is necessary to match the specific illuminator optics design.
--[p454]-- The possibility of scaling the emission volume from 0.8-mm length and 0.25-mm diameter to more than 6-mm length and 1.3-mm diameter has been demonstrated.
The most important technologies and components for GDPP Z-pinch EUV sources are
• the emitter material (also called fuel, target, or working gas) and emitter supply,
• the discharge electrode system configuration for efficiently collectible plasma volumes,
• the pulsed-power electrical energy supply circuit,
--[p453]-- The effect used is that of self-compression of a cylindrical plasma by the azimuthal magnetic field generated by the axial discharge current. This effect is called the pinch effect, and the compressed plasma is called a pinch plasma.
Its discoverer, Willard H. Bennet, described the pinch effect as magnetic selffocusing in a plasma with electrical current flow.
--[p454]-- A typical design for such a discharge unit, which generates pinch plasmas with high efficiency, is currently under investigation at XTREME technologies— the surface-discharge pre-ionized Z-pinch discharge<sup>5,6</sup> (see Fig. 14.3). The plasma generator consists of two cylindrical electrodes that are properly shaped to achieve the desired plasma size and emission angle. A cylindrical insulator separates anode and cathode.
--[p454]-- The total energy in the magnetic field, plasma, and external circuit can be estimated as 5–10 J. A stable plasma cylinder would possess a resistance of 50 m. The plasma is heated with some $1 0 ^ { 7 }$ W due to its ohmic resistance. Because of the heating of the plasma, the current decreases significantly after several hundred nanoseconds. The discharge can be operated only in a pulsed regime.

===== [p226-227] Radiative Collapse in Z Pinches > 6.12 Axial Size of the EUV Source; Zippering Effect (5块) =====
--[p226]-- Figure 6.10 demonstrates experimental evidence of the subsequent appearance of EUV-radiating micropinches in different positions on the discharge axis. Evidently the initial plasma column created by ablation of one of the electrodes is axially strongly inhomogeneous. As a result appropriate conditions for the development of necks in the radiative collapse regime may appear at slightly different moments of time for different axial positions.
--[p227]-- Experiments show that proper choice of time profile and focusing of the laser (electron) ablating beam are able to mitigate zippering and maintain the axial size of the EUV source inside the specification limits of the imaging optics.
--[p226]-- In parallel with increase of the pinch length we detect some increase of the EUV yield. For observation (collecting of radiation) in the direction perpendicular to the discharge axis, which was proposed in our concept source, such an increase in length is of no of use—restrictions imposed by the imaging optics do not allow utilization of radiation from a source with dimension larger than 1 mm. Time-gated pinhole images of the radiating plasma permit understanding of this phenomenon.
--[p227]-- Figure 6.10 shows time-framed and space-resolved spectra of a tin plasma in the VUV spectral region. Usually the appearance of subsequent micropinches correlates with a multipeak (in this case, double-peak—see Fig. 6.6) structure of the EUV time-resolved signal. For the scheme where useful radiation is collected perpendicular to the discharge axis, such an increase of the EUV source size could be unfavorable and must be avoided.
--[p226]-- 6.12 Axial Size of the EUV Source; Zippering Effect
The axial dimension of the neck micropinch cannot be calculated in the zerodimensional analytical model we have used to introduce some important features of the pinching of plasmas of heavy atoms. More advanced 2D modeling predicts $\gamma \approx 2 – 5$ for a single neck, and thus the axial size of our source is expected to be between 0.5 and 1 mm. Nevertheless, time-integrated images often reveal larger sizes—up to 1.5–2 mm.

===== [p299-300] Z∗ Code for DPP and LPP Source Modeling > 8.5 Summary (4块) =====
--[p299]-- It models plasma dynamics in sophisticated geometries, self-consistently with the radiation transfer in an electromagnetic field.
The RMHD code $Z ^ { * }$ allows one
• to carry out complete simulations of plasma radiation sources in geometry and conditions close to the actual experimental setup,
• to evaluate the functionality and suitability of different plasma systems for the purposes of plasma radiation sources, and
--[p299]-- These requirements and the underlying physics description have been briefly discussed in this chapter. The solution implemented, in the 2D radiation MHD code $Z ^ { * }$ , satisfies a majority of these requirements. It calculates atomic and ionization properties, equation of state, kinetic and transport coefficients, rates of ionization and excitation, and detailed spectral properties of complex ion compound plasmas (such as those of Xe, Sn, or their admixtures) in the nonequilibrium regime.
--[p299]-- 8.5 Summary
To model adequately the multicharged ion plasma in EUV radiation sources, a sufficiently complex physical model must be developed to take into account the plasma dynamics under the influence of an electromagnetic field, as well as the self-consistent ionization and radiation phenomena. The calculations of radiation transport and ionization kinetics should be able to treat nonequilibrium, nonstationary plasmas under conditions of partial radiation reabsorption.
--[p300]-- • to define optimal plasma, as well as device, parameters for high radiation emission.
In the practical examples given, we have shown how $Z ^ { * }$ can be applied to
• obtain the time evolution and dimensions of an EUV-radiation emitter,
• study preionization and 3D plasma compression in a gradient capillary discharge,
• evaluate the parameter dependence of DPF radiation,
• evaluate the efficiency of Sn and Xe EUV radiators in LPP sources, and
• generally optimize geometries and plasma conditions for better EUV radiation yield.

===== [p71-71] EUV Source Requirements for EUV Lithography > 2.2.5 Source cleanliness (4块) =====
--[p71]-- It is anticipated that the collector mirror that faces the source emission point will be damaged by debris and will be replaced periodically. But other illuminator mirrors after the IF cannot be replaced easily, because they are integrated into a wafer exposure tool and aligned precisely with each other.
--[p71]-- More than 30,000 light-on hours of source cleanliness after the IF is required to obtain a 10-year lifetime of the illuminator, where the exposure time is expected to be $1 / 3$ of the wafer processing time. The amount of debris that is discharged through the opening between the source and the wafer exposure tool should be controlled.
--[p71]-- In addition, $\mathrm { C } _ { x } \mathrm { H } _ { y }$ and $_ { \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } }$ , which flow into the wafer exposure tool through the opening, should be controlled because they contaminate the illuminator mirrors and the projection mirrors. In order to achieve the required source cleanliness, metrology and evaluation techniques are very important.
--[p71]-- 2.2.5 Source cleanliness
Next to output, cleanliness is the most critical characteristic of an EUV source, because it affects the wafer throughput and the CoO directly. It is desirable to minimize debris from the target, nozzle, or electrode reaching the IF. Residual debris hits and damages illuminator mirrors, and the mirror reflectivity will drop in proportion to the amount of debris and its kinetic energy.

===== [p50-50] EUV Source Technology: Challenges and Status > 1.3.3.1 Xe DPP (7块) =====
--[p50]-- In summary, thermal extraction is the showstopper for Xe DPP technology, limiting it to 50 W of maximum power at IF. Remaining challenges for Xe DPPbased EUV sources are debris mitigation, collector lifetime, and collector cooling.
--[p50]-- The current data for thermal extraction indicate that up to 20 kW<sup>10,11</sup> of input power can be mitigated. The use of porous-metal cooling technology,<sup>58</sup> in which high-pressure water is forced through porous metal electrodes to cool them, has allowed increased power input to the sources. An additional increase in the thermal mitigation is expected from design changes and the new electrode cooling technologies.
--[p50]-- 1.3.3.1 Xe DPP
EUV sources for existing EUV microsteppers are based on Xe DPP technology. They provide about 1 W of power at the IF.<sup>11</sup> However, the showstopper for Xe DPP is thermal extraction. It is now widely agreed that this technology cannot meet the power need for HVM sources, since the upper limit for thermal mitigation is expected to be 30 kW. All current Xe DPP projects<sup>10,11</sup> are now focused on delivering a low-power source for an alpha-level scanner.
--[p50]-- Sputtering is the next leading cause of erosion of electrodes.
For Xe DPP, it is reasonable to expect that close to 1% can be achieved for the upper limit of the CE, something already seen with Xe LPP. Today most suppliers are working with 1.8-sr collectors and plan to integrate 3.14-sr collectors in the near future. In Table 1.3, the debris mitigation device transmission is simply an estimate; the same is true to for SPF filters available today.
--[p50]-- To reduce the thermal heat load on the electrodes, the distance between the plasma and electrode also needs to be increased to allow higher power generation.<sup>11,15,22</sup> An electrode configuration called Star Pinch has been demonstrated to allow a higher thermal load than other DPP sources,<sup>59</sup> and for this electrode configuration a 10<sup>10</sup>-pulse lifetime has been predicted by the supplier.
--[p50]-- With a 75% etendue match expected, a 4% effective collection can be expected today for Xe DPP, which can potentially increase to 17% as the SPF and collector efficiency improve. Since power measurements are made directly at the source, 200 W in 2π sr with 4% collection will mean that a minimum of 8 W of power can be expected at the IF. With 30-kW power input and 17% collection, a maximum of 50 W of power at the IF can be expected for Xe DPP.
--[p50]-- Input energy to a DPP source is dissipated in various components of the system, from which the heat must be extracted. According to calorimetric measurements for the Star Pinch configuration,<sup>59</sup> in the cathode 8%, anode 6%, foil comb 13%, and chamber 73% of the input power is dissipated. Electrode thermal extraction is therefore only part of the issue, but still the most important part, since rising temperatures can increase the erosion of electrodes and reduce their lifetime.

===== [p340-340] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.3.2 Analytical description of plasma expansion (6块) =====
--[p340]-- 10.3.2 Analytical description of plasma expansion
As the plasma is produced, it develops and expands in the surrounding vacuum. The expansion speed is determined by the temperature of the electrons and the mass of the ions. It determines how fast energy must be supplied to the plasma if it is to reach a high temperature. The electron-ion thermal expansion velocity is roughly equal to the ion acoustic velocity<sup>15–17</sup>
$$
--[p340]-- v _ { \mathrm { e x p } } \approx c _ { \mathrm { s } } = { \sqrt { \frac { Z ^ { * } \gamma k _ { \mathrm { B } } T _ { \mathrm { e } } } { M _ { \mathrm { i } } } } } ,\tag{10.4}
$$
where $T _ { \mathrm { i } }$ and $Z ^ { * }$ are the ion temperature and the average ion charge, respectively, $M _ { \mathrm { i } }$ is the ion mass, and $\gamma = 1 + 2 / N$ is the thermodynamic ratio of specific heats for a system with N degrees of freedom.
--[p340]-- The expansion of LPPs leads to a rapid decrease of electron (and ion) density. This results in less absorption by the IBA process, as shown by Eq. (10.1). As soon as the generated plasma has sufficiently expanded, the absorption of the incident laser power will become weak. Hence, to obtain high CE, the laser pulses should not be too long.
--[p340]-- The xenon plasma rate estimated from this acoustic velocity (using $M _ { \mathrm { i } } =$ $1 3 1 . 2 9 , Z ^ { * } = 1 0$ , and $T _ { \mathrm { e } } \sim 1 0 ~ \mathrm { e V } )$ is about $1 . 1 \times 1 0 ^ { 6 }$ cm/s. And the expansion velocity of a tin plasma (with $M _ { \mathrm { i } } = 1 1 8 . 7 , Z ^ { * } = 1 0$ , and $T _ { \mathrm { e } } \approx 3 0 ~ \mathrm { e V } )$ is about $2 \times 1 0 ^ { 6 }$ cm/s.
--[p340]-- 2 6 \times 1 0 ^ { 8 } \biggl ( \frac { Z ^ { * } k _ { \mathrm { B } } T _ { \mathrm { e } } } { M _ { \mathrm { i } } } \biggr ) ^ { 1 / 2 } \ : \frac { \mathrm { c m } } { \mathrm { s } } ,\tag{10.5}
$$
where $k _ { \mathrm { B } } T _ { \mathrm { e } }$ is in electron volts, the ion mass $M _ { \mathrm { i } }$ is expressed in units of the proton mass, and γ is taken as $5 / 3$
As the plasma expands, thermal energy is then converted into direct kinetic energy.
--[p340]-- The expansion velocity is in large part dominated by the electron thermal pressure. It is driven by the electron temperature $k _ { \mathrm { B } } T _ { \mathrm { e } }$ but limited by the inertia of the ions through their mass Mi, as can be seen in Eq. (10.4). In practical units the expansion velocity can be expressed as

--[p199]-- 5.12 for different values of $n ,$ from which it is evident that the optimum electron temperature is close to 40 eV. Note that this figure is based on the assumption that the theoretical spectra and therefore the scaling factors used are the most appropriate. To determine the precise scaling factors requires a high-resolution study and identification of a number of the lines, which for some stages may be impossible, as the line separation may be less than the individual linewidths.
--[p199]-- It is immediately evident that the peak brightness is obtained for $\Phi \overset { \cdot } { = } 1 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 1 } \mathrm { ~ W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . A similar result was obtained for mass-limited targets containing tin.<sup>36</sup> From the CR model, the value of $T _ { e }$ corresponding to this flux density is 49 eV.

===== [p53-53] EUV Source Technology: Challenges and Status > 1.3.4.3 Sn LPP (4块) =====
--[p53]-- 1.3.4.3 Sn LPP
Due to its higher efficiency, Sn is also favored as a fuel in LPP EUV sources. In addition to high-power lasers, the potential technical challenges for Sn LPP are Sn delivery and Sn debris mitigation. In LPP, the geometrical arrangement allows for a large collection angle; however, this geometry also does not allow debris mitigation devices (e.g., a foil trap) between the source and the collector.
--[p53]-- For Xe LPP, progress has been made in mitigating debris (high-energy Xe ions) using gas curtains.<sup>15,49</sup> However, for Sn, which is a metal, Sn debris mitigation may be a showstopper for LPP.
The most promising approach to addressing Sn debris is the use of an enclosed Sn source,<sup>68</sup> in which heated Sn is contained in a cavity, the laser beam enters through heated silicon windows, and EUV exits through other windows.
--[p53]-- Today the expected collection efficiency is 11%, but progress in collector design and improved SPF will increase that to 33%. This means that for a 15-kW laser, up to 149 W of power can be obtained at the IF for Sn LPP. In summary, the remaining technical challenges for Sn LPP technology are laser power, debris mitigation, and collector lifetime.
--[p53]-- In the past, development of such metal sources for EUV applications has been difficult for cadmium targets,<sup>69</sup> because silicon windows degraded and metal eventually leaked out.
At this time, the highest reported power is 25 W at the source, with a 2.5% CE for Sn tape-based targets.<sup>13</sup> Other researchers have reported higher CEs for Sn $\mathrm { L P P ^ { 7 0 } }$ but with much lower laser power.

===== [p496-496] High-Power GDPP Z-Pinch EUV Source Technology > 15.2.2 Colliding-beam plasma source (4块) =====
--[p496]-- It was estimated that the required ion count of ${ > } 1 0 ^ { \hat { 1 } 5 }$ ions could not be delivered to the central location without substantial neutralization, either by resonant charge exchange or by copropagating electrons; otherwise a high positive potential would repel many of the ions. The resonant charge-exchange cross section is very large<sup>20</sup> and able to provide substantial neutralization at the xenon density of interest.
--[p496]-- This prototype directed discharge led directly to the development of the Star Pinch discharge, in which a heating pulse was introduced at the time the pulsed astron plasma had formed, to additionally pinch and heat the plasma to the temperature and density for 13.5-nm emission.<sup>22,23</sup>
--[p496]-- 15.2.2 Colliding-beam plasma source
Experiments were performed with a pulsed astron discharge to attempt to form a hot plasma at the intersection of the many through-cathode ion beams, which were known to be very intense in single pseudospark channels.<sup>17–19</sup> The first necessity was simultaneous ignition of all channels, which was found to occur after minimal conditioning when the pulsed discharge was preceded by a dc discharge.
--[p496]-- Experiments with this colliding-neutral-beam $\mathrm { d e v i c e } ^ { 2 1 }$ yielded a warm plasma that was not sufficiently hot and dense to yield 13.5-nm radiation from xenon. As a method to estimate the plasma conditions, an argon spectrum was analyzed in the 40–120-nm region, and ions up to $\mathrm { A r } ^ { 3 + }$ contributed plentifully to the emitted radiation (Fig. 15.4). The plasma diameter was less than 3 mm, even although the nearest wall was 25 mm away.

===== [p338-338] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.3 Physical Processes in Laser Plasmas (2块) =====
--[p338]-- 10.3 Physical Processes in Laser Plasmas
Here we describe the primary interaction processes that occur in the formation and development of plasmas created by nanosecond lasers. We largely summarize more detailed treatises on this topic.<sup>11–13</sup> Laser pulse intensities above $1 0 ^ { 1 0 } \ \mathrm { W / c m ^ { 2 } }$ are sufficient to ionize atoms, transforming any matter to plasma.
--[p338]-- The spectral nature of the emission from the produced plasma is characteristic of its temperature and the species of ions created. EUV radiation is best produced by plasmas having an electronic temperature $T _ { \mathrm { e } }$ of several tens of electron volts and electron densities $n _ { \mathrm { e } } = 1 0 ^ { 1 9 } \ \mathrm { t o } \ \mathrm { i } \mathrm { \hat { 0 } } ^ { 2 1 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ .
To achieve this temperature in plasmas of Xe or Sn, the laser intensity should exceed $1 0 ^ { 1 1 } \mathrm { W / c m } ^ { 2 }$

===== [p364-364] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.6 Future Trends (5块) =====
--[p364]-- 10.6 Future Trends
This review outlines the detailed theory involved in laser plasmas and the complex radiation physics involved in the emission of EUV light from plasmas created from materials such as Xe and Sn, and summarizes the current computer models being used to make realistic predictions of this emission. We have shown how hydrodynamic plasma codes such as Med 103 and CHIVAS effectively model the plasma expansion and simulate the electron density and temperature distributions.
--[p364]-- In CRETIN, each element in the plasma is modeled with numerous atomic states, corresponding to the distribution of electrons in various atomic levels. Transitions between levels are caused by interactions between electrons, ions, and photons. CRETIN itself contains no atomic data. The level structure and transition processes for each element included in a simulation are specified in an external data file, referred to as an atomic model.
--[p364]-- We have described a number of collisional-radiative codes used to describe LTE and non-LTE AA-based models for estimating the relative ion abundance, excitation, and emission (SCROLL, AVERROES, SCAALP, and HULLAC) and made comparisons of experimental data with HULLAC. Towards acquiring a more comprehensive non-LTE model of the emission from these plasmas, we are implementing the non-LTE radiative-transfer CRETIN code.
--[p364]-- We are currently using atomic codes such as COWAN and FAC to calculate these data. For reasons of convenience, fits to hydrodynamics parameters are currently used to drive the CRETIN simulations, rather than using the hydrodynamic results directly. The fit can easily be extended or modified to investigate different scenarios without redoing the hydrodynamic simulation. Simulated detector spectra are shown in Fig. 10.12 for one position, integrated over time.
--[p364]-- More detailed calculations are in progress.

===== [p225-226] Radiative Collapse in Z Pinches > 6.11 Stability of Radiative-Collapse Trajectory, EUV Yield, and Shot-to-Shot Reproducibility (6块) =====
--[p226]-- We want to point out that visible smearing of both curves in Fig. 6.9(A) is mainly due to time jittering of the oscilloscope start-up recording time. Figure 6.9(B) illustrates an unstable discharge at a low current. If the current in the discharge only slightly exceeds the critical one, the radiative collapse may be interrupted at early stages of its development. For some good shots the CE may be as high as for the stable regime, but the EUV signal has a very unstable character.
--[p225]-- The existence of a stability zone explains well the stability of radiation yield even at badly reproducible initial conditions when material is fed into the discharge by third-electrode triggering or by ablation from one or both electrodes by a laser pulse.<sup>10,21</sup>
Figure 6.9(A) demonstrates reasonably high stability of the EUV signal at properly chosen parameters of ablating laser and discharge design parameters. It shows oscilloscope traces for current and EUV signal for 256 shots.
--[p226]-- Our modeling and experiments indicate that there exists a mechanism of selfstabilization of the trajectory of the micropinch development. Nevertheless, triggering of this stabilization mechanism depends on the initial parameters of the plasma column and on the discharge design characteristics.
--[p225]-- 6.11 Stability of Radiative-Collapse Trajectory, EUV Yield, and Shot-to-Shot Reproducibility
When studying the physics of neck instabilities in vacuum sparks with current 100– 200 kA, it was found that, depending on the initial conditions, micropinches could be subdivided into two types.<sup>21</sup> The first, a “good” type, was characterized by deep compression, high brightness, and rather good reproducibility of such plasma parameters as size and radiation yield.
--[p225]-- The second type was characterized by a low level of compression, with low and very unstable x-ray and VUV yield. Numerical modeling and experimental studies resulted in the conclusion that a region of stable initial parameters (radius and N) exists where the neck reaches a stable $R _ { \mathrm { E Q } } [ T ( N ) ]$ trajectory rather soon after breakdown.
--[p225]-- There exists also a zone of initial parameters, characterized by either too high an initial radius or too low an initial linear density in the pinch. For such pinches energy losses due to plasma outflow from the neck exceed radiative losses, and the neck does not reach the regime of radiative collapse. Both cases are illustrated in Fig. 6.8.

===== [p235-236] Fundamentals and Limits of Plasma-based EUV Sources > 7.2.3 Single-pulse conversion and scalability with repetition rate (4块) =====
--[p236]-- The concept must allow for generating and for heating of a suitable radiator, and it must allow for scaling the repetition rates into the multikilohertz range while conserving the single-pulse features.
• Optimization of the driver. This depends on finding a driver that generates the best starting conditions and feeds sufficient power into the radiator with the highest possible efficiency in a way that is matched to reach the highest CEs.
--[p235]-- This means reaching an intrinsic conversion efficiency much larger than 2% in 2π sr for the given input power from a volume small enough to allow collection of radiation into the specified solid angle. This task is mainly connected with basic plasma physics, as will be seen later.
• Finding a source concept suited for being scaled up.
--[p236]-- • Solving engineering problems for tool architecture and lifetime. These include thermal management to sustain this operation mode for a long enough time, and avoiding erosion.
Unfortunately, these problems cannot be solved independently. Features of the driver influence the plasma and vice versa. Best CEs may not be suited for long lifetime, or best conversion may lead to a radiator that is not scalable, for example due to crosstalk from one pulse to the next.
In this chapter, we concentrate on the first task, i.e., single-pulse conversion.
--[p235]-- 7.2.3 Single-pulse conversion and scalability with repetition rate
In principle the recipe to develop the best-suited source can be separated into the following tasks:
• Optimization of the single-pulse radiator. This depends on finding condi tions for a radiator that emits single pulses of EUV inband emission most efficiently.

===== [p421-421] Dense Plasma Focus Source > 12.12 EUV Collector (4块) =====
--[p421]-- In the past,<sup>4,5</sup> we have therefore investigated grazing-incidence collector shells coated with palladium and ruthenium. A computation program was developed to assist in the optimization of the optical design by ray tracing and to model the angle-dependent reflectivity. The individual shells are fabricated by electroplating nickel onto a polished mandrel.
--[p421]-- 12.12 EUV Collector
For a discharge-based EUV light source, the plasma size and related etendue considerations point toward the use of a nested-shell collection optics employing grazing angles of incidence.<sup>1,26</sup> The requirement of an intermediate focus (IF) aperture separating the source-collector module from the remaining illumination optics leads to an ellipsoidal shape of collector surface.
--[p421]-- The results of far- and near-field testing with visible light were described previously.<sup>5</sup> Wavefront errors become more pronounced for the outer shells of the collector, due to deformation of the shells under their own weight. Although optical testing has been carried out for several prototypes with thicker shells, limitations due to lifetime were encountered.
--[p421]-- The overall EUV collection efficiency is significantly influenced by the transmission of the debris shield and, to a lesser extent, by the shell support structure.

===== [p439-439] Hollow-Cathode-Triggered Plasma Pinch Discharge > 13.3.2 Conversion efficiency (7块) =====
--[p439]-- The impedance matching of the system is such that more than 90% of the energy stored on the capacitors is coupled into the plasma. The highest CE for Xe is 0.8% for a long pinch; for a small pinch, in practical cases, values around 0.5% are achieved. Another way of looking at this number is to say that roughly 15% of the total energy is converted into EUV radiation between 9 and 19 nm (1% in 4π sr divided by the fraction 0.066 of inband energy).
--[p439]-- The final output energy must be recalculated from the measured diode signal and the measured spectrum of the radiating species. Tools are calibrated at the Bessy synchrotron in Berlin. Spectra for Sn and Xe are shown in Fig. 13.5. The inband portion around 13.5 nm is shaded and calculated as a fraction of the total energy between 9 and 18 nm.
--[p439]-- 13.3.2 Conversion efficiency
The CE is defined as the output energy divided by the energy initially stored on the capacitor bank. Here, the output energy is the radiation energy in a solid angle of 2π and in a bandwidth of ±1% around the center wavelength of 13.5 nm. The output energy is measured with a standard measuring tool that consists of a diode and two multilayer filters that filter out roughly a 4% bandwidth around 13.5 nm.
--[p439]-- With another 10% of the energy left in the circuitry, this means that the remaining 75% of the total energy is dissipated in other loss channels. The major part of this is attributed to fast ions, bypass currents, and VUV/DUV radiation.
From Fig. 13.5, it is apparent that Sn has a more favorable spectral distribution than Xe and would lead to a factor 3 improvement if everything else were equal.
--[p439]-- In fact, we have demonstrated CEs of up to 2.5% in a Sn pinch plasma discharge with 3-J pulse energy. In this experiment, we employed the same hollow-cathode configuration as in the Xe case, but added a mechanism to deliver Sn into the vapor phase. The value 2.5% is an extreme case achieved only after fine-tuning discharge parameters. In a more usual environment, CE values of 2% are achieved for a frequency range of 0–6 kHz and a pulse energy between 1.5 and 4 J.
--[p439]-- The lamp has been operated up to very high frequencies. The highest frequency for the Xe lamp was 7 kHz (20-kW input power) and for the Sn lamp was 6 kHz (14-kW input power). In both cases, CEs did not depend strongly on input power and were almost the same as for low-power operation.
--[p439]-- The CE is determined by many factors: how much energy remains in the circuitry, resistive losses in the electrode system and the cathode fall, current leakage in the plasma outside of the pinch plasma, out-of-band radiation from EUV all the way up to infrared, ionization, and acceleration of particles. To set up an accurate energy balance is still a matter for research, since a number of data are not easily accessible to experiments (e.g., cathode fall, ionization distribution).

===== [p347-348] Chapter 10 Modeling LPP Sources > 10.5.1.1 Average-atom model (5块) =====
--[p347]-- The introduction of the densityfunctional theory<sup>48</sup> was an occasion to consider the variational character of the ioncell TF model at finite temperature.<sup>49</sup> A comprehensive inclusion of the quantummechanical shell effects for bound electrons in a self-consistent AA model has been proposed by Rozsnyai.<sup>50</sup> In Rozsnyai’s model the bound-electron density is calculated from a set of fictitious bound shells using the fractional occupation numbers given by the Fermi-Dirac function. The continuum-electron density is calculated in the TF approximation.
--[p348]-- Let us note that the direct applications of the AA models are in the field of plasma thermodynamics and not of plasma optical properties. Indeed, the AA models provide reasonable equations of state and mean ionization charges. Their direct use for the calculation of the optical properties is in principle not allowed. That is because the AA quantum orbitals should be considered as auxiliary quantities to construct the electron density.
--[p348]-- Despite that, various heuristic extensions of the AA model to NLTE situations have been proposed (see, for instance, Ref. 52), especially for rapid calculation of the NLTE opacities needed in hydrodynamic codes. In the NLTE codes the populations of the bound AA levels are determined from collisional-radiative rate equations (see Sec. 10.5.1.7 below). The methods using screened hydrogenic models<sup>53</sup> could be especially rapid.
One of the recent screened hydrogenic models has been elaborated by Perrot,<sup>54</sup> who proposed to include l splitting.
--[p347]-- 10.5.1.1 Average-atom model
The AA model has been proposed as a theoretical approach to the hot dense plasma for various astrophysical and thermonuclear fusion application. Its origins are connected with the use of the Thomas-Fermi (TF) model<sup>44</sup> in dense plasmas.<sup>45–47</sup> All these models have been proposed for LTE plasmas.
--[p347]-- The bound shells stem from a spherically symmetric self-consistent potential, which is the sum of two parts: the Coulomb term and exchange-correlation correction; the first term comes from the electron density and the nuclear charge Ze, and the second can be calculated in the local density approximation (at present one of the best formulas for that potential can be found in Ref. 51). The ion cell is neutral, which allows one to find the electronic chemical potential of the plasma.

===== [p228-228] Radiative Collapse in Z Pinches > 6.13 Conclusions (5块) =====
--[p228]-- One chapter in a book does not allow adequate coverage of even a small part of the physics of discharges with axial symmetry—Z pinches. Nevertheless, where possible, we have tried to show that understanding of the physical processes taking place in discharge plasmas is essential for EUVL source design.
--[p228]-- 6.10) was an example of importance of 2D modeling for understanding the pinch physics relevant to EUV production. --[p228]-- One of them, relevant to EUVL source design, the reader can find in Chapter 11; another—code Z<sup>∗</sup>—was presented at the first EUVL symposium in Dallas in 2002.<sup>22</sup>

--[p228]-- The use of first-order approximation decreases the precision of the computations, though this is compensated by the high stability of the code, which yields physically reasonable results even on a rather crude grid. The main problem for all numerical models working with heavyion dense plasmas is radiation transport. Together with the THERMOS group, we are trying to incorporate atomic-physics calculations and radiation transport into the full treatment code.
