===== [p308-308] Metrology for EUVL Sources and Tools > 29.5.2.1 NIST photodiode calibration facilities (4块) =====
--[p308]-- 29.5.2.1 NIST photodiode calibration facilities
The NIST photodiode calibration activities in the EUV are carried out at the EUV Detector Radiometry Beamline<sup>20</sup> at SURF III. This beamline is a grazingincidence toroidal grating monochromator with a fixed exit slit. There are no collection optics at the front of the beamline, so the solid angle of collected radiation, and hence the beamline throughput, are quite modest (a few nanowatts).
--[p308]-- However, the monochromator exit beam is well collimated, allowing measurement stations to be separated by about 1 m of path length without significant change in the beam size. Also, effects arising from oblique incidence on the detector that are present in beams with a high numerical aperture are absent in this beamline. There are two interchangeable gratings, one covering the spectral region from 5 to 18 nm, and the other from 17 to 50 nm.
--[p308]-- A second end station with an adjustable aperture can be installed to calibrate small photodiodes or to scan large-area detectors to measure the spatial uniformity of the quantum efficiency. The details of the calibration procedures are described elsewhere.<sup>22</sup>
--[p308]-- The beamline houses an ionization chamber for absolute measurement of the photon flux from the monochromator.<sup>21</sup> A WS photodiode is calibrated against the ionization chamber, and then outgoing transfer standard detectors are calibrated against the WS by interchanging the two detectors in the photon beam.

===== [p130-131] Chapter 21 Modular LPP Source > 21.3.2 The high-power laser system (7块) =====
--[p130]-- 21.3.2 The high-power laser system
The concept of 10 spatially and temporally multiplexed laser modules of 500-W average power in the infrared is chosen to reach the total power of 5 kW.
--[p130]-- The 500-W laser module design is based on patented homogeneous pumping structures, used in Thalès Laser commercial lasers, and which represent the technological base of Thalès Laser.
--[p130]-- We believe that this solution is the best adapted to higher-power LPP sources, because of (1) cost optimization of each individual module, (2) easy and fast replacement of a module in case of failure, (3) no interruption of the EUV process with one module offline, (4) cw diode technology for low cost of ownership, and (5) satisfactory beam quality of high-power modules through innovative design.
--[p130]-- The main specifications of the 500-W laser module developed in collaboration with the CEA/SCP, and currently prepared for industrialization by Thalès Laser, are: 1064-nm wavelength, 6- to 20-kHz pulse repetition rate, average power 500 W at 10 kHz, beam quality $M ^ { 2 }$ better than 15, and pulse durations shorter than 40 ns.

===== [p282-283] Flying Circus EUV Source Metrology and Source Development Assessment > 28.5.2 Electrostatic analyzer with TOF spectrometer (7块) =====
--[p283]-- The group at UCF uses a 90-deg $\mathrm { E S A } . ^ { 4 2 }$ The base pressure in the main vacuum chamber is below $1 . 3 3 \times 1 0 ^ { - 2 }$ Pa $( 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 }$ Torr), and consequently does not require any differential pumping. In order for the electron multiplier detector to operate properly, the vacuum must be maintained below $1 . 3 3 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 }$ Pa $( 1 . 0 \times$ $1 \bar { 0 } ^ { - 5 }$ Torr).
--[p282]-- 28.5.2 Electrostatic analyzer with TOF spectrometer
Electrostatic analyzers (ESAs) consist mainly of two curved deflection electrodes. These electrodes create a radially directed electric field through which entrance and exit apertures restrict the ions to travel along a circular path with a known radius.
--[p283]-- The most abundant ion charge state was $\mathrm { X e } ^ { 2 + }$ . The maxima of the ion energy distributions were approximately at 3 and <1 keV for the 8-ns and 150-ps laser pulse widths, respectively. The maximum ion energies were approximately 8 and >10 keV, respectively.
--[p283]-- The entrance aperture is 10 cm from the LPP with a total path length of 64 cm. The different ions could be easily distinguished by the detector at the measured energies of 250 and 313 eV.
The ESA at EUVA used by Komori’s research group is a commercial device.<sup>45</sup> It is located in a separate vacuum chamber that is differentially pumped. The entrance aperture to the differentially pumped region is 42 cm from the LPP, and the ions traverse a total distance of 845 cm.
--[p282]-- In terms of the applied voltage, assuming the ions travel midway between the plates, the energy-to-charge ratio becomes equal to $E / q = V / \ln ( b / a )$ , where V is the applied voltage, $q$ is the ion charge, and b and a are the radii of the deflection electrodes.
Typically, ESAs are not used alone but in combination with a mass spectrometer. The simplest combination is an ESA with a TOF spectrometer. Consequently, both the $E / q$ and the $m / q$ of the transmitted ions can be determined.
--[p283]-- The analyzer deflects ions through an angle of almost 180 deg, and they are then detected with an MCP detector. Excellent mass resolution is obtained, and the natural isotope abundance for each charge state can be easily resolved. The group has been using its ESA-TOF detector to study an LPP source using a Xe jet. A typical measurement is shown in Fig. 28.7. Only Xe ions have been observed, and the ion charge states were $\leq 6 +$ .
--[p283]-- Because the detector is no longer directed at the plasma, spurious signals due to x rays and fast electrons are not present. Consequently, an external timing signal from the plasma is necessary to measure the ion arrival times.
The research groups of both Richardson at $\mathrm { U C F } ^ { 4 2 }$ and Komori at $\mathrm { E U V A } ^ { 4 5 }$ have used this technique. Schematics of their experimental apparatus are shown in Fig. 28.5 and Fig. 28.6, respectively.

===== [p279-279] Flying Circus EUV Source Metrology and Source Development Assessment > 28.4.2 Thomson scattering (11块) =====
--[p279]-- 5$ , and $n _ { \mathrm { e } } = ( 1 . 3 0 \pm 0 . 0 5 ) \times 1 0 ^ { 2 0 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { \hat { - } 3 }$ . This LPP source is significantly different from other EUV sources in which electron temperatures on the order of 30 eV optimize the 13.5-nm radiation from xenon.<sup>4</sup>
--[p279]-- The spectrum of scattered light in a Thomson scattering experiment is determined by the parameter $\alpha = ( \lambda / 4 \pi \lambda _ { \mathrm { D } } ) \sin ( \theta / 2 )$ , where $\lambda _ { \mathrm { D } }$ is the Debye length, θ is the scattering angle, and λ is the wavelength of the incident laser light. When $\alpha \ll 1$ , the spectrum is directly related to the electron energy distribution function.
--[p279]-- If the plasma has a well-defined electron temperature, the scattered light will have a Gaussian shape. When $\propto \gg 1$ , the collective motion of the plasma becomes dominant. The scattered spectrum is dominated by a central peak at $\omega _ { 0 }$ and satellite peaks at $\omega _ { 0 } \pm \omega _ { \mathrm { p } }$ , where $\omega _ { 0 }$ is the incident laser frequency and $\omega _ { \mathrm { p } }$ is the plasma frequency.
--[p279]-- A frequency-doubled Nd:glass laser was focused into a $1 6 0 { \mathrm { - } } { \mu } \mathrm { m } { \mathrm { - } } \mathrm { F W H M }$ focal spot. The laser pulse was flat-topped with a 650-ps duration. The scattered light was collected at 45 deg to the incident laser beam and observed from a $2 0 0 \times 1 0 0 \times 1 0 0 – \mu \mathrm { m } ^ { 3 }$ volume. The estimated scattering parameter was $\alpha = 3 .
--[p279]-- Carefully designed beam dumps, optical baffles, and polarizing filters are often used to help reduce the scattered laser light. In addition, the scattered radiation must be distinguished from the background of optical emissions from the plasma.
--[p279]-- 4 3$ , and therefore the spectrum was dominated by the collective plasma motions. Two separate spectrometers were used to measure the electronic and ion satellite peaks. A high spectral resolution (0.025 nm) was used to measure the ion plasma frequency, and a lower spectral resolution (10 nm) for the electron plasma frequency. They found for the condition measured that the electron temperature $T _ { \mathrm { e } } = 4 1 5 \pm 4 0 \ \mathrm { e V } , \langle Z \rangle = 2 7 . 4 \pm 1 .
--[p279]-- The plasma frequency is $\omega _ { \mathrm { p } x } = ( 4 \pi n _ { x } e ^ { 2 } / \dot { m _ { x } } ) ^ { 1 / 2 }$ , where $n _ { x }$ and $m _ { x }$ are respectively the electron $( x = \mathtt { e } )$ or ion $( x = \mathrm { i } )$ density and mass. Therefore, by measuring the plasma frequencies from the Thomson scattering spectrum, the charged-particle densities can be determined.
--[p279]-- They studied the properties of a laser-produced gas-jet xenon plasma. Instead of having a separate laser for the Thomson scattering, they measured the scattered light originating from the same laser pulse used to create the plasma. The xenon target was a sonic gas jet formed with a 1-mm-diameter nozzle. The nozzle created a parabolic density profile that was essentially uniform over the central $4 0 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ of the jet.
--[p279]-- The ratio of the electron and ion densities can then be used to estimate the average ion charge state in the plasma.
Thomson scattering has not been used widely as a diagnostic for EUV or other similar plasma sources. The intense optical emissions from these plasma sources make measuring the weak scattered light very difficult. The technique has been applied by Chenais-Popovics et al.<sup>37</sup> at the Laboratoire pour l’Utilisation des Lasers Intenses facility at École Polytechnique, France.
--[p279]-- 28.4.2 Thomson scattering
Thomson scattering measurements can provide information concerning the electron temperature, electron density, and average ion charge state of plasmas. This information is obtained from the frequency shifts of light scattered from the plasma. The scattered radiation is typically quite small and often difficult to measure. Great care also is needed to suppress scattered laser light from optical components and other surfaces within the plasma vacuum chamber.
--[p279]-- The width of the central peak is associated with the ion motion and can be used to determine the ion temperature. The satellite peaks can form from both the electron $( \omega _ { \mathrm { p e } } )$ and ion $( \omega _ { \mathrm { p i } } )$ plasma frequencies.

===== [p376-379] Synchrotron Radiation Sources for EUVL Applications > 32.1 Electron Storage Rings and Synchrotron Radiation (21块) =====
--[p376]-- The energy lost by the circulating electrons to synchrotron radiation is replenished by longitudinal electrical kicks imparted to the beam as it transverses one or more radio frequency (rf) cavities incorporated in the ring. The rf power in these cavities chops the circulating electron beam into bunches and hence determines the duration of the synchrotron radiation pulses; its frequency determines the minimum bunch spacing.
--[p376]-- If the momentum loss is too high, the electron is lost from within the storage-ring acceptance. To reduce electron-molecule collisions, the inside of a storage ring is maintained at extremely low pressure (in the range $1 0 ^ { - 9 } \mathrm { t o } \ 1 0 ^ { - 1 0 } \mathrm { T o r r } )$ . Changing the electron beam’s size can change the electron-electron collision rate, but the photoemission process is inherent in the quantum nature of photoemission.
--[p377]-- For example, undulator radiation is produced when a relativistic electron beam traverses an insertion device with a sufficiently weak periodic magnetic field.
--[p379]-- The spectral shape of wiggler radiation is similar to that of bending-magnet radiation but shifted to higher photon energies by the higher magnetic fields and increased photon flux. Due to constructive interference, the spectrum of undulator radiation consists of a series of sharp intense peaks at harmonics of the fundamental energy, as shown in Fig. 32.2(b).
--[p379]-- Next, we discuss four applications of synchrotron radiation to EUVL that illustrate why synchrotron EUV sources have played such an important role in the development of this technology. Finally, we comment on the applications that are likely to continue to play an important role in this technologically important field.
--[p379]-- The spectral brightness of synchrotron radiation from some typical insertions devices at several representative synchrotron radiation facilities<sup>2</sup> is shown in Fig. 32.2(c). A more detailed description of the characteristics of synchrotron radiation is provided in Sec. 32.2.
By tradition, storage rings are generally classified according to generation.
--[p376]-- A drawing of a typical synchrotron radiation source built around a storage ring is shown in Fig. 32.1. The storage ring, a many-sided doughnut-shaped tube, enables a current of electrons to circulate at essentially the speed of light in a closed orbit for many hours, all the while emitting synchrotron radiation. The electron beam decays slowly because of electron momentum loss during collisions with residual gas molecules, electron-electron collisions, and photoemission.
--[p377]-- Due to the stronger transverse fields, the oscillation amplitude is larger and the radiation cone angle is broader [with cone angle $K ( \gamma ) ^ { - 1 }$ , where K is the electron deflection parameter], as shown in Fig. 32.2(a) (middle).
Typical radiation spectra from a bending magnet, a wiggler, and an undulator<sup>2</sup> are shown in Fig. 32.2(b). For bending-magnet and wiggler sources, the spectrum is a smooth continuum.
--[p376]-- This so-called lattice determines the basic features of the circulating beam, such as its emittance and its transverse dimensions, and also determines the number, length, and location of any straight sections in the ring available for insertion magnets: devices that provide radiation with enhanced flux, brightness, and spectral range.
--[p377]-- Bendingmagnet (or dipole) radiation is produced when relativistic electrons (with energy $\gamma m c ^ { 2 }$ , where $\gamma$ is the Lorentz contraction factor, m is the electron mass, and c is the speed of light in vacuum) travel in a uniform magnetic field.
--[p377]-- The periodic magnetic field causes the electrons to wiggle, or undulate, from side to side as they pass through the device. The magnet period, field strength, and other geometric properties of the insertion device can be chosen to optimize one or more properties of the radiation: photon flux, wavelength selectability, spatial resolution, etc.
--[p377]-- The characteristic emission angle from an undulator is narrowed by constructive interference of radiation from the array of magnets, resulting in a pencil-shaped beam of photons [with cone angle $( \dot { \gamma } \sqrt { N } ) ^ { - 1 }$ , where N is the number of magnet periods] that in many ways resembles the output from a laser, as shown in Fig. 32.2(a) (bottom). Wiggler radiation is produced when relativistic electrons transverse an insertion device with a strong periodic magnet field.
--[p376]-- Some of the synchrotron radiation from the bending magnets and most of the radiation from the insertion magnets (wigglers and undulators) escapes the storage ring through tangential ports, called beamlines, that allow the radiation to pass to experimental end stations located at convenient distances from the ring.
Some of the more important characteristics of the three different types of radiation available from a synchrotron light source<sup>1</sup> are illustrated in Fig. 32.2.
--[p376]-- The storage ring is filled with electrons from a source called an injector, e.g., a linear accelerator fed from an electron gun, a microtron, or a small booster ring fed by a linac or a microtron.
--[p379]-- A first-generation storage ring is one that was originally built for use in high energy physics research and that has subsequently been outfitted with one or more parasitic beam ports to utilize the otherwise lost synchrotron radiation. Somewhat later, a second generation of storage rings, specifically designed as dedicated light sources, was constructed. In general, these second-generation rings have a larger number of bending-magnet beamlines and serve a large user community.
--[p377]-- In this case the emission is confined to a sharp cone (with cone angle $\bar { \gamma } ^ { - 1 } )$ that sweeps around like the headlight on a toy train, producing a continuous swath of radiation in the plane of the bend, as shown in Fig. 32.2(a) (top). Synchrotron radiation with additional useful properties is produced when relativistic electrons traverse an insertion device with a spatially periodic magnetic field.
--[p376]-- A system of magnetic lenses, bending magnets (dipoles), focusing magnets (quadrupoles), and steering magnets (sextupoles), strategically located around the ring, guides and focuses the electron beam.
--[p379]-- In this chapter, we review the fundamentals of synchrotron radiation, especially as they relate to EUVL.<sup>3–5</sup> We begin by briefly reviewing the important characteristics of bending-magnet, undulator, and wiggler radiation in the EUV spectral region. We then list some of the important characteristics of the various synchrotron radiation facilities worldwide.
--[p376]-- 32.1 Electron Storage Rings and Synchrotron Radiation
It is well known that when charged particles are accelerated they emit electromagnetic radiation. For example, when electrons traveling at nearly the speed of light are forced to move along a curved path by the magnetic fields of a storage ring, they emit photons into a narrow cone.
--[p379]-- The latest synchrotron-radiation facilities, so-called third-generation storage rings, are characterized by much lower electron-beam emittance and contain many straight sections specifically designed for insertion devices. Third-generation rings generally provide synchrotron radiation with much higher brightness. A fairly comprehensive survey of synchrotron-radiation facilities presently available around the world is presented in Sec. 32.3.
--[p376]-- Depending on the electron energy, this so-called synchrotron radiation can be extremely intense over a broad wavelength range extending all the way from the microwave to the x-ray spectral region. Because this radiation also tends to be vertically collimated and polarized, it has been used as a powerful research and development tool in chemistry, physics, material science, biology and medicine, and, in the last decade or so, has played a key role in the development of EUVL.

--[p167]-- This means that the jet and the source hardware must be able to handle this power. The challenge is to predict if this is possible before the lasers become available, since so far only lasers in the few-kilowatt range have been available for laser-plasma experiments.<sup>54,58</sup>

--[p167]-- 23.4.4 Thermal-load capability
It is evident from the design example above that drive powers of several tens of kilowatts will be required. It is a great challenge for any source to handle such powers. Since the plasma will be optimized to absorb most of the drive power, approaching 100%, basically the same amount of power that drives the plasma will be emitted from the plasma as broadband radiation and energetic particles.

===== [p467-468] Electrode and Condenser Materials for Plasma Pinch Sources > 35.4 Testing of Materials in Plasma-Gun Facilities (8块) =====
--[p467]-- 35.4 Testing of Materials in Plasma-Gun Facilities
Small plasma pinch devices operating with frequencies of 5–10 kHz, pulse energies on the order of 1–100 J, and gas mixtures of Xe and He are very promising as sources of EUVL radiation $( \lambda = 1 3 . 5 \mathrm { n m } )$ .
--[p468]-- The experiments performed are a first step toward understanding the problem of material damage induced by hot Xe plasma. They were focused mainly on the development of appropriate experimental techniques relevant to conditions in highheat-flux regions on electrodes in DPP EUV devices.
--[p467]-- A serious problem in the design of such EUV sources concerns erosion of the pinch components under the action of electric currents, hot plasma particles, and photon radiation.<sup>27</sup> Material erosion limits the lifetime of plasma-facing components, thereby reducing the practical feasibility of DPP EUV sources. Investigation of erosion mechanisms and their dependences on the operational parameters is quite important for successful development of commercial DPP EUV devices.
--[p468]-- Initial results indicate various mechanisms of material erosion (such as vaporization, sputtering, and melt splashing) and surface modification (bubble and blister growth and cavity formation) that can all exist in regions of high heat flux in DPP EUV device electrodes.<sup>7,8</sup>
--[p467]-- Due to collision of the supersonic plasma stream with the solid target, a shock front arises in the plasma stream, and a cloud of hot, dense Xe plasma is formed near the target surface. Thus the target surface is exposed to the interaction of energetic particles and photon radiation from the hot Xe plasma, as in DPP EUV devices.
--[p468]-- Theoretical analysis shows that the required temperature can be obtained in the shock wave if the plasma stream moves with a velocity of the order of $1 0 ^ { 7 } \mathrm { c m / s }$ . Therefore, the first task of the experiment was to produce Xe plasma streams with sufficiently high velocity. Besides a high velocity, the plasma stream must have a rather large energy and pulse duration. In this manner, material testing and lifetime assessment could be realized during a short time.
--[p467]-- Experiments described in this section investigate material erosion caused by hot, dense Xe and H plasmas on copper and tungsten sample targets. The experiments were carried out at the plasma-gun facility MK-200, at TRINITI, Russia. A pulsed plasma gun is used as the source of Xe or H plasma. The gun accelerates low-temperature Xe plasma to a high velocity. Then the plasma stream collides with the structural material to be investigated.
--[p468]-- A cloud of Xe plasma is formed at a temperature $\begin{array} { r } { T = 3 0 { - } 5 0 \mathrm { e V } , } \end{array}$ similar to those found in EUV plasma pinch devices. This magnitude of temperature is needed for the tenfold ionization of Xe to produce ${ \tt X e } ^ { + { \tilde { 1 0 } } }$ ions emitting spectral lines at the wavelength $\lambda = 1 3 . 5$ nm.

===== [p55-55] Chapter 17 Capillary Z-Pinch Source > 17.5 Conclusions (3块) =====
--[p55]-- Lifetime tests for electrodes and collector mirror have started, and a component lifetime of more than $1 0 ^ { 7 }$ shots has been checked so far. Although the lifetime of neither electrodes nor collector optics meets the requirements yet, the causes of the problem have always been identified.
Using our experimental test stand, many aspects of the radiation characteristics were evaluated.
--[p55]-- 17.5 Conclusions
This chapter described features and characteristics of the capillary Z-pinch EUV source. An EUV source power of 54.4 W (2π sr, 2% bandwidth) was achieved in 2-kHz operation. At this time, a power of 121 W (2π sr, 2% bandwidth) has been achieved with a newly developed source in 7-kHz operation. An IF power of 8.4 W has been obtained with the use of a single grazing-incidence mirror.
--[p55]-- The properties of the EUV output power in 2-kHz operation were different from those at low repetition rate. The angular distributions of inband EUV radiation were explained, and the equivalent solid angle was calculated as 1.45 sr. Inband EUV images taken by a pinhole camera showed very interesting behavior of the radiating plasma in the capillary and explained the angular distribution of radiation.
Moreover, two types of collectors were introduced, and EUVA has established experimental evaluation and simulation tools.

===== [p307-307] Metrology for EUVL Sources and Tools > 29.5.1.3 Speed (2块) =====
--[p307]-- Junction capacitance scales linearly with the photodiode active area, so smaller devices are faster devices. The capacitance can be decreased by reverse-biasing a photodiode, as described in Sec. 29.5.3. The calibration of small devices is problematic, since it is crucial for the detector to be underfilled during the calibration. Traditionally, 10 × 10-mm devices have been used for transfer standards because of their large active area.
--[p307]-- 29.5.1.3 Speed
In a pulsed application, the detector’s intrinsic speed is a significant factor. The response from one pulse must be completely discharged prior to the arrival of the next pulse, or pulse-stacking will occur. The device speed is determined principally by the junction capacitance, which appears with the load resistance as the RC time constant in a capacitive discharge circuit.

===== [p98-99] Spatially and Temporally Multiplexed Laser Modules for LPP Sources > 20.1 Introduction (4块) =====
--[p98]-- We have successfully generated a high-power EUV source using an LPP scheme. In this scheme, we spatially multiplex (combine) several of our lasers and focus them onto a xenon target. To achieve this we have recently made significant steps forward in the performance of the laser-driver module employed in our LPP EUV source. We have increased the average power output from the laser whilst minimizing the overall cost of ownership (CoO) and footprint of the system.
--[p99]-- In addition to sustained laser development, we are taking the responsibility of developing an appropriate target to achieve what we have projected in our EUV development source roadmap. The target development is not restricted to Xe solid jets, but other targets materials are also investigated in order to increase the inband EUV conversion efficiency (CE). The combination of highly efficient lasers and high CE of the inband EUV through target development drives down the CoO of the EUV source.
--[p98]-- These advantages can be summarized as power scalability through tuning of laser parameters, low debris, pulse-to-pulse stability (optimum dose control), flexibility in dimensions, spatial stability, minimal heat load, and large solid angle of collection.
The main objective of the EUV program at Powerlase is to develop a highpower, cost-effective source able to deliver enough usable power for use in the microlithography process.
--[p98]-- 20.1 Introduction
EUVL is considered to be one of the most attractive candidates to succeed conventional optical lithography in the coming years. This will permit reduction of structure sizes in semiconductor devices to less than 45 nm. To enable this technology, a light source is required that emits in the spectral range around 13.5 nm. The LPP EUV source has great potential to be the future source for EUVL, and offers several advantages over discharge-based EUV sources.

===== [p223-223] Laser Plasma EUV Sources based on Droplet Target Technology > 26.1.1 Source requirements for EUVL (7块) =====
--[p223]-- Yet this thermal loading limit creates a practical maximum power above which discharge sources will not operate. The laser plasma, on the other hand, suffers no imposed limit on the available power. This can be increased simply by increasing the total laser power. In that case, however, low values of the inband CE will drive laser costs through the economically imposed ceilings on total scanner costs.
--[p223]-- Gas curtains,<sup>3</sup> mechanical shutters,<sup>4</sup> electric and magnetic fields,<sup>5</sup> and other devices can be the basis of a number of inhibition techniques. Moreover, the relative particle and ion fluxes depend greatly on the source materials and characteristics. Discharge sources tend to have higher particle fluxes, while the larger-solid-angle collection optics possible with laser plasmas place more stringent requirements on protection against ion erosion.
--[p223]-- Out-of-band (OOB) radiation poses a threat for both sources.
By far the most difficult challenge after source power is the need to limit the effects of plasma and particulate debris on the collection optics. These must last for 30,000 h. Meeting this latter requirement can be approached in several ways. Particles and ions emanating from the source can be stopped by a number of means before they damage the optics.
--[p223]-- Though the key requirements of inband power, stability, lifetime, and cost pertain both to discharge sources and to laser-plasma sources, their relative importance as threats to the collection optics differs. For instance, thermal loading on the electrodes will limit the maximum inband power available from a discharge source. Thus, any improvement in inband conversion efficiency (CE) will increase the maximum available power.
--[p223]-- Hopefully we will not be challenged by still higher fluence levels, since, in large part, the fabrication industry seems to have settled on 300-mm wafer formats running at ∼100 wafers per hour. Other requirements have different degrees of difficulty for discharge and for laser plasmas. The maximum source size of 1 mm is easily met with laser plasmas, but not with discharge plasmas—likewise for the repetition rate, which affects the EUV dose stability.
--[p223]-- 26.1.1 Source requirements for EUVL
The complete set of diverse source requirements for EUVL is summarized in Chapter 2. This chapter concentrates on those requirements that present the stiffest challenges to the successful development of a source for EUVL, with particular reference to a laser-plasma source.
--[p223]-- As the anticipated insertion date of EUVL into fabrication has receded, and both the assessment of its technology and its required performance level have matured, it is not surprising that the required source parameters have increased in magnitude—and maybe, too, in level of attainment. By far the most dramatic change has occurred in the required source power, jumping tenfold in the last six years (Fig. 26.1).

--[p133]-- However, due to the physical properties of xenon (small thermal expansion coefficient and large atomic weight), this gas is difficult to pump. To meet the EUV source specifications, Alcatel designed an innovative pumping system based on three differential pumping stages and on advanced pumps optimized for xenon.
The main part of the xenon jet is directly pumped through a catcher by a dry primary pumping system based on advanced multistage Roots pumps.
--[p133]-- In particular, our modeling is based on a stationary approach assuming monophase gaseous xenon (i.e., no liquid phase), and finally the xenon target is taken as a dense, gaseous xenon flow out of the injector nozzle. --[p133]-- Thus, the pressure in the collector chamber remains one order of magnitude below that of the plasma chamber, thereby keeping EUV-light absorption at a negligible level and limiting contamination of optical elements.
This optimization was first made with simple conductance calculations, and then detailed with a 3D computational-flow-dynamics modeling of the whole vacuum system.
--[p133]-- 21.3.4.1 The xenon pumping system
Vacuum and contamination controls are key issues for the production of EUV light. First of all, for current systems using xenon, the reabsorption of EUV light by residual contamination gas and in particular by residual xenon strongly affects the useful EUV generation. Therefore, the source chamber partial pressure of xenon should be limited to $1 0 ^ { - 3 }$ mbar on the EUV light path.
--[p133]-- The evaporated xenon in the source chamber is pumped by magnetically levitated turbomolecular hybrid pumps, which are directly connected to the plasma chamber and to the EUV collecting chamber. Figure 21.21 summarizes schematically the ELSAC pumping system for xenon and shows all subunits.
The diaphragm between the two chambers is optimized so that only a small amount of evaporated xenon can flow through it toward the collector.
--[p133]-- Second, contamination could be critical for the optical components’ lifetime. Indeed, EUV sources contain optical components, such as focusing elements or collector modules, that are fragile and very sensitive to contamination. Therefore the partial pressure of water and hydrocarbons must be kept as low as possible, typically below the $1 0 ^ { - 9 }$ mbar range.
--[p133]-- Optimization of the vacuum systems was obtained by combining gas flow modeling with experimental tests.

===== [p225-226] Laser Plasma EUV Sources based on Droplet Target Technology > 26.1.3 Motivation for droplet sources (9块) =====
--[p225]-- Early investigations of tin as a source material, by others and ourselves,<sup>8,9</sup> showed its potential as an efficient emitter at 13 nm, but simple witness-plate tests identified high-velocity, micron-size aerosols flying from the target,<sup>10</sup> which convinced us and others of the danger of using solid metallic targets.
--[p225]-- Depending on the material, such a target will have a diameter of ${ \sim } 1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . Assuming that this target is uniformly energized, there should be no particulate debris at all. The sole problem will now be to protect the collection mirrors from the ions coming from the plasma. Ions can be controlled with electric and magnetic fields, and are slowed by recombination, in contrast with particulate neutral matter.
--[p226]-- More recently, we have introduced the tin-doped liquid droplet target, which combines the advantages of tin over xenon (see below) with the mass-limited target concept.<sup>17</sup>
In this chapter we describe the experimental and theoretical foundations for mass-limited droplet targets for EUV sources. We place special emphasis on our latest progress with the tin-doped droplet target, since this is showing some promise for satisfying the needs of EUVL.
--[p226]-- Calibrated spectroscopy and metrology of the 13.5-nm emission help to identify the optimum laser and irradiation conditions, and these are equated with the predicted plasma conditions. Details of the laser and target technologies used in precisely synchronizing the streaming microscopic droplet targets with the focused laser beam are summarized, and at-wavelength imaging of the target confirms a small, submillimeter source size.
--[p225]-- 26.1.3 Motivation for droplet sources
From the outset of our involvement in laser plasma sources for lithography, we have expressed concern for the effects of material debris from the target on the collection optics.
--[p226]-- Extensive measurements of the energy of the ions emanating from the plasma, particularly those that can cause erosion of the collection optics, are summarized, as well as characteristics of the particulate emission. Measures to stop or inhibit this particulate and ion emission are described. Lastly, we summarize our current view of the expectations of this approach with respect to a high-efficiency EUV source and describe the developments needed to demonstrate its practicality.
--[p226]-- We describe the basic physics of the interaction leading to plasma generation, and the associated radiation physics. We place strong emphasis on using plasma fluid and radiation transfer codes to model the ion emission. Included are brief descriptions of our characterization of the evolution of the plasma, and comparisons made with hydrodynamic plasma code predictions of the plasma density and temperature.
--[p225]-- Our approach has since been to configure the laser plasma from a mass-limited target, that is, one whose mass yields just the total number of required atomic radiators. With this target concept, for example, a 100-mJ laser pulse (energy $\approx 6 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { e V } )$ will produce an ${ \approx } 3 0 – \mathrm { e V }$ plasma of ${ \sim } 1 0 ^ { 1 5 }$ atoms, taking into account the energy needed for ionization and excitation.
--[p225]-- With this philosophy, we began investigating a water droplet target, which fortunately emits a strong narrow line at 13 nm (the 4d-2p transition in Li-like oxygen).<sup>2,11</sup> Another approach, which quickly gained favor, was to use jets of liquid Xe atomic clusters produced by pulsed supersonic ejection through a microscopic nozzle.<sup>12,13</sup> Xenon was recognized as a broadband emitter of EUV radiation from previous general studies of soft-x-ray emission from laser plasmas.<sup>14</sup> It was felt that Xe, being a gas, would pose less serious threats to collection mirrors. Subsequently liquid $\mathrm { j e t } ^ { \bar { 1 } 5 }$ and liquid Xe droplet<sup>16</sup> targets have been developed.

--[p101]-- 20.2.3 Powerlase Starlase laser system
Having considered the optimum laser parameters for efficient EUV generation, the laser solution under development at Powerlase is now presented.
The Starlase range of lasers is based on completely solid state technology that employs diode pumping of Nd:YAG rods in order to generate laser radiation at a wavelength of $1 . 0 6 4 \mu \mathrm { m }$ .
--[p102]-- This type of target has been $\mathrm { s h o w n } ^ { 7 }$ to exhibit an EUV CE of up to 0.95% (2π sr, 2% bandwidth). We have so far demonstrated a CE of up to 0.8% (2π sr, 2% bandwidth) using a $5 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ -diameter xenon filament. Table 20.1 shows a section of the Powerlase EUV source roadmap, which was prepared in response to industry demands.
--[p102 [表]]-- In order to produce the required level of laser power and be able to deliver it to the LPP target, Powerlase is continuing to increase the output power of the EO-switched laser module whilst employing spatial multiplexing (discussed in the next subsection) to combine multiple beams on target. The output power of the laser module is scaled up using a combination of increased repetition rate with enhancements to key laser components such as the cavity, gain module, and switch.
--[p101]-- The system currently under development for EUV generation utilizes electrooptical (EO) switching to generate short laser pulses with 9-ns duration, and is therefore ideal for use with micron-scale, solid-density targets. At the present time, the laser is capable of producing an average output power of up to 1 kW at a repetition rate of 3.5 kHz, and operates with a beam $M ^ { 2 }$ of 12.
One key feature of the laser technology is that very high electrical-to-optical CE has been achieved.
--[p102]-- Within the context of the complete EUV light source, a key efficiency factor is the CE of laser energy into inband EUV radiation. To date, we have measured an EUV CE of 0.8% (2π sr, 2% bandwidth) using the Starlase system to irradiate a jet of xenon clusters a short distance (∼1 mm) away from the gas supply nozzle. However, in order to reduce source-induced debris and increase CE, work has begun on developing a high-density xenon filament as the next stage in LPP target development.

===== [p256-256] Flying Circus EUV Source Metrology and Source Development Assessment > 27.1 Historical Overview of Metrology Development and Standardization (7块) =====
--[p256]-- Collecting data from sources on different locations worldwide, the activity became known as Flying Circus, or FC for short, and initially resulted in a full benchmark characterization of five candidate EUV light sources and the development of a common diagnostic standard.<sup>6,7</sup> The follow-up project, Flying Circus 2 (FC2), sponsored by International SEMATECH, had the broader scope of further assessing the progress of EUV source performance, calibrating EUV source metrology equipment from different EUV source suppliers, and continuing the development of globally accepted EUV source measurement procedures. Nowadays, more then a dozen sources are characterized in this way, and the FC-type diagnostic has found permanent use at the majority of the source development laboratories.
--[p256]-- FC diagnostics are commercially offered by Scientec Engineering (www.scientec.nl). The general acceptance of the method and the continued program of on-site calibration using the portable FC equipment at the different source labs, as well as furtherdeveloped FC hardware, considerably assisted in the standardization of source performance representation.<sup>8</sup>
--[p256]-- The approach was to assess each of the different sources with one single diagnostics set, circumventing any uncertainty introduced by the specific properties or calibration of the various metrology devices. In addition, the measurement procedure was standardized.
--[p256]-- 27.1 Historical Overview of Metrology Development and Standardization
Soon after the first explorations of the potential of EUVL, it became obvious that the wafer throughput of future EUVL systems, and thus the EUV source brightness, was a key factor in the industrial value of this new imaging technology.
--[p256]-- From the data collected with these devices, extrapolations were then made to the most relevant quantity, namely, the true EUV power within the bandwidth and the radiation acceptance angle of the total EUVL system. In order to allow a direct comparison of the performance of the different candidate EUV sources, in 2000 ASML sponsored a source metrology activity by FOM and Philips Research for which a portable, absolutely calibrated set of diagnostics was used.
--[p256]-- The need for plasma-based light sources of moderate temperature, though strongly confined in space and critically optimized for emission at 13.5 nm, implied the use of suitable diagnostics, well adjusted for the particular application. Especially in the early days of EUVL development, a variety of source diagnostics were being used by the different source developers, each having backgrounds in different research and technology areas.
--[p256]-- These diagnostics ranged from uncalibrated grating spectrographs and luminescent detectors to broadband detection systems, such as filtered calorimeters and photocathodes, each detector obviously having its own characteristics.<sup>1–3</sup> The measurement units applied varied correspondingly, ranging from $\mathbf { J } { \cdot } \mathbf { e } \mathbf { V } ^ { - 1 } { \cdot } \mathbf { J } _ { \boldsymbol { 1 } } ^ { - 1 }$ to percent. 4,5

--[p479]-- 35.4.9 Conclusions on testing materials in plasma-gun facilities
Tungsten and copper targets have been tested with hot Xe plasma $( T = 3 0 – 5 0 \mathrm { e V } )$ formed near the target surface due to collision of a supersonic Xe plasma stream with the solid target. The same materials have been tested also with a H plasma stream having similar energy density to the Xe one. Plasma-induced erosion and surface damage were studied.
The experimental results can be summarized briefly as follows:
--[p480]-- The details of surface damage are relevant, since the experiments presented here produce the same net energy deposition as that found in DPP devices. A Xe self-shielding effect should be expected during operation of DPP devices, and thus melt motion can be expected in certain regions on DPP electrode surfaces.
--[p480]-- • Copper and tungsten erosion caused by material evaporation, sputtering, and droplet injection (the erosion mechanisms leading to target mass loss) is about 0.1 µm per shot of Xe or H plasma.
• Hot Xe or H plasma produces a melt layer at the exposed target surface.
• Under the action of a plasma stream, copper melt is splashed from the exposed target area. Erosion of copper due to melt movement is about 1 µm per shot of H plasma. Xe plasma causes much less splashing of copper melt.
--[p480]-- A H plasma produces small flakes at the tungsten surface, causing brittle destruction of the tungsten. A Xe plasma produces a wavy structure on the tungsten surface, consisting of bubbles. These results show that surface damage induced by Xe plasma differs from that induced by H plasma.
One important observation is the variety of erosion mechanisms under highintensity plasma exposure for materials such as copper and tungsten. The erosion is not only due to normal physical sputtering.
--[p480]-- The net energy deposited into the materials tested in the MK-200 plasma guns is between 1.5 and 2.5 J/cm<sup>2</sup>, resembling conditions in DPP electrode regions exposed to high heat flux.
--[p480]-- • Splashing of tungsten melt is practically absent.
• The microstructures of target surfaces exposed to Xe and H plasmas are quite different.
For copper, a H plasma causes melt boiling, producing open cavities at the exposed target surface. A copper target irradiated with a Xe plasma is entirely covered with surface waves. For tungsten, a H plasma causes severe cracking of the surface. A Xe plasma causes considerably milder cracking.
--[p480]-- It also depends on the effectiveness of the vapor shielding, which, in the case of Xe bombardment and the conditions in these experiments, is quite effective. Thus normal sputtering is not the only erosion mechanism, though the overall mass losses from Xe and from H are measured to be of the same order of magnitude.
Concerning implications of these results for DPP EUV devices, the following points are concluded. Xe damage at the surface is quite distinct from that due to other gases such as H.

--[p332]-- 30.4.2 Spectral responsivity of different types
The high absorption of EUV radiation in any material is a major problem for the use of semiconductor photodiodes as detectors, because the radiation must penetrate through the passivation layer and the front region (either p- or n-doped) into the pn junction region. Therefore, silicon photodiodes with a thick oxide passivation are not useful for EUV radiation. An alternative is to use Schottky diodes.
--[p334]-- Although these diodes have a nearly ideal performance regarding their responsivity, it turned out that the nitrided oxide is not sufficiently stable over time (see next subsection). For 157-nm F<sub>2</sub> laser radiation, PtSi Schottky-barrier diodes have been shown to be most stable.<sup>39,40</sup> Regarding their homogeneity, these diodes suffer from the same problem of the highly absorbing front layer as discussed above for GaAsP-Au diodes.
--[p333]-- The development of silicon photodiodes for the VUV and EUV spectral range was initiated by needs of the second-generation synchrotron radiation sources as well as the applications in x-ray astronomy, x-ray microscopy, and plasma diagnostics and the first investigations for EUVL in the late 1980s.<sup>35</sup> These diodes (called AXUV) were soon improved regarding their radiation stability<sup>36</sup> and used for radiometric applications.<sup>11,37,38</sup>
--[p335]-- Diodes from different lots have a rather similar spectral responsivity at 13.5 nm, between 0.20 and 0.23 A/W; the responsivity at 10 nm, however, depends strongly on the individual device, varying between 0.05 and 0.15 A/W. ===== [p106-107] Spatially and Temporally Multiplexed Laser Modules for LPP Sources > 20.3.1 High-density xenon target (6块) =====
--[p107]-- The diode assembly is also equipped with multilayer mirror (MLM) samples to study debris from the source. A cross section of our vacuum chamber illustrating these diagnostics is shown in Fig. 20.5. OOB measurements using a Xe target showed that almost 60% of the emitted plasma radiation is in the region 5–20 nm. The OOB measurements were conducted using combinations of different filters such as Al, Si, Zr, and $\mathrm { C a F } _ { 2 }$ with XUV diodes.
Angular distribution measurements, shown in Fig. 20.7, exhibit less than 10% variation of the EUV intensity.
--[p106]-- 20.3.1 High-density xenon target
The principal objective of LPP target design is to create a localized region of highdensity material such that laser absorption is maximized, whilst absorption of the generated EUV radiation in the chamber environment is minimized. Furthermore, if a nozzle is used to deliver the target material, the plasma must be created far enough away from the nozzle that nozzle debris does not limit the lifetime of the collection optics.
--[p106]-- In the system currently under development at Powerlase, a high-density xenon filament with diameter of $5 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ is injected into the vacuum system shown in Fig. 20.5. This system uses two $3 0 0 0 { - } \mathrm { l } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ turbopumps to achieve an ultimate pressure of $5 \times 1 0 ^ { - \mathrm { i } 0 }$ mbar and a background pressure of $5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 }$ mbar when operating the xenon target.
--[p107]-- The main issue currently being addressed is the stability of the target, as changes in the filament direction can lead to substantial variations in the EUV output.<sup>10</sup> However, several strategies exist to circumvent this problem, and they are currently being investigated.
In order to determine the angular distribution and the out-of-band (OOB) radiation, we have assembled a photodiode array at a distance of 110 mm from the EUV source.
--[p106]-- The xenon is recycled in a closed loop employing continuous gas filtration in order to achieve extremely low levels of contamination. Residual gas analyzer (RGA) measurements indicate hydrocarbon levels of $\leq 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 1 0 }$ mbar (for molecular masses $\sum 4 5 - 2 0 0 )$ and a water level of $\sim 1 0 ^ { - 9 }$ mbar. The recycling system is capable of delivering a stable xenon pressure of up to 50 bar at the nozzle inlet.
Figure 20.6 shows two images of the xenon filament.
--[p106]-- The target should be refreshable and able to support the high repetition rates (>3.5 kHz) that are produced by the Starlase range of lasers and are required for optimum EUV dose control during the lithographic process. The source environment must also be debris-free, and the hydrocarbon and water levels must not exceed specified limits.
A promising method of achieving these requirements is provided by a cryogenic, high-density xenon filament target.

===== [p93-93] Chapter 19 Technology for LPP Sources > 19.8 Summary and Conclusion (3块) =====
--[p93]-- The most reliable target material in practice is xenon, the use of which should allow sufficiently long optics lifetime of the lithography exposure tool. Experimentally 2.5-W inband power was achieved in 2π sr and 2% bandwidth, which corresponds to an IF power of 1 W. With a recently developed 1.2-kW laser, a demonstration of 3.5-W IF power is in preparation. The necessary laser power for HVM sources based on xenon is estimated to be 34 kW.
--[p93]-- The more efficient target material tin would reduce the laser-driver power needed to 8.5–24 kW and therefore reduce the cost of ownership (CoO) of the laser. However, because of condensation on the optics the use of tin may impose fundamental restrictions with respect to the lifetime of the optics. This may finally override the laser CoO reduction by far. Research to clarify this question is currently going on.
A choice of tin, lithium, or xenon fuel is expected for 2006 to support the introduction of LPP-based HVM EUV sources in 2008.
--[p93]-- 19.8 Summary and Conclusion
LPP EUV sources with diode-pumped solid-state driver lasers are promising candidates for HVM lithography light sources. With respect to the required power and lifetime, these sources do not show physical limitations in principle that might prevent the achievement of the required specifications. The driver-laser design is based on diode-pumped solid-state lasers.

--[p48]-- 17.4.2 Angular distribution of EUV radiation
In the case of the DPP source, almost all schemes seem to have a nonuniform radiation profile. Since a 9-mm-long capillary was used in our capillary Z-pinch plasma, a nonuniform distribution had been expected. In order to confirm it, the EUV energy was measured at different angular positions using ADMs and an FC-II (Fig. 17.3). ADM units were placed at 0, 5, 15, 20, 25, 30, and 40 deg.
--[p49]-- When the gas flow rate was low, the radiating plasma was located upstream inside the capillary. With increasing gas flow rate, it came to cover the whole capillary. Surprisingly, a small portion of plasma ejected from the capillary was observed at 40 sccm of gas flow rate. The length of this plasma ejection was estimated to be a few millimeters. The edge of the capillary is completely open, so that plasma can be ejected to the outside of the capillary during and after the Z-pinch implosion.
--[p49]-- The broader angular distribution of higher-gas-flow shots was in good agreement with this plasma location. From the viewpoint of collection efficiency of the collector mirror, it is an advantage that radiating plasma is located outside and near the electrode. Also, the higher gas flow rates seemed likely to yield better EUV energy stability. However, the plasma ejection might cause a difficulty.
--[p49]-- In a DPP EUV source system, a debris-mitigation system must be placed in front of the capillary to prevent debris from damaging the collector mirrors. Plasma ejection, however, could damage the debris shield. There is thus great concern about the interaction between the plasma jet and the debris shield. Further investigation of this EUV image should allow good understanding of the physics of EUV-radiating Z-pinch plasmas.
--[p48]-- Altogether eight channels were used simultaneously, including the FC-II (at 10 deg). Figure 17.10 shows the 200-shot-averaged angular distribution of EUV energy in millijoules per steradian (2% bandwidth) for 9-, 21-, and 40-sccm gas flow rates. Only data obtained at 2 kHz are provided here. At each flow rate, there was not a large difference in the EUV energy from 0 through 15 deg. At larger angular positions, it was clearly seen that a higher flow rate made the profile broader.
--[p48]-- Therefore, the highest EUV energy (in other words, the highest equivalent solid angle) was obtained at 40 sccm, although the on-axis EUV energies did not differ from each other. On comparing these data with the previously measured data,<sup>9</sup> the distribution profile was expected to fit the previous data at angles above 40 deg. Therefore, it can be estimated that EUV radiation existed in the region from 0 through about 70 deg.

--[p66]-- 18.5 Different Additives

===== [p24-25] Xenon and Tin Pinch Discharge Sources > 16.4.2 Rotating multi-discharge-unit source (8块) =====
--[p25]-- Despite the attractiveness of this approach, it may meet with numerous difficulties on the way to its implementation because of its complexity and high cost.
One obvious step toward creating an HVM EUV source is to increase the CE. Research has shown that a considerable increase in CE is possible through utilization of an alternative medium, such as Sn vapor, which will be considered in the following section.
--[p25]-- Another approach to reduce heat loading on a discharge unit is the use of N spatially fixed discharge units equidistant from a rotating mirror, which reflects radiation from each discharge unit onto one common axis.<sup>26</sup> The rotating mirror is installed near to N intermediate foci, symmetrically distributed around a common axis, at which the EUV beams are focused by means of N optical collectors.
--[p25]-- The total EUV flux reflected by the rotating mirror onto the common axis will be the sum of the N fluxes from all discharge units, and the resulting pulse repetition rate on the common axis will be a factor N higher than the pulse repetition rate of each discharge unit. Thus in the EUV source containing N discharge units and a common rotating mirror, the heat load on the electrodes can be greatly reduced.
--[p24]-- The principle of the RMDU source with many rotating discharge units<sup>25</sup> consists in the fact that the discharge happens in one of N discharge units positioned on two metal disks separated by a dielectric (Fig. 16.11). Both disks are rotated by an electric motor with rotational speed ν. The N pairs of coaxial holes in which the discharge can be produced are positioned on a circle with diameter
B on the disk.
--[p25]-- The dependence of the pulse repetition rate f on the main parameters of the RMDU source is determined by the following relation:
$$
f = { \frac { \pi B \ v } { C } } = N \ v .\tag{16.2}
$$
For the RMDU source with Xe the dimension C can be ≈3 cm, and at moderate B = 0.5 m the rotational speed of the disks should be as high as 200 rev/s to provide f ≈10 kHz.
--[p25]-- The discharge is initiated in a fixed location by means of a fixed ignition system (preionizer). The next discharge is initiated in the same location in the volume restricted by another set of holes. The holes inside which the discharge took place will be used again to produce the discharge after a complete rotation of the disks. Thus in the RMDU source the heat load on the electrodes can be reduced by a factor N.
--[p24]-- 16.4.2 Rotating multi-discharge-unit source
One of the approaches to meet the requirements for the HVM EUV source can be to utilize a source containing many discharge units triggered sequentially so that the total EUV power will be provided by the sum of the EUV power emitted by all the discharge units.
--[p25]-- Preliminary research has shown that at such high rotation speeds a serious technical problem of electrode vibration—and, accordingly, of pinch pointto-point instability—appears.

===== [p289-289] Flying Circus EUV Source Metrology and Source Development Assessment > 28.7 Summary (2块) =====
--[p289]-- 28.7 Summary
In order for an EUV plasma light source to become the NGL source, many critical challenges still need to be addressed. An understanding of the plasma and the emitted plasma debris is critical for the optimization of EUV sources and suppression of plasma debris. This is important for achieving the necessary source intensity and component lifetimes for EUV plasmas to be an economically viable lithography source.
--[p289]-- Fortunately, a wide variety of different diagnostics are available for characterizing the plasmas found in EUVL sources. Many of these diagnostics have been developed previously for other high-energy plasma applications such as fusion and x-ray lasers. Each plasma diagnostic provides only a small piece of information concerning the actual plasma state. In order to fully characterize EUV sources, a variety of different diagnostic techniques need to be employed.

--[p494]-- 36.2.1.1 Estimation of J
There are two methods to estimate a maximum value for J. The first is through energy conservation. Say 5 J of energy goes into the pulse. This number is quite reasonable for the XTS 13-35, where similar numbers have been measured. Experience with plasma guns in general has shown that the energy taken away by the electrode coolant system approximately equals the energy going into the device.
--[p494]-- That would imply that at most 25% of the energy could have turned into energetic particles and photons that could travel away from the pinch region, or 50% turned into energetic particles and photons traveling all directions, since the solid angle the electrodes intercept is at best $2 \pi$ (50%).
To be able to produce approximately 100-eV photons, the electron temperatures, $T _ { \mathrm { e } }$ , must be on the order of 30 eV.
--[p495]-- Less of the input energy may be conveyed to the particles, more energy may go to radiation, there may be much lower ion energies produced, and/or all the input fuel atoms may not get ionized or trapped. All estimates of the debris source will be made in terms of J, so the remaining calculations can be scaled as needed.
--[p495]-- Since these plasma are very dense and self-compress quickly, high ionization states of the fuel occur. The desired EUV light comes from $\mathrm { X e ^ { 9 + } }$ through $\mathrm { X e ^ { 1 1 + } }$ or $\mathrm { S n } ^ { 6 + }$ through $\mathrm { S n } ^ { 1 3 + }$ . A given radiating ion may be reexcited many times during the brief pinch duration. Finally, the plasma begins to expand and cool—reducing the charge state through recombination.

$$
J = 4 . 6 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { i o n s . }
$$
This estimate is for a temperature of 300 K. Different geometries, temperatures, and pressures would change this number, but it is of the same magnitude as given by the energy estimate.
I will use an average value of $5 . 0 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 5 }$ energetic ions for J. Note that the actual value of J may be lower.
--[p495]-- In this process a certain number of fast electrons are expelled, causing a charge imbalance. This results in a Coulomb explosion, which then accelerates the ions away from the pinch region.<sup>3</sup> Instabilities can also cause ion emission.
Measurements<sup>4</sup> and modeling<sup>5</sup> have shown that the average energy from our XTS 13-35 source is 8 keV $( \mathrm { X e ^ { + } } )$ .
--[p494]-- This implies that almost all of the energy from the pulse turns into ohmic heating or into photons or energetic particles that lose their energy to the electrodes. Obviously some fraction of the energy is not returned to the electrodes, or there would be no energetic debris to worry about mitigating! Say the maximum amount that could be unaccounted for is 25%.

===== [p324-326] Calibration of Detectors and Tools for EUV-Source Metrology > 30.2.2 EUV irradiation beamline (9块) =====
--[p326]-- At this position, the beam has a wedge-shaped structure with a high-intensity re gion of about 2 by 1 mm adjacent to a region of about 3 times lower intensity, about 4 by 2 mm in size. About 40% of the power is focused onto the hot-spot region at the tip of the wedge. The intensity profile at the irradiation position was measured using a calibrated CCD (for a detailed picture see Refs. 26,27).
--[p324]-- 30.2.2 EUV irradiation beamline
EUV lifetime studies for detectors and optics are performed at a bending-magnet beamline. The irradiation beamline<sup>23</sup> supplies broadband radiation with a total power of 900 mW (in the wavelength range from 5 to 100 nm) for a typical ring current of 200 mA. Synchrotron radiation from a bending magnet is focused with a grazing-incidence mirror into a contamination test chamber at the end of the beamline.
--[p326]-- The irradiation test chamber can accommodate up to $1 0 ^ { - 2 }$ mbar of gas pressure.<sup>24</sup> It is separated from the beamline through a differential pumping section. --[p311]-- 29.5.3.2 Saturation
It has recently been demonstrated<sup>8</sup> that the response of a Si photodiode to 10-ns pulses of visible (532-nm wavelength) radiation shows evidence of saturation effects at even the lowest peak power levels measured (1 nJ in 8.25 ns, ${ \approx } 1 2 0 ~ \mathrm { m W } )$ The useful dynamic range of the photodiode depends on the accuracy required for the radiometry and the knowledge of the nonlinear dependence of quantum efficiency on power.
--[p311]-- The model predicts, and experiment confirms, that the photodiode responsivity can be fitted with a curve that requires two calibration factors: one is the cw responsivity, and the other describes the saturation characteristics of the device. The responsivity R as a function of pulse energy $E _ { \mathrm { p u l s e } } \mathrm { i s } ^ { 8 }$
$$
R ( E _ { \mathrm { p u l s e } } ) = \frac { R _ { \mathrm { c w } } } { 1 + \beta E _ { \mathrm { p u l s e } } } ,\tag{29.3}
$$
--[p311]-- A model has been developed that attributes the loss of efficiency to increased recombination loss of the photogenerated carriers. The presence of these photogenerated carriers is responsible for the decreased carrier lifetime in the semiconductor, and thus for the reduction in external quantum efficiency.

--[p100]-- For instance, there is a relaxation time scale corresponding to the time required for the plasma ionization (which can be regarded as an internal degree of freedom) to reach steady state: In the early stages of the interaction, free electrons are produced via high-field ionization to produce a cold plasma, after which laser energy is deposited primarily into the electrons through collisional absorption.
--[p100]-- Further ionization occurs when energy is transferred from the electrons to the ions via inelastic collisions. This process continues until a steady ionization state is reached. For temperatures of interest here, this time scale is ${ \approx } 0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { n s } . ^ { 2 }$
Another time scale concerns the time taken for the expanding plasma to become optically thick to its own emitted radiation (which for $T \approx 3 0 ~ \mathrm { e V }$ means primarily EUV radiation).

===== [p13-16] Xenon and Tin Pinch Discharge Sources > 16.2 Pinch Effect (15块) =====
--[p14]-- Z-pinch configurations with dimensions L and D up to several tens of centimeters were investigated. The energy stored in the capacitor battery could reach about $1 0 ^ { 6 } \ \mathrm { J } .$ , so through the gas at pressures of $1 0 ^ { - 3 } – 1 0 ^ { - 4 }$ Torr a current of $1 0 ^ { 4 } – 1 0 ^ { 6 } \mathrm { ~ A ~ }$ was obtained.
--[p15]-- No measurements of EUV radiation were made in Ref. 4; nevertheless, the form and features of the spouting pinch have brought us to a better understanding of plasma pinch dynamics and also to the development of the new discharge configuration described in Sec. 16.4.1.
The most attractive works dealing with the classic Z pinch as a source for EUVL are McGeoch’s investigations.
--[p14]-- Researchers who were trying to obtain neutrons from Z-pinch plasmas registered the compression of the plasma toward the cylinder axis during the first phase of the discharge. Then they registered the development of plasma instabilities in the current channel. Plasma instabilities limited the lifetime of the high-temperature plasma volume, and that was one reason amongst others why the attempts to obtain a thermonuclear effect in a Z-pinch plasma were unsuccessful.<sup>3</sup>
--[p16]-- In the present day the pinch effect is widely used for the development of DPP sources with different electrode configurations, such as the noncylindrical configuration of the Z pinch, or dense plasmafocus (DPF),<sup>13</sup> the hollow-cathode triggered Z pinch (HCT-Z),<sup>14</sup> the capillary Z pinch,<sup>15,16</sup> and the Star Pinch.<sup>17</sup>
--[p14]-- However, even such a description, considered within the framework of magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), is rather simplified and cannot explain repeated compression processes in a plasma pinch or various plasma instabilities that may arise.
--[p13]-- The lines of force of the magnetic field B created by the current look like concentric circles arranged on planes perpendicular to the Z axis. The resulting electrodynamic force F acting on a unit gas volume with a current density j is equal to $c ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { j }$ · B, where c is the light velocity. F is directed inward along the radius to the cylinder axis and causes compression of the current channel.
--[p13]-- However such a mechanism of pseudo-steady compression contradicts the experimental data, and the model offered by Leontovich and Osovets<sup>11</sup> is more correct. In accordance with this model, after the breakdown of an electrode gap the discharge is displaced to the walls of the insulator due to the skin effect, after which the surface plasma layer, under the action of electrodynamic forces, is accelerated toward the axis.
--[p15]-- The more stable spouting pinch was obtained in Ref. 4. As shown in Fig. 16.2, the ring electrodes connected to the capacitor battery were separated by a ceramic disk with a central hole. The discharge volume was isolated from the external atmosphere by two glass caps. When a $1 3 0 \mathrm { - \mu F }$ capacitor battery charged up to 20 kV was switched onto the ring electrode, the spouting pinch was observed as shown schematically in Fig. 16.2.
--[p15]-- Investigation of the discharge dynamics<sup>4</sup> has shown that a bright central current cord (pinch) moves behind the plasma front with a speed of ${ \approx } 3 . \bar { 3 } \ \times 1 0 ^ { 6 }$ cm/s. The pinch closes the electrodes through a coaxial plasma shell. In the experiments,<sup>4</sup> the pinch, with a diameter of ${ \approx } 2$ cm and a length of ≈65 cm, was stable without any necks during the few microseconds of the first half period of the discharge current.
--[p14]-- In this model the inertial forces are taken into account, and it is assumed that during the whole compression there is no equality of magnetic and gas-kinetic pressure. The model allows one to calculate the time of compression, which agrees well with experimental data, including the data obtained for our experimental conditions.
--[p14]-- The intensive investigation of high-power installations on the basis of the pinch effect began in the 1950s within the framework of controlled-fusion programs.<sup>3</sup> The initial investigations at Kurchatov Institute of Atomic Energy were based on electrode systems similar to that shown in Fig. 16.1. The anode and the cathode are insulated from each other by the ceramic tube with diameter D. The low-inductance capacitor battery was connected to electrodes separated by a distance L.
--[p13]-- The equation of motion during the initial phase of compression is thus
$$
\frac { d } { d t } \bigg [ \bigg ( 1 - \frac { r ^ { 2 } } { r _ { 0 } ^ { 2 } } \bigg ) \frac { d r } { d t } \bigg ] = - \frac { I ^ { 2 } ( t ) } { c ^ { 2 } M r } ,\tag{16.1}
$$
where r and $r _ { 0 }$ are the present and initial radii of the plasma layer, respectively, $M = \pi r ^ { 2 } \rho$ is the mass of gas per unit length, and ρ is the gas density.
--[p13]-- 16.2 Pinch Effect
The pinch effect arises from compression of a previously created plasma by the magnetic field of its own current. The phenomenon of plasma compression was first described in 1934 by W. H. Bennett.<sup>10</sup> The mechanism and characteristic features of a pinch effect can be usefully considered using the examples of the classical Z pinch (Fig. 16.1) and the spouting pinch (Fig. 16.2). In the classical Z pinch the current flows along the Z axis of a cylindrical plasma volume.
--[p13]-- The magnetic compression of the plasma is counteracted by the gas-kinetic pressure of the plasma. At equilibrium the moving boundary of the pinch is a surface of equal pressure. From this condition the so-called Bennett equilibrium follows: $B ^ { 2 } / 8 \pi = 2 n k T$ , where T is the plasma temperature and n is the gas concentration.
--[p15]-- He reduced the energy dissipated in the discharge while keeping the initial plasma uniformity by the use of radio-frequency preionization.<sup>12</sup> For an electrode system similar to the ones shown in Fig. 16.1, McGeoch used a ceramic tube with $D = 2 5$ mm and $L = 4 0$ mm. At a stored energy of about 240 J the brightness of the source was found to be $9 . 4 \ : \mathrm { J } \ : \mathrm { s r } ^ { - 1 } \ : \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ per pulse.

===== [p21-23] Xenon and Tin Pinch Discharge Sources > 16.3.4 EUV source lifetime, electrode erosion (12块) =====
--[p21]-- If the average electrode temperature comes close to the melting temperature, the whole of the radiation energy coming from the plasma and being absorbed in a thin surface layer will be spent in intensive vaporization, causing significant electrode mass loss.
--[p23]-- The essence of the phenomenon is that under the interaction of high-power plasma fluxes with a wall it starts to evaporate intensely. The vaporized wall material is ionized under the action of external radiation and forms a plasma wall layer. This layer protects the wall surface against plasma fluxes. Now it is not clear whether such a phenomenon takes place in the EUV source, and further detailed research into the electrode erosion mechanism is necessary.
--[p21]-- Our experiments have shown that the lifetime of the discharge system depends on the geometry and material of electrodes and dielectric, the method of cooling, the amount of electrical power dissipated in the discharge $( W _ { \mathrm { d } } )$ , and the parameters of the pulsed discharge $( E _ { \mathrm { d } }$ , current, pulse duration). In our experiments both the anode and the cathode were fabricated from copper and reveted with tungsten.
--[p21]-- For each level of $W _ { \mathrm { d } }$ the electrodes were weighed before and after the test run. Thus the mass loss of the electrodes (their erosion) for each level of $W _ { \mathrm { d } }$ was determined.
As can be seen from Fig. 16.9(a), the EUV source using Xe can provide about 250 W of inband EUV power close to the plasma pinch region in continuous operation. After $4 5 \times 1 0 ^ { 6 }$ pulses the EUV power began to be significantly decreased even at $W _ { \mathrm { d } } = 1 0 .
--[p23]-- 16.9(b) it also follows that the increase of $W _ { \mathrm { d } }$ from 5 to 20 kW does not result in an increase of erosion per pulse. This result contradicts the common notion that the increase of $W _ { \mathrm { d } }$ should result in nonlinear growth of erosion. Probably it is possible to explain this by a phenomenon known as vapor shielding, which was studied in detail in Ref. 24, for example.
--[p21]-- Investigation of the character of anode surface destruction in the initial stage of the pulse discharge has shown that under electron bombardment in the presence of an electric field, it involved such phenomena as plastic strain of the surface layer, its melting and the growth of hanging indentations (microhillocks) from the melt, and evaporation or breakoff of the tops of the microhillocks.<sup>23</sup> The radiation from the hot plasma pinch forming in a later stage of the discharge leads to further heating of the electrodes and to evaporation of their surface layers.
--[p21]-- So increasing the plasma-wall distance is an effective way to reduce the electrode surface temperature. During continuous operation of an EUV source at a high repetition rate, the surface electrode temperature can attain the melting temperature of tungsten (3650 K).
--[p23]-- 5 \mathrm { \ k W }$ was essentially restored and the source produced an additional 75 million pulses at 1.11 kHz. In this test the anode operated for 150 million pulses. The values of mass loss for both cathode and anode measured during the test at different $W _ { \mathrm { d } }$ are shown in Fig. 16.9(b). The anode erosion was higher than the cathode erosion. That difference had already been noted in a number of publications, for example in Ref. 23. From Fig.

--[p21]-- A typical model consideration for a tungsten electrode $( E _ { \mathrm { d } } = 4 { \mathrm { ~ J ) } }$ shows that during the discharge pulse about $70 \%$ of all deposited energy remains in an electrode surface layer of a few micrometers’ thickness. During the discharge pulse the temperature of tungsten electrode surface layer jumps by approximately 200 K if the plasma-wall distance is 10 mm, and by more than 2000 K if it is 2.5 mm.
--[p21]-- 16.3.4 EUV source lifetime, electrode erosion
The lifetime of the EUV source is determined first of all by electrode erosion, which is determined by the whole collection of interdependent physical processes on the electrodes under the action of both high discharge current and high power radiated from the plasma.

--[p301]-- However, these measurements cannot be made simultaneously, and the stored beam current is continuously decaying. The output of the monochromator is normalized by incorporating a unique double-exit slit design. Two slits lie in the exit slit plane of the monochromator: one is open, and the second, 5 mm below the first, incorporates a detector that is butted directly at the slit’s output. The open slit allows light to exit the monochromator and impinge on the sample plane 30 cm beyond the slit.
--[p301]-- The vertical focus is at the exit slit, which is 247 cm downstream from the gratings, while the horizontal focus is at the sample, 30 cm farther downstream. All reflections are in the vertical plane, and the radiation incident on the sample is 96% horizontally polarized.
Higher grating orders are reduced by the use of thin-foil filters.
--[p302]-- Resolving power up to 1000 can be achieved using the 1500-line/mm grating; however, this grating does not cover the full range of a typical EUVL MLM measurement.
--[p301]-- Both toroids operate at a 3-deg grazing angle. The gratings are 40 cm from the second toroid. The gratings are plane, varied-linespace ruled gratings with gold surfaces. The first operates at a 5-deg grazing angle, from 10 to 40 nm, with 600 lines/mm. The second operates at a 3.5-deg grazing angle from 3 to 14 nm, with 1500 lines/mm. Wavelength is scanned by rotating and translating a gold-coated plane mirror.
--[p301]-- The spectral purity of the monochromator’s output near 13.5 nm has been characterized by running it under various electron-beam and filtering conditions.<sup>6</sup> In this study it was found that under standard operating conditions of 380-MeV stored beam energy, there is a contribution due to broadband scatter of 0.5%, with an additional contribution of higher-order radiation (third order and above) of 0.2%.

SURF III. This mirror collects virtually all of the vertical emission and 20 mrad of the horizontal emission of EUV radiation from SURF III. The radiation is focused 1:1 onto the entrance slit, then is deflected by a second toroidal mirror 325 cm downstream from the entrance slit.
--[p301]-- Peak throughput in the region around 13 nm is about $\bar { 1 } 0 ^ { 1 1 }$ photons/s, corresponding to about $2 \mu \mathrm { W } .$ A typical EUV detector has a noise floor of a few picowatts, leading to a dynamic range in the beamline of over five orders of magnitude.
Reflectivity measurements are made by measuring the photocurrent generated in the detector when it is exposed to the incident beam and then the reflected beam.
--[p301]-- The signal from the detector at the lower slit accurately follows the open slit’s output with an uncertainty approaching 0.1%. This system allows for accurate tracking of the input power on a sample under test.
The spectral resolution of the monochromator is modest. The beamline is generally run with slit widths of 0.5 mm, which gives a resolving power of about 200.
