--[p16]-- Schematically, one of the electrode configurations with L = 4 mm is shown in Fig. 16.3. In order to create uniform plasma we have proposed<sup>18</sup> and implement-$\mathrm { e d } ^ { \breve { 5 } - 8 , 1 9 - 2 2 }$ preionization by an auxiliary creeping discharge. Preionization leads to the ignition of a uniform discharge in the main discharge gap, repeatability of EUV energy, and increased CE.
--[p16]-- 16.1 and 16.2, was to understand how the reduction of $E _ { \mathrm { d } }$ would affect the conversion efficiency (CE). The study of EUV energy as a function of $E _ { \mathrm { d } }$ for the electrode configuration as shown in Fig. 16.1, with L ranging from 28 to 2 mm and D from 16 to 8 mm, have shown that the Z-pinch plasma can effectively radiate around 13.5 nm with $E _ { \mathrm { d } }$ of about 5–10 J, depending on $D$ and $L$
--[p16]-- The pulsed power system included two stages of magnetic compression and allowed variation of the stored energy from 10 J up to 30 J. The highest voltage (≈6 kV) was used for ignition of the auxiliary creeping discharge. Such preionization provides lower voltages $( { < } 4 \mathrm { k V } )$ in the main discharge gap. It reduces the electrical loads on the ceramic insulator separating the cathode and the anode, and it magnifies the lifetime of the EUV source.
--[p16]-- However, in the process of decreasing L it is more difficult to match the pulsed power system with the discharge load. Our experiments have shown<sup>5,6</sup> that for $L >$ 13 mm the pulsed power system is well matched to the discharge load $( E _ { \mathrm { d } } / E >$ 86%). When L was decreased, $E _ { \mathrm { d } } / E$ was decreased also; for example, we found $E _ { \mathrm { d } } / E = 4 5 \%$ for $L = 2 ~ \mathrm { m m }$
--[p16]-- 16.3.1 Optimization and performance
We take into account the fact that in accordance with the HVM lithography tool requirements the pulse repetition rate of the EUV source should be 7–10 kHz, so the energy dissipated in the discharge $( E _ { \mathrm { d } } )$ should be not too high (∼10 J). The first step of our research, with the use of configurations similar to the ones in Figs.
--[p16]-- It is known that ideally EUV radiation should be isotropic in a solid angle of ${ \approx } 1 . 8 ~ \mathrm { s r . } ^ { 9 }$ Our measurements of the angular distribution of EUV radiation from a Z-pinch plasma for different electrode distances L (D = 9 mm, $E _ { \mathrm { d } } = 1 0 ~ \mathrm { J } )$ have demonstrated<sup>6</sup> that the EUV radiation becomes more isotropic with reduction of L.

===== [p239-239] Laser Plasma EUV Sources based on Droplet Target Technology > 26.5 Ion Emission from Droplet Laser Plasmas (4块) =====
--[p239]-- Although the IP has limitations in estimating the spectrum of the ions emitted by the plasma, it is a very useful device for measuring the total charge, and therefore the approximate flux of ions, at points remote from the source. It can therefore be used to estimate the ion flux that would be incident on a collection mirror’s substrate.
The second diagnostic is a custom-designed ion spectrometer configured as an ion energy analyzer (IEA). The IP and IEA configurations are shown in Fig. 26.13.
--[p239]-- Both of these techniques utilize time-of-flight (TOF) analysis and are both commonly used in many fields.<sup>42–44</sup>
--[p239]-- Second, a knowledge of the ion composition of the plasma and the relative ion velocity distributions will provide further understanding of the plasma state, the laser light coupling mechanisms, and the fractional ablation of the target material. To this end, we have established an experimental facility dedicated to quantitative ion measurements.
Two different approaches are currently being used to measure ionic emission. The first is a Faraday-cup ion probe (IP).
--[p239]-- 26.5 Ion Emission from Droplet Laser Plasmas
A precise characterization of the ion emission from the plasma is imperative to meeting the requirements of laser plasma EUV sources. First, this characterization is necessary to assess the potential erosion effects of these ions, if they are allowed to expand freely, at the first collector mirrors.

===== [p473-473] Electrode and Condenser Materials for Plasma Pinch Sources > 35.4.6 Irradiation by Xe and H plasmas (2块) =====
--[p473]-- Thus the performed mass loss measurements have shown that copper and tungsten erosion caused by material evaporation, sputtering, and droplet ejection is limited to 0.1 µm per shot of Xe and only slightly less for H.
--[p473]-- 35.4.6 Irradiation by Xe and H plasmas
Copper and tungsten targets were exposed to 15 shots of Xe and H plasma at practically identical heat loads: $1 5 0 { - } 2 5 0 ~ \mathrm { J / c m ^ { 2 } }$ . The material erosion evaluated from the measured mass loss was found to be about 0.1 µm per shot for both copper and tungsten, under Xe and H plasma exposure. In principle, H plasma should cause lower mass loss, by about 30%, but the mass loss measured was nearly the same as for Xe.

--[p161]-- 23.2.3 Liquid-xenon-jet freezing
Normally, a liquid jet will spontaneously break up into droplets.<sup>43</sup> However, highly volatile liquids, such as liquefied gases, may freeze due to evaporation-induced cooling before traveling the droplet formation distance, thereby avoiding drop formation. Whether droplets will form or not is therefore a question of the rate of the droplet formation process contra the rate of the jet cooling process.

This is supported by experimental evidence shown in Fig. 23.8. Here the xenon jet is photographed several centimeters from the nozzle orifice.

===== [p121-123] Chapter 21 Modular LPP Source > 21.2.3 Laser development for the modular LPP source (14块) =====
--[p121]-- Another advantage is the possibility of accurately controlling the EUV dose on the wafer, as explained later in Sec. 21.2.6.
To develop a laser chain suitable for an LPP source, we considered a Nd:YAG rod as laser material, pumped by high-power cw diode bars. As a matter of fact, to obtain high repetition rate (>3 kHz), cw pumping is more efficient than pulsed pumping, due to the lifetime of the upper laser level.
--[p121]-- The power oscillator is based on specially developed, now commercially available pump modules.<sup>22</sup> These modules exhibit excellent pump uniformity to limit the spherical aberration and a high (90%) transfer efficiency, defined as the ratio of the light absorbed by the rod to the light emitted by the diode bars.
--[p123]-- 26 have shown that in this way the power can be doubled without degradation of the beam quality. First calculations show that the extraction in the first amplifier can be as high as 70% of the stored energy with 50-mJ input, and in the second one 80%.
--[p121]-- The spherical aberration was measured, and we found typical values between 0.5λ and 1.6λ rms at the maximum pump power, depending on the diode cooling temperature, i.e., the pump profile. Unlike the birefringence, the spherical aberration cannot be easily compensated and should be minimized.
For Q switching of the laser, we use acousto-optical (AO) devices.
--[p122]-- The optical-to-optical and the optical-to-electrical efficiencies of the laser module are respectively 21% and 7%. The time jitter of the laser is 1.2 ns rms, and the power fluctuations less than 3%.
To increase the laser power of each module, we will add amplifier stages to the oscillator. The amplifier is a duplicate of the oscillator design without the mirrors. The schema of the POPA design is given in Fig. 21.10. The authors of Ref.
--[p121]-- In the POPA there is no need for preamplifiers, because the output from the oscillator efficiently extracts the energy stored in the first amplifier.
The beam quality of the power oscillator must be a compromise between good system efficiency and good focusability to generate sufficiently high intensities on the target. The beam quality<sup>20,21</sup> should be on the order of $M ^ { 2 } = 1 0 \mathrm { - } 1 5$ and maintained throughout the amplification chain.
--[p121]-- To fulfil the throughput requirements of EUVL production tools, the laser system of an LPP source must deliver, in the most optimistic case, at least 20 kW of average power. In our opinion, this can hardly be obtained with only a few laser chains.
--[p121]-- In a short cavity, the cw output power of a pump module is 450 W for 1100-W pump power, yielding 40% optical-to-optical efficiency and 17% optical-to-electrical efficiency for the optical pumping structures.<sup>23</sup>
Particular efforts were devoted to the management of the thermal effects.
--[p121]-- Briefly, we use two identical pump modules in combination with a polarization rotator to compensate for the induced birefringence.<sup>24</sup> The spherical aberration, mainly due to pump inhomogeneities and the temperature dependence of the thermal conductivity,<sup>25</sup> limits the efficiency of the oscillator.
--[p121]-- 21.2.3 Laser development for the modular LPP source
The laser system is by far the most expensive part of an LPP source. Thus the designers have to take into account not only its technical performance but also such essential characteristics as cost, efficiency, reliability, and industrial availability.
In the present state of the art, the maximum CEs achieved with commonly used xenon and tin targets are respectively 1% and 3%.
--[p121]-- Starting from this consideration, we have proposed<sup>18</sup> the concept of a modular LPP source based on the use of 10 to 20 identical, moderate-power laser chains (with typically 1.5 to 2 kW each) that are simultaneously focused on the same spot.<sup>19</sup>
Among other advantages, this leads to a simpler, more compact laser-chain concept and to a more robust system with enhanced redundancy (e.g., still allowing EUV operation when one chain is down).
--[p122]-- They allow simple, reliable, and cost-effective switching for unpolarized cavities at high (multikilohertz) repetition rates, but two of them are necessary to hold off the relatively high gain $( g _ { 0 } l \approx 1 . 8 )$
A schematic diagram of the laser resonator is given in Fig. 21.8. Two divergent lenses are used to reduce both the divergence of the beam (so as to improve the hold-off of the Q-switch system) and the power density on the mirrors.
--[p121]-- Moreover, the lifetime of cw diode bars may approach 20,000 hours—much longer than that of quasicontinuous-wave diodes—and cw diodes are at least 2 times cheaper for the same average power.
In order to obtain a good optical-to-electrical efficiency we have chosen to develop a power oscillator–power amplifier (POPA) configuration instead of the standard MOPA (master oscillator–power amplifier) system.
--[p122]-- Figure 21.9 shows the average laser output power as a function of the repetition rate. It ranges from 480 W at 10 kHz to 550 W at 30 kHz. The pulse duration (Fig. 21.9) is linearly dependent on the repetition rate and can be as low as 32 ns. This leads to peak densities on the order of 75 GW/cm<sup>2</sup> on a 50-µm-diameter spot. The measured beam quality is 13 and mainly limited by the spherical aberration.

===== [p295-296] Metrology for EUVL Sources and Tools > 29.2.1 Synchrotron Ultraviolet Radiation Facility (5块) =====
--[p296]-- At all synchrotron-based calibration facilities, the pulse frequency is sufficiently high that the radiation is essentially a continuous stream of photons for all but the fastest detectors. Therefore, all EUV calibrations are performed in the cw mode.
Compared to the sources for EUVL, synchrotron radiation sources are extremely low-power devices. At SURF III the typical EUV power on a sample being measured rarely gets higher than a few microwatts.
--[p296]-- The low-power nature of synchrotron sources must be considered when calibrations are transferred from a synchrotron radiation source to a pulsed, high-peak-power EUV light source such as the DPPs and LPPs for EUVL, because nonlinear effects such as detector saturation will not be revealed with low-power measurements.
--[p295]-- 29.2.1 Synchrotron Ultraviolet Radiation Facility
Synchrotron radiation sources are the sources of choice for setting radiometric standards and calibration. This is because they are stable, calculable sources with a smooth, spectrally continuous emission. An output spectrum of NIST’s Synchrotron Ultraviolet Radiation Facility<sup>4,5</sup> (SURF III) is shown in Fig. 29.1.
--[p296]-- Synchrotron radiation sources are generally considered cw sources; however, they are actually pulsed in nature. The radiation is pulsed at n times the synchrotron orbital frequency, where n is the number of electron bunches stored in the ring. At SURF III the radiation incident on a calibration sample is pulsed at 114 MHz.
--[p295]-- It shows the continuous output spectrum as a function of wavelength for several different electron energies of the stored beam. SURF III is somewhat unusual in that it is possible to change the electron energy over a broad range and thereby tune the output spectrum as needed. This property is often exploited at SURF III to reduce the presence of higher-order and OOB radiation.<sup>6</sup>

A second priority was to keep the pressure in the source chamber low to avoid both the reabsorption of the generated EUV light and the contamination of the laser-focusing and EUV-collecting optics.

Furthermore, the injector has its own integrated temperature control system.
--[p129]-- 21.3.1 The ELSAC source architecture
Right at the beginning of Exulite, the main idea was to take into account the constraints on all subelements of the ELSAC source and those generated by the relationship between those elements.
--[p129]-- Note that the choice of a massive chamber also permits us to reach the required positioning precision of the focusing mirrors and to facilitate the implantation of all necessary windows for the inlet and outlet of the laser beams.
Finally, the second chamber for the EUV collecting elements has lower mechanical and thermal constraints. Its design was optimized to be modular in order to accept a complete set of diagnostics and thereby allow numerous different studies.
Figure 21.16 shows the resulting architecture for ELSAC.
--[p129]-- This architecture optimization was achieved thanks to a complete functional analysis of the source and of all subelements: the target vacuum chamber, the injection system, the laser module, the xenon pumping and recycling system, the laser-beam transportation and focusing system, the EUV collector, and the global control system.
First of all, the design takes into account the injection and optical systems. For example, the mechanical implantation of the injection system is modular.

===== [p163-163] Driver Laser, Xenon Target, and System Development for LPP Sources > 23.2.4 Jet stabilization through nozzle heating (5块) =====
--[p163]-- 23.2.4 Jet stabilization through nozzle heating
The stability of the xenon jet is very important in order to allow for stable plasma operation far from the nozzle. It was mentioned above that it is important to operate the jet at a temperature close to the freezing point of xenon in order to avoid spraying.
--[p163]-- This instability and a way to avoid it are discussed in Hansson et al.<sup>41</sup> It is believed that the instability is due to some substance, most probably the liquefied gas itself, freezing in or around the nozzle orifice, and thus changing the flow characteristics at the orifice. One can assume that the rapid evaporation of the jet cools the nozzle to temperatures below the freezing point of the liquefied gas used.
--[p163]-- 23.9. It is believed that this heating will keep the nozzle tip at a high enough temperature to avoid the freezing of material in the tip that may alter the flow profile and induce an instability. However, it is important to apply this heating very locally at the nozzle tip, since otherwise the liquid jet itself will be heated, leading to spraying. This is consistent with the observation reported above, that the jet will spray when the liquid is too warm.
--[p163]-- The cooling process could be due either to evaporation of the liquid that wets the edges of the orifice or to heat transfer from the jet, which in its turn is cooled by evaporation. Nozzle cooling has in fact previously been observed for normal liquids.<sup>49</sup>
Localized heating of the nozzle tip is a possible way to avoid this problem and to achieve a stable jet.<sup>50</sup> The heating can, e.g., be applied through resistive heating at the tip with a thin wire, as is illustrated in Fig.
--[p163]-- However, apart from spraying, a directional instability of an otherwise stable jet can be present on occasion.<sup>21,23,48</sup> This instability can be as large as 1 deg, and when it is present it makes stable plasma generation at practical distances from the orifice difficult.

===== [p41-42] Chapter 17 Capillary Z-Pinch Source > 17.2 Discharge Head and Magnetic Pulse Compression Generator (5块) =====
--[p41]-- 17.2 Discharge Head and Magnetic Pulse Compression Generator
Figure 17.1 shows the cross section of the discharge head. The head consists of an anode, capillary, cathode, vacuum interface, and coaxial current feed. Both electrodes are cooled by circulated deionized water. The electrode material determines the heat and debris generation. Since tantalum has good thermal conductivity and sputtering resistance, currently tantalum electrodes are applied.
--[p42]-- The capillary could serve both as the discharge space and as an orifice for differential pumping, because the diameter of the capillary was small enough to maintain the pressure of the downstream region low enough to avoid absorbing the EUV radiation.
Figure 17.2 shows a circuit diagram of the magnetic pulse compression (MPC) generator. The final compression stage of the 5-stage MPC generator is shown in this figure.
--[p41]-- Although several geometries were tested to examine their characteristics, in this section only the results obtained from a capillary of diameter and length 5 and 9 mm will be described.
The discharge head was installed in the vacuum chamber. Xenon gas was fed from the cathode side and evacuated from the anode side.
--[p42]-- The final capacitor of 132.5 nF was charged to 14.5 kV, which is equal to 14 J of electrical energy storage. In order to decrease the output inductance, 16 coaxial cables were used to connect the MPC and discharge head. The all-solidstate MPC generator allows very stable operation at up to 2 kHz. Depending on the circuit resistance and inductance, a typical current amplitude and duration were 17 kA and 350 ns, respectively.
--[p41]-- A silicon carbide (SiC) disk is used as the capillary body. The capillary diameter and length are among the important parameters for a Z-pinch discharge. They must be chosen together with the pulse shape of the driving current, because the magnetic field induced by the current is determined by the current amplitude and the capillary diameter. The radiation energy and its spatial and spectral profiles also depend on the capillary length.

===== [p155-157] Driver Laser, Xenon Target, and System Development for LPP Sources > 23.1.4 Laser-plasma targets (8块) =====
--[p156]-- The tape target limits the debris by allowing the shock wave to escape through the tape rather than be reflected back to the surface.<sup>9</sup> However, the debris emission is still substantial from a tape target.<sup>10</sup> In addition, tape targets are limited to materials that can be processed into a tape, and the tape will eventually run out during prolonged high-repetition-rate operation.
For gaseous target materials, the gas-puff target is an alternative as illustrated in Fig.
--[p156]-- Normally, the jet will naturally break up into droplets after traveling some distance, leading to a liquid droplet target<sup>20</sup> [Fig. 23.1(e)]. However, as will be discussed below, a liquid xenon jet may freeze before natural droplet formation, resulting in a solid jet, often referred to as a filament.
The liquid-droplet target was early shown to reduce the debris deposition, compared to a tape target, by a factor<sup>20</sup> of 200–300.
--[p155]-- 23.1.4 Laser-plasma targets
For each new laser shot, fresh target material must be available at the laser focus position. Since a source for an EUVL scanner is anticipated to operate at a repetition rate of >7 kHz with 25% duty cycle for almost 24 hours a day,<sup>8</sup> this puts high demands on the target delivery system. Traditionally, solid bulk targets have been employed for laser-plasma generation.
--[p156]-- Compared to the gas/cluster target, this target has the advantage of higher density, which leads to improved EUV generation, and better collimation of the target flow, which allows for slightly longer working distances, although still in the few-millimeter range.<sup>16,17</sup>
This chapter, however, describes the liquid-jet<sup>18,19</sup> target [Fig. 23.1(d)]. It is formed by forcing a liquid through a small nozzle orifice, thereby creating a collimated jet.
--[p155]-- They are typically translated between shots to provide a fresh target surface and can therefore only operate for a very limited time until the whole surface is filled with craters. In addition, large fractions of molten material will be ejected due to the shock wave reflected in the bulk material.<sup>9</sup>
An alternative is to use a thin tape as a target, as illustrated in Fig. 23.1(a).
--[p156]-- 23.1(b).<sup>11</sup> The clear advantage is that no large debris particles can be ejected from the plasma target. However, the laser must be focused close to the nozzle in order for the target gas to have sufficient density for effective laser-plasma generation.
--[p157]-- It has furthermore been shown that the liquid-jet target yields as low deposition as the droplet target.<sup>18</sup> A disadvantage of the liquid-jet and droplet target types is that not all substances can be used, but many are available that are not room-temperature liquids through various techniques, e.g., liquefied gases,<sup>21–23</sup> molten metals,<sup>24,25</sup> solutions,<sup>25–27</sup> and liquids doped with metal in various ways.<sup>28</sup>
--[p156]-- This may lead to sputtering of nozzle material that, in turn, may coat sensitive components.<sup>12</sup> Under the right operating conditions, the gas will form clusters enhancing the EUV production from the gas target.<sup>13–15</sup>
A similar target is the liquid-spray target [Fig. 23.1(c)], which can be applied to liquids or condensing gases, where larger droplets are formed.

--[p165]-- 23.4.2 Repetition-rate capability
At a given pulse-to-pulse emission stability, increasing the repetition rate of the EUV source will improve the dose accuracy and thus the critical dimension control.
--[p165]-- It is believed that the limiting factor for the repetition rate of a liquid-xenon-jet laser-plasma source is the time after one plasma event until new unaffected target material is available at the laser focus point. This is influenced by the jet speed and the length of the jet that is destroyed by a plasma event. Figure 23.10 shows the jet just after a plasma event.<sup>57</sup> As can be seen in the image, the jet is basically unaffected at a point 1.3 mm upstream toward the nozzle.
--[p165]-- 23.11 illustrates how a significant stability transition from 3.8% (1σ) to 36% was found on changing the delay from 60 to 50 µs, corresponding to an increase in repetition rate from 17 to 20 kHz.
At the shorter time separation, the second pulse is not always fired on an intact jet target, but rather on the jet region that may have been damaged by the first pulse. The experiment indicates that a liquid-xenon-jet laser-plasma source can be operated with a repetition rate of at least 17 kHz.
--[p165]-- With a typical jet velocity of 50 m/s, this corresponds to a maximum repetition rate of 30 kHz. A similar experiment is reported by Shields et al.,<sup>52</sup> arriving at a maximum repetition rate of 10 kHz, the lower value probably being due to lower jet speed.

===== [p320-321] Calibration of Detectors and Tools for EUV-Source Metrology > 30.1 Introduction (8块) =====
--[p320]-- 30.1 Introduction
The routine availability of high-accuracy soft-x-ray radiometry is a prerequisite for the development of EUVL as the next-generation lithography (NGL).<sup>1,2</sup> A main issue for EUVL is the ability to produce sufficient levels of EUV radiant power.<sup>3,4</sup> Therefore, well-characterized radiation detectors that work reliably over long periods of time at high irradiation levels are needed.
--[p321]-- The calibrations at PTB use monochromatized synchrotron radiation, a quasidc radiation with a rather low radiant power of about 1 $\mu \mathrm { W } .$ . For EUV source characterization, strongly pulsed radiation and very different radiant powers must be measured. High-accuracy calibrations for EUVL therefore require further investigations of the detector performance.
--[p321]-- The radiant power equals the change in the electrical heater power required for keeping the absorber temperature at a constant value when the radiation shutter is opened. Photodiodes are calibrated as transfer detector standards with a relative uncertainty of $u = 0 . 2 6 \%$ by direct comparison with the radiometer.<sup>16</sup> The calibration of tools for source characterization is thus directly traced to the SI system of units.<sup>18,19</sup>
--[p321]-- The radiometric approach made at PTB to the calibration of detectors in the EUV spectral range is the comparison with a primary detector standard, a cryogenic electrical substitution radiometer (ESR) operated at liquid-He temperature<sup>17</sup> using monochromatized synchrotron radiation. The operating principle of an ESR is that an absorber transforms the incident radiant power into a heat flow directed through a heat link to a heat sink kept at constant temperature.
--[p321]-- A large reflectometer enables the PTB to characterize EUVL optics up to 550 mm in diameter and 50 kg in mass,<sup>13,14</sup> meeting the demands for the present designs of projection optics.<sup>15</sup> For the spectral reflectance of a mirror in the EUV spectral region, a relative uncertainty of $u = 0 . 1 4 \%$ is achieved.<sup>16</sup>
--[p321]-- Therefore, high-power beamlines for investigations of the linearity of the response and stability under irradiation with EUV were installed by PTB.
This chapter gives an overview of the measurement capabilities of PTB at the BESSY II storage ring and presents the status of the calibration of detectors and tools for EUV source metrology achieved at PTB.
--[p320]-- This development has caused an increasing need for radiometric standards and quantitative radiometric measurements.<sup>5</sup> In order to meet these demands, the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt (PTB) radiometry laboratory at the BESSY II electron storage ring pursues the characterization and calibration of radiation detectors and tools in the VUV and soft-x-ray spectral regions as a major task.<sup>6</sup>
--[p321]-- The PTB has been providing EUV calibration services for many years within the European EUCLIDES<sup>7</sup> and $\mathrm { \Delta \ k D E A ^ { 8 } }$ projects at a dedicated radiometry beamline at the BESSY $\displaystyle { \mathrm { I } } ^ { 9 - 1 1 }$ electron storage ring and, from the year 2000, at the BESSY II electron storage ring,<sup>12</sup> exploiting the benefits offered by this thirdgeneration facility.

===== [p126-129] Chapter 21 Modular LPP Source > 21.2.6 EUV dose control (9块) =====
--[p127]-- Our dose control system is based on the principle<sup>31</sup> that the EUV pulse energy can be modified quickly and precisely with the number of lasers that is effectively contributing to the plasma heating. Whereas it is not recommended to vary quickly the power of a laser module for thermal reasons, it is easy to shift temporally the pulse trigger instant or to shift spatially the focus point with a moving mirror. We have preferred the solution based on temporal shifting.
--[p126 [表]]-- Using LPP sources, the EUV energy is a particular function of the injected laser power, which means that the delivered EUV dose can be adjusted with the laser power. It is very difficult to adjust, quickly and precisely, the output power from a single laser chain without having any thermal problems. The approach we propose is straightforward when using a modular, multibeam LPP source.
--[p126]-- Hitherto, common EUV sources have been much less stable, approaching only 2% in 3σ over 50 shots, despite the fact that they still do not have enough power.<sup>32,33</sup> Thus, a specific system allowing one to control the dose stability is essential. To do so, one must consider in detail how the scanner proceeds. During the continuous translation of the exposure slit on the wafer, only one different-energy pulse is delivered between two consecutive doses of 50 pulses each.
--[p127]-- The results of these simulations (Fig. 21.15) show that even with an EUV source presenting 5 times more shot-to-shot instability than other existing sources,<sup>32,33</sup> we can meet the tough stability requirements.
Of course, this method works with more pulses per dose, or with more lasers, or with a different pulse repetition rate.
--[p127]-- In practice, the problem is a little more complicated in that, between two consecutive energy doses, there is only one available different-energy pulse. So we must use algorithms to reduce the noise level and to decide the next pulse energy. Different simulations were needed to choose the best algorithms and to calculate the performance according to the different parameters: maximum EUV power, ratio of the EUV power with the laser power, and shot-to-shot stability.
--[p126]-- 21.2.6 EUV dose control
Each part of the wafer must receive a well-defined energy dose in order to be correctly exposed for the lithographic process. With an EUV source power of 115 W at a repetition rate of 10 kHz, the correct dose corresponds to 50 pulses and the source dose stability has to be ±0.30% in 3σ.<sup>30</sup> Without an energy-dose control system, this requirement is hard to achieve, due to the multiple instabilities of the different source systems.
--[p127]-- As the EUV energy produced by a single laser is quite low, the energy of the temporally shifted laser does not disturb the EUV source, if the temporal shift is judiciously chosen. The way that our dose control works is actually quite simple: the system measures the energy of the first 49 pulses, calculates the pulse energy necessary to obtain the energy dose, and commands the number of lasers to be used.
--[p129]-- However, good stability can be achieved only if the average EUV power necessary for the lithographic process is below the maximal useful EUV power of the source. For this reason, a system to optimize the EUV power has also been developed within Exulite. This system, between wafer changes, looks for the best working point of the LPP source and its lasers. The modular LLP source is thus an excellent concept to apply for a simple and efficient EUV dose control system.

===== [p306-307] Metrology for EUVL Sources and Tools > 29.5.1.2 Stability (5块) =====
--[p306]-- The native $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ passivating layer on photodiodes is easily damaged by the incident radiation, particularly when there is strong absorption in the $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ .
--[p307]-- A high degree of stability has also been demonstrated in a 100%- relative-humidity environment over a four-week period.<sup>13</sup> This resistance to watervapor-induced degradation is a significant improvement over native oxides.
--[p306]-- 29.5.1.2 Stability
The stability of the quantum efficiency will help determine the recalibration frequency for any radiometry tool. There are two types of stability that are important: temporal stability during storage, and radiation hardness during use. Si photodiodes with radiation-hardened passivating oxide layers exhibit significantly improved performance in both types of stability over native oxide passivated devices.
--[p306]-- The damage is a result of trap sites that form in the $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ and collect at the $\mathrm { S i } { - } \mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ interface.<sup>18</sup> The presence of these trap sites increases the surface recombination loss of photogenerated carriers and decreases the quantum efficiency of the device.
Incorporating nitrogen into the passivating layer significantly reduces the device’s susceptibility to radiation-induced damage.<sup>13</sup>
--[p307]-- The long-term stability of these devices when stored has been demonstrated by repeated calibration of detectors at NIST. Over the course of a year, the quantum efficiency of a family of three devices was observed to be constant, varying only randomly with a standard deviation on the order of 0.2%, which is the measurement repeatability.

===== [p297-299] Metrology for EUVL Sources and Tools > 29.2.2 LPP source (7块) =====
--[p297]-- The linear curve fit included shows that the shot-to-shot variation has little effect on the normalization and also shows that neither of the two channels is affected by saturation. Removing the WS channel and repeating the process with a test instrument in the WS channel generates a similar curve. The ratio of the slopes of the two curves determines the ratio of the inband responsivity of the WS and the test instrument, thus transferring the WS’s calibration to the test instrument.
--[p297]-- 29.2.2 LPP source
NIST has assembled a Xe-based LPP source for use as a calibration tool for assembled metrology instrumentation. The source incorporates a 10-Hz Nd:YAG flashlamp-pumped Q-switched laser, which delivers approximately 800 mJ of 1.06-µm light in a 10-ns pulse on target. The target is a pulsed-valve Xe or Kr gas target operating at 1 Hz. The source can be cooled to cryogenic temperatures to facilitate droplet formation and increased EUV production.
--[p297]-- This method significantly reduces the measurement uncertainty by accurately mapping the shot-to-shot performance of the source.
This source has no grating monochromator, but uses the bandwidth of the Mo/Si multilayer mirrors (MLMs) to control the spectral throughput of the WS channel. A schematic of the system is shown in Fig. 29.2. The figure shows light from the LPP being collected by two separate Mo/Si MLMs and being relayed onto two detectors: one WS and one normalizing detector.
--[p299]-- The output spectrum of the WS channel greatly influences the calibration of tested EUV instrumentation, so that spectrum has been measured and is shown in Fig. 29.3(B). In order to accurately transfer a calibration, the overlap between the WS channel’s output spectrum and the test instrument’s acceptance spectrum must be determined. Therefore the effects of individual components within a test instrument must be characterized to calculate the final absolute calibration.
The characterization of these individual components is done at NIST on beamlines at SURF III and is described in the following sections.
--[p297]-- Despite fluctuations in laser intensity and other shot-to-shot variations, the two-channel system is reliable and repeatable. The WS channel can insert as much as 100 nJ per pulse into a test instrument and can be varied to generate a continuous scale of input energies. A typical normalization run is shown in Fig. 29.3(A). It shows the ratio of the charge collected by the WS and normalization channels.
--[p297]-- An identical pulsedvalve system is in place at the University of Maryland and is used to characterize the interactions of ultrashort laser pulses with clusters and droplets.<sup>7</sup> Calibrations are done with a detector-based method by incorporating a working standard (WS) channel and a normalization channel for monitoring the shot-to-shot variability of source output.
--[p297]-- Each detector has a directly deposited Zr-based filter that is approximately 300 nm thick and effectively minimizes the OOB light recorded by the detectors. After recording the ratio of the WS to the normalization detector, the WS detector’s calibration can be transferred to an instrument by removing the WS detector and placing an instrument to be calibrated in the WS channel beam path.

===== [p312-312] Metrology for EUVL Sources and Tools > 29.6 Calibration of EUV Radiometry Tools (3块) =====
--[p312]-- Therefore the cost and availability of individual component calibrations are more appropriate for the frequent calibrations necessary to maintain a well-characterized radiometry tool. With this said, it is still necessary to do an occasional calibration on a fully assembled calibration tool. Though the response of an assembled tool can be modeled through the responsivity of individual components, it may not reveal the full story of the calibration of the instrument.
--[p312]-- 29.6 Calibration of EUV Radiometry Tools
This chapter has mostly discussed the calibration of individual components, not assembled radiometry instruments. This is due to the fact that individual components are routinely calibrated at synchrotron radiation facilities, because it requires less effort to ship and calibrate components than to ship an assembled tool and possibly design custom hardware to interface the tool to an existing beamline.
--[p312]-- Apertures, filter and mirror nonuniformities, and mirror angle of incidence all have an effect on the total throughput of an instrument and its resulting responsivity. In this section a calibration of a fully assembled radiometry tool will be described.

===== [p312-312] Metrology for EUVL Sources and Tools > 29.6.1 Tool description (1块) =====
--[p312]-- 29.6.1 Tool description
The Flying Circus 2 (FC2) is an instrument that has been in development for several years and is often used by EUV source developers to determine the performance of an EUV source under various conditions. It is has been designed to measure the performance of sources under a variety of conditions and configurations. It is composed of a single-apertured MLM, thin foil filters, and an EUV-sensitive photodetector. The FC2’s performance has been well documented.<sup>28</sup>

===== [p249-249] Laser Plasma EUV Sources based on Droplet Target Technology > 26.9 Summary (3块) =====
--[p249]-- 26.9 Summary
This chapter describes a promising approach to the development of a high-power source for EUVL. It has evolved from the long-term efforts of a university group and its collaborators. Significant gains have been made in the efficiency of inband emission generation, and we believe further improvements can be made. There seems no impediment to running these sources at high repetition rates (>10 kHz). A future high-power demonstration of this concept should substantiate this confidence.
--[p249]-- This source should easily satisfy the required levels of stability, average source size, and dose stability. Although not yet fully characterized, the level of OOB emission and the consequent heating of the first collimator mirrors are probably manageable.
--[p249]-- Studies of the ion emission and the particle emission from the droplet laser source show that long-term operation in conjunction with a multilayer collimator is possible, but that mitigation schemes will need to demonstrate greater effectiveness. We believe that a firmer understanding of MLM erosion by ions and greater effort devoted to the integration of mitigation schemes with this source will help this development.

===== [p222-223] Laser Plasma EUV Sources based on Droplet Target Technology > 26.1 Introduction (3块) =====
--[p222]-- 26.1 Introduction
The development of a source bright enough for EUVL, possessing the required long-term stability within a reasonable cost, is forcing plasma physicists to address issues associated with dense plasmas that have up until now received scant attention. With both discharge plasmas and laser plasmas, addressing these issues has stimulated many new ideas and concepts for source design and measures associated with them.
--[p222]-- Although these new developments are currently directed toward satisfying the needs of next-generation lithography (NGL), it is likely they will also open new fields of application in the years ahead.
--[p223]-- Early on in the development of EUVL sources, when the required source power (2π sr, 2% bandwidth) was ∼10 W, we speculated that the so-called debris problem would be the most difficult to overcome.<sup>1</sup> It was for this reason that we proposed the notion of the mass-limited target for the laser plasma source.<sup>2</sup> In this scenario, the material supplied to the source should consist only of a mass sufficient to provide the minimum required number of atomic radiators.

===== [p67-67] Chapter 18 Plasma Capillary Source > 18.6 Conclusion (3块) =====
--[p67]-- 18.6 Conclusion
In conclusion, inband EUV radiation can be produced with high efficiency by employing a PVC ablative capillary discharge. However, these discharges are only suitable where low EUV power is asked for—as, for instance, for EUV MLM calibration, EUV mask inspection (which requires high power and high brightness), and EUV spectrometer calibration.
--[p67]-- As the spectrum showed no indication of self-absorption, it is possible in principle to increase the efficiency further by simply employing PVC with a higher concentration of Sn. A CE of 2.4% with a Sn concentration of 2% in PVC seems entirely feasible.
--[p67]-- It will be extremely difficult to develop this into a source for EUVL because of the ablation from the wall of the capillary, which limits the lifetime, causes problems with the discharges themselves, and last but not least, produces debris that will damage the MLM optics. These features are certainly inherent in all ablative capillary discharges.

===== [p335-335] Calibration of Detectors and Tools for EUV-Source Metrology > 30.4.3 Self-calibration (8块) =====
--[p335]-- The uncertainty is proportional to $1 - s _ { \mathrm { r } } ( h \nu )$ . For AXUV diodes with nearly ideal responsivity $[ s _ { \mathrm { r } } ( h \nu )$ close to 1], reasonable results might be obtained, while for Schottky diodes and SXUV-type diodes the uncertainty is about 10%.
--[p335]-- The relative uncertainties were estimated to be about 4% for $n { \mathrm { - } } 0 \mathbf { n } { \mathrm { - } } p$ silicon diodes, and about 6% for GaAsP Schottky diodes.<sup>43</sup> Later on, this approach was improved to allow for a thin layer beneath the diode front contact where the charge generated is only partially collected.<sup>33</sup> This approach was successfully used to derive the mean energy for the production of electron-hole pairs in semiconductors from the absolutely measured responsivity of photodiodes using the ESR.<sup>33</sup> Measurements in the soft-x-ray range at PTB revealed a quantum efficiency proportional to the photon energy, i.e., a constant value of $w = 3 .
--[p335]-- This is the basis for an alternative approach to the determination of the spectral responsivity of photodiodes used earlier at PTB in the softx-ray spectral range,<sup>43</sup> the so-called self-calibration.<sup>44</sup> The absorptance of the front layers can be determined from the ratio $s _ { \Theta } ( h \nu )$ of the responsivity for 60-deg-tonormal incidence to that for normal incidence of the radiation.
--[p335]-- 6 6 ( 3 )$ eV for the generation of an electron-hole pair in silicon in the wavelength range from 0.5 to 20 nm. In the wavelength range above 330 nm, exactly one electron-hole pair per absorbed photon is created, and for wavelengths shorter than 150 nm, the mean energy per electron-hole pair converges to the constant value for shorter wavelengths.<sup>34,39</sup> For GaAsP, a value of $w = 4 . 5 8 ( 7 )$ eV was measured in the EUV and soft-x-ray spectral range.<sup>34</sup>
--[p335]-- Reflection at normal incidence is negligible in the EUV spectral range. Thus for an ideal detector with 100% internal charge collection, only the absorption in the front layer needs to be known.
--[p335]-- 30.4.3 Self-calibration
The AXUV-type photodiodes with nearly ideal responsivity have in the past been proposed as absolute detectors<sup>42</sup> for $\mathrm { E U V } .
--[p335]-- The relative uncertainty achievable by the self-calibration method, however, is limited by the quality of the optical data used for the calculation of $s _ { \mathrm { r } } ( h \nu )$ from the measured ratio $s _ { \Theta } ( h \nu )$ . For the above-mentioned determination of w for silicon, the optical data on the nitrided oxide had to be deduced from reflection measurements. The situation becomes even worse for highly absorbing front layers such as gold or silicides.
--[p335]-- ^ { 3 6 }$ The basic idea is that the spectral responsivity $s ( h \nu )$ of a photodiode for photons of energy hν in the soft-x-ray region can be expressed as $s ( h v ) = ( e / w ) s _ { \mathrm { r } } ( h v )$ with e the elementary charge, w the mean electron-hole pair creation energy, and $s _ { \mathrm { r } } ( h \nu )$ a relative responsivity taking account of all loss processes, including reflection and absorption in the front layer.

===== [p277-278] Flying Circus EUV Source Metrology and Source Development Assessment > 28.4.1 Langmuir probes (5块) =====
--[p278]-- The research group at Sandia National Laboratories in Livermore, CA, has attempted to make Langmuir probe measurements of its LPP source.<sup>35,36</sup> A stainless steel spherical Langmuir probe approximately 6.35 mm in diameter was located 12.7 cm from the laser focus. Ion saturation currents were monitored with a −350-V bias. The Langmuir probe data indicated the presence of ions long after the laser shot.
Such low-energy ions could contribute to a continuum ion background when a high-repetition-rate laser is used.
--[p278]-- Over time, deposition or oxidation on electrode surfaces can change in an unpredictable manner the already poorly quantified secondary-electron emission coefficient.<sup>33</sup> Because the plasmas in EUV sources are rapidly expanding, a different theoretical treatment of the data is typically required, similar to that derived for moving probes.
--[p278]-- The ion saturation current $I _ { \mathrm { i } }$ can be approximated by $I _ { \mathrm { i } } = ( 1 + \varepsilon ) e U A \sum n _ { i } z _ { i }$ where ε is the secondary-electron emission coefficient, U is the plasma velocity, A is the cross-sectional area of the probe perpendicular to the flow, $n _ { i }$ is the density of an ion $j , e$ is the electric charge, and $z _ { i }$ is the charge state of the ion.<sup>34</sup>
--[p277]-- Unfortunately, placing the biased electrode in the plasma can, under certain circumstances, significantly perturb the plasma, making the results unreliable.
Langmuir and other types of electrostatic probes have been used frequently to study LPP sources. Unfortunately, the quantitative results obtained from Langmuir probes in these plasmas are of questionable quality.<sup>32</sup> Secondary-electron emission from the probe surfaces can significantly alter the measured signals.
--[p277]-- 28.4.1 Langmuir probes
Langmuir probes were one of the fundamental techniques first used in plasma diagnostics. Essentially, a biased electrode was inserted into the plasma, and the resulting current provided information concerning the properties of the plasma. A great deal of information can be determined from this simple diagnostic, including electron and ion densities and electron distribution functions.

===== [p245-245] Laser Plasma EUV Sources based on Droplet Target Technology > 26.7 Inhibition of Ion and Particle Emission (5块) =====
--[p245]-- In earlier studies we examined the effects of mechanical shutters, spinning apertures, and other mechanical systems for intercepting debris.<sup>4</sup> The use of the droplet approach radically reduces particulate debris. But ions can still threaten the mirror lifetime. This was demonstrated in our earlier studies with water droplets, which created no particulate debris (Fig. 26.17), but in which erosion by oxygen ions was observed (Fig. 26.21).
--[p245]-- Magnetic fields helped steer ions to benign areas of the source facility, but we are concerned about the long-term presence of strong magnets in locations where precision optomechanical systems need to be located. The greatest effect on ions in mitigating mirror erosion we have so far found is through the use of electric fields, the so-called repeller field concept. We have demonstrated a more than order-of-magnitude improvement in mirror lifetime with simple embodiments of this concept.
--[p245]-- We examined several methods to inhibit this erosion<sup>53</sup> including the use of electric and magnetic fields and the use of a transmitting background gas, helium. The latter we found did lead to reduction in erosion, but through x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) surface analysis, we found it also led to an undesirable effect, oxidation of the top silicon layer of the multilayer. This effect had a more devastating effect on the mirror lifetime than did erosion.
--[p245]-- Moreover, we have recently found that it is effective in inhibiting charged particulate matter as well, as illustrated below. However, it is our view that this approach alone will provide insufficient protection to the collimating mirrors. It is most likely that a combination of techniques will be needed, and we are therefore investigating other approaches.
--[p245]-- 26.7 Inhibition of Ion and Particle Emission
The previous section illustrates how imperative is the need to prevent both particles and ions from reaching the multilayer collection mirrors in any large numbers. This is also the case for discharge sources, and may pose even a more serious threat in that case. Thus we have embarked on a multidimensional approach to mitigating damage to these mirrors.

===== [p271-272] Flying Circus EUV Source Metrology and Source Development Assessment > 28.2.1 Witness plates (6块) =====
--[p272]-- Reasonable microscopic imaging of the surface can be done with either SIMS or AES with spatial resolutions on the order of 0.1 and 1 µm, respectively.<sup>1</sup>
One problem involved with witness plates is that not all surface depositions are related to plasma-surface interactions.
--[p272]-- EUV radiation can crack carboncontaining molecules, resulting in surface deposits of carbon.<sup>2</sup> Hydrocarbon molecules can come from a variety of different sources, including outgassing from the photoresists.<sup>3</sup> The presence of this deposition mechanism can be verified by inserting an EUV transmitting filter between the plasma and the witness plate. In many cases most of the carbon deposits can be attributed to this EUV cracking mechanism.<sup>4</sup>
--[p272]-- The presence of concentrated surface deposits instead of a uniform deposition layer can be evidence of large clusters or droplets being emitted from the EUV light source. Surface scanning techniques such as scanning electron microscopy (SEM) or atomic force microscopy (AFM) can provide very high spatial resolution, but probably will not have the necessary chemical discrimination between different materials.
--[p271]-- After an extended exposure to the plasma, a post mortem analysis of the witness plate can be performed to identify the chemical identity of the deposited materials.
A wide variety of different surface analysis techniques can be applied to analyze the witness plates. The chemical composition of material on the witness surface can be obtained from such techniques as x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) or Auger electron spectroscopy (AES).
--[p271]-- 28.2.1 Witness plates
Although primarily used for monitoring the degradation of optical surfaces in EUVL sources, witness plates can also be utilized as a simple plasma diagnostic. Material ejected from the plasma can form a deposit on the surface or, if the particle energy is high enough, embed beneath the surface. Even if the surface is being etched, some of the plasma debris may still reside beneath or on the surface.
--[p271]-- Surface sensitivities better than $1 0 ^ { 1 2 }$ atoms/cm<sup>2</sup> for certain materials can be obtained.<sup>1</sup> Depth profiling of material embedded in the surface can be achieved by sequentially combining these techniques with ion milling. Even higher surface sensitivity can be obtained using secondary-ion mass spectroscopy (SIMS), achieving sensitivities of 10<sup>9</sup> atoms/cm<sup>2</sup>.<sup>1</sup>
Microscopic analysis of the surface depositions can be very important as well.

===== [p307-307] Metrology for EUVL Sources and Tools > 29.5.1.4 Uniformity (2块) =====
--[p307]-- The radiation-hardened Si photodiodes have been measured to have a peak-to-valley variation in quantum efficiency on the order of $1 \% ^ { 1 1 }$ at 121.6 nm and $0 . 1 \% ^ { 1 2 }$ at 11.3 nm over the full $1 0 0 { \cdot } \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ active area.
--[p307]-- 29.5.1.4 Uniformity
The spatial uniformity of quantum efficiency is another important detector characteristic. Errors in measurement will result when two photon beams (e.g., incident and reflected beams in a reflectometer) strike different parts of the photodiode. Errors will occur even if the two beams are both well centered if the intensity profiles of the beams are different, as may be the case in transferring a calibration from the NIST laboratory to the user’s laboratory.

===== [p412-412] Chapter 33 Grazing-Incidence EUV Collectors > 33.3.1.3 General requirements on the collector optics (3块) =====
--[p412]-- Most porous materials accumulate water or other volatile substances, and continuous outgassing of these substances over long time periods causes vacuum problems.
--[p412]-- 33.3.1.3 General requirements on the collector optics
The collector optics must fulfill the following general requirements:
Chip manufacturers must contend with limited installation space for lithography tools. This requirement puts limitations on the distance between the EUV source and the IF.
Because EUV light is strongly absorbed by most media, including air and inert gases, the light path is kept in vacuum.
--[p412]-- The whole EUV collector assembly must therefore comply with ultrahigh-vacuum requirements, including outgassing specifications.
In order to provide a reasonable lifetime, all materials used within the collector assembly must be stable against EUV and other short-wavelength radiation. Most organic materials, such as glues or rubber gaskets, decompose if irradiated by DUV or shorter-wavelength light.

===== [p418-418] Chapter 33 Grazing-Incidence EUV Collectors > 33.3.3.4 Nickel deposition (2块) =====
--[p418]-- 33.3.3.4 Nickel deposition
Coated mandrels are mounted in suitable holding fixtures and immersed in a nickel electrolyte bath. They serve as the cathode during the electroforming process. Nickel is deposited on the mandrel surface by application of an electric field between the electrodes. The current density on the mandrel surface is controlled to keep internal stress low during nickel deposition.
--[p418]-- After having achieved the required thickness of the nickel layer (i.e., mirror-shell thickness), the electrodeposition process is stopped. The mandrel is extracted from the galvanic bath, cleaned, dried, and finally prepared for the next production step.

===== [p136-136] Chapter 21 Modular LPP Source > 21.4 Conclusion (2块) =====
--[p136]-- 21.4 Conclusion
Within the frame of the European MEDEA+ T405 project, the Exulite consortium is currently developing a modular LPP source based on spatial multiplexing of several laser beams. This innovative approach using many identical, compact poweroscillator modules was first proposed by Exulite partners in 2000 to overcome the economic constraints of common LPP sources.
--[p136]-- This chapter summarizes in a condensed way the spectrum of efforts at Exulite that allow us to propose technical solutions concerning lasers, EUV optics, and system-oriented aspects, including for example thermal studies, pumping and recycling of xenon, tolerancing of the multibeam optical interface, and EUV dose control. The LPP prototype (ELSAC) is currently built and will be fully operational on an intermediate EUV power level in mid-2005 with 3-kW laser power on the target.

--[p26]-- 16.5 Pinch Discharges Based on Sn Vapor and Gas Mixtures

===== [p155-155] Driver Laser, Xenon Target, and System Development for LPP Sources > 23.1.2 EUV sources (3块) =====
--[p155]-- 23.1.2 EUV sources
Synchrotron radiation from electron storage rings<sup>1</sup> is today the most common source of EUV radiation.
--[p155]-- However, it is difficult to install an electron storage ring in an existing fab, especially given the required radiation shielding, which weighs at least 100–200 tons.<sup>2</sup> Furthermore, a traditional synchrotron source cannot meet the power requirements of EUVL.<sup>2,3</sup> Instead, all sources under consideration for EUVL are based on hot plasmas, and there are two major ways to generate the plasma: electrical discharge and laser irradiation.
--[p155]-- Since the various electricaldischarge sources are covered elsewhere in this volume, this chapter will mainly discuss the laser plasma. It should also be mentioned that other means to generate EUV radiation are available, including high-harmonic generation,<sup>4,5</sup> table-top soft-x-ray lasers,<sup>6</sup> and conventional electron impact sources,<sup>7</sup> but since they are not expected to reach the specifications for EUVL, they are not discussed further here.

===== [p271-271] Flying Circus EUV Source Metrology and Source Development Assessment > 28.2 Surface Accumulators (2块) =====
--[p271]-- Although some in situ measurements such as mirror reflectivity can be performed, most measurements that will provide information concerning plasma conditions require ex situ measurements of the accumulator. Typically, no spatial or temporal information is obtained using these techniques.
--[p271]-- 28.2 Surface Accumulators
Surface accumulators are typically designed to monitor plasma-surface interactions within the plasma. While extremely important, they provide very limited, indirect information concerning the actual plasma conditions. In EUVL plasmas, one of the goals is to minimize mirror degradation, and consequently plasma surface erosion or deposition is slow. Surface accumulators typically need to be exposed to the plasma for an extended period of time.

===== [p155-155] Driver Laser, Xenon Target, and System Development for LPP Sources > 23.1.1 General background (2块) =====
--[p155]-- 23.1.1 General background
The liquid-xenon-jet laser-plasma EUV source is one of the source types under development for EUVL. This chapter focuses on the initial development of the source type performed by the authors and their coworkers at the Royal Institute of Technology (KTH) and at the former company Innolite AB, both in Stockholm, Sweden.
--[p155]-- Where relevant, it also presents results on this source type achieved by others; results given without specific references were obtained at KTH or Innolite AB.

===== [p295-295] Metrology for EUVL Sources and Tools > 29.1 Introduction (5块) =====
--[p295]-- Now, however, EUV sources bright enough to be suitable for EUVL are all based on very high temperature plasmas that must be generated by extremely high power pulses.
--[p295]-- Recently some experience in pulsed radiometry has been gained through the creation of standards for pulsed radiometry connected with DUV lithography with its pulsed 248- and 193-nm laser sources.<sup>1</sup> However, important differences in the spectral, temporal, and spatial characteristics of the EUV sources as contrasted with the DUV laser sources necessitate specialized approaches, still under development, that are described in Sec. 29.3.
--[p295]-- Soon after the demonstration in 1986 of the first practicable EUV mirror in the form of a Mo/Si multilayer,<sup>2</sup> NIST established a capability to measure the reflectivity of EUV mirrors for such applications as solar astronomy, plasma diagnostics, EUV laser development, and EUV microscopy. At that point, measurement accuracy of order 0.01 nm in wavelength and 2% in reflectivity seemed to provide more than adequate characterization for the applications at hand.
--[p295]-- 29.1 Introduction
The effort to develop EUVL has presented the metrologist with a set of unique challenges both in radiometry and in measuring reflectivity. Since the inception of the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST’s) EUV-detector-based radiometry program in 1970, there has been little need for accurate measurements of pulsed EUV sources, and the radiometric techniques in this spectral range were all tailored to continuous wave (cw) measurements.
--[p295]-- However, the advent of EUVL made the demands much more stringent due to the imaging and illumination needs of the process.<sup>3</sup> NIST has continued to perform EUV mirror calibrations since the program’s inception, has increased its capabilities to meet many of the reflectometry demands of EUVL, and will continue to expand and improve the program to help meet the future needs of the industry.

--[p371]-- 31.3.2 Characterization of EUV optics and reflectometry

===== [p358-360] Electron-based EUV Sources for At-Wavelength Metrology > 31.1 The EUV Tube—an Old Solution for New Applications (10块) =====
--[p359]-- The Kα line of beryllium $( Z = 4 )$ and the L-shell radiation of silicon $( Z = 1 4 )$ are located at 11.4 and 13.5 nm, respectively. Therefore, electron-induced emission from these materials (especially from silicon) is potentially of high practical importance for EUV-related applications.
--[p358]-- Therefore, compact, cheap, and easy-to-operate tools and systems are badly required for atwavelength control and inspection, directly at the mirror fabrication labs and companies. Several attempts to develop laboratory EUV sources for metrology, based on laser- or discharge-produced plasmas,<sup>1</sup> are currently being made. Unfortunately, these sources have rather complex setups and high running costs.
--[p358]-- 31.1 The EUV Tube—an Old Solution for New Applications
During the past few years, significant progress has been achieved in the development of multilayer-coated optical components for the EUV spectral range. At present, the characterization of EUV optics is carried out at synchrotron radiation facilities. Synchrotrons are high-quality sources that are ideal for scientific research, but they are very complex and expensive for applications.
--[p359]-- However, the possibility of using this technique for the generation of EUV radiation has fallen into oblivion. Now, due to the rapid technological developments in EUVL, this technique has been rediscovered as a promising tool for EUV metrology.<sup>2</sup> An interesting but more complicated version of an EUV source based on narrowband Si L-edge Cherenkov emission induced by relativistic electrons also has been suggested.<sup>4</sup>
--[p358]-- They operate at a relatively low repetition rate, exhibit considerable temporal and spatial fluctuations, and always require special efforts for debris mitigation.
Usually it is overlooked that one can produce EUV radiation directly from solid targets, avoiding all these plasma-related drawbacks.<sup>2</sup> This can be done by using electron-induced characteristic emission from solids. The electron-based EUV source can be considered as an analog to a conventional x-ray tube.
--[p359]-- For radiation sources based on the electron bombardment of solid targets, it is well known that the fluorescence yield is less for lighter elements due to the competition between the radiative and Auger decays. As an example, in Fig. 31.1(b) the
--[p360]-- Nevertheless, the EUV tube can play an important role for various at-wavelength metrology applications: EUV reflectometry of multilayer mirrors (MLMs) and masks, calibration of EUV instruments, characterization of EUV optics, etc.
In Sec. 31.2, the spectral, spatial, and temporal properties of the EUV tube are presented in detail. The long-term stability and the debris-free operation of the source are demonstrated, and prospects for further power scaling are outlined. In Sec.
31.3, different applications of the source in the field of at-wavelength metrology are provided.
--[p360]-- K-shell fluorescence yield as a function of the atomic number Z is shown.<sup>5</sup> The solid line represents a fit corresponding to ${ \cal A } / ( A + W ) \sim Z ^ { 4 } / ( Z ^ { 4 } + \mathrm { c o n s t } )$ , where A and W are the radiative and Auger decay probabilities. For the generation of high-power characteristic emission with beryllium and silicon targets, this behavior can be considered as a serious drawback.
--[p359]-- Electrons are generated by a tungsten filament, accelerated in a high-voltage electric field toward an anode, and focused onto a solid target, which allows the generation of characteristic emission in the EUV spectral range. This radiation is produced by electron-impact ionization (excitation) of atomic inner shells, which is followed by radiative decay. In Fig. 31.1(a), dependences of the wavelengths of the characteristic K- and L-shell emission on the atomic number Z are shown.
--[p359]-- An EUV source operating via this mechanism (EUV tube) fulfills practically all requirements for a metrology source: stable, long-term, and debris-free operation; compact, low-cost, and user-friendly setup; and welldefined, easy-to-calibrate, and controllable output.
For several decades soft-x-ray sources based on the electron bombardment of solid targets have been studied<sup>3</sup> and applied to the calibration of soft-x-ray spectrographs and detectors.

===== [p374-374] Electron-based EUV Sources for At-Wavelength Metrology > 31.4 Summary and Outlook (2块) =====
--[p374]-- Since no debris is produced, this source, called an EUV tube, promises to become a very important tool for EUV optics characterization and metrology. First application examples of this source have been presented.
--[p374]-- 31.4 Summary and Outlook
A compact, stable, debris-free, low-cost, computer-controlled continuous-wave EUV radiation source for off-synchrotron, on-site, at-wavelength metrology has been described. Different target materials allow one to easily access a broad EUV– soft-x-ray wavelength range for various applications. The EUV radiation power can be absolutely calibrated and varied by controlling the electron current and the accelerating voltage.

===== [p417-417] Chapter 33 Grazing-Incidence EUV Collectors > 33.3.3.3 Mandrel coating (2块) =====
--[p417]-- It is the delicate balance between the adhesive forces of the reflective coating on adjacent surfaces that decides a successful release and replication process.
--[p417]-- 33.3.3.3 Mandrel coating
A thin metal layer is deposited in high vacuum (PVD coating process) on the superpolished and cleaned mandrel surface, which later is transferred—by a replication process—to the electroformed mirror shell substrate. This metal layer must provide good properties for EUV photon reflection and also act as a suitable release agent for a soft replication process.

===== [p366-366] Electron-based EUV Sources for At-Wavelength Metrology > 31.2.3 Long-term stability and debris-free operation (3块) =====
--[p366]-- 31.2.3 Long-term stability and debris-free operation
A great benefit of the electron-based EUV tube compared to plasma-based sources is the excellent temporal long-term stability of the EUV emission. To record this stability, the radiation emitted from the sem|20 EUV tube is reflected by a 45-deg Mo/Si MLM and detected using an EUV photodiode (IRD Inc., model AXUV-100) coated with a Ti/Zr/C layer to block visible radiation. The diode current is measured with a picoammeter.
--[p366]-- Since no additional filters between the source and the mirror are used and the recorded signal does not show any decrease, this measurement also demonstrates that the EUV tube is a completely debris-free source. No degradation of the MLM can be observed.
Both aspects, the high stability and the debris-free operation, make the electronbased EUV tube an ideal source for metrological applications.
--[p366]-- The distances from the mirror to the EUV source and from the mirror to the diode are 10 and 15 cm, respectively.
In Fig. 31.10, the stability of the source operation with a total running time of nearly 70 h is illustrated. In this case an accelerating voltage of 7 kV and a target current of $7 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { A }$ were used. The small apparent fluctuations of the signal are probably due to the inaccuracy of the photodiode current measurements and are below ±0.5%.

===== [p470-470] Electrode and Condenser Materials for Plasma Pinch Sources > 35.4.3 Irradiation of target materials by hot Xe plasma (3块) =====
--[p470]-- Besides Xe plasma, the targets were also tested with hydrogen plasma streams having practically the same energy density as Xe plasma streams. The experiment focused on investigation and comparison of surface damage caused by Xe and H plasmas.
--[p470]-- 35.4.3 Irradiation of target materials by hot Xe plasma
Tungsten and copper are typically used as structural materials for DPP electrodes. These materials were exposed to Xe plasma streams in the MK-200CUSP. The targets were irradiated by Xe plasma with energy density $1 0 0 { - } 2 0 0 \ \mathrm { J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ . Since a hot Xe plasma cloud is formed in front of the exposed target, the target surface is exposed to the interaction of Xe plasma particles and photon radiation.
--[p470]-- This type of experimental data is quite important for understanding whether the numerical models used in HEIGHTS-EUV, for example, which are being developed for simulation of material damage caused by H plasmas, can also be applied and benchmarked for modeling of material damage induced by Xe plasmas with applications to numerical modeling of DPP high-intensity-plasma–material interactions.

===== [p471-471] Electrode and Condenser Materials for Plasma Pinch Sources > 35.4.4 Target design (3块) =====
--[p471]-- 35.4.4 Target design
Four targets were tested: two identical tungsten targets and two identical copper targets. The targets were produced in the form of rectangular plates fully overlapping the plasma stream. The plates were manufactured absolutely flat, and their face surfaces were prepolished, which is required for profilometry measurement of the exposed surface after irradiation.
Each target was equipped with a diaphragm having a 3-cm hole [Fig. 35.9(a)].
--[p471]-- When the target is exposed to the whole plasma stream, the diameter of the eroded area is larger than 5 cm.
The melt, which is splashed from the plasma-irradiated region, falls outside the region protected by the diaphragm from plasma irradiation. Therefore the splashed metal melts again in subsequent plasma shots, and it retains its original properties. This clarifies whether the melt is splashed in the form of droplets and jets or moves as a whole.
--[p471]-- The diaphragm was placed in front of the target face at a distance of 1–2 mm. A gap between the target surface and the diaphragm was produced by using an intermediate plate as shown in Fig. 35.9(b).
The target was equipped with a diaphragm for the following reasons. The diaphragm reduces the size of the plasma-irradiated area to a diameter of 3 cm. This allows the surface profile to be analyzed using a standard mechanical profilometer. The scanning length of the profilometer is limited to 5 cm.

===== [p58-59] Chapter 18 Plasma Capillary Source > 18.1 Introduction (7块) =====
--[p58]-- Also, a two-step operation employing a prepulse to evaporate wall material for the main discharge has been demonstrated.<sup>3</sup> Gas-filled capillaries have diameters typically larger than 1 mm, the diameters of ablative setups being 1 mm and smaller.
The high current through the capillary results in pinching of the plasma to form the hot plasma column along the axis. In fast discharges this pinch effect is preceded by a cylindrical shock wave with consequent heating.
--[p58]-- The radiating hot plasma is either produced from a gas filling the discharge tube or, when operated at nearvacuum, from material ablated from the wall by an initial sliding spark, radiation from the hot plasma and heat flow to the wall providing further wall ablation. The smaller the capillary diameter, the stronger the wall ablation is.
--[p59]-- An extraordinarily short duration of emission, 5 ns, has been achieved in a device that combines the features of a transient hollow-cathode discharge with the inherent characteristics of a capillary discharge.<sup>6</sup> Half-cycle durations of 100 ns and above are achieved by conventionally discharging capacitors but in carefully designed low-inductance arrangements. Rather straightforward designs of the discharge circuit are used for pulse durations of 0.5 µs and longer.
--[p58]-- Exceptions are possible, and the plasma becomes unstable if conditions can be found under which the plasma indeed is fully detached from the wall.<sup>4</sup>
Capillary discharges can be characterized also by the period of the discharge and consequently by the current driver. Extremely fast discharges with a first halfcycle duration of the current well below 100 ns are driven by transmission lines, which are pulse-charged by appropriate Marx generators.
--[p58]-- Although in quasisteady state, standard Z pinches are inherently unstable against the growth of the $m = 0$ sausage and the $m = 1$ kink instability over an Alfvén transit time, in capillary discharges weakly ionized plasma and/or the influx of ablated wall material more or less bridges the region between the wall and the hot plasma column and stabilizes the latter.
--[p58]-- 18.1 Introduction
Capillary discharges provide a simple means to produce hot and dense plasmas that are brilliant radiators in the EUV and soft x-ray spectral regions. Early investigations by Bogen et al.<sup>1</sup> revealed strong line emission down to 3 nm, and McCorkle was the first to point out a possible application to lithography.<sup>2</sup>
Capillary discharges are usually compact, allow efficient energy coupling, and are characterized by a small diameter-to-length ratio.
--[p59]-- Operation of such fast discharges is usually at high voltages. The fast rise time is mandatory for driving collisionally excited soft-x-ray lasers,<sup>5</sup> but the short duration of EUV emission discourages application to lithography, where the delivered radiant energy is important.

===== [p277-277] Flying Circus EUV Source Metrology and Source Development Assessment > 28.4 Electron Diagnostics (3块) =====
--[p277]-- Although the electrons are probably not directly responsible for much of the optics erosion found in EUV sources, they certainly play an important role in the ion and neutral-atom behavior. Several of the plasma imaging techniques described in Sec. 28.3 (shadowgraphs, schlieren, and interferometric imaging) provide information on the spatial distribution of the electron density.
--[p277]-- This section will discuss two additional nonimaging electron diagnostics that can provide information related to both the electron temperature and the density.
--[p277]-- 28.4 Electron Diagnostics
Optical emission measurements have indicated that electron temperatures on the order of 30 eV occur in EUVL sources optimized for 13.5-nm emission from xenon. But it is the nonthermal electrons that drive many of the important plasma processes, including the generation of high-energy ions.

===== [p488-488] Electrode and Condenser Materials for Plasma Pinch Sources > 35.6 Conclusions (3块) =====
--[p488]-- 35.6 Conclusions
Plasma-facing EUV-source device materials will need to be carefully designed to stand up to the harsh environment they will be exposed to. Electrode materials must be designed to provide erosion resistance and good thermal conductivity. Highdensity plasmas in DPP devices will lead to serious erosion challenges as HVM conditions are attained. However, with proper electrode design and robust debris mitigation schemes, some opportunity exists for operation in HVM.
--[p488]-- This specification requires that only a 10% loss in EUV reflectivity occurs over 30,000 operating hours.
Proper design coupled with debris mitigation schemes will enable emerging lithography technologies to operate under HVM conditions. This goal can be attained in timely fashion by designing well-diagnosed, controlled off-line experiments, such as the IMPACT experiment, to understand synergistic erosion mechanisms that can lead to advanced mirror designs.
--[p488]-- Condensermirror optics face the same challenge. The mirror surface will have to be designed to contend with incident debris, highly energetic singly charged and multicharged particles, and fast neutrals. More importantly, the synergy of such fluxes combined with background impurities and OOB radiation will ultimately decide the fate of plasma-facing mirrors. This is mainly dictated by the specification of the condenser-optic lifetime for the collector optics.

--[p227]-- For these conditions and a sufficiently short plasma scale length $( { \approx } 2 0 \lambda _ { \mathrm { L } } )$ , most of the laser energy is deposited near critical density.
--[p227]-- Here, $\omega _ { \mathrm { { L } } }$ is the laser frequency (rad/s); $\omega _ { \mathrm { p } }$ is the electron plasma frequency; $T _ { \mathrm { e } }$ is the electron temperature; ln is the Coulomb logarithm, which is related to the minimum impact parameter; and $Z$ is the average charge per ion. Thus, IBA is more effective for high electron densities, low plasma temperatures, short laser wavelengths, and a highly ionized plasma.
--[p226]-- 26.2.1 Inverse bremsstrahlung absorption
Inverse bremsstrahlung absorption (IBA) occurs in a laser plasma when oscillating electrons, driven by the laser electromagnetic field, collide with ions, transferring energy from the field to the ions.
