===== [p155-155] Driver Laser, Xenon Target, and System Development for LPP Sources > 23.1.3 Laser plasma (2块) =====
--[p155]-- These power densities are sufficient to raise the temperature of the plasmas to the several times 100,000 K needed to achieve emission in the EUV wavelength region.<sup>1</sup>
--[p155]-- 23.1.3 Laser plasma
In a laser plasma, the plasma is created through the interaction of short high-peakpower laser pulses with a target. Pulse energies on the order of 1 J with pulse lengths of a few nanoseconds are typically used, leading to peak powers in the range of megawatts to gigawatts. Furthermore, by focusing the laser pulses down to diameters in the 100-µm range, power densities of $1 0 ^ { 1 1 } \mathrm { ~ t o ~ } 1 0 ^ { 1 2 } \mathrm { ~ W / c m } ^ { 2 }$ are achieved.

===== [p159-159] Driver Laser, Xenon Target, and System Development for LPP Sources > 23.2.1 Typical source arrangement (4块) =====
--[p159]-- 23.2.1 Typical source arrangement
A typical arrangement for operation of a liquid-xenon-jet laser-plasma target is as illustrated in Fig. 23.5. The liquid jet is formed by forcing xenon gas under high pressure into a reservoir cooled to liquefy the xenon. A tapered glass capillary nozzle with an orifice diameter of typically 10–30 µm is attached to the reservoir, producing a microscopic liquid jet into an ultrahigh-vacuum-compatible chamber.
--[p159]-- The plasma is typically generated by focusing Nd:YAG-laser pulses of λ = 1064 nm, ≈5-ns pulse length, and up to 350-mJ pulse energy onto the jet through a focusing system theoretically capable of obtaining a FWHM-10-µm spot. Finally, the EUV emission is generally monitored using a Flying Circus tool.<sup>39</sup>
--[p159]-- Vacuum is maintained by two ≈2000-l/s turbomolecular pumps, result ing in pressures of $1 0 ^ { - 4 } – 1 0 ^ { - 3 }$ mbar during operation. The base pressure of the system, before jet operation, is typically in the $1 0 ^ { - 8 } – 1 0 ^ { - 7 }$ -mbar range, but could be further reduced through, e.g., baking of the system.
--[p159]-- To reduce the load on the turbomolecular pumps during operation, the nonevaporated part of the xenon jet is extracted from the chamber through a differential-pumping scheme. The xenon evacuated through both the turbomolecular pumps and the jet-extraction system is further collected by a recycling, purification, and pressurization system allowing for closed-loop usage of xenon. Without such a recycling system, the high cost of xenon strongly limits the experimental time.

--[p204]-- Xenon Target and High-Power Laser Module Development for LPP Sources
Richard Moyer, Harry Shields, Steven Fornaca, Randall St. Pierre, Armando Martos, James Zamel, Fernando Martos, Samuel Ponti, R. D. McGregor, Mark Michaelian, Jeffrey Hartlove, Stuart McNaught, Lawrence Iwaki, Rocco Orsini, Michael Petach, Mark Thomas, Armando Villarreal, and Vivek Bakshi

===== [p273-273] Flying Circus EUV Source Metrology and Source Development Assessment > 28.3 Plasma Imaging (1块) =====
--[p273]-- 28.3 Plasma Imaging
Plasma imaging techniques provide a direct measure of the spatial extent of the plasma. Not only does this type of technique provide important information concerning the evolution of the pulsed plasma, it is also important for understanding the optical properties of the emitted EUV radiation. Imaging of EUV plasmas is complicated by the lack of refractive materials for lenses. Therefore, lensless techniques such as pinhole cameras or mirror optics are required.
Optical spectroscopy techniques can often be combined with plasma imaging, but these techniques are covered in more detail in Chapter 27.

===== [p280-280] Flying Circus EUV Source Metrology and Source Development Assessment > 28.5 Ion Diagnostics (1块) =====
--[p280]-- 28.5 Ion Diagnostics
It is expected that the ion flux from the EUVL sources will be the main factor in source problems involving optics degradation. Even small numbers of highly charged ions could have a big effect on surface erosion due to their high sputtering efficiency. In addition, unexpected ions could be present due to erosion or melting of electrodes or outgassing of materials such as resists.
Being able to characterize the ion flux from the plasma can aid in source optimization and damage mitigation techniques.

===== [p61-61] Chapter 18 Plasma Capillary Source > 18.4 Ablative Capillary Discharges (2块) =====
--[p61]-- 18.4 Ablative Capillary Discharges
Ablative capillaries allow us to exploit plasmas of solid materials and thus expand our choice of ions capable of producing EUV radiation. The discharge device is even simpler than the one needed for gas discharges, because a fast switch is not needed to apply the high voltage (HV) to the capillary electrodes. The HV can be applied directly to them, and triggering is done by a low-energy HV pulse between a small auxiliary electrode and one capillary electrode.
--[p61]-- On the other hand, a lot of debris is produced, and capillaries have limited lifetime, both of which effects seriously restrict the utilization of such a device in applications where a high repetition rate and/or absence of debris are required.

===== [p311-311] Metrology for EUVL Sources and Tools > 29.5.3.1 Bias electronics (2块) =====
--[p311]-- The capacitance and resistance values in the bias circuit must be chosen to minimize the effect on the load resistance seen by the photodiode and the reduction in the photodiode capacitive-discharge time constant. Additionally, the voltage supply must be able to restore the full reverse bias potential across the photodiode in the interval between pulses. Bias electronics design is not a trivial task and should be approached with some care.
--[p311]-- 29.5.3.1 Bias electronics
In pulsed radiometry, the photodiode should always be reverse biased to increase the speed of the device. To fairly good approximation, the junction capacitance varies inversely as the square root of the reverse bias, and the time constant is linearly related to the junction capacitance. The bias circuit should provide an accoupled path to the measurement instrumentation (typically an oscilloscope) and a current-limited path from the voltage source.

===== [p50-50] Chapter 17 Capillary Z-Pinch Source > 17.4.3 Total EUV power (1块) =====
--[p50]-- 17.4.3 Total EUV power
Knowing the characteristics described above, we can calculate the EUV power from the source plasma as shown in Table 17.2. All data were obtained from the results of 2-kHz operation. It was experimentally found that the EUV energy increases as $I ^ { 2 } T$ , where I and T are the current amplitude and the current pulse duration. Modifying the output inductance resulted in shortening of the pulse and increase of current amplitude.
The value $I ^ { 2 } T$ increased by a factor of 1.5, which almost equals the factor of increase of the EUV power from previously acquired data.

===== [p308-308] Metrology for EUVL Sources and Tools > 29.5.2.2 Ionization chamber (2块) =====
--[p308]-- From knowledge of the gas photoabsorption cross section, the path length in the Ne, and the gas density (usually calculated from pressure and temperature), one can derive the incident photon flux. A photodiode is calibrated by inserting it into the photon beam of known flux and measuring the photogenerated current.
--[p308]-- 29.5.2.2 Ionization chamber
NIST has a calibration system<sup>23</sup> based on an ionization chamber that covers the entire region from 5 to 50 nm. The ionization chamber uses Ne as the absorbing rare gas and operates in the single-plate mode. Incident photons are absorbed in the Ne and generate ion-electron pairs that are separated by an applied electric field. The ions are collected at the cathode, and the photocurrent is measured.

===== [p420-420] Chapter 33 Grazing-Incidence EUV Collectors > 33.3.3.7 Mirror-shell integration (4块) =====
--[p420]-- However, an additional support structure and an alignment stage had to be developed and built for the massive EUV spider wheel. The spider wheel must be moved in the axial direction (vertically) in order to allow for insertion of the next mirror shell. Both support systems are adjustable in the lateral directions (with an x–y stage), can be tilted, and allow very fine movement in the axial direction (along the z axis).
--[p420]-- Mirror-shell assembly is started with the innermost (smallest) shell and is continued step by step with the next larger shell until all reflectors have been inserted in the collector.
All mirror shells are coaligned with respect to a reference optic, and the correct focus position of each individual mirror shell is achieved through active alignment along the optical axis. All adjustment and alignment tasks on the reflectors are carried out under real-time optical control.
--[p420]-- Aligned mirror shells are fixed to the spokes by bonding with an appropriate cement. During bonding and curing of the cement, the mirror shell’s optical performance can be checked online by optical means. After curing of the cement, the next mirror shell is inserted, aligned, and finally bonded to the collector spider wheel. Figure 33.9 shows a spider wheel with four integrated mirror shells.
--[p420]-- 33.3.3.7 Mirror-shell integration
Integration of EUV mirror shells into their holding fixture (spider wheel) is carried out in a similar way as for the ABRIXAS telescope modules.<sup>11,12</sup> The major difference from ABRIXAS is that the EUV mirrors are inserted into the spider wheel from the bottom and the EUV mirror shells are suspended at appropriate support rings.
The EUV collector integration stand is more or less a 1:1 copy of the EUV mirror shell test stand.

===== [p300-300] Metrology for EUVL Sources and Tools > 29.4 Reflectometry (2块) =====
--[p300]-- The sample chamber was designed to measure actual EUVL optics. In 1994 the largest optics predicted for a commercial system were 35 cm in diameter. The goniometer was designed to be able to measure the entire surface of an optic 35 cm in diameter and 15 cm thick.
--[p300]-- 29.4 Reflectometry
The NIST/DARPA EUV Reflectometry Facility was installed in the late 1980s to serve the community of multilayer optics developers. The earliest work took place on an existing beamline of what was then SURF II while a new beamline was being designed. The monochromator was designed with the goal of optimizing performance for measurement of Mo/Si MLMs. The wavelength coverage is 3 to 40 nm, with high throughput and modest resolution.

===== [p134-135] Chapter 21 Modular LPP Source > 21.3.5 The xenon recycler (4块) =====
--[p134]-- 21.3.5 The xenon recycler
Since xenon is a rare and expensive material, a recycling and purifying system is crucial to keep the cost of ownership for an industrial LPP source at a reasonable level. Alcatel Vacuum Technology/Adixen developed a xenon recycling system, and a first prototype has been working continuously since 2002 at the CEA labs.
--[p134]-- The specifications for the second system for the ELSAC source prototype have been set much more severely in terms of purity (1 ppm $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } ;$ 1 ppm ${ \bf O } _ { 2 } ;$ ; 1 ppm $\mathrm { C } _ { x } \mathrm { H } _ { y } ; 1$ ppm $\mathrm { N H } _ { 3 } , \mathrm { C l } _ { 2 }$ , and $\mathrm { F } _ { 2 }$ ; 10 ppm $\Nu _ { 2 }$ and rare gases; 1 ppm for all other trace gases), in terms of injection pressure (up to 50 bars), in terms of xenon charge (up to 400 L), and in terms of flow rate of xenon (up to 3 slm), thereby keeping the leak rate below $1 0 ^ { - 9 }$ mbar L/s. This system has continuous automatic flow operation, for potential every-day and round-the-clock operation. The physical principle of the recycling system is illustrated in Fig.
--[p135]-- At the same time, another reservoir is in evaporation mode and is delivering xenon gas at room temperature to the source injector. The third reservoir is in transition mode between liquefaction and evaporation, so that the cyclic system is able to deliver purified xenon gas in continuous flow. The output pressure delivered is regulated by a mass flow regulation system. The entire machine is controlled by an automatic device and a supervisor computer.
--[p134]-- 21.23.
The xenon is extracted from the exhaust of the dry pumping system in a gas phase to a buffer gas tank. This xenon gas is then purified through chemical filters to eliminate $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } , \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ , and $\mathrm { C } _ { x } \mathrm { H } _ { y }$ molecules. Liquefaction is performed in the next phase in one of the three reservoirs by cryogenic means.

===== [p73-73] Chapter 19 Technology for LPP Sources > 19.1.1 Roadmap (2块) =====
--[p73]-- 19.1.1 Roadmap
The roadmap for the development of EUV sources until the stage of HVM using EUVL requires so-called microexposure tools (α and β tools), as well as early pre-HVM tools, for the development of the technology. Some of the leading semiconductor manufacturers are expected to ramp up EUVL for HVM at the beginning of 2009, in parallel with 193-nm immersion excimer laser lithography.
--[p73]-- To support this roadmap, first microexposure tools with small field size were installed in the semiconductor industry as technology pathfinders in 2004. α tools needed to be equipped with sources with 5-W output at lithography exposure-tool manufacturers in 2004. β exposure tools required 15-W EUV sources in 2005. Pre-HVM EUV exposure tools will need the integration of sources with 25–50-W power in late 2006. Finally, HVM sources with 115 W power will be needed starting in 2008.

===== [p416-416] Chapter 33 Grazing-Incidence EUV Collectors > 33.3.3.2 Mandrel fabrication (3块) =====
--[p416]-- 33.3.3.2 Mandrel fabrication
High-precision mandrels, having exactly the negative of the shape of the required mirror shells, are needed for the fabrication of high-efficiency EUV mirror reflectors. Not only the exact surface figure, but also a very smooth, superpolished surface is an absolute must for good mandrels.
A set of mandrels for all mirror shells has been manufactured at Carl Zeiss.
--[p416]-- All mandrels contain a rigid core of an aluminum alloy and are plated with a thin layer of high-quality electroless nickel. By application of state-of-the-art lapping, metrology, and superpolishing processes,<sup>8</sup> high-quality replication mandrels with very smooth surfaces (microroughness below 0.5 nm rms; see Fig. 33.7) have been manufactured. Figure 33.6 shows the mandrel figure metrology setup before the superpolishing process, and Fig.
--[p416]-- 33.7 shows an example ProMap (phase-shift optical interferometric measurement) result for the superpolished mandrel surface.
<sup>∗</sup>The term “figure” describes the surface topography on a centimeter-to-meter scale.

===== [p133-133] Chapter 21 Modular LPP Source > 21.3.4 The EUV collector (1块) =====
--[p133]-- 21.3.4 The EUV collector
The designed EUV collector will not be built during the first phase of Exulite, which runs until mid-2005. For the realization of ELSAC, we intend to use a rough collector module that mimics the future optical collector without presenting an optimal optical surface (with respect to shape, roughness, and treatment).

===== [p176-176] Driver Laser, Xenon Target, and System Development for LPP Sources > Acknowledgments (1块) =====

===== [p167-167] Driver Laser, Xenon Target, and System Development for LPP Sources > 23.4.3 Emission stability (2块) =====
--[p167]-- 23.4.3 Emission stability
A pulse-to-pulse emission stability $0 \mathrm { f } \pm 8 . 4 \% ( 3 \sigma )$ at plasma operation 50 mm from the nozzle has been reported.<sup>57</sup> As will be evident in the next section, the ability to operate a stable jet at a large distance from the nozzle is especially important to reduce the thermal load. This measured emission stability should correspond to $\pm 8 . 4 \% / \sqrt { 5 0 } = \pm 1 .
--[p167]-- 2 \%$ for a 50-pulse running average, to be compared with the specification of ±0.3%. However, the repetition-rate specification is $1 0 \mathrm { k H z } ,$ and if a liquid-xenon-jet laser plasma source can be operated at 20 kHz, the specification should be given for a 100-pulse average, which means that the published stability would be $\pm 8 . 4 \% / \sqrt { 1 0 0 } = \pm 0 . 8 4 \%$ .
This number is within a factor of 3 of the specification, and it should therefore be possible to reach the final specification.

===== [p62-62] Chapter 18 Plasma Capillary Source > 18.4.1 Polyacetal capillary (3块) =====
--[p62]-- Similarly, capillaries made of polyethylene are almost oxygen-free, and their spectrum is dominated by carbon lines. The broad peak around 13.5 nm is composed of individual C VI and C V lines, some of which are lines of shorter wavelength whose higher spectral orders appear here. The intensity of this “peak” is very low, and hence the polyethylene spectrum in Fig. 18.3 was multiplied by factor 5 relative to the POM spectrum to make details visible.
--[p62]-- The spectrum of the POM plasma is of some interest for us because POM is often used as the capping material for the PVC capillaries and thus contributes to some extent to the EUV spectra of such composites.
--[p62]-- 18.4.1 Polyacetal capillary
Polyacetal (POM) is a standard material for ablative capillaries. It is robust, withstands many discharges, and does not produce too much debris. In the last few decades ablative capillary discharges utilizing POM as the capillary material have been extensively studied in connection with EUV lasing of the C VI Balmer α line at 18.2 nm. The noncoherent spectrum of a plasma produced in a POM capillary is dominated by strong O V and O VI lines.

===== [p109-109] Spatially and Temporally Multiplexed Laser Modules for LPP Sources > 20.4 Conclusion (1块) =====
--[p109]-- 20.4 Conclusion
LPPs provide a flexible and scalable route toward a production-level EUV source for lithography. The key technological components of the EUV source, namely the target and (most importantly) the laser-driver solution, have already been demonstrated to be technically viable. In addition, CoO calculations indicate that the LPP source is a commercially viable solution that will satisfy the requirements specified by EUV scanner manufacturers.

===== [p307-307] Metrology for EUVL Sources and Tools > 29.5.1.5 Linearity (2块) =====
--[p307]-- Devices with an internal quantum efficiency less than unity show an increase in quantum efficiency at low incident powers as trap sites are filled and the recombination losses are mitigated. At higher incident powers, the quantum efficiency falls dramatically. Saturation effects are a major concern in the measurement of pulse energy, because the peak power of a short pulse is very high, even when the average power is low. This problem is discussed more fully in Sec. 29.5.3.
--[p307]-- 29.5.1.5 Linearity
At high signal strengths, the linearity of the photodiode is important. As saturation sets in, the quantum efficiency of the photodiode can change. Devices with 100% internal quantum efficiency $[ \boldsymbol { \eta } ( E ) / T ( E ) ]$ show good linearity at photocurrents in excess of 3 mA when unbiased and illuminated with visible cw radiation.<sup>11</sup> A lower internal efficiency indicates the presence of trap sites that lead to surface recombination losses.

===== [p150-150] Driver Laser, Xenon Target, and System Development for LPP Sources > 22.5 Summary (2块) =====
--[p150]-- Xenon jet and droplet targets are being investigated; droplet targets are becoming more attractive for higher laser repetition rates. The currently developed light source delivers 4-W inband power at a repetition rate of 10 kHz. Important light-source characteristics such as the emission spectrum and the inband emission plasma size have also been presented.
--[p150]-- 22.5 Summary
The EU LPP light-source development for lithography currently done in Japan under the management of EUVA has been presented. A MOPA Nd:YAG laser system is being developed as a driver laser. The system has currently an average power of 1 kW at a repetition rate of 10 kHz. The FWHM pulse duration is 6 ns, and the wavelength 1064 nm. Xenon has been chosen for the plasma target to minimize debris and thus maximize optical-component lifetime.

===== [p264-265] Flying Circus EUV Source Metrology and Source Development Assessment > 27.6 Summary and Future Directions (3块) =====
--[p264]-- For the coming years, though, a continued need to assess the progress of EUV source performance can be foreseen, as well as a need to have a noncommercial liaison activity on EUV metrology equipment in a position between EUV source suppliers and synchrotron-based or lab-scale calibration facilities. The FC formula is well suited for that purpose, though possibly with small adaptations.
--[p265]-- In general, the range of available EUV metrology equipment is becoming noticeably broader, with more emphasis on the ability to monitor system-specific source parameters such as true inband power, inband source size, and spectral contributions in the VUV.<sup>33</sup> This development calls for an ongoing standardization effort in order to continue the development of EUV source measurement procedures.
--[p264]-- 27.6 Summary and Future Directions
The rapid progress of EUV source development and an increase in commercial interest will have the consequence that a considerably larger fraction of the results becomes proprietary. In response, the nature of FC may gradually change into a more facilitating cross-calibration-like activity.

===== [p342-342] Calibration of Detectors and Tools for EUV-Source Metrology > 30.5 Spectrally Filtered Tools and Spectrographs (1块) =====
--[p342]-- 30.5 Spectrally Filtered Tools and Spectrographs
For the optimization of radiation sources for EUVL and for the determination of the parameters needed for the system design and the system integration, these sources must be characterized in terms of the absolute inband power, the spectral distribution in the EUV spectral region and the out-of-band (OOB) spectral regions, the spatial distribution of the emitting volume, and the angular distribution of the emission.
Also, the source debris has to be investigated. We present here some examples for the calibration of such tools at PTB.
